def: markedly different from an accepted norm

exs.t: When the financial director started screaming and throwing food at his co-workers, the police had to come in to deal with his aberrant behavior.
Most of the seedlings grew straight toward the lamp, but a few aberrant specimens curled away from the light, prompting the botanist to test them for a genetic mutation.
The auditors flagged the account not because its totals were large but because its pattern of late-night transfers was so aberrant compared with every other client's routine activity.
Critics who expected another conventional sonnet sequence were startled by the poet's aberrant new volume, which abandoned rhyme, meter and even punctuation.

def: a deviation from what is normal or expected

exs.t: Aberrations in climate have become the norm: rarely a week goes by without some meteorological phenomenon making headlines.
The manager insisted that the quarter's losses were a temporary aberration rather than a trend, noting that sales had risen steadily for the previous nine years.
For a composer known for cheerful, tuneful pieces, the dissonant and brooding final quartet struck many listeners as an aberration in an otherwise consistent career.
The researchers discarded one reading as an aberration caused by a faulty sensor, since it contradicted hundreds of measurements taken under identical conditions.

def: choose not to consume or take part in (particularly something enjoyable)

exs.t: Considered a health nut, Jessica abstained from anything containing sugar--even chocolate.
Although the banquet offered wine at every course, the surgeon abstained, knowing she might be called to the operating room before midnight.
Several committee members chose to abstain from the vote rather than take a side in a dispute that pitted two of their closest colleagues against each other.
During the fasting month, observant families abstain from food and drink from dawn until sunset, breaking the fast together only after dark.

def: difficult to understand; incomprehensible

exs.t: Physics textbooks can seem so abstruse to the uninitiated that readers feel as though they are looking at hieroglyphics.
The philosopher's argument was so abstruse that even specialists in the field needed several readings, and a glossary, before they could follow its central claim.
Far from being abstruse, the physicist's popular lectures made quantum theory accessible to audiences with no mathematics beyond high school algebra.
Because the tax code is written in such abstruse language, many small business owners hire accountants simply to learn which rules apply to them.

def: refusing to change one's mind

exs.t: Civil rights icon Rosa Parks will forever be remembered for adamantly refusing to give up her seat on a public bus--even after the bus driver insisted, she remained rooted in place.
Despite repeated pleas from her editor to soften the ending, the novelist remained adamant that the protagonist must die in the final chapter.
The union was adamant about its demand for safer equipment; no offer of higher wages could persuade its leaders to drop the issue.
Although his advisers urged a compromise, the governor was adamant in refusing to reopen the negotiations, insisting that the matter was already settled.

def: to warn strongly, even to the point of reprimanding

exs.t: Before the concert began, security personnel admonished the crowd not to come up on stage during the performance.
The librarian admonished the students for talking in the reading room, warning that a second disturbance would cost them their study privileges.
Rather than praising the report, the supervisor admonished its authors to check their figures more carefully before circulating anything to clients.
The judge admonished the jurors not to discuss the case with anyone, cautioning that even a casual conversation could force a mistrial.

def: serving to warn; expressing reproof or reproach especially as a corrective

exs.t: At the assembly, the high school vice-principal gave the students an admonitory speech, warning them of the many risks and dangers of prom night.
The museum posted admonitory signs beside the fragile tapestries, reminding visitors in stern language that touching the fabric was strictly forbidden.
Her mentor's letter was less congratulatory than admonitory: it praised the promotion briefly and then devoted three pages to the mistakes she must avoid.
With a single admonitory glance over his spectacles, the conductor silenced the violinist who had begun tuning during the pianist's solo.

def: one who professes great sensitivity to the beauty of art and nature

exs.t: A true aesthete, Marty would spend hours at the Guggenheim Museum, staring at the same Picasso.
An aesthete to the core, the collector would rearrange a single vase for an hour until the light fell on its glaze exactly as he wished.
Whereas her pragmatic brother judged furniture only by its durability, Clara was an aesthete who could be moved to tears by the grain of a walnut table.
The novel satirizes a self-styled aesthete who claims to swoon at every sunset yet cannot name a single painter whose work he has actually studied.

label: adj.
def: concerned with the appreciation of beauty

exs.t: The director, not known for his aesthetic sensibilities, decided not to use costumes at all, and put on the play in everyday clothing.
The city council approved the bridge for engineering reasons, but critics complained that no one had considered its aesthetic impact on the historic skyline.
Although the software was functional, its designers paid little attention to aesthetic concerns, and users found its cluttered gray screens unpleasant to look at.
For the gardener, pruning was never merely practical; it was an aesthetic pursuit in which each cut shaped the beauty of the whole hedge.

label: n.
def: a set of principles underlying and guiding the work of a particular artist or artistic movement

exs.t: The artist operated according to a peculiar aesthetic, not considering any photograph to be worth publishing unless it contained a marine mammal.
The studio's minimalist aesthetic, which favored bare concrete, raw steel and a single accent color, could be recognized in every building it designed.
Rejecting the lush orchestration of his teachers, the young composer developed a spare aesthetic built on silence, repetition and a handful of notes.
Scholars have traced the magazine's cool, ironic aesthetic, visible in everything from its typography to its photography, to a small circle of founding editors.

def: a mixture of multiple things

exs.t: The band's music was an amalgam of hip-hop, flamenco and jazz, blending the three styles with surprising results.
The city's cuisine is an amalgam of the dishes brought by successive waves of immigrants, combining spices, grains and techniques from three continents.
The committee's final proposal was an awkward amalgam of competing plans, stitched together so that every faction could claim some part of it.
Rather than inventing a new character, the novelist created an amalgam of several relatives, borrowing one uncle's temper and another's wit.

def: open to more than one interpretation

exs.t: The coach told his team, "Move towards that side of the field"; because he did not point, his directions were ambiguous, and the team had no idea to which side he was referring.
The contract's wording was ambiguous: 'within thirty days' could refer either to the date of signing or to the date of delivery, and both parties exploited the confusion.
Critics still argue over the painting's ambiguous expression, which some read as a smile of contentment and others as a grimace of quiet despair.
Because the poll's question was ambiguous, respondents who supported the policy and those who opposed it sometimes gave the same answer.

def: mixed or conflicting emotions about something

exs.t: Sam was ambivalent about studying for the exam because doing so ate up a lot of his time, yet he was able to improve his analytical skills.
The scientist felt ambivalent about the prize: she was proud of the recognition, yet uneasy that it credited her alone for work her whole lab had done.
Many residents are ambivalent about the new stadium, welcoming the jobs it will bring while dreading the traffic and noise it will create.
In his letters the poet seems ambivalent toward his hometown, alternately praising its quiet beauty and cursing its stifling narrowness.

def: make something bad better

exs.t: Three Cups of Tea tells the story of western man who hopes to ameliorate poverty and the lack of education in Afghanistan.
The city planted thousands of trees along its busiest avenues, hoping to ameliorate the heat that had made summers nearly unbearable in poorer neighborhoods.
Although the new medication cannot cure the disease, it does ameliorate the worst symptoms, allowing patients to sleep through the night.
Rather than ameliorating tensions between the two departments, the hasty reorganization only deepened their mutual suspicion and made cooperation even harder.

def: easily persuaded

exs.t: Even though she did not like the outdoors, Shirley was generally amenable and so her brother was able to persuade her to go camping.
The landlord proved surprisingly amenable to our request; after a brief conversation, he agreed to repaint the apartment at his own expense.
Unlike her stubborn predecessor, the new director is amenable to suggestions from junior staff and has already adopted several of their ideas.
The negotiators hoped that a modest concession on wages would make the union more amenable to a longer contract.

def: shapeless

exs.t: His study plan for the GRE was at best amorphous; he would do questions from random pages in any one of seven test prep books.
The protest movement remained amorphous for months, lacking leaders, a platform or even a name, before it finally coalesced around a single demand.
Under the microscope the cells were amorphous blobs, with none of the regular structure the biologists had expected to see.
The consultant's amorphous recommendations, which urged the firm to 'embrace change' without specifying how, left the managers with nothing concrete to do.

def: not normal

exs.t: According to those who do not believe in climate change, the extreme weather over the last five years is simply anomalous--average temps should return to average, they believe.
The astronomers could not explain the anomalous dimming of the star, which did not match the pattern of any known planet or dust cloud.
In a family of accountants and engineers, her decision to become a sculptor seemed anomalous, yet her parents supported it without hesitation.
Because one patient's reaction was so anomalous, the doctors reviewed her medical history to see what set her apart from the others in the trial.

def: something that is not normal, standard, or expected

exs.t: After finding an anomaly in the data, she knew that she would have to conduct her experiment again.
A warm day in January is no anomaly in this region, where mild spells regularly interrupt the winter.
The historian noted that the treaty was something of an anomaly: in a century of bitter rivalry, it was the only agreement the two kingdoms ever honored.
Engineers traced the anomaly in the bridge's readings to a loose cable, reassuring the public that the structure itself was sound.

def: an intense feeling of dislike or aversion

exs.t: Maria had an antipathy for tour groups, often bolting to the other side of the museum as soon as she saw a chaperone leading a group of wide-eyed tourists.
The novelist's antipathy toward critics was well known; she refused interviews and once returned a glowing review with an angry note.
Despite their shared politics, the two senators felt a deep antipathy for each other that no amount of party loyalty could conceal.
Her antipathy to cities was so strong that she turned down a prestigious job rather than move away from her quiet valley.

def: sharply contrasted in character or purpose

exs.t: His deep emotional involvement with these ideas is, in fact, antithetical to the detachment Buddhism preaches.
Rote memorization, the reformers argued, is antithetical to genuine inquiry, since it rewards students for repeating answers rather than questioning them.
The director's flashy, crowd-pleasing style seemed antithetical to the spare and meditative novel he had chosen to adapt.
For the monks, the pursuit of wealth was antithetical to their mission; they gave away every gift they received.

def: marked by a lack of interest

exs.t: Mr. Thompson was so talented at teaching math that even normally apathetic students took interest.
The candidate's speech, though full of passion, failed to stir an apathetic audience that had long since stopped believing politicians could change anything.
Most students were apathetic about the new curriculum, but a small group of passionate parents attended every meeting to fight it.
After years of being ignored by management, the employees grew apathetic, doing the minimum required and no longer offering ideas.

def: an absence of emotion or enthusiasm

exs.t: Widespread apathy among voters led to a very small turnout on election day.
The charity's greatest obstacle was not hostility but apathy: most people agreed the cause was worthy and then simply did nothing.
His apathy toward his studies puzzled his teachers, who remembered him as a boy eager to read every book in the classroom.
Rather than outrage, the scandal produced only public apathy, as citizens shrugged and assumed that every official behaved the same way.

def: being of questionable authenticity

exs.t: The web is notorious for sandwiching apocryphal stories between actual news.
The tale of the young composer writing an entire symphony in one night is probably apocryphal; no letters or diaries from the period mention it.
Although the quotation appears on countless posters, scholars regard it as apocryphal, since it cannot be found in any of the statesman's writings.
Company legend holds that the founder sketched the first design on a napkin, but longtime employees suspect the story is apocryphal.

def: pacify by acceding to the demands of

exs.t: Neville Chamberlain, the British prime minister during WWII, tried to appease Hitler and in doing so sent a clear message: you can walk all over us.
To appease the angry customers, the airline offered free hotel rooms and vouchers, though many travelers remained furious about the cancellation.
The emperor tried to appease the rebellious provinces by lowering their taxes, but the concession only encouraged them to demand independence.
Rather than appeasing the critics by cutting the controversial scene, the director defended it in an open letter.

def: based on a random, groundless decision

exs.t: One of the arbitrary decrees in place during the emperor's rule is that all citizens pay him weekly homage at his palace.
Employees resented the arbitrary schedule changes, which seemed to follow no pattern and were announced without explanation.
The judge's decision was hardly arbitrary; she cited three precedents and explained in detail why each applied to the case.
Any cutoff score is somewhat arbitrary, the admissions officer admitted, since a student one point below the line is scarcely different from one just above it.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: requiring secret or mysterious knowledge

exs.t: Most college fraternities are known for arcane rituals that those hoping to the join the fraternity must learn.
The lawyer navigated the arcane procedures of maritime law with ease, though most of her colleagues had never even heard of the statutes she cited.
Only a handful of scholars can read the arcane notation used by medieval alchemists, whose symbols were designed to conceal their methods from outsiders.
To the uninitiated, the rules of the ancient board game seemed arcane, but the players had learned them as children and followed them effortlessly.

def: demanding considerable mental effort and skill; testing powers of endurance

exs.t: In order to deal with the arduous cross-country journey, truck drivers often survive on a string of caffeinated drinks, staying awake for up to 30 hours at a time.
Restoring the damaged fresco was an arduous task, requiring the conservators to clean each square inch by hand over the course of four years.
Although the summit trail is short, it is arduous: hikers must climb nearly vertical rock for hours with little shade and no water.
The translator described her work on the epic as arduous, since every line demanded weeks of research into forgotten idioms and allusions.

label: adj.1
def: exhibiting artistic skill

exs.t: Picasso is generally considered the most artful member of the Cubist movement.
The pianist's artful phrasing turned a simple folk melody into something so refined that the audience sat in stunned silence afterward.
The critic praised the film's artful composition, noting how each frame was arranged with the care of a classical painting.
Far from clumsy, the potter's glazes were artful, layering subtle blues and greens so that each bowl seemed to shimmer like water.

label: adj.2
def: clever in a cunning way

exs.t: Bernie Madoff's artful Ponzi scheme stole billions of dollars from investors and is considered the largest financial fraud in U.S. history.
The con man's artful excuses fooled even the skeptical detective, who realized only weeks later how thoroughly he had been manipulated.
With artful evasions, the witness managed to answer every question without ever revealing where she had been that night.
The lobbyist was an artful schemer who flattered legislators in public while quietly arranging for their rivals to fund his causes.

label: adj.
def: practicing self-denial

exs.t: His ascetic life is the main reason he inspired so many followers, especially since he gave up wealth and power to live in poverty.
The philosopher led an ascetic existence, sleeping on a wooden plank, eating one plain meal a day and owning nothing but a few books.
Though heir to a vast fortune, she adopted an ascetic routine, giving away her jewels and refusing even small comforts such as heated rooms.
The monastery's ascetic rules forbade meat, conversation after sunset and any possessions beyond a robe and a bowl.

label: n.
def: one who practices great self-denial

exs.t: Historically, ascetics like Gandhi are often considered wise men partially because of their restraint.
The hermit was a true ascetic, living for decades in a cave on a diet of bread and water and refusing every gift offered by pilgrims.
Unlike his lavish brother, the younger prince became an ascetic, renouncing his inheritance to live in a bare cell among the monks.
Visitors expected the famous ascetic to be gloomy, yet the man who had forsaken all comforts greeted them with cheerful warmth.

def: with a look of suspicion or disapproval

exs.t: The old couple looked askance on the teenagers seated next to them, whispering to each other, "They've got rings through their noses and purple hair!"
The veteran editors looked askance at the intern's proposal to abolish the print edition, doubting that a newcomer understood the paper's finances.
Traditional physicians initially viewed the new therapy askance, suspecting that its dramatic results were too good to be true.
When the stranger offered to buy the entire orchard for cash, the farmer eyed him askance and asked to see his credentials first.

def: willing to be bold in social situations or to take risks

exs.t: As all of the other campers cowered in their tents, Bill, armed only with a flashlight, audaciously tracked down the bear that had raided their food.
The general's audacious plan called for marching the entire army across the frozen lake at night, a risk no commander before him had dared to take.
Critics called the young architect's design audacious, since it balanced a heavy concert hall on a single slender column.
It was an audacious move for a first-year associate to challenge the senior partner's argument in front of the client, but her boldness won the case.

def: aggressive boldness in social situations

exs.t: She surprised her colleagues by having the audacity to publicly criticize the findings of an distinguished scientist.
The intern had the audacity to correct the chairman in the middle of his speech, a breach of etiquette that left the room silent.
Few journalists would have shown the audacity to question the dictator directly, yet she asked him about the missing prisoners on live television.
The committee was shocked by the audacity of the applicant, who demanded a salary higher than the director's before he had even been interviewed.

def: favorable, the opposite of sinister

exs.t: Despite an auspicious beginning, Mike's road trip became a series of mishaps, and he was soon stranded and penniless, leaning against his wrecked automobile.
The clear skies on launch day seemed auspicious, and the engineers began the countdown confident that the mission would succeed.
The album's launch was hardly auspicious: on the day of its release the lead single was pulled from radio, and the opening concert of the tour was canceled for lack of ticket sales.
A strong first quarter provided an auspicious start for the new chief executive, who had promised investors a rapid recovery.

label: adj.1
def: practicing self-denial

exs.t: His lifestyle of revelry and luxurious excess could hardly be called austere.
After years of lavish spending, the heiress adopted an austere way of life, forgoing servants, rich food and every luxury she had once enjoyed.
The monks' austere discipline included long fasts, cold baths and nights spent kneeling on stone floors in silent prayer.
Though he could afford comfort, the scholar remained austere in his habits, allowing himself nothing beyond bread, tea and his books.

label: adj.2
def: unadorned in style or appearance

exs.t: Late Soviet architecture, although remaining largely austere, moved into experimental territory that employed previously unused shapes and structures.
The chapel's austere interior, with whitewashed walls and plain wooden benches, contrasted sharply with the gilded cathedral across the square.
The designer favored an austere layout for the book, with wide margins, a single typeface and not one decorative flourish.
Visitors expecting ornate furnishings were surprised by the austere rooms of the palace, which held little more than a table and a few chairs.

label: adj.3
def: harsh in manner of temperament

exs.t: The principal of my elementary school was a cold, austere woman; I could never understand why she chose to work with children.
The headmaster's austere manner, with his cold stare and clipped commands, frightened even the most rebellious pupils into silence.
Colleagues found the judge austere and forbidding, yet her clerks insisted that she was warm once one got past her severe demeanor.
Unlike his genial predecessor, the new abbot was austere, rebuking the novices sharply for the slightest lapse.

def: excessively greedy

exs.t: Since avaricious desire is similar to gluttony or lust--sins of excess--it was listed as one of the seven deadly sins by the Catholic church.
The avaricious landlord raised the rent every year, even as the building's plumbing failed and its tenants struggled to pay.
In the fable, an avaricious merchant hoards so much gold that he starves in his vault rather than spend a single coin on bread.
Critics accused the firm's executives of being avaricious, noting that they awarded themselves record bonuses while laying off thousands of workers.

def: repeated too often; overfamiliar through overuse

exs.t: The professor used such banal expression that many students in the class either fell asleep from boredom or stayed awake to complete his sentences and humor friends.
The novel's plot was banal, recycling the same tired story of a small-town girl who moves to the city and finds love.
Hoping for insight, the students were disappointed by the speaker's banal advice to 'follow your passion' and 'never give up.'
What begins as a banal detective story is transformed in its final chapters into a strikingly original meditation on memory.

def: a trite or obvious remark

exs.t: Herbert regarded the minister's remark as a mere banality until Sharon pointed out profound implications to the seemingly obvious words.
The graduation speech was a string of banalities, each one as predictable as the last, and the audience soon stopped listening.
The diplomat's statement contained nothing but the usual banality that 'both sides must work toward peace,' offering no concrete proposal.
Although the letter seemed to contain only banalities about the weather, the historian read it as a coded report on troop movements.

def: to give a false representation to; misrepresent

exs.t: The smile on her face belies the pain she must feel after the death of her husband.
Her surface calm belied her roiling emotions.
The effortless fluidity with which the pianist's fingers moved belied the countless hours he had practiced.
Her upbeat attitude during the group project belied her inherent pessimism towards any collective endeavor.
The calm voice of the pilot belied the gravity of the situation, for the plane had lost an engine and was losing altitude fast.
The modest facade of the house belies its enormous interior, which extends far back into the hillside.
Her cheerful public statements belied the company's real financial state, which was far worse than investors had been told.

def: characteristic of one eager to fight

exs.t: Tom said that he was arguing the matter purely for philosophical reasons, but his belligerent tone indicated an underlying anger about the issue.
After losing the argument, the delegate grew belligerent, shouting at the chair and threatening to walk out of the conference.
The ambassador's belligerent rhetoric alarmed the neighboring states, which feared that his words foreshadowed an actual invasion.
Though usually mild-mannered, the professor became belligerent whenever anyone questioned his theory, challenging critics to public debates.

def: to reveal or make known something, usually unintentionally

exs.t: With the gold medal at stake, the gymnast awaited his turn, his quivering lip betraying his intense emotions.

As we age, our political leanings tend to become less pronounced; the once dyed-in-the-wool conservative can betray liberal leanings, and the staunch progressive may suddenly embrace conservative policies.
Although she claimed to be indifferent to the verdict, her trembling hands betrayed how anxious she really was.
The spy's slight accent betrayed his foreign origins, despite years of training to speak like a native.
The poet's careful revisions betray a deep insecurity, for she rewrote even her most celebrated lines dozens of times.

def: without any attempt at concealment; completely obvious

exs.t: Allen was often punished in school for blatantly disrespecting teachers.
The essay was a blatant case of plagiarism: entire paragraphs had been copied word for word from a well-known textbook.
The referee's call was so blatant a mistake that even the home crowd booed the decision.
Rather than hiding their favoritism, the officials showed blatant partiality, awarding every contract to firms owned by their relatives.

def: support and strengthen

exs.t: The case for the suspect's innocence was bolstered considerably by the fact that neither fingerprints nor DNA were found at the scene.
The new fossil discovery bolstered the theory that birds evolved from dinosaurs, adding yet another piece of supporting evidence.
Hoping to bolster morale after the layoffs, the company organized team retreats and announced modest raises for those who remained.
The city bolstered the old seawall with steel and concrete, strengthening it against the storms that had grown more frequent.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: unrestrained by convention or propriety

exs.t: Their large "donations" to the local police department gave the drug cartel the brazen confidence to do their business out in the open.
In a brazen breach of protocol, the junior diplomat interrupted the treaty signing to announce his own objections to the press.
The thieves were so brazen that they robbed the gallery in broad daylight, walking out with the painting while visitors watched.
Her brazen defiance of the dress code, arriving at the formal gala in hiking boots, delighted some guests and scandalized others.

def: relating to the pleasant aspects of the country

exs.t: The noble families of England once owned vast expanses of beautiful, bucolic land.
Tired of the noise and traffic of the city, the couple moved to a bucolic village surrounded by orchards, meadows and grazing sheep.
The painter's bucolic landscapes, full of shepherds and gentle streams, offered viewers a nostalgic escape from the industrial cities of his time.
Although the region looks bucolic in tourist brochures, its farms have in fact been largely replaced by factories and warehouses.

def: lacking physical movement skills, especially with the hands

exs.t: Within a week of starting, the bumbling new waiter was unceremoniously fired.
The bumbling apprentice dropped three porcelain cups in a single morning, and the potter finally assigned him to sweeping the floor.
In the comedy, a bumbling inspector knocks over lamps and trips on rugs, yet somehow solves the case by accident.
Though bumbling in the kitchen, where he burned and spilled nearly everything, the chemist was remarkably precise in his laboratory.

def: grow and flourish

exs.t: China's housing market is burgeoning, but some predict that the growth is merely a bubble and will burst much like the U.S. real estate bubble of 2008.
As interest in local history burgeoned, the tiny archive expanded into a museum that now draws thousands of visitors each year.
The software industry burgeoned in the valley, transforming a quiet farming region into one of the country's busiest economic centers.
Scholars expected the movement to fade quickly; instead, it burgeoned, attracting new members in dozens of countries within a few years.

def: making of a false statement meant to injure a person's reputation

exs.t: With the presidential primaries well under way, the air is thick with calumny, and the mud already waist- high.
The candidate's rivals spread calumny about his finances, falsely claiming that he had embezzled funds from the charity he founded.
The scientist sued the tabloid for calumny after it printed invented accusations that she had fabricated her research data.
Although the rumors were eventually proven false, the calumny had already ruined the merchant's reputation and driven away his customers.

def: determined by chance or impulse or whim rather than by necessity or reason

exs.t: Nearly every month our capricious CEO had a new plan to turn the company around, and none of them worked because we never gave them the time they needed to succeed.
The capricious weather of the mountains, which could shift from sunshine to blizzard within an hour, made planning the climb nearly impossible.
Employees never knew what to expect from their capricious manager, who might praise a report one day and reject the same work the next.
The king's decisions were capricious rather than reasoned; he once exiled a minister simply because he disliked the color of his coat.

def: to reprimand harshly

exs.t: Drill sergeants are known to castigate new recruits so mercilessly that the latter often break down during their first week in training.
The editor castigated the reporter for publishing an unverified story, calling it the most careless error the paper had made in decades.
In a scathing review, the critic castigated the orchestra for its sloppy tempo and out-of-tune brass.
Rather than castigating the student in front of the class, the teacher chose to discuss his mistakes privately after the lesson.

def: to express strong disapproval

exs.t: After being caught in bed with a mistress, the mayor was quickly censured by the city council.
The senate voted to censure the member for misusing public funds, a formal rebuke that stopped short of expelling him.
The medical board censured the surgeon for operating without consent, though it allowed him to keep his license.
Several scientists censured the journal for publishing the flawed study, arguing in a public letter that its reviewers had failed their duty.

def: to reprimand harshly

exs.t: Though chastised for his wanton abuse of the pantry, Lawrence shrugged off his mother's harsh words, and continued to plow through jars of cookies and boxes of donuts.
The coach chastised his players for their lack of effort, lecturing them sternly in the locker room for nearly an hour.
After the mistake cost the firm a major client, the partner chastised the associate so severely that he considered resigning.
Rather than chastising her son for breaking the vase, the mother calmly asked him to help sweep up the pieces.

def: to chuckle, laugh merrily

exs.t: Walking past the bar, I could hear happy, chortling people and the blast of horns from a jazz band.
The audience chortled with delight as the clown stumbled through his routine, their laughter growing louder with each pratfall.
Reading his friend's witty letter, the old professor chortled to himself, pausing every few lines to wipe his eyes.
Instead of scowling at the child's prank, the grandfather chortled and asked to hear the joke again, his shoulders still shaking long after the others had stopped.

def: restrict or confine

exs.t: Their tour of South America was circumscribed so that they saw only popular destinations and avoided the dangerous parts of cities.
The new regulations circumscribe the agency's authority, limiting its investigations to cases that involve interstate commerce.
Her freedom was sharply circumscribed during the illness; she could not leave her room and could receive visitors only for an hour each day.
Because the scholar drew only on the archives of one provincial town, critics argued that his sources circumscribed his conclusions far more than his sweeping title implied.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: cleverly find a way out of one's duties or obligations

exs.t: One way of circumventing the GRE is to apply to a grad school that does not require GRE scores.
The company circumvented the export ban by routing its shipments through a third country, a practice regulators later deemed illegal.
Rather than confronting the bureaucracy directly, the activists found a clever way to circumvent it, delivering aid through local churches.
Some students try to circumvent the school's plagiarism software by paraphrasing entire articles, but the teachers usually catch them anyway.

def: to be in proportion or corresponding in degree or amount

exs.t: The convicted felon's life sentence was commensurate to the heinousness of his crime.
The engineers argued that their salaries should be commensurate with their responsibilities, which had doubled after the merger.
The punishment seemed far from commensurate with the offense: the student was expelled for a minor clerical error.
Investors expect returns commensurate with the risks they take, so a speculative venture must promise far greater gains than a government bond.

label: v.1
def: acknowledge defeat

exs.t: I concede. You win!
After a long night of counting ballots showed him trailing by thousands of votes, the candidate finally conceded and congratulated his opponent.
With only his king left on the board, the grandmaster conceded the game rather than prolong the inevitable.
The defending champion refused to concede even when she trailed by two sets, and her persistence carried her to an improbable comeback.

label: v.2
def: admit (to a wrongdoing)

exs.t: After a long, stern lecture from her father, Olivia conceded to having broken the window.
Confronted with the emails, the executive conceded that he had misled investors about the company's debts.
The senator eventually conceded to having accepted improper gifts, though he denied that they had influenced his votes.
Although he long insisted on his innocence, the clerk finally conceded that he had altered the records to hide the missing funds.

label: v.3
def: give over; surrender or relinquish to the physical control of another

exs.t: The Spanish were forced to concede much of the territory they had previously conquered.
Under the terms of the treaty, the defeated kingdom was forced to concede its northern provinces to the victors.
The family conceded control of the estate to the bank after failing to repay the mortgage for several years.
Unwilling to concede the fortress to the besieging army, the garrison held out for months on dwindling supplies.

label: v.1
def: be confusing or perplexing to

exs.t: Though Harry loved numbers, he found calculus confounding.
The results confounded the researchers, who had predicted the opposite outcome and could find no flaw in their experiment.
The riddle confounded every guest at the dinner party; no one could explain how the answer fit the clues.
Economists were confounded by the market's behavior, which rose sharply even as every indicator pointed toward a recession.

label: v.2
def: mistake one thing for another

exs.t: Americans often confound sweet potatoes with yams, and refer to both vegetables by the same name.
Beginning students often confound correlation with causation, assuming that because two things occur together, one must cause the other.
The two sisters looked so alike that even their teachers confounded them, calling each by the other's name.
Critics who confound the narrator with the author miss the irony of the novel, whose speaker holds views the writer clearly rejects.

def: without any attempt at concealment; completely obvious

exs.t: American basketball players are always conspicuous when they go abroad--not only are they American, but some are over seven feet tall.
In a room full of dark suits, the guest in a bright yellow coat was conspicuous, and every photographer turned toward him.
The editor's name was conspicuous by its absence from the acknowledgments, a pointed omission that many readers noticed.
The new tower, far taller than anything around it, is conspicuous from every part of the city.

label: n.1
def: a citizen who is represented in a government by officials for whom he or she votes

exs.t: The mayor's constituents are no longer happy with her performance and plan to vote for another candidate in the upcoming election.
The representative held town meetings every month, listening to her constituents' concerns about schools, roads and taxes.
After thousands of letters from angry constituents, the senator reversed his position and voted against the bill.
A legislator who ignores the needs of his constituents may find that the voters of his district replace him at the next election.

label: n.2
def: an abstract part of something

exs.t: The constituents of the metal alloy are nickel, copper, and tin.
Trust, the sociologist argued, is an essential constituent of any functioning community, as vital as shared laws or institutions.
Irony is such an essential constituent of the novelist's style that her books lose much of their charm in translations that flatten it.
Rhythm, melody and harmony are the basic constituents of most Western music, though some modern composers have discarded one or more of them.

def: interpreted in a particular way

exs.t: The author's inability to take a side on the issue was construed by both his opponents and supporters as a sign of weakness.
The diplomat's silence was construed as agreement, though he later insisted that he had simply been waiting for instructions.
Judges must construe ambiguous statutes in light of the legislature's intent, reading the text alongside the debates that produced it.
She construed his brief reply as a rejection, but he had merely been too busy to write more.

label: n.
def: a gathering of persons representative of some larger group

exs.t: A small contingent of those loyal to the king have gathered around the castle to defend it.
A small contingent of scientists from the university attended the conference, representing their department in the international debate.
The largest contingent at the parade came from the veterans' association, whose members marched in uniform behind a brass band.
Each member nation sent a contingent of peacekeepers, so that the mission included soldiers from a dozen countries.

label: adj.
def: possible but not certain to occur

exs.t: Whether the former world champions can win again this year is contingent upon none of its star players getting injured.
The loan is contingent on the company's passing an independent audit; if the auditors find irregularities, the bank will withdraw its offer.
His acceptance to the program was contingent upon his completing a final course in statistics during the summer.
Historians stress that the war's outcome was contingent rather than inevitable, depending on a few chance decisions made in its opening weeks.

def: the feeling of remorse or guilt that comes from doing something bad

exs.t: Those who show contrition during their prison terms--especially when under review by a parole board-- often get shortened sentences.
The defendant's apparent contrition, including his tearful apology to the victims, persuaded the judge to reduce his sentence.
Far from showing contrition, the executive blamed his subordinates and insisted that the company had done nothing wrong.
In a letter full of contrition, the student admitted to cheating and asked the professor for a chance to redeem himself.

def: to pull off a plan or scheme, usually through skill or trickery

exs.t: Despite a low GPA, he contrived to get into college, going so far as to write his own glowing letters of recommendation.
The prisoners contrived to escape by digging a tunnel beneath the kitchen, concealing the dirt in their mattresses for months.
Although the invitation list was closed, the reporter contrived to get into the gala by posing as a caterer.
The clever steward contrived a meeting between the feuding cousins, arranging for both to arrive at the same inn on the same night.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: in abundant supply

exs.t: In midsummer, there are copious popsicle stands at the beach; in the winter, there are none.
The researcher took copious notes during each interview, filling several notebooks with details that she later organized into her book.
Despite copious rainfall in the spring, the reservoir remained low because of the previous year's drought.
The feast featured copious amounts of food, far more than the guests could possibly eat.

def: pathetically cowardly

exs.t: Though the man could have at least alerted the police, he crouched cravenly in the corner as the old woman was mugged.
The king's craven retreat, abandoning his troops to flee the battle, cost him the respect of his entire army.
Fearing the minister's anger, the manager made the craven decision to blame his assistant for a mistake he himself had made rather than face the consequences.
Unlike her craven colleagues, who stayed silent to protect their positions, the young auditor reported the fraud despite the risk.

def: mysterious or vague, usually intentionally

exs.t: Since Sarah did not want her husband to guess the Christmas present she had bought him, she only answered cryptically when he would ask her questions about it.
The poet's cryptic final lines have puzzled readers for generations, since they seem to hint at a secret without ever naming it.
When asked about his plans, the director gave only a cryptic reply, saying that 'the answer lies in the question.'
The spy left a cryptic message on the cafe table, a string of numbers and symbols that only her handler could decode.

def: reach the highest or most decisive point

exs.t: Beethoven's musical genius culminated in the 9th Symphony, which many consider his greatest work.
The months of negotiations culminated in a historic treaty, signed with great ceremony in the capital.
Her long career culminated in a lifetime achievement award, the highest honor her profession offers and a fitting end to decades of work.
The festival culminates in a grand fireworks display over the harbor on its final night.

def: a state of guilt

exs.t: Since John had left his banana peel at the top of the stairwell, he accepted culpability for Martha's broken leg.
The investigation established the airline's culpability for the crash, finding that it had ignored repeated warnings about the faulty engine.
Although the driver denied culpability, the security footage clearly showed him running the red light.
The committee sought to determine the degree of each official's culpability, distinguishing those who approved the scheme from those merely unaware of it.

def: characterized by good taste in manners and conduct

exs.t: Sally's parties are decorous affairs, and instead of the usual beer and music, there is tea and intellectual conversation.
The ceremony was a decorous affair, with guests speaking in hushed tones and bowing politely to the elders.
Although the debate was heated, the candidates remained decorous, avoiding personal insults and addressing each other with courtesy.
The children, usually rowdy, were unexpectedly decorous during the visit to their grandmother, sitting still and thanking her for every treat.

def: propriety in manners and conduct

exs.t: You will obey the rules of decorum for this courtroom or spend the night in a jail cell, said the judge to the prosecutor.
The chairman reminded the committee members to observe decorum, since shouting and personal attacks had no place in the hearing.
Despite the tense atmosphere, the diplomat maintained perfect decorum, never raising his voice or showing irritation.
The student's loud outburst during the solemn memorial ceremony was a shocking breach of decorum that embarrassed his entire family.

def: showing respect

exs.t: If you ever have the chance to meet the president, stand up straight and be deferential.
The junior associates were deferential toward the senior partner, never interrupting him and always waiting for his opinion before offering their own.
Visitors to the temple adopted a deferential posture, bowing their heads and speaking only in whispers.
Although the young scientist was deferential to her mentor in public, she privately disagreed with many of his conclusions.

def: harmful to living things

exs.t: The BP oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico was deleterious to the fishing industry in the southern states.
Prolonged exposure to loud noise can have deleterious effects on hearing, causing damage that is often permanent.
The pesticide was banned after studies showed that it was deleterious to bees, whose populations had collapsed in treated areas.
Rather than helping the fish, the chemical proved deleterious, killing thousands of them within weeks of its release.

def: describe in detail

exs.t: After a brief summary of proper swimming technique, the coach delineated the specifics of each stroke, spending 30 minutes alone on the backstroke.
In her opening chapter, the historian delineates the causes of the famine one by one, devoting several pages to drought, trade policy and war.
The contract carefully delineated each party's responsibilities, specifying who would pay for materials, labor and any delays.
Rather than offering vague promises, the candidate delineated her plan, walking voters through exactly how each program would be funded and which agency would run it.

def: to object or show reluctance

exs.t: Wallace disliked the cold, so he demurred when his friends suggested they going skiing in the Alps.
When asked if she wanted to visit the war-torn region without a translator by her side, the journalist demurred.
When the committee asked him to chair the new project, the professor demurred, explaining that his research already consumed all of his time.
Most members approved the merger enthusiastically, but a few demurred, voicing doubts about the partner company's finances.
She usually accepted invitations eagerly, yet she demurred at the offer to speak at the ceremony, preferring to remain in the audience.

def: charge falsely or with malicious intent; attack the good name and reputation of someone

exs.t: Count Rumford denigrated the new theory of heat, demonstrating that it was wholly inadequate to explain the observations.
Rather than engaging with his rival's arguments, the candidate tried to denigrate her character, spreading insinuations about her past.
The tabloid's attempt to denigrate the scientist backfired when her colleagues publicly defended both her integrity and her research.
Jealous of his success, the older composer denigrated the young man's work in every interview, dismissing it as noisy and shallow.

def: be a sign or indication of; have as a meaning

exs.t: Even if the text is not visible, the red octagon denotes "stop" to all motorists in America.
On the map, a small blue triangle denotes a campsite, while a red circle marks a ranger station.
In musical notation, a dot above a note denotes that it should be played short and detached.
The term 'renaissance' originally denoted a rebirth of classical learning, though it is now used far more loosely.

def: (of a creative product, e.g. music or writing) not original; drawing on the work of another person

exs.t: Although the movies were utterly derivative of other popular movies, they did well at the box office.
Although the band's first album was praised for its originality, its second was derivative, borrowing heavily from the groups it had once mocked.
The critic dismissed the novel as derivative, noting that its plot, characters and even its setting closely echoed a famous nineteenth-century work.
Far from being derivative, the painter's style owed nothing to her teachers; she invented her techniques entirely on her own.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

label: v.1
def: come from; be connected by a relationship of blood, for example

exs.t: Many words in the English language are derived from Latin, including the word "derive."
The name of the town derives from an old word for 'ford,' reflecting its origin as a crossing point on the river.
Much of the family's wealth derived from a single shipping company founded by a great-grandfather.
Many modern breeds of dog are derived from a small number of ancestral lines that humans domesticated thousands of years ago.

label: v.2
def: reason by deduction; establish by deduction

exs.t: From the multiple set of footprints in the living room, the investigator derived an important clue: Sheila was not alone in the room at the time of the murder.
From the pattern of cracks in the plaster, the engineer derived the direction in which the foundation had shifted.
Working only from a few observations of the planet's orbit, the astronomer derived its mass with remarkable accuracy.
Students in the logic course must derive each conclusion step by step from the stated premises, justifying every move.

def: expecting unquestioning obedience; characteristic of an absolute ruler

exs.t: The coach was dictatorial in his approach: no players could ever argue or question his approach.
The editor's dictatorial management style, in which every decision required his personal approval, drove several talented writers to quit.
Although the committee was supposed to reach decisions collectively, its chairman behaved in a dictatorial manner, ignoring every objection.
The country slid into dictatorial rule as the president dissolved the legislature and silenced the press.

def: instructive (especially excessively)

exs.t: Tolstoy's The Death of Ivan Ilyich is a didactic novel, instructing the reader on how to live a good life.
The children's book is so didactic that its story disappears beneath a constant stream of lessons about sharing and honesty.
Unlike his earlier plays, which preached moral lessons, the playwright's late work is not didactic; it presents dilemmas without resolving them.
The curators insisted that every exhibit leave visitors with a lesson about the region's history, so the galleries felt didactic and offered little room for simple wonder.

def: showing modest reserve; lacking self-confidence

exs.t: As a young girl she was diffident and reserved, but now as an adult, she is confident and assertive.
The diffident young scholar rarely spoke at seminars, though her papers revealed that she understood the material better than anyone.
Although diffident in social gatherings, where he hardly said a word, the pianist became commanding the moment he sat at the keyboard.
Her diffident manner, which led her to preface every opinion with an apology, concealed a sharp and original mind.

def: wasting time

exs.t: Lawyers use dilatory tactics so that it takes years before the case is actually decided.
The committee's dilatory approach to the investigation, including months of postponed hearings, allowed crucial evidence to disappear.
Frustrated by the contractor's dilatory pace, the homeowners hired another firm, which finished the renovation in a few weeks.
The student was dilatory about his thesis, spending the year organizing his desk and reading unrelated novels instead of writing.

def: an amateur who engages in an activity without serious intentions and who pretends to have knowledge

exs.t: Fred has no formal medical training; while he likes to claim authority on medical issues, he is little more than a dilettante.
Although he spoke confidently about Renaissance painting, the gallery owner soon realized that the collector was a dilettante who had read only a few popular books.
The serious musicians resented the dilettante who joined their ensemble, since he practiced rarely and treated rehearsals as social occasions.
Having dabbled in poetry, pottery and astronomy without mastering any of them, the heiress was dismissed by critics as a mere dilettante.

def: discontented as toward authority

exs.t: After watching his superior take rations from the soldiers, he quickly became disaffected and rebelled.
Disaffected with the party leadership, which had ignored their concerns for years, many younger members left to form a new organization.
The rebellion drew its strength from disaffected soldiers who had not been paid for months.
Teachers worried about the growing number of disaffected students who saw school as irrelevant to their lives and resented its rules.

def: constituting a separate entity or part

exs.t: What was once known as Czechoslovakia has since split into two discrete, independent nations.
The course is divided into discrete modules, each of which can be completed independently of the others.
What appears to be a continuous line on the screen is actually a row of discrete pixels, as anyone who magnifies the image enough to count them will discover.
The researchers identified three discrete stages in the disease, each with its own distinct symptoms.

def: unbiased; neutral

exs.t: The potential juror knew the defendant, and therefore could not serve on the jury, which must consist only of disinterested members.
To resolve the dispute fairly, both companies agreed to hire a disinterested arbitrator who had no financial ties to either side.
A disinterested observer, with no stake in the outcome, would have seen that both teams had played unfairly.
The scholar's review was disinterested, praising and criticizing the book on its merits even though its author was her longtime rival.

def: unaffected by strong emotion or prejudice

exs.t: A good scientist should be dispassionate, focusing purely on what the evidence says, without personal attachment.
Even while describing the atrocities, the historian maintained a dispassionate tone, letting the documents speak for themselves.
Judges must be dispassionate, setting aside their own sympathies and resentments in order to weigh the evidence impartially.
Unlike her fiery colleague, the negotiator remained dispassionate throughout the crisis, calmly analyzing each option.

def: cause to become widely known

exs.t: Before the effects of anesthesia were disseminated, patients had to experience the full pain of a surgery.
The health agency disseminated information about the vaccine through radio broadcasts, posters and community meetings.
The invention of the printing press allowed scholars to disseminate their ideas far more widely than hand-copied manuscripts ever could.
The activists used social media to disseminate their message, reaching millions of people within days.

def: highly opinionated, not accepting that your belief may not be correct

exs.t: Bryan is dogmatic in his belief that the earth is flat, claiming that all pictures of a spherical earth are computer generated.
The professor was so dogmatic about his theory that he refused even to read studies that contradicted it.
Unlike his dogmatic predecessor, who insisted that there was only one correct way to run every play, the new coach encouraged players to experiment.
Her dogmatic views on nutrition, which she presented as beyond question, alienated colleagues who valued open debate.

def: compulsory force or threat

exs.t: The witness said he signed the contract under duress and argued that the court should cancel the agreement.
The court threw out the confession because it had been obtained under duress, after the suspect was threatened and denied sleep.
Treaties signed under duress, the historian argued, rarely last, since the weaker party seeks to overturn them as soon as it can.
The employee claimed that she had approved the payments only under duress, fearing that her supervisor would fire her if she refused.

def: comprised of a variety of styles

exs.t: Joey was known for his eclectic tastes in music, one moment dancing to disco the next "air conducting" along to Beethoven's 9th symphony.
The restaurant's eclectic menu featured dishes from Japan, Peru and Morocco side by side, often combining two cuisines on a single plate.
The architect's eclectic style combined Gothic arches, modernist glass walls and traditional tile roofs, borrowing freely from every period she admired.
Her library was eclectic, with books on quantum physics shelved beside medieval poetry and cookbooks.

def: avoiding waste, efficient

exs.t: Journalists favor an economical style of writing, in which no unnecessary words are used and every sentence is as short as possible.
The novelist's economical prose, in which not a single word is wasted, conveys more in a paragraph than many writers achieve in a chapter.
The engineers designed an economical heating system that used half the fuel of the old one while keeping the building just as warm.
Rather than hiring a large staff, the startup remained economical, relying on a few versatile employees who handled many tasks.

def: enlightening or uplifting so as to encourage intellectual or moral improvement

exs.t: I recently read an article in the Times about whether good literature is edifying or not; specifically, does reading more make a person more moral.
The lecture was edifying, leaving the audience with a deeper understanding of the moral questions raised by modern medicine.
Although the documentary was billed as edifying, it offered little more than sensational footage with no insight at all.
Victorian parents favored edifying novels for their children, stories meant to improve both the mind and the character.

def: producing the intended result

exs.t: Since Maggie's cough syrup, which had expired five years back, was no longer efficacious, she coughed through the night.
The new treatment proved efficacious in the clinical trial, reducing patients' symptoms in nearly every case the researchers studied.
The city's anti-litter campaign was surprisingly efficacious; within months, the streets were noticeably cleaner.
Many folk remedies turn out not to be efficacious: in controlled trials, patients who took them recovered no faster than those who took nothing at all.

def: standing out in negative way; shockingly bad

exs.t: The dictator's abuse of human rights was so egregious that many world leaders asked that he be tried in an international court for genocide.
The referee's egregious error, awarding a goal that had clearly gone wide, prompted an official investigation.
The report documented egregious violations of safety rules, including locked fire exits and missing alarms.
Among the many mistakes in the translation, the most egregious was rendering 'peace' as 'war' in the treaty's opening line.

def: call forth (emotions, feelings, and responses)

exs.t: Just smiling--even if you are depressed--can elicit feelings of pleasure and happiness.
The comedian's joke elicited only a few scattered laughs, and he quickly moved on to his next routine.
The survey was designed to elicit honest responses, so it guaranteed anonymity to every participant.
The novel's ambiguous ending elicited strong reactions from readers, some of whom wrote delighted letters to the author while others demanded a sequel that explained it.

def: make clearer and easier to understand

exs.t: Youtube is great place to learn just about anything--an expert elucidates finer points so that even a complete novice can learn.
The professor used a simple diagram to elucidate the concept, and students who had been confused for weeks finally understood it.
Rather than elucidating the policy, the spokesman's long statement only left reporters more puzzled than before.
The editor added footnotes to elucidate the poet's obscure references to local legends and forgotten politicians.

def: standing above others in quality or position

exs.t: Shakespeare is an eminent author in the English language, but I find his writing uninteresting and melodramatic.
The conference featured several eminent physicists, including two Nobel laureates and the director of the national laboratory.
Although she later became an eminent historian, respected throughout the field, her first book was rejected by a dozen publishers.
The university invited an eminent judge to deliver the commencement address, a jurist admired for decades of distinguished service on the high court.

def: to sap energy from

exs.t: John preferred to avoid equatorial countries; the intense sun would always leave him enervated after he'd spent the day sightseeing.
Dave found the professor's lecture so enervating that not even a potent cup of joe could keep his eyes from drooping.
The long, humid summer enervated the workers, who by August could barely summon the energy to finish their shifts.
Far from invigorating her, the months of chemotherapy enervated the patient so thoroughly that she slept most of each day.
Endless committee meetings enervate even the most enthusiastic faculty members, leaving them too drained to pursue their research.

def: give rise to

exs.t: The restrictions of the Treaty of Versailles were so severe that they engendered deep hatred and resentment in the German people.
The new policy engendered widespread resentment among employees, who felt they had not been consulted.
The teacher's patient encouragement engendered in her students a lasting love of reading that many of them carried into adulthood.
Economic inequality, the sociologist argued, tends to engender distrust, since those left behind suspect that the system is rigged.

def: fixed firmly or securely

exs.t: By the time we reach 60-years old, most of our habits are so entrenched that it is difficult for us to change.
Reformers struggled against the entrenched interests of the old guild, whose members had controlled the trade for centuries.
The belief that women could not do mathematics was so entrenched in the culture that even brilliant girls were discouraged from studying it.
Once a bureaucracy becomes entrenched, it resists every attempt at change, protecting its procedures long after they have outlived their purpose.

def: lasting a very short time

exs.t: The lifespan of a mayfly is ephemeral, lasting from a few hours to a couple of days.
The artist creates ephemeral sculptures of sand and ice that vanish within hours, preserved only in photographs.
Unlike the ephemeral fame of internet celebrities, the composer's reputation has endured for more than two centuries.
The joy of the victory proved ephemeral; within days, the team was mired in scandal.

def: confusing or ambiguous

exs.t: The findings of the study were equivocal--the two researchers had different opinions on what the results signified.
Whether we can glean an artist's unconscious urges through his or her art remains equivocal; that we can ever even really tap into another person's hidden motives remains in doubt.
The minister's equivocal answer, which could be read as either support or opposition, satisfied neither side of the debate.
The results of the trial were equivocal: some patients improved, others worsened, and the researchers could not say whether the drug worked.
Rather than giving an equivocal reply, the candidate stated plainly that she opposed the tax increase.

def: to completely destroy

exs.t: I tried eradicating the mosquitos in my apartment with a rolled up newspaper, but there were too many. of them.
A decades-long vaccination campaign finally eradicated the disease, which has not been seen anywhere in the world since.
The new manager vowed to eradicate corruption in the department, firing every official involved in the bribery scheme.
Although the gardeners worked tirelessly to eradicate the invasive weed, it returned each spring from roots buried deep underground.

def: having or showing profound knowledge

exs.t: Before the Internet, the library was typically were you would find erudite readers.
The erudite professor could quote Greek poetry, discuss Chinese philosophy and explain quantum mechanics with equal ease.
Although the essay was erudite, filled with references to obscure scholars, it was accessible to general readers.
The librarian was surprisingly erudite; she had read nearly every book in the collection and could discuss each one in depth.

def: avoid and stay away from deliberately; stay clear of

exs.t: Politicians are the masters of eschewing morals; academics are the masters of eschewing clarity.
The chef eschews processed ingredients, insisting on preparing every sauce and bread from scratch.
Hoping to appeal to ordinary voters, the candidate eschewed technical jargon and spoke in plain, simple language.
The monks eschew all forms of luxury, living in bare cells and wearing only coarse robes.

def: confined to and understandable by only an enlightened inner circle

exs.t: Map collecting is an esoteric hobby to most, but to geography geeks it is a highly enjoyable pastime.
The seminar focused on an esoteric branch of mathematics that only a handful of specialists in the world fully understand.
The poet's allusions are so esoteric that even well-read critics need footnotes to understand them.
What began as an esoteric practice among a small circle of mystics eventually spread to millions of ordinary followers.

def: to adopt or support an idea or cause

exs.t: As a college student, Charlie espoused Marxism, growing his beard out and railing against the evils of the free-market.
Although he had once espoused free-market principles, the economist later became a vocal advocate for government regulation.
The organization espouses a philosophy of nonviolence, training its members to resist injustice without ever using force.
Few scientists were willing to espouse the controversial theory publicly, fearing damage to their reputations.

def: make worse

exs.t: Her sleeplessness exacerbated her cold--when she woke up the next day, her sinuses were completely blocked.
The drought was exacerbated by poor water management, which allowed much of the remaining supply to leak away.
Rather than calming the crisis, the government's heavy-handed response exacerbated it, sparking even larger protests.
Chronic stress can exacerbate many physical ailments, so doctors often advise patients with heart disease to reduce the pressures in their lives.

def: requiring and demanding accuracy

exs.t: Though his childhood piano teacher was so exacting, Max is thankful now, as a professional pianist.
The surgeon's exacting standards meant that her residents rehearsed every procedure until it was flawless.
Restoring antique clocks is exacting work; a single misplaced gear can prevent the entire mechanism from functioning.
The editor was notoriously exacting, returning manuscripts covered in corrections for even the smallest error of grammar or fact.

def: praise or glorify

exs.t: The teenagers exalted the rock star, covering their bedrooms with posters of him.
The poem exalts the humble farmer, portraying him as a hero whose labor sustains the entire nation.
Because the river goddess was believed to bring the floods that fertilized their fields, the villagers exalted her in hymns sung at every harvest festival.
Critics who once exalted the painter as a genius later dismissed his work as derivative and shallow.

def: pronounce not guilty of criminal charges

exs.t: The document clearly indicated that Nick was out of the state at the time of the crime, and so served to exonerate him of any charges.
New DNA evidence exonerated the prisoner, who had spent twenty years in jail for a crime he did not commit.
The investigation exonerated the pilot, finding that the crash had been caused by a mechanical failure rather than human error.
Although the committee exonerated the senator of wrongdoing, many voters remained convinced of his guilt.

def: add details or explanation; clarify the meaning; state in depth

exs.t: The CEO refused to expound on the decision to merge our department with another one, and so I quit.
The professor expounded on his theory for two hours, explaining each assumption and answering every objection in detail.
In her latest book, the philosopher expounds a new approach to ethics, laying out its principles chapter by chapter.
Asked to expound on his brief remark, the witness declined to provide any further details.

def: the opposite of extinct

exs.t: Despite many bookstores closing, experts predict that some form of book dealing will still be extant generations from now.
Only three copies of the original manuscript are extant; the rest were destroyed in the fire that consumed the monastery's library.
Although many ancient languages have disappeared, some of their descendants remain extant and are still spoken today.
The oldest extant map of the city dates from the sixteenth century, though earlier maps are mentioned in records.

def: of a belief that is based on faulty reasoning

exs.t: The widespread belief that Eskimos have forty different words for snow is fallacious, based on one false report.
The argument that a policy must be good because it is popular is fallacious, confusing public approval with actual merit.
The report's conclusions were fallacious, resting on a flawed sample that included only the most successful companies.
Critics exposed the fallacious reasoning behind the advertisement, which implied that correlation proved causation.

def: overly concerned with details; fussy

exs.t: Whitney is fastidious about her shoes, arranging them on a shelf in a specific order, each pair evenly spaced.
The fastidious editor insisted on checking every comma and footnote, sometimes delaying publication by weeks.
A fastidious dresser, the diplomat never appeared in public without a perfectly pressed suit and polished shoes.
Unlike his fastidious roommate, who alphabetized the spice rack, he left dishes piled in the sink for days.

def: a state of uncertainty about what should be done (usually following some important event)

exs.t: Ever since Elvira resigned as the head of marketing, everything about our sales strategy has been in a state of flux.
After the founder's sudden death, the company was in a state of flux, with no clear successor and no agreed strategy.
After the election produced no clear winner, the ministry's economic policy remained in flux for months, as officials hesitated to commit to any plan before learning who would lead them.
Because the rules of the new program are still in flux, applicants cannot be sure which requirements will apply to them.

def: try to stir up public opinion

exs.t: After having his pay cut, Phil spread vicious rumors about his boss, hoping to foment a general feeling of discontent.
Agitators tried to foment unrest among the workers, spreading rumors that the factory would soon close.
The pamphlets were designed to foment rebellion, urging citizens to rise up against the colonial government.
Accused of fomenting discord within the party, the senator insisted that he had merely voiced legitimate concerns.

def: marked by or showing hopelessness

exs.t: After her third pet dog died, Marcia was simply forlorn: this time even the possibility of buying a new dog no longer held any joy.
The forlorn child sat alone at the bus station, having given up hope that anyone would come to collect her.
After the factory closed, the town took on a forlorn appearance, its empty storefronts and silent streets reflecting the residents' despair.
Her letters from the besieged city grew increasingly forlorn, abandoning all talk of rescue and asking only that her family remember her kindly.

label: adj.1
def: available when required or as promised

exs.t: The President announced that the senators were about to reach a compromise, and that he was eager to read the forthcoming details of the bill.
The company promised that a full explanation would be forthcoming, but weeks passed without any statement.
Although funding for the project had been approved, the money was slow to be forthcoming, delaying construction for months.
When no help was forthcoming from the government, the villagers organized their own relief efforts.

label: adj.2
def: at ease in talking to others

exs.t: As a husband, Larry was not forthcoming: if Jill didn't demand to know details, Larry would never share them with her.
The witness was unusually forthcoming, volunteering details that the investigators had not even thought to ask about.
Unlike her guarded predecessor, the new spokeswoman was forthcoming with reporters, answering their questions openly and at length.
The biographer found the novelist's family less than forthcoming; they refused to discuss his early life.

def: occurring by happy chance; having no cause or apparent cause

exs.t: While the real objects are vastly different sizes in space, the sun and the moon seem to have the same fortuitous size in the sky.
The discovery was fortuitous rather than planned: the chemist noticed the new compound only because a contaminated dish happened to be left out over a holiday.
Their meeting was entirely fortuitous: both had missed the same train and ended up sharing a taxi.
A fortuitous change in the weather allowed the climbers to reach the summit just before the storm returned.

def: not serious in content or attitude or behavior

exs.t: Compared to Juliet's passionate concern for human rights, Jake's non-stop concern about football seems somewhat frivolous.
The judge dismissed the lawsuit as frivolous, noting that it had no legal basis and seemed intended only to harass the defendant.
While his colleagues debated serious policy questions, the young aide made frivolous jokes that irritated everyone in the room.
Although critics dismissed the novel as frivolous, its playful surface concealed a serious meditation on grief.

def: not spending much money (but spending wisely)

exs.t: Monte was no miser, but was simply frugal, wisely spending the little that he earned.
Though she earned a modest salary, her frugal habits allowed her to save enough to buy a house by the age of thirty.
The frugal family repaired their own furniture, grew their own vegetables and rarely ate at restaurants.
Unlike his extravagant brother, who spent every penny he earned, the younger son was frugal, investing carefully and avoiding debt.

def: hinder or prevent (the efforts, plans, or desires) of

exs.t: I thought I would finish writing the paper by lunchtime, but a number of urgent interruptions served to frustrate my plan.
The senator's allies hoped that a lengthy series of procedural objections would frustrate the bill's passage, delaying the final vote until the session expired.
Repeated equipment failures frustrated the research team's efforts to replicate the experiment, so the promising results remained unconfirmed for another year.
A fragmented permitting process often frustrates architects' plans to build affordable housing quickly, since each additional review adds months of costly delay and some projects never break ground.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: marked by quiet and caution and secrecy; taking pains to avoid being observed

exs.t: While at work, George and his boss Regina felt the need to be as furtive as possible about their romantic relationship.
Before snatching the fruit, the young monkey cast furtive glances toward the dominant male, as if it hoped to avoid being seen and punished.
Unlike the open deliberations of the council, the negotiations were furtive: envoys met at night in unmarked houses and destroyed their notes before dawn.
Ashamed of his taste in novels, the narrator made furtive trips to the library, always checking that no colleague was nearby before he borrowed a book.

def: deny or contradict; speak against or oppose

exs.t: I can't gainsay a single piece of evidence James has presented, but I still don't trust his conclusion.
The data from three independent laboratories were so consistent that even the theory's harshest critics could not gainsay the central finding.
No one at the meeting dared to gainsay the founder, since contradicting her in public had ended more than one promising career at the firm.
Although the historian's conclusions are open to debate, one can hardly gainsay the thoroughness of her research, which draws on hundreds of unpublished letters.

label: n.1
def: the trait of being rude and impertinent

exs.t: Even though Carly was only recently hired, she had the gall to question her boss's judgment in front of the office.
After missing every deadline that semester, the student had the gall to ask the professor for an extension on the final paper as well.
Critics were astonished by the gall of the young playwright, who, after one modest success, publicly lectured veteran directors on how to stage his work.
It takes considerable gall for a company recently fined for polluting the river to advertise itself as a champion of environmental stewardship.

label: n.2
def: feeling of deep and bitter anger and ill-will

exs.t: In an act of gall, Leah sent compromising photos of her ex-boyfriend to all his co-workers and professional contacts.
Decades after the disputed inheritance divided the family, the brothers still felt nothing but gall toward one another, refusing even to attend the same funerals.
The memoir is steeped in gall: never having forgiven the colleagues who took credit for her discovery, the author revisits each slight with undiminished resentment.
Rather than reconciling after the bitter election, the defeated faction nursed its gall for years, obstructing every initiative the victors proposed out of sheer rancor.

def: to excite or inspire (someone) to action
