exs.t: At mile 23 of his first marathon, Kyle had all but given up, until he noticed his friends and family holding a banner that read, "Go Kyle"; galvanized, he broke into a gallop, finishing the last three miles in less than 20 minutes.
The colonel's speech galvanized the troops, who had all but given up.
The report's stark photographs of the polluted harbor galvanized a previously apathetic public, and within weeks thousands of residents had joined the cleanup effort.
The coach hoped that a rousing halftime speech would galvanize her demoralized players into mounting a comeback in the second half.
Although the scientific community had long neglected the disease, a single outbreak in a major city galvanized researchers, who soon launched dozens of new studies.

def: full of trivial conversation

exs.t: Lynne was garrulous: once, she had a fifteen minute conversation with a stranger before she realized the woman didn't speak English.
The documentary's garrulous narrator filled every silence with trivial asides about his lunch and the weather, so viewers often lost track of the actual subject.
Whereas her reserved sister rarely spoke at dinner, Elena was garrulous, chattering about neighbors, recipes, and television plots until the dessert was cleared.
Long flights can be exhausting when one is seated beside a garrulous passenger who insists on narrating every minor detail of his vacation photographs.

def: lacking social polish

exs.t: Sylvester says the most gauche things, such as telling a girl he liked that she was much prettier when she wore makeup.
At the formal embassy dinner, the young attache made the gauche mistake of asking the host about his salary, a lapse that embarrassed everyone at the table.
Though brilliant in the laboratory, the physicist was notoriously gauche at receptions, where he interrupted conversations and forgot to introduce his own guests.
Etiquette manuals of the period warned that it was gauche to mention the price of a gift, since polite society regarded such talk as a mark of poor breeding.

def: relevant and appropriate

exs.t: The professor wanted to tell the jury in detail about his new book, but the lawyer said it wasn't germane to the charges in the cases.
The committee chair repeatedly steered the discussion back to the budget, reminding members that anecdotes about past conferences were not germane to the vote.
In a strong essay, every example should be germane to the thesis; a digression, however vivid, only distracts the reader from the argument.
The judge excluded testimony about the defendant's childhood, ruling that events from four decades earlier were not germane to a contract dispute that began last spring.

label: n.
def: an excessive supply

exs.t: The Internet offers such a glut of news related stories that many find it difficult to know which story to read first.
A glut of new apartments in the city center forced landlords to offer months of free rent, since there were far more units than tenants.
Economists warned that the bumper harvest would create a glut of wheat, driving prices so low that many farmers would lose money on every bushel.
Rather than suffering from a shortage of information, today's researchers face a glut: thousands of papers appear each week, far more than anyone could read.

label: v.
def: supply with an excess of

exs.t: In the middle of economic crises, hiring managers find their inboxes glutted with resumes.
Aggressive planting across the region glutted the market with avocados, and by summer growers were leaving fruit to rot on the trees.
When several studios release blockbusters in the same month, they glut the theaters, and even well-reviewed films struggle to find an audience.
Cheap imports threatened to glut the domestic steel market, so the ministry imposed temporary quotas to keep supply in line with demand.

def: characterized by unusual lightness and delicacy

exs.t: The gossamer wings of a butterfly, which allow it to fly, are also a curse, so delicate that they are often damaged.
The designer's gown was made of a gossamer silk so fine that it seemed to float around the model rather than hang from her shoulders.
Early morning light revealed gossamer threads strung between the hedges, each so delicate that a single breath could have broken it.
Critics praised the pianist's gossamer touch in the nocturne, noting that even the fastest passages sounded weightless rather than heavy or forced.

def: to be likely to socialize with others

exs.t: Often we think that great leaders are those who are gregarious, always in the middle of a large group of people; yet, as Mahatma Gandhi and many others have shown us, leaders can also be introverted.
Unlike the solitary leopard, the lion is a gregarious animal, living and hunting in prides that may include more than a dozen members.
Although he was gregarious at parties, moving easily from one circle of guests to the next, the novelist insisted on complete solitude when he wrote.
The firm deliberately hired gregarious salespeople, reasoning that those who enjoyed meeting strangers would thrive in a role built on constant networking.

def: free of deceit

exs.t: At first I thought my niece was guileless, but I then found myself buying her ice cream every time we passed a shop.
The swindler never recruited guileless villagers as accomplices, since their candid faces and inability to tell even a small lie would have betrayed his scheme at once.
Her testimony was so guileless, full of admissions that damaged her own case, that the jury concluded she could not possibly be lying.
The child's guileless answer, offered without any attempt to hide the broken vase, disarmed parents who had braced themselves for an elaborate excuse.

def: lacking significance through having been overused

exs.t: Cheryl rolled her eyes when she heard the lecturer's hackneyed advice to "be true to yourself."
The screenwriter's first draft relied on hackneyed devices, such as the amnesiac hero and the villain who explains his plan, that audiences had seen countless times.
Although the speech was meant to inspire, its hackneyed phrases about thinking outside the box and reaching for the stars left the graduates yawning.
Once fresh and startling, the metaphor of the city as a jungle has become hackneyed through endless repetition in newspaper columns.

def: marked by great carelessness; dependent upon or characterized by chance

exs.t: Many golf courses are designed with great care, but the greens on the county golf course seem entirely haphazard.
The museum's early collection was assembled in haphazard fashion, with curators buying whatever happened to be for sale rather than following any coherent plan.
Because the files had been stored in such a haphazard manner, the auditors spent weeks locating receipts that should have taken minutes to find.
Critics argue that the city's haphazard development, with factories beside schools and highways cutting through parks, reflects decades without any zoning.

label: n.
def: a long pompous speech; a tirade

exs.t: Dinner at Billy's was more a punishment than a reward, since anyone who sat at the dinner table would have to listen to Billy's father's interminable harangues against the government.
The chairman's harangue lasted nearly an hour, and by the time he finished berating the staff for low sales, several employees had quietly left the room.
Instead of a reasoned rebuttal, the candidate delivered a harangue, shouting accusations at his opponent while the moderator tried in vain to intervene.
The pamphlet reads less like a scholarly analysis than a harangue: page after page denounces modern architecture in increasingly overheated language.

label: v.
def: to deliver a long pompous speech or tirade

exs.t: Tired of his parents haranguing him about his laziness and lack of initiative, Tyler finally moved out of home at the age of thirty-five.
Every morning the foreman would harangue the crew for twenty minutes about safety lapses, although most of the workers had heard the same lecture hundreds of times.
Rather than persuading the undecided delegates, the speaker harangued them at such length that many walked out before the vote.
Frustrated by the slow pace of reform, the activist stood on the courthouse steps haranguing passersby about corruption until the police asked him to move.

def: troubled persistently especially with petty annoyances

exs.t: With a team of new hires to train, Martha was constantly harried with little questions and could not focus on her projects.
The harried receptionist, fielding a dozen calls while patients lined up with minor complaints, barely had time to glance at her own lunch.
Constantly interrupted by small requests from every department, the harried office manager began to dread the sound of his telephone.
Parents of toddlers often look harried by late afternoon, having spent the day refereeing squabbles, fetching snacks, and cleaning up spills.

def: having or showing arrogant superiority to and disdain of those one views as unworthy

exs.t: The haughty manager didn't believe that any of his subordinates could ever have an insight as brilliant his own.
The haughty curator refused even to look at the amateur's paintings, remarking that he did not waste his time on people without formal training.
Although she had been raised in great wealth, the heiress was never haughty; she treated the household staff as equals and remembered each of their birthdays.
The diplomat's haughty tone, which implied that the smaller nation's concerns were beneath his notice, doomed the negotiations from the start.

def: dominance over a certain area

exs.t: Until the Spanish Armada was defeated in 1587, Spain had hegemony over the seas, controlling waters stretching as far as the Americas.
For centuries the empire's naval hegemony allowed it to dictate trade terms to its neighbors, none of whom could challenge its fleets.
Some cultural critics worry about the hegemony of a few streaming platforms, which now largely decide what audiences around the world watch.
Although the party had enjoyed decades of unchallenged hegemony in the region, a series of scandals finally allowed rival groups to win power.

def: a person who holds unorthodox opinions in any field (not merely religion)

exs.t: Though everybody at the gym told Mikey to do cardio before weights, Mikey was a heretic and always did the reverse.
In a department devoted to classical economics, the young scholar was regarded as a heretic because she argued that markets rarely correct themselves.
Chefs who once dismissed him as a heretic for serving dessert first now imitate his menus, which have become the new orthodoxy.
The physician was treated as a heretic by his colleagues when he insisted that surgeons wash their hands, an idea that contradicted the accepted medical wisdom of his day.

def: somebody who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions

exs.t: Lady Gaga, in challenging what it means to be clothed, is an iconoclast for wearing a "meat dress" to a prominent awards show.
An iconoclast by temperament, the philosopher delighted in attacking the most revered doctrines of her discipline, including those her own teachers had championed.
The architect was hailed as an iconoclast for rejecting the ornate traditions that the city's elite considered sacred, building stark concrete towers instead.
Though he began his career as a reverent student of the national epic, the critic became an iconoclast, arguing that its heroes were petty tyrants unworthy of veneration.

def: defying tradition or convention

exs.t: Jackson Pollack was an iconoclastic artist, totally breaking with tradition by splashing paint on a blank canvas.
The composer's iconoclastic symphony abandoned melody altogether, an affront to audiences who expected the lush romantic style of his predecessors.
Far from conventional, the chef's iconoclastic menu paired ice cream with anchovies and served the courses in reverse order.
The magazine built its reputation on iconoclastic essays that mocked cherished national myths rather than repeating them.

def: a behavioral attribute that is distinctive and peculiar to an individual

exs.t: Peggy's numerous idiosyncrasies include wearing mismatched shoes, laughing loudly to herself, and. owning a pet aardvark.
One idiosyncrasy of the novelist was that he wrote standing at a tall lectern, a habit that none of his contemporaries shared.
Good biographers resist the temptation to catalog every idiosyncrasy of their subjects, such as a fondness for green ink, unless those quirks illuminate character.
The new manager learned to accommodate each employee's idiosyncrasies: one needed total silence, another worked only after midnight, and a third refused to use email.

def: dishonorable

exs.t: In the 1920s, the World Series was rigged--an ignoble act which baseball took decades to recover from.
Although the general was celebrated as a hero, historians later uncovered the ignoble truth that he had abandoned his wounded soldiers to save himself.
The board rejected the proposal to profit from the disaster, calling it an ignoble scheme unworthy of an organization founded to help victims.
Rather than conceding defeat gracefully, the chess champion accused his opponent of cheating without any evidence, an ignoble end to a distinguished career.

def: (used of conduct or character) deserving or bringing disgrace or shame

exs.t: Since the politician preached ethics and morality, his texting of revealing photographs was ignominious, bringing shame on both himself and his party.
After promising voters a sweeping victory, the party suffered an ignominious defeat, losing even the districts it had held for generations.
The once admired financier met an ignominious end: convicted of fraud, he was stripped of his honors and shunned by his former friends.
The expedition's ignominious retreat, with soldiers abandoning their supplies and fleeing in panic, became a lasting source of national embarrassment.

def: not able to be changed

exs.t: Taxes are one of the immutable laws of the land, so there is no use arguing about paying them.
Early chemists believed that the elements were immutable, so the discovery that one element could transform into another overturned a basic assumption of their science.
Although the club's founders treated the bylaws as immutable, later members amended nearly every rule within a decade.
For the ancient philosophers, the heavens represented an immutable order, in contrast to the constant decay and change they observed on Earth.

def: free from undue bias or preconceived opinions

exs.t: The judge was not impartial since he had been bribed by the witness's family.
Because both teams distrusted the local referees, the league appointed an impartial official from another country to oversee the final match.
A good judge must remain impartial, setting aside personal sympathies so that each side receives an equal hearing.
The researchers hired an outside firm to analyze the data, hoping that an impartial review would dispel suspicions that the drug's makers had skewed the results.

def: being disrespectful; improperly forward or bold

exs.t: Dexter, distraught over losing his pet dachshund, Madeline, found the police officer's questions impertinent--after all, he thought, did she have to pry into such details as to what Madeline's favorite snack was?
The intern's impertinent remark about the director's outdated methods, delivered during her first week, stunned the senior staff into silence.
Victorian children were expected to be seen and not heard, so a child who questioned an adult's authority was scolded for being impertinent.
The reporter's impertinent questions about the host's income and marriage, asked loudly in front of his guests, embarrassed everyone at the gala.

def: incapable of making less angry or hostile

exs.t: Win or lose, the coach was always implacable, never giving the athletes an easy practice or a break.
Despite repeated apologies and offers of compensation, the offended landowner remained implacable, vowing to pursue the lawsuit to the highest court.
The two clans were implacable enemies whose hatred no treaty, gift, or marriage between their families could ever soften.
Negotiators hoped that generous concessions would soothe the union, but its leaders proved implacable, rejecting every offer as an insult.

def: describing a statement that is not believable

exs.t: The teacher found it implausible that the student was late to school because he had been kidnapped by outlaws on horseback.
The defendant's alibi, that he had been sleepwalking across town at the time of the robbery, struck the jury as wholly implausible.
While the novel's premise is implausible, the author renders her characters so vividly that readers willingly suspend their disbelief.
Physicists dismissed the inventor's claim of a perpetual motion machine as implausible, since such a device would violate the basic laws of thermodynamics.

def: not wise

exs.t: Hitler, like Napoleon, made the imprudent move of invading Russia in winter, suffering even more casualties than Napoleon had.
It would be imprudent to invest one's entire savings in a single untested company, however persuasive its founders may seem.
The mountaineers made the imprudent decision to continue toward the summit despite the gathering storm, and they barely made it back to camp alive.
Critics called the city's decision to build on the floodplain imprudent, noting that the area had flooded repeatedly within living memory.

def: improperly forward or bold

exs.t: In an impudent move, the defendant spoke out of order to say terribly insulting things to the judge.
The impudent apprentice corrected the master carpenter in front of a client, a breach of workshop etiquette that nearly cost him his position.
When the teacher asked the class to be quiet, one impudent student replied that he would talk whenever he pleased.
Far from being grateful for the scholarship, the young man made the impudent demand that the committee also pay for his travel and lodging.

def: having or demonstrating ability to recognize or draw fine distinctions

exs.t: The lawyer had an incisive mind, able in a flash to dissect a hopelessly tangled issue and isolate the essential laws at play.
The critic's incisive review distinguished between the novel's genuine innovations and its merely fashionable gimmicks, a distinction other reviewers had missed.
Although the debate was long and muddled, the moderator's incisive questions cut straight to the key differences between the two proposals.
Her incisive analysis of the survey data revealed that what appeared to be a single trend was actually two separate patterns affecting different age groups.

def: lacking in harmony or compatibility or appropriateness

exs.t: The vast economic inequality of modern society is incongruous with America's ideals.
The modern glass tower looks incongruous among the medieval churches of the old town, clashing with their weathered stone facades.
It seemed incongruous that a festival celebrating local farmers would be sponsored by a corporation that had bought up most of their land.
The comedian relies on incongruous pairings, such as a solemn funeral march played on a kazoo, to provoke laughter from his audience.

def: impervious to correction by punishment

exs.t: Tom Sawyer seems like an incorrigible youth until Huck Finn enters the novel; even Sawyer can't match. his fierce individual spirit.
Despite detentions, suspensions, and countless meetings with his parents, the boy remained incorrigible, returning to his pranks the moment each punishment ended.
An incorrigible gambler, the count lost the family estate even after his creditors had twice seized his property and barred him from the casino.
Prison reformers argued that few offenders are truly incorrigible; given education rather than ever harsher penalties, most could be rehabilitated.

def: not in keeping with accepted standards of what is right or proper in polite society

exs.t: Eating with elbows on the table is considered indecorous in refined circles.
At the solemn memorial service, the guest's loud laughter and ringing phone struck the mourners as deeply indecorous.
Under the rigid court etiquette of the era, it was considered indecorous for a courtier to turn his back on the king, however briefly.
The senator apologized for his indecorous remarks, conceding that insulting a colleague's family on the chamber floor violated the norms of legislative debate.

def: the trait of seeming not to care

exs.t: In an effort to fight indifference, the president of the college introduced a new, stricter grading system.
The scientist was dismayed by the public's indifference to her findings; despite the alarming data, few people bothered even to read the report.
Although the novel's hero professes indifference to wealth, he spends most of the story scheming to marry an heiress.
Teachers often find apathy harder to address than hostility, since a student's indifference offers no strong feeling that might be redirected toward learning.

def: impossible to stop or prevent

exs.t: The rise of the computer was an inexorable shift in technology and culture.
The glacier's inexorable advance, though only a few centimeters a day, eventually buried the entire village despite every effort to divert it.
Many historians reject the idea that the empire's decline was inexorable, arguing that wiser leaders could have averted collapse.
Like the tide, the aging process is inexorable; cosmetics and surgery may disguise its effects, but nothing can halt it.

def: to be naïve and innocent

exs.t: Two-years in Manhattan had changed Jenna from an ingenuous girl from the suburbs to a jaded urbanite, unlikely to fall for any ruse, regardless of how elaborate.
The ingenuous young clerk believed every promise the salesman made, never suspecting that the bargain was a trap.
Critics found the film's heroine too ingenuous to be credible: after years in the political capital, she still trusts every smiling official she meets.
His ingenuous question about why the adults were whispering revealed that the child had no idea his parents were separating.

def: gain favor with somebody by deliberate efforts

exs.t: Even though Tom didn't like his new boss, he decided to ingratiate himself to her in order to advance his career.
Hoping to ingratiate himself with the new director, the junior curator praised her every decision and volunteered for the tasks nobody else wanted.
The ambassador ingratiated herself with the local elite by learning their dialect and hosting lavish dinners in their honor.
Candidates who try too obviously to ingratiate themselves with voters, praising every town they visit as the finest in the nation, often provoke suspicion rather than affection.

def: hostile (usually describes conditions or environments)

exs.t: Venus, with a surface temperature that would turn rubber to liquid, is inimical to any form of life.
The high salinity of the lake is inimical to most fish, so only a few hardy species of brine shrimp survive in its waters.
Economists warned that sudden, unpredictable changes in tax policy are inimical to long-term investment, because firms cannot plan under such uncertainty.
The open-plan office, with its constant chatter and interruptions, proved inimical to the deep concentration that the programmers' work required.

def: harmless and doesn't produce any ill effects

exs.t: Everyone found Nancy's banter innocuous--except for Mike, who felt like she was intentionally picking on him.
What seemed an innocuous question about the budget provoked a furious reaction from the minister, who evidently had something to hide.
Although the mushroom closely resembles a deadly species, it is entirely innocuous and can be eaten safely by anyone who identifies it correctly.
Most of the bacteria living on human skin are innocuous; only a small fraction ever cause infection, and many actually help to protect their host.

def: not easily understood; unfathomable

exs.t: His speech was so dense and confusing that many in the audience found it inscrutable.
The poker champion's inscrutable expression gave her opponents no hint as to whether she held a winning hand or nothing at all.
To modern readers the medieval manuscript remains inscrutable, written in a cipher that no scholar has yet managed to decode.
The villain's motives are deliberately inscrutable; the author never explains why he betrays his closest friend, and critics still argue about it.

def: working in a subtle but destructive way

exs.t: Plaque is insidious: we cannot see it, but each day it eats away at our enamel, causing cavities and other dental problems.
High blood pressure is especially insidious because it produces few symptoms while steadily damaging the heart and kidneys over many years.
The propaganda was insidious rather than blatant, slipping small distortions into otherwise accurate reports until readers' views had quietly shifted.
Rot is an insidious threat to wooden buildings: it spreads unseen behind walls for years before a floor suddenly gives way.

def: rude and arrogant

exs.t: Lilian could not help herself from being insolent, commenting that the Queen's shoes were showing too much toe.
When the customs officer asked for his papers, the smuggler responded with an insolent sneer and tossed them onto the ground at the man's feet.
The household dismissed the insolent servant, who had openly mocked his master's guests and then refused to apologize.
Though merely a junior partner, he adopted an insolent tone with the firm's founders, openly calling their strategy foolish and their experience irrelevant.

def: to suggest something subtly

exs.t: At first Manfred's teachers intimated to his parents that he was not suited to skip a grade; when his parents protested, teachers explicitly told them that, notwithstanding the boy's precocity, he was simply too immature to jump to the 6th grade.
Without saying so directly, the editor intimated that the manuscript would need substantial revisions before it could be accepted.
Choosing her words carefully, the diplomat intimated that her government might soon change its position, though she never stated any such intention outright.
The board's statement seemed to intimate that the chief executive would soon step down, although no one would confirm it openly.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: unwilling to change one's beliefs or course of action

exs.t: Despite many calls for mercy, the judge remained intransigent, citing strict legal precedence.
Because both sides remained intransigent, refusing to budge on a single demand, the negotiations collapsed after only two days.
The committee chair was intransigent about the deadline, rejecting every request for an extension no matter how compelling the reason.
Although she welcomed criticism in most matters, the author was intransigent when editors tried to alter her novel's bleak ending.

def: fearless

exs.t: Captain Ahab was an intrepid captain whose reckless and fearless style ultimate leads to his downfall.
The intrepid reporter ventured into the war zone without an escort, determined to document conditions that other journalists were too frightened to approach.
Early polar explorers had to be intrepid, since they faced months of darkness, bitter cold, and the constant risk of death.
Though timid in social settings, the botanist became intrepid in the field, scaling cliffs and wading through rivers to collect rare specimens.

def: habitual

exs.t: He is an inveterate smoker and has told his family and friends that there is no way he will ever quit.
An inveterate traveler, the historian spent nearly every summer of her adult life exploring remote archives in a different country.
The senator was an inveterate interrupter: for thirty years, in committee and on the floor, he had never let a colleague finish a sentence, and no rebuke could break the habit.
His inveterate habit of arriving late, formed in childhood and never broken, eventually cost him his position at the firm.

def: complicated, and difficult to comprehend

exs.t: The physics lecture became so involved that the undergraduate's eyes glazed over.
The plot of the opera is so involved, with its disguised twins, secret marriages, and mistaken identities, that most audiences rely on the program notes to follow it.
Applying for the grant proved an involved process, requiring dozens of forms, three separate budgets, and letters of support from several institutions.
Rather than giving a simple explanation, the lawyer offered an involved argument whose many clauses and exceptions left the jury more confused than before.

def: incapable of being retracted or revoked

exs.t: Once you enter your plea to the court, it is irrevocable so think carefully about what you will say.
Once the treaty was ratified, its provisions were irrevocable, so the delegates debated each clause with great care beforehand.
The decision to demolish the historic theater was irrevocable; once the wrecking crews finished, no amount of regret could restore it.
Some philosophers argue that promises are not irrevocable, since circumstances may change so drastically that keeping one would cause great harm.

def: traveling from place to place to work

exs.t: Doctors used to be itinerant, traveling between patients' homes.
In the nineteenth century, itinerant preachers rode from settlement to settlement, holding services wherever a crowd would gather.
Unlike the settled farmers of the valley, the itinerant shearers moved with the seasons, finding work wherever flocks needed tending.
Because her work as an itinerant consultant took her to a different city every week, she kept only a small apartment that she rarely saw.

def: fanatical patriotism

exs.t: North Korea maintains intense control over its population through a combination of jingoism and cult of personality.
Wartime newspapers were filled with jingoism, portraying the enemy as subhuman and urging readers to accept any sacrifice for the nation's glory.
The historian warned that jingoism can masquerade as ordinary patriotism, though it differs in its eagerness for war and its contempt for other nations.
Critics accused the film of jingoism, noting that it celebrated every battlefield victory while ignoring the suffering of civilians on both sides.

def: full of or showing high-spirited merriment

exs.t: The political candidate and his supporters were jovial once it was clear that she had won.
The jovial innkeeper greeted every guest with a hearty laugh and a joke, and his cheerful mood soon spread through the dining room.
Although the meeting began tensely, the atmosphere became jovial once the unexpected profits were announced and the directors began trading toasts.
Known for his jovial manner, the professor opened each lecture with a humorous anecdote that set his nervous students at ease.

def: full of high-spirited delight because of triumph or success

exs.t: My hard work paid off, and I was jubilant to receive a perfect score on the GRE.
The jubilant fans poured onto the field after their team's unlikely championship victory, hugging strangers and singing late into the night.
The scientists were jubilant when the probe finally transmitted its first images, the triumphant culmination of two decades of work.
Though exhausted after the long campaign, the volunteers were jubilant when the final count confirmed that the referendum had passed.

def: place side by side

exs.t: The meaning of her paintings comes from a classical style which juxtaposes modern themes.
The exhibition juxtaposes ancient masks with contemporary portraits, inviting viewers to compare how different eras represented the human face.
By juxtaposing the lavish banquet with the starving crowds outside the palace gates, the director makes the film's critique of inequality unmistakable.
The poet likes to juxtapose images of industrial decay and natural beauty, setting a rusted factory beside a field of wildflowers in the same stanza.

def: one who says very few words

exs.t: While Martha always swooned over the hunky, laconic types in romantic comedies, her boyfriends inevitably were very talkative--and not very hunky.
Asked to explain his victory, the laconic champion replied only, 'I trained,' and then left the press conference.
Whereas her predecessor gave lengthy speeches, the new chair was laconic, often ending meetings after a few terse sentences.
The general's laconic dispatches, rarely more than a line or two, frustrated officials in the capital who wanted detailed accounts of the campaign.

def: criticize severely or angrily

exs.t: Showing no patience, the manager utterly lambasted the sales team that lost the big account.
Critics who had praised the director's early work lambasted his latest film, calling its plot incoherent and its dialogue embarrassingly clumsy.
The auditor's report lambasts the agency for wasting millions on consultants, describing its oversight as negligent in the extreme.
Although the coach privately praised the players, in public she chose to lambast their lazy defense, hoping the harsh words would spur improvement.

def: not inclined towards physical exertion or effort; slow and relaxed

exs.t: As the sun beat down and the temperature climbed higher, we spent a languid week lying around the house.
The novel captures the languid pace of summer in a southern town, where residents spend long afternoons dozing on shaded porches.
After the frenetic first movement, the symphony shifts to a languid adagio, its phrases drifting unhurriedly as if the orchestra itself had grown drowsy in the afternoon heat.
The cat stretched in a languid way, clearly in no hurry to abandon its sunny spot on the windowsill.

def: extreme generosity and giving

exs.t: Uncle Frank was known for his largess, so his nephew was sad when he did not receive a present for his birthday.
The university's new library was made possible by the largess of an anonymous donor, who gave far more than the fundraisers had dared to request.
The king's largess toward his courtiers, showering them with estates and titles, eventually emptied the royal treasury.
Although the company advertised its charitable largess, critics noted that its donations amounted to a tiny fraction of its annual profits.

def: worthy of high praise

exs.t: To say that Gandhi's actions were laudable is the greatest understatement; he overthrew an empire without violence.
The charity's goal of providing clean water to every village is laudable, though critics question whether its methods are effective.
Her laudable decision to return the reward money to the family she had helped earned her admiration throughout the city.
While the committee found the student's ambition laudable, it worried that the proposed project was far too large to complete in a single year.

def: assign great social importance to

exs.t: Students in the U.S. learn to lionize Jefferson, Franklin, and Washington because they are the founding fathers of the nation.
After his first novel became a surprise success, the young writer was lionized by the city's literary society, which invited him to every salon and gala.
Popular culture tends to lionize the few daring entrepreneurs who struck it rich, celebrating them in magazines and films while ignoring the many whose ventures failed.
Although she was lionized in her lifetime as the greatest actress of her generation, she is now largely forgotten.

def: noble and generous in spirit, especially towards a rival or someone less powerful

exs.t: He was a great sportsman: in defeat he was complementary and in victory he was magnanimous.
In victory the general was magnanimous, allowing the defeated soldiers to return home with their weapons and their dignity intact.
Rather than gloating over the bankruptcy of the rival firm that had tried to ruin her, the magnanimous chief executive offered jobs to its laid-off employees.
The former champion's magnanimous tribute to the young challenger who had just dethroned him surprised fans who had expected bitterness.

def: to assert

exs.t: The scientist maintained that the extinction of dinosaurs was most likely brought about by a drastic change in climate.
Despite mounting evidence against him, the defendant maintained throughout the trial that he had never met the victim and had been abroad that week.
Some linguists maintain that all human languages share a common underlying grammar, though others dismiss the claim as untestable.
The architect maintains that ornament is not a luxury but a necessity, arguing that bare facades alienate the people who must live beside them.

def: clumsy

exs.t: As a child she was quite maladroit, but as an adult, she has become an adept dancer.
The maladroit waiter managed to spill soup on two guests and drop a tray of glasses within the first hour of the banquet.
Although she was maladroit on the dance floor, stumbling over every step, the young diplomat moved with great grace through tense negotiations.
His maladroit handling of the chisel left the sculpture scarred with gouges, and the master quietly reassigned him to sweeping the studio.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: someone who exhibits great independence in thought and action

exs.t: Officer Kelly was a maverick, rarely following police protocols or adopting the conventions for speech common among his fellow officers.
A maverick among economists, she ignored the prevailing models and built her own, which turned out to predict the crisis far better.
The legislator earned a reputation as a maverick by voting against his own party whenever he disagreed with its position.
Unlike the studio directors who followed established formulas, the maverick filmmaker financed his own projects and shot them without scripts.

def: overly sentimental to the point that it is disgusting

exs.t: The film was incredibly mawkish, introducing highly likeable characters only to have them succumb to a devastating illnesses by the end of the movie.
The film's ending, with its swelling violins, tearful reunions, and orphaned puppy, struck critics as mawkish rather than moving.
Though the eulogy began with genuine feeling, it soon became mawkish, dwelling so heavily on sentimental commonplaces that several mourners winced.
The editor urged the poet to cut the mawkish final stanza, arguing that its gushing tributes to childhood innocence would make readers cringe.

def: the tendency to be untruthful

exs.t: I can forgive her for her mendacity but only because she is a child and is seeing what she can get away with.
The minister's mendacity became so well known that journalists routinely checked even his most trivial statements against independent sources.
Critics of the advertising industry decry its mendacity, arguing that many campaigns rely on claims the companies know to be false.
Although the memoirist presents herself as scrupulously honest, readers soon discover her mendacity, as one invented anecdote follows another.

def: (of a person) prone to unexpected and unpredictable changes in mood

exs.t: The fact that Ella's moods were as mercurial as the weather was problematic for her relationships--it didn't help that she lived in Chicago.

Martha Argerich's mercurial nature is perfectly matched with playing Chopin: she'll toss off, with aplomb, effervescent passages, before moments later plumbing the depths of her soul to give voice to bars of music steeped in the utmost melancholy.
The orchestra struggled to work with its mercurial conductor, who might praise the musicians warmly one moment and storm out of rehearsal the next.
Biographers attribute the poet's uneven output to his mercurial temperament, which swung without warning from euphoria to despair.
Investors grew wary of the founder's mercurial leadership, since her sudden changes of mood often produced abrupt reversals in strategy.

def: marked by extreme care in treatment of details

exs.t: The Japanese noodle maker was meticulous in making his noodles and would never let another person take over the task.
The restorer was meticulous, spending weeks cleaning a single square inch of the fresco with tiny brushes to avoid damaging the original pigment.
Because the experiment depended on precise measurements, the lab kept meticulous records, logging every temperature reading to a hundredth of a degree.
Although his early drafts were careless, the novelist became meticulous in revision, checking every date and name against his sources.

def: interpret in the wrong way

exs.t: The politician never trusted journalists because he though that they misconstrue his words and misrepresent his positions.
The ambassador's cautious silence was misconstrued as approval, and the neighboring government proceeded with plans he actually opposed.
Students often misconstrue the principle of natural selection, wrongly believing that organisms change deliberately to suit their environments.
Fearing that readers might misconstrue her satire as a sincere endorsement, the author added a preface explaining her ironic intent.

label: v.1
def: make less severe or harsh

exs.t: I can only spend so much time mitigating your disagreements with your wife, and at a certain point, you need to do it on your own.
Planting trees along city streets can mitigate the effects of summer heat, lowering surface temperatures by providing shade.
The company introduced flexible schedules to mitigate the stress of the long commute, although many employees still arrived exhausted.
Although nothing could undo the damage of the flood, the relief fund mitigated the hardship of families who had lost their homes.

label: v.2
def: lessen the severity of an offense

exs.t: If it weren't for the mitigating circumstances, he would have certainly lost his job.
The judge accepted that the defendant's youth and genuine remorse mitigated his crime, and she imposed a far lighter sentence than the prosecution had sought.
His lawyer argued that the extreme provocation he had endured mitigated the assault, though it could not excuse it entirely.
The review board condemned the officer's misconduct but agreed that his lack of training did mitigate his culpability, so it recommended retraining rather than dismissal.

def: to make someone angry less angry; placate

exs.t: In the morning, Harriat was unable to mollify Harry, if he happened to become angry, unless he had his cup of coffee.
To mollify the furious customers whose flights had been canceled, the airline offered free hotel rooms and vouchers for future travel.
The mayor's apology did little to mollify residents who were outraged by the sudden rise in water rates.
Hoping to mollify his irate editor, the reporter promised to deliver the overdue article before the morning deadline.

label: adj.1
def: repetitive and boring; not spiritual

exs.t: Nancy found doing dishes a thoroughly mundane task, although Peter found a kind of Zen pleasure in the chore.
Although the job came with a glamorous title, most of her days were consumed by mundane tasks such as filing reports and answering routine email.
The novelist's precise and lyrical prose makes even mundane chores like washing dishes and sorting mail seem fascinating, a feat few writers achieve.
Astronauts report that, contrary to popular belief, much of life in orbit is mundane: repeated maintenance checks and exercise routines fill most of each day.

label: adj.2
def: relating to the ordinary world

exs.t: Though we think of the pope as someone always dealing in holy matters, he is also concerned with mundane events, such as deciding when to set his alarm each morning.
The monks were expected to renounce mundane concerns such as property and politics in order to devote themselves wholly to prayer.
Medieval painters often placed saints in mundane settings, such as a merchant's kitchen or a busy marketplace, linking the sacred with the everyday world.
The anthropologist cared less about the tribe's sacred rituals than about its mundane life: how people farmed, traded, and raised their children.

def: very generous

exs.t: Uncle Charley was known for his munificence, giving all seven of his nephews lavish Christmas presents each year.
Thanks to a munificent bequest from a former student, the college was able to offer full scholarships to every admitted applicant.
The patron was munificent toward young composers, funding their studies, commissioning their works, and even paying their rent.
Though notoriously stingy with his own family, the industrialist was munificent in public, endowing museums and hospitals across the city.

def: lacking foresight or imagination

exs.t: The company ultimately went out of business because the myopic managers couldn't predict the changes in their industry.
Cutting the research budget to boost this quarter's profits was a myopic decision that left the company without new products a few years later.
Critics called the zoning plan myopic, arguing that it ignored the population growth the region would certainly experience over the next two decades.
Far from being myopic, the city's founders laid out avenues wide enough to accommodate a population ten times larger than the one they governed.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: a large indefinite number

exs.t: There are a myriad of internet sites hawking pills that claim to boost energy for hours on end.
The rainforest canopy is home to a myriad of insect species, many of which scientists have not yet even named.
A newcomer to the city faces a myriad of decisions, from choosing a neighborhood to navigating an unfamiliar transit system.
Myriads of stars, too faint to be seen individually, combine to produce the pale glow of the galaxy's band across the night sky.

def: so small as to be meaningless; insignificant

exs.t: The GRE tests cumulative knowledge, so if you cram the night before it is, at best, likely to only have a negligible impact on your score.
The new filter's effect on water quality was negligible; tests showed virtually no difference in contaminant levels before and after installation.
Although the tax increase was negligible for wealthy households, it imposed a real burden on families with lower incomes.
The engineers dismissed the risk as negligible, since the probability of both backup systems failing at once was less than one in a billion.

def: unsure how to act or respond

exs.t: Shirley was totally nonplussed when the angry motorist cut her off and then stuck his finger out the window.
The seasoned lecturer was nonplussed by the student's question, which exposed a flaw he had never considered, and he stood silent for a long moment.
Nonplussed by the conflicting instructions from her two supervisors, the new employee simply did not know which task to begin first.
Visitors are often nonplussed by the old city's nameless streets, unsure which way to turn at each intersection and unable to find their hotels.

def: a subtle difference in meaning or opinion or attitude

exs.t: Because of the nuances involved in this case, I hired an outside consultant to advice us and help.
The translator struggled to capture every nuance of the poem, since a single word in the original could carry shades of both irony and tenderness.
Although the two philosophers' positions look identical at first, careful readers notice a nuance: one treats duty as absolute, while the other allows exceptions.
The actor's performance was praised for its nuances, conveying the character's grief through slight changes in posture and tone rather than dramatic outbursts.

label: v.
def: make unclear

exs.t: On the Smith's drive through the Grand Canyon, Mr. Smith's big head obscured much of Mrs. Robinson's view, so that she only saw momentary patches of red rock.
The report's dense technical jargon tends to obscure its central finding, so many readers never realize that the study contradicts earlier research.
The translator's heavy footnotes obscured rather than clarified the poem's meaning, burying each simple image beneath paragraphs of commentary.
Critics accused the company of using convoluted accounting to obscure its mounting losses, leaving investors unable to judge its true condition.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

label: adj.
def: known by only a few

exs.t: Many of the biggest movie stars were once obscure actors who got only bit roles in long forgotten films.
The scholar built her career on obscure poets of the eighteenth century, figures whose names appear in few anthologies and on fewer syllabi.
Although the composer was obscure during his lifetime, performing only for small provincial audiences, his symphonies are now staples of the concert repertoire.
The foundation often gives its prize to obscure researchers rather than celebrated ones, hoping to draw attention to work that has been overlooked.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: attentive in an ingratiating or servile manner; attempting to win favor from influential people by flattery

exs.t: The obsequious waiter did not give the couple a moment's peace all through the meal, constantly returning to their table to refill their water glasses and to tell them what a handsome pair they made.
The obsequious courtier praised every decree the king issued, however foolish, hoping to secure a lucrative appointment.
Diners complained that the obsequious staff hovered over them, refilling glasses after every sip and bowing whenever the owner's wealthy friends arrived.
Although he was obsequious toward the board members who controlled his salary, the manager treated his own subordinates with open contempt.

def: not clearly understood or expressed

exs.t: The meaning of the professor's new research was opaque to most people, so no one asked any questions.
The contract's language was so opaque that even the company's own lawyers disagreed about what obligations it imposed.
Critics complain that the agency's decision-making process remains opaque, since it never publishes the criteria it uses to award grants.
Although the philosopher's early essays are lucid, his later work is opaque, full of invented terminology that few readers can decipher.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: wealth as evidenced by sumptuous living

exs.t: Russian oligarchs are famous for their opulence, living in fancy homes and dining on expensive caviar.
Visitors to the palace are struck by its opulence: gilded ceilings, marble staircases, and chandeliers of hand-cut crystal fill every room.
The novel contrasts the opulence of the banker's mansion with the squalid tenements where the workers in his factories live.
During the port city's commercial boom, merchant families displayed their opulence through lavish balls, imported silks, and private art collections.

def: intended to attract notice and impress others; tawdry or vulgar

exs.t: Matt wanted to buy stone lions for front of the house, but Cynthia convinced him that such a display would be too ostentatious for a modest house in an unassuming neighborhood.
The newly rich banker built an ostentatious mansion with gold-plated faucets and a fountain in the foyer, determined that no visitor would overlook his wealth.
Although she could easily afford luxury, the heiress avoided ostentatious displays, preferring plain clothing and a modest car.
Critics found the monument ostentatious, arguing that its towering columns and gilded eagles were designed to impress rather than to honor the dead.

def: exclude from a community or group

exs.t: Later in his life, Leo Tolstoy was ostracized from the Russian Orthodox Church for his writings that contradicted church doctrine.
After he reported the fraud to regulators, the accountant was ostracized by his colleagues, who stopped inviting him to meetings and refused to eat lunch with him.
In many small villages, a family that broke the community's customs risked being ostracized, cut off from trade and social life alike.
Rather than ostracize the dissenting member, the society invited her to present her objections at its annual meeting.

def: distinctive and stylish elegance

exs.t: Jim, with his typical panache, came to the wedding reception with a top hat, a cane, and a long cape covered in sequins.
The pianist played with such panache, flourishing her hands and adding improvised ornaments, that even the plainest etude seemed dazzling.
Although the restaurant's food was ordinary, the owner ran it with panache, greeting guests in a velvet jacket and presenting each dish with theatrical flair.
The architect's designs lacked panache; they were sound and practical but so plain that they rarely attracted a second glance.

def: narrowly restricted in scope or outlook

exs.t: Jasmine was sad to admit it, but her fledgling relationship with Jacob did not work out because his culinary tastes were simply too parochial; "After all," she quipped on her blog, "he considered Chef Boyardee ethnic food."
The newspaper's parochial coverage, focused almost entirely on local gossip, left readers ignorant of events beyond the county line.
Critics accused the committee of parochial thinking, since it judged every proposal solely by its effect on a single department rather than on the university as a whole.
Traveling abroad for the first time, the student realized how parochial her views had been, shaped entirely by the small town where she had grown up.

def: extremely frugal; miserly

exs.t: Katie is so parsimonious that she only buys a pair of socks if all of her other socks have holes in them.
Even with millions in his bank account, Fred was so parsimonious that he followed a diet consisting of nothing more than bread and canned soup.
The parsimonious landlord refused to repair the broken heater, insisting that tenants could simply wear more sweaters during the winter.
Although he was a millionaire, the collector was so parsimonious that he reused tea bags and walked miles to avoid paying bus fare.
The foundation's parsimonious grants, rarely enough to cover even basic expenses, disappointed researchers who had hoped for generous support.

def: marked by a narrow focus on or display of learning especially its trivial aspects

exs.t: Professor Thompson was regarded as an expert in his field, but his lectures were utterly pedantic, focused on rigorous details of the most trivial conventions in the field.
The pedantic reviewer devoted half of his critique to the author's misuse of a semicolon, ignoring the novel's ambitious themes entirely.
Students found the lecturer pedantic, since he interrupted every discussion to correct minor points of Latin grammar.
Although the scholar's footnotes are exhaustive, they are never pedantic; each one illuminates the argument rather than merely displaying erudition.

def: lacking imagination

exs.t: While Nan was always engaged in philosophical speculation, her brother was occupied with far more pedestrian concerns: how to earn a salary and run a household.
Critics dismissed the novel as pedestrian, noting that its predictable plot and flat prose offered nothing readers had not seen many times before.
Although the architect's early sketches were daring, the final building was pedestrian: a plain box indistinguishable from the offices around it.
The menu was surprisingly pedestrian for a restaurant with such lofty ambitions, relying on familiar dishes prepared without any creative twist.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: expressing disapproval (usually refers to a term)

exs.t: Most psychologists object to the pejorative term "shrink", believing that they expand the human mind, not limit it.
The word 'bureaucrat' has acquired such a pejorative sense that many civil servants prefer to describe themselves as public administrators.
Many art historians note that 'Gothic' began as a pejorative label, applied by critics who regarded medieval architecture as crude and barbaric.
The editor removed several pejorative terms from the article, explaining that such disparaging language undermined the author's claim to objectivity.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: an act of deliberate betrayal; a breach of a trust

exs.t: The lowest circles in Dante's Inferno were for those who had practiced perfidy, and among these, the very lowest was for those, such as Judas, who had been treacherous to one of their benefactors.
The general never forgave the perfidy of his closest adviser, who had secretly sold the army's battle plans to the enemy.
Many revenge tragedies turn on an act of perfidy, as a trusted friend or relative betrays the hero for personal gain.
When the partner who had sworn loyalty to the firm was caught leaking client files to a competitor, his colleagues were stunned by such perfidy.

def: exceedingly harmful; working or spreading in a hidden and injurious way

exs.t: The most successful viruses are pernicious: an infected person may feel perfectly healthy for several months while incubating and spreading the virus.
Economists warn that inflation has a pernicious effect on savings, quietly eroding their value year after year without the owners noticing.
The pernicious rumor spread slowly through the town, and by the time the mayor learned of it, his reputation had been irreparably damaged.
Some invasive vines are pernicious because they grow unnoticed beneath the canopy, gradually strangling the trees that support them.

def: easily irritated or annoyed

exs.t: When Ed first met Ruth, he didn't realize she was so petulant, but now that they are three months into their relationship, Ed feels a day doesn't go by in which she isn't whining about some minor issue.
When the committee rejected his proposal, the petulant professor stormed out of the meeting and refused to speak to his colleagues for a week.
The toddler grew petulant whenever his nap was delayed, whining and swatting at anyone who tried to comfort him.
Critics found the tennis star's petulant outbursts, smashing rackets and snapping at line judges over minor calls, unworthy of a champion.

def: cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of

exs.t: I was able to placate the angry mob of students by promising to bring cookies on Monday.
To placate the angry investors, the company promised to replace its chief executive and to publish independent audits every quarter.
The ministry placated the striking dockworkers with a modest raise and a promise of safer equipment, and the ports reopened within days.
The king hoped that lowering the grain tax would placate the rebellious provinces, but the unrest only spread.

def: a trite or obvious remark

exs.t: The professor argued that many statements regarded as wise in previous times, such as the Golden Rule, are now regarded as mere platitudes.
Instead of offering concrete plans, the candidate relied on platitudes such as 'the future belongs to all of us,' which no voter could possibly dispute.
Grieving families often find a platitude like 'everything happens for a reason' more hurtful than simple silence.
The critic dismissed the novel's closing moral, that honesty is the best policy, as a platitude unworthy of such a sophisticated writer.

def: emotionally touching

exs.t: After the Montagues and Capulets discover the dead bodies of Romeo and Juliet, in the play's most poignant moment, the two grief-stricken families agree to end their feud once and for all.
The documentary's most poignant scene shows an elderly man returning to the village where he was born, only to find it submerged beneath a reservoir.
Letters from soldiers to their children are especially poignant, since many of the writers never returned home to see the families they addressed.
Though the novel is often comic, its final chapter is poignant, and many readers admit to weeping as the old friends say goodbye.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: a strong verbal or written attack on someone or something

exs.t: The professor launched into a polemic, claiming that Freudian theory was a pack of lies that absolutely destroyed European literary theory.
The pamphlet was less a balanced analysis than a polemic: its author never once acknowledged a reasonable point made by the reformers, and he questioned their motives on every page.
In a fierce polemic published in the journal, the economist denounced her rivals' models as not merely flawed but intellectually dishonest.
Although the author intended the book as a calm historical survey, reviewers read it as a polemic against the modern art establishment.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: assume as fact

exs.t: Initially, Einstein posited a repulsive force to balance Gravity, but then rejected that idea as a blunder.
To explain the planet's irregular orbit, astronomers posited an unseen companion body, a hypothesis that later telescopes confirmed.
Classical economic models simply posit a perfectly rational consumer without testing the premise, an assumption that behavioral researchers have repeatedly challenged.
The detective's theory rested on a single unproven premise: she posited that the victim knew his attacker, and every later inference followed from that assumption.

def: guided by practical experience and observation rather than theory

exs.t: Rather than make a philosophical appeal to the Congressmen, the Speaker decided to take a far more pragmatic approach, making small side-deals that would add votes to his bill.
Rather than waiting for a perfect theoretical model, the engineers took a pragmatic approach, testing dozens of prototypes and keeping whatever worked.
The new mayor was pragmatic rather than ideological, adopting policies from any source if experience showed that they reduced crime.
Although her training was highly theoretical, years in rural clinics made the doctor pragmatic, trusting what she observed in patients over what textbooks predicted.

def: done with very great haste and without due deliberation

exs.t: He was expecting a precipitous rise in the value of a "hot" tech stock, so he was disappointed when it only inched up a dollar or two each day.
The board's precipitous decision to fire the director, made within hours of a single critical article, was soon regretted when the accusations proved false.
Historians argue that the precipitous withdrawal of troops, ordered without any plan for transferring security, left the region vulnerable to chaos.
Rather than making a precipitous commitment to the merger, the cautious chairwoman insisted on months of study and independent review.

def: keep from happening or arising; make impossible

exs.t: The manager specified that all other gates be locked, to preclude the possibility of persons without tickets entering the arena undetected.
The contract's exclusivity clause precludes the author from publishing with any other house for five years, so her next two novels must go to the same firm.
A single contaminated sample may not preclude the study's publication, but it does require the researchers to repeat several experiments.
The knee injury precluded any chance of her competing in the final, so she watched from the stands as her rival won the title.

def: characterized by or characteristic of exceptionally early development or maturity (especially in mental aptitude)

exs.t: Though only seven years old, she was a precocious chess prodigy, able to beat players twice her age.
A precocious reader, the girl was working her way through her parents' collection of Victorian novels by the age of six.
The composer's precocious talent astonished his teachers, who found that by the age of eight he could write fugues more polished than their own.
Although precocious children often attract admiring attention, early brilliance does not necessarily predict great achievement in adulthood, and many prodigies settle into ordinary careers.

def: a strong liking

exs.t: Monte had a predilection for the fine things in life: Cuban cigars, 200 dollar bottles of wine, and trips to the French Riviera.
The critic's predilection for experimental fiction led him to champion little-known writers while ignoring more conventional bestsellers.
Despite her own predilection for fiery food, the chef designed a mild menu to suit the tastes of the conference guests.
The collector's predilection for maritime paintings was obvious to every visitor: seascapes lined each hallway, and model ships crowded the shelves.

def: the power to foresee the future

exs.t: Baxter's warnings about investing in technology stocks seemed like an act of prescience after the whole market declined significantly.
The economist's prescience was confirmed when the housing market collapsed exactly as she had predicted in a paper that most of her peers had ignored.
Some early science fiction writers showed remarkable prescience, describing video calls and pocket computers long before such devices existed.
Lacking any prescience about the coming drought, the farmers planted thirsty crops and lost nearly their entire harvest.

def: to speak in an evasive way

exs.t: The cynic quipped, "There is not much variance in politicians; they all seem to prevaricate".
Bobby learned not to prevaricate when his teacher asked him where his homework was; by giving a straightforward answer, he would avoid invoking the teacher's wrath.
When asked directly whether he had seen the documents, the witness prevaricated, talking at length about the office layout without ever answering yes or no.
Rather than prevaricate about the budget shortfall, the new treasurer stated the figures plainly and proposed immediate cuts.
Journalists grew frustrated as the spokesperson continued to prevaricate, answering every pointed question with vague references to ongoing reviews.

def: rashly or wastefully extravagant

exs.t: Successful professional athletes who do not fall prey to prodigality seem to be the exception--most live decadent lives.
The prodigal heir squandered his inheritance within five years, spending lavishly on racehorses, yachts, and parties for hundreds of guests.
Critics accused the government of prodigal spending, pointing to a new presidential palace built while hospitals lacked basic supplies.
Unlike her prodigal brother, who bought every expensive gadget that caught his eye, Maria saved nearly half of her modest salary.

def: so great in size or force or extent as to elicit awe

exs.t: After the relatively small home run totals in the "dead ball" era, Babe Ruth's home run totals were truly prodigious: every year, he set a new all-time record.
The young violinist's prodigious memory allowed her to perform dozens of concertos without ever consulting a score.
Building the cathedral required a prodigious effort, involving thousands of workers and more than a century of labor.
The storm dumped a prodigious amount of snow on the city, burying cars entirely and closing the roads for a week.

label: adj.
def: spending money recklessly or wastefully

exs.t: The profligate administration borrowed heavily to fund lavish festivals and monuments, leaving its successors with debts they could scarcely repay.
Although he earned a modest salary, the clerk led a profligate life, spending each paycheck on fine wines and tailored suits within days of receiving it.
Economists warned that profligate use of the emergency fund, drawn down to cover routine expenses, would leave the state unprepared for a genuine crisis.
Far from being profligate, the museum's director stretched each small grant remarkably far, buying secondhand display cases and relying on volunteer carpenters.

label: n.
def: someone who spends money recklessly or wastefully

exs.t: Most lottery winners go from being conservative, frugal types to outright profligates who blow millions on fast cars, lavish homes, and giant yachts.
The novel's hero is a profligate who gambles away three fortunes before finally learning the value of thrift.
Although his creditors dismissed the young count as a profligate, his lavish spending on artists eventually produced one of the finest collections in the country.
The bank refused to lend to such a notorious profligate, since he had already squandered his inheritance and defaulted on several previous loans.

def: intellectually productive

exs.t: Schubert was the most prolific composer, producing hundreds of hours of music before he died at the age of 31.
A prolific scholar, the historian published a new book nearly every year while also editing two journals.
Although she wrote only two novels, the author was prolific as an essayist, producing hundreds of reviews and columns over four decades.
The painter's prolific output, thousands of canvases over a long career, has made it difficult for curators to distinguish his masterpieces from his routine work.

def: presenting favorable circumstances; likely to result in or show signs of success

exs.t: The child's heartbeat is still weak, but I am seeing many propitious signs and I think that she may be healing.
With interest rates low and consumer demand rising, the moment seemed propitious for launching the new product line.
The sailors waited for propitious winds before setting out, since a strong headwind could delay the crossing by weeks.
Although the early test results were propitious, the researchers cautioned that larger trials might yet reveal serious problems.

def: characteristic of the a limited perspective; not fashionable or sophisticated

exs.t: Maggie's enthusiasm about her high school teams seemed provincial to her college classmates, all of whom were following a nationally ranked college team.
Having never left his hometown, the young editor held provincial views that his cosmopolitan colleagues in the capital found quaint.
The designer's collection was criticized as provincial, reflecting fashions that the great cities had abandoned years earlier.
Sophisticated visitors from the capital once dismissed the town's theater as provincial, yet its daring productions soon made the capital's own stages look stale.

def: someone who has been admitted to membership in a scholarly field

exs.t: Steven Pinker's credentials are unquestioned as a pundit; he has taught at MIT and Stanford, teaches at Harvard, and has published a number of influential books on cognition, language, and psychology.
The committee invited a leading pundit on medieval law to testify, since none of its members could interpret the ancient charters themselves.
Although he held no formal degree, the self-taught astronomer was consulted as a pundit by professors who valued his decades of careful observation.
Recognized as a pundit in Sanskrit grammar, the elderly scholar was asked to settle a dispute that had divided younger linguists for years.

def: to be legally competent or capable

exs.t: If James had made more than $50,000 last year, then he wouldn't have qualified for the low-income scholarship.
Because she had lived in the district for less than a year, the candidate did not qualify to run for the city council.
Applicants qualify for the grant only if their household income falls below the threshold set by the agency.
After passing the bar examination, he finally qualified to practice law in the state, ending years of work as a paralegal.

def: to make less severe; to limit (a statement)

exs.t: Chris qualified his love for San Francisco, adding that he didn't like the weather as much as the weather in Los Angeles.
The scientist praised the study's methods but qualified her endorsement, noting that its small sample limited how broadly the results could be applied.
Asked whether the policy had succeeded, the minister qualified his answer, conceding that it had worked in cities but not in rural areas.
Careful historians qualify their generalizations about an era, acknowledging the many exceptions that a sweeping claim might conceal.

def: habitually complaining

exs.t: The querulous old woman was beginning to wear down even the happier members of the staff with her ceaseless complaining.
The querulous passenger complained about the legroom, the temperature, the meal, and the pilot's announcements before the plane had even left the gate.
Although he had once been cheerful, long illness made the old sailor querulous, and his nurses dreaded his constant grumbling.
The letters reveal a querulous side of the poet, who filled page after page with grievances about his publishers, his neighbors, and his health.

def: found in the ordinary course of events

exs.t: Phil gets so involved thinking about Aristotle's arguments that he totally forgets quotidian concerns, such as exercising and eating regularly.
The painter found beauty in quotidian scenes, such as a woman peeling potatoes or a child tying her shoes, that other artists overlooked.
Although the diary describes a momentous war, most entries record quotidian matters: the price of bread, the weather, a neighbor's cough.
Tourists marvel at the city's grand cathedrals, but the anthropologist studied its quotidian rhythms of commuting, shopping, and cooking.

def: extremely hungry; devouring or craving food in great quantities

exs.t: John didn't each much at all during the week he had the flu, so now that he is regaining his health, it's not surprising that he has a ravenous appetite.
After hiking for nine hours without food, the climbers were ravenous and devoured an entire pot of stew within minutes.
Bears emerge from hibernation ravenous, having eaten nothing for months, and they spend the spring foraging almost constantly.
The ravenous caterpillars stripped the orchard bare in a single week, consuming leaves far faster than the trees could replace them.

def: criticize severely or angrily; censure

exs.t: The police chief rebuked the two officers whose irresponsible decisions almost led to the deaths of seven innocent by-standers.
The judge rebuked the prosecutor for withholding evidence, warning that any further misconduct would lead to sanctions.
Rather than praising the report, the director sharply rebuked its authors for their careless errors and unsupported conclusions.
The coach chose not to rebuke the young player in front of the team, preferring to discuss his mistakes privately after practice.

def: make (one thing) compatible with (another)

exs.t: Peggy was unable to reconcile her kind friend Jane with the cruel and merciless character Jane played on television.
Physicists have long struggled to reconcile quantum mechanics with general relativity, since the two theories make incompatible predictions at extreme scales.
It is difficult to reconcile the company's pledge to cut emissions with its plan to open three new coal mines next year.
The committee worked late to reconcile the two budgets, trimming some programs and delaying others until the figures finally agreed.

def: difficult to penetrate; incomprehensible to one of ordinary understanding or knowledge

exs.t: I found Ulysses recondite and never finished the book, waiting instead to read it with someone else so we could penetrate its meaning together.
The lecture on medieval numerology was so recondite that even the specialists in the audience struggled to follow its references.
Although the poet's allusions are recondite, drawing on forgotten myths and little-known treatises, the emotions of her verse are immediately accessible.
The editors rejected the article as too recondite for a general readership, advising the author to explain her technical terms.

def: stubbornly resistant to authority or control

exs.t: Used to studious high school students, Martha was unprepared for the refractory Kindergarteners who neither sat still nor listened to a single word she said.
The refractory mule refused to cross the bridge, planting its hooves no matter how the farmer coaxed or pulled.
Teachers who had tamed the rowdiest classes admitted defeat with the refractory students of the fourth period, who ignored every rule and defied every punishment.
The colonial governor found the northern provinces refractory, their leaders openly resisting his decrees and refusing to pay taxes.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: prove to be false or incorrect

exs.t: No one could refute his theories or propositions, and that is why he was esteemed by all his colleagues in the philosophy department.
The new fossil evidence appeared to refute the long-held theory that the species had evolved only on the island.
The defense attorney refuted the witness's testimony by producing receipts proving that her client had been in another city on the night of the crime.
Although the claim was widely repeated, a careful study refuted it, showing that the supposed link between the two diseases was a statistical artifact.

def: to express criticism towards

exs.t: At first, Sarah was going to yell at the boy, but she didn't want to reproach him for telling the truth about the situation.
The teacher gently reproached the student for plagiarizing, reminding him that honesty mattered more than a perfect grade.
Although he had broken no law, the senator was reproached by his colleagues for accepting lavish gifts from lobbyists.
The reviewer was careful not to reproach the young author too harshly, framing his criticisms as suggestions for her next book.

def: reject as untrue or unfounded

exs.t: Many in the public believed the rumors of a UFO crash outside town, so the chief of police did everything he could to repudiate the rumors.
The scientist publicly repudiated the rumor that her data had been fabricated, releasing all of her original laboratory notebooks for inspection.
The company issued a statement repudiating the allegations of child labor in its factories, though independent investigators continued to demand evidence.
Later scholars repudiated the once popular theory that the ancient city had been destroyed by a flood, pointing to evidence of a prolonged drought instead.

def: cancel officially

exs.t: The man's driver's license was rescinded after his tenth car accident, which meant he would never be allowed to legally drive again.
After widespread protests, the university rescinded its decision to raise tuition, restoring the previous fees for the coming year.
The city council voted to rescind the ordinance banning street musicians, conceding that the law had been both unpopular and unenforceable.
The publisher threatened to rescind the author's contract if she failed to deliver the manuscript by the agreed deadline.

def: restless

exs.t: The crowd grew restive as the comedian's opening jokes fell flat.
As the delayed train sat motionless for a third hour, the passengers grew restive, pacing the aisles and demanding answers from the conductor.
The horse became restive in its stall before the storm, stamping and tossing its head at every distant roll of thunder.
Years of rising prices made the urban workers increasingly restive, and the government feared that strikes would soon spread across the country.

def: rising again as to new life and vigor

exs.t: The team sank to fourth place in June, but is now resurgent and about to win the division.
After decades in which the dialect seemed destined for extinction, it is now resurgent, taught in village schools and heard again on regional radio.
Economists who had written off the textile district were surprised by its resurgent factories, which, after years of closure, now hum with new orders.
Far from fading after the founder's death, the movement proved resurgent: membership doubled within two years as a younger generation revived its ideals.
