def: reluctant to draw attention to yourself; temperamentally disinclined to talk

exs.t: When asked about her father, Helen lost her outward enthusiasm and became rather reticent.
Although the novelist's books are intensely confessional, she herself is famously reticent in interviews, deflecting personal questions with a polite shrug.
Colleagues were startled when the ordinarily reticent engineer spoke at length during the review; in five years he had hardly offered an opinion in a meeting.
Diplomats found the envoy reticent about his government's intentions, since he answered every probing question with brief, noncommittal remarks.

def: feeling or showing profound respect or veneration

exs.t: The professor could speak objectively about the other composers, but he always lectured about Brahms with a particularly reverent air, unable to offer a single criticism of his compositions.
Visitors fell into a reverent hush as they entered the ancient library, lowering their voices as if the manuscripts themselves deserved deference.
Rather than mocking the old masters as some modernists did, the young painter adopted a reverent attitude toward them, copying their canvases with devout care.
Critics complained that the biography was too reverent to be useful: the author treated her subject as a saint and ignored every documented flaw.

def: being in the earliest stages of development; being or involving basic facts or principles

exs.t: I would love to be able to present a fully polished proposal to the board, but right now, our plans for the product are still in the most rudimentary stages.
The prototype's navigation system is still rudimentary, able to detect large obstacles but not yet to plan a route around them.
Although she had only a rudimentary grasp of Portuguese, enough to order a meal and ask directions, she was unprepared for the technical vocabulary of the conference.
Early mammals possessed only rudimentary versions of the intricate inner ear that later species would develop over millions of years.

def: characteristic of rural life; awkwardly simple and provincial

exs.t: The vacation cabin had no electricity and no indoor plumbing, but despite these inconveniences, Nigel adored its rustic charm.
The architect rejected polished marble in favor of rough timber beams and stone floors, giving the lodge a deliberately rustic character suited to its mountain setting.
City visitors often found the villagers' customs charmingly rustic, though the villagers themselves resented being treated as quaint relics of farm life.
The composer drew on shepherds' dances and harvest festivals, and the resulting suite has a rustic simplicity that contrasts sharply with his ornate urban operas.

label: v.
def: give authority or permission to

exs.t: The authorities have sanctioned the use of the wilderness reserve for public use; many expect to see. hikers an campers enjoying the park in the coming months.
Because the university had not formally sanctioned the experiment, the researchers were forced to suspend it until the ethics board granted its approval.
The league refused to sanction the exhibition match, so the players who took part could not count it toward their official records.
Although local custom seemed to sanction the hiring of relatives, the new charter explicitly prohibited the practice, citing concerns about fairness.

label: n.
def: a legal penalty for a forbidden action

exs.t: International sanctions have been placed on certain shipping lanes that were thought to be involved in human trafficking.
Players who leave the field without the referee's permission face stiff sanctions, including fines and suspension from future matches.
The regulatory agency warned that firms concealing their emissions data would incur sanctions severe enough to threaten their operating licenses.
Because the professional code carried no real sanction for violations, many practitioners ignored its provisions with impunity, knowing that nothing would happen to them.

label: adj.1
def: characterized by extreme care and great effort

exs.t: Because of his scrupulous nature, Mary put him in charge of numbering and cataloging the entire collection of rare stamps.
The restorers were scrupulous in their work, cleaning each square inch of the fresco with a cotton swab and documenting every fleck of pigment they removed.
Her scrupulous attention to footnotes, comparing every citation against the original source, made her the journal's most valued copy editor.
Unlike his predecessor, whose data tables were riddled with transcription errors, the new analyst was scrupulous, confirming each figure twice before submitting a report.

label: adj.2
def: having a sense of right and wrong; principled

exs.t: Everyone trusted what he said and followed his example because he was scrupulous and honest.
A scrupulous official, she declined even the modest gifts that vendors customarily offered, lest anyone suspect that her decisions could be bought.
The dealer was scrupulous about disclosing every flaw in the paintings he sold, even when silence would have earned him a far higher price.
Though many of his rivals padded their expense claims, the scrupulous mayor reimbursed the treasury for a single personal phone call made on an official line.

def: inducing mental lethargy; sleep inducing

exs.t: Although the professor is brilliant, his bland monotone gives his lectures a soporific effect.
The committee chair's soporific recitation of budget figures left half the audience nodding off before the first question was even asked.
Some antihistamines have a soporific side effect, so patients are warned not to drive or operate heavy machinery after taking them.
Far from the gripping thriller its publisher promised, the novel proved soporific: its long descriptive passages lulled even devoted readers into drowsiness.

label: adj.1
def: based on pretense; deceptively pleasing

exs.t: Almost every image on TV is specious and not to be trusted.
The development's glossy brochure offered a specious vision of lakeside tranquility; the lake, buyers later discovered, was a drainage pond beside a highway.
Behind the specious charm of the courtier lay cold calculation, for his gracious manners were merely a mask for ruthless ambition.
The renovated storefronts gave the district a specious air of prosperity, since most of the attractive shops behind the fresh paint stood empty.

label: adj.2
def: plausible but false

exs.t: He made a career out of specious arguments and fictional lab results, but lost his job and reputation when his lies were exposed by an article in The New York Times.
The lawyer's reasoning seemed persuasive at first, but it proved specious once the jury realized that it rested on a misreading of the contract.
Students are taught to spot specious causal claims, such as the argument that ice cream sales cause drownings merely because both rise in summer.
Although the pamphlet's statistics sounded authoritative, they supported only a specious conclusion, since the sample had been chosen to favor the author's thesis.

def: recurring in scattered and irregular or unpredictable instances

exs.t: The signals were at first sporadic, but now we detect a clear, consistent pattern of electromagnetic radiation emanating from deep space.
Fighting along the border has been sporadic rather than continuous, with brief skirmishes erupting at unpredictable intervals over the past year.
Because her attendance at rehearsals was sporadic (she would appear one week and vanish for the next three), the director eventually gave her part to an understudy.
The survey team found only sporadic evidence of settlement in the valley: a hearth here, a few potsherds there, scattered across several centuries.

def: plausible but false

exs.t: When listening to a politician speak, it is hard to distinguish the spurious claims from the authentic ones.
The historian dismissed the letter as spurious, noting that its paper and ink could not have been manufactured until decades after the supposed author's death.
Researchers warned that the apparent link between the two variables might be spurious, an artifact of a flawed sampling method rather than a genuine relationship.
Although the company promoted its supplement with impressive testimonials, regulators found the health claims spurious and ordered them removed from the label.

def: firm and dependable especially in loyalty

exs.t: No longer a staunch supporter of the movement, Todd now will openly question whether its goals are worthwhile.
Even when the rest of the board turned against the director, she remained a staunch ally, defending his decisions at every meeting.
For forty years the widow was the orchestra's most staunch patron, funding its seasons even when wealthier donors abandoned it during hard times.
The critic had been the playwright's staunchest defender through years of failed productions, which made his sudden condemnation of her latest work all the more startling.

def: demanding strict attention to rules and procedures

exs.t: Most of the students disliked the teacher because of his stringent homework policy, but many students would later thank him for demanding so much from them.
Because the laboratory handles dangerous pathogens, it enforces stringent safety protocols: every visitor must shower, change clothing, and sign a detailed log.
The journal's review standards are notoriously stringent, and manuscripts with even minor methodological lapses are returned to their authors for revision.
Critics argued that the building code was too lax, while developers complained that its requirements were already so stringent that affordable construction had become impossible.

label: v.1
def: contain or include

exs.t: The rogue wave quickly subsumed the pier and boardwalk, destroying everything in its path.
When the two agencies merged, the smaller one was subsumed into the larger, and its staff, budget, and mission were folded into the new department.
The new curriculum subsumes the old courses on rhetoric and composition within a single writing sequence rather than eliminating them.
Over several centuries the independent duchy was gradually subsumed by its powerful neighbor until it existed only as a province within the kingdom.

label: v.2
def: consider (an instance of something) as part of a general rule or principle

exs.t: Don Quixote of La Mancha subsumes all other modern novels, demonstrating modern literary devices. and predating even the idea of a postmodern, metanarrative.
The philosopher argued that aesthetic judgments cannot be subsumed under general rules, since each work of art demands to be evaluated on its own terms.
Rather than treating the new disease as a unique phenomenon, the researchers subsumed it under a known class of autoimmune disorders that share the same mechanism.
A good legal theory should subsume particular rulings under broad principles, so that each verdict appears as an instance of a coherent doctrine.

def: in opposition to a civil authority or government

exs.t: The ruling political party has begun a campaign to shut down subversive websites that it deems as a threat to "national safety."
The regime banned the poet's collections as subversive, fearing that their veiled allegories encouraged readers to question the authority of the state.
Under the military government, even a folk song about freedom could be deemed subversive, and its singers were arrested for threatening public order.
The pamphlets appeared innocuous (recipes and weather notes), yet their coded passages carried subversive instructions for organizing resistance against the occupying authorities.

def: showing a brooding ill humor

exs.t: Herbert took board games too seriously, often appearing sullen after losing.
Denied permission to join the expedition, the young apprentice spent the evening in sullen silence, refusing to eat and glaring at anyone who spoke to him.
The once cheerful workforce grew sullen after the layoffs, going about their tasks with resentful glances and muttered complaints.
Unlike her sunny older sister, the teenager was sullen at family gatherings, answering questions in monosyllables and moping in a corner.

label: adj.1
def: serving no useful purpose

exs.t: How can we hope to stay open if we don't eliminate all superfluous spending, like catered meetings and free acupuncture Tuesday?
The editor struck out the ornate introductory paragraph as superfluous, since it contributed nothing to the argument that followed.
Engineers removed the superfluous buttons from the remote control after usage studies showed that several of them had never once been pressed.
Once the bridge opened, the ferry service was rendered superfluous, and its boats sat idle at the dock with no passengers left to carry.

label: adj.2
def: more than is needed, desired, or required

exs.t: Everything in this closet is superfluous and can be given to charity.
With three generators already able to power the entire hospital, a fourth struck the budget committee as superfluous, and the money went to hiring nurses instead.
The chef believed that a truly ripe tomato needs only a pinch of salt, and that any further seasoning is superfluous.
Having ordered five times the packing material it could use in a year, the warehouse stacked the superfluous cartons in its hallways.

def: take the place or move into the position of

exs.t: For many, a cell phone has supplanted a traditional phone; in fact, most 20-somethings don't even have a traditional phone anymore.
Within a generation, the railroad had supplanted the canal as the region's chief means of transport, and the old waterways fell into disuse.
The ambitious deputy schemed for years to supplant her superior, courting the board members whose votes would decide who led the agency.
Linguists have documented how the colonial language gradually supplanted local tongues in commerce and schooling, until few children could speak their grandparents' dialect.

def: a person who tries to please someone in order to gain a personal advantage

exs.t: The CEO was unaware of the damaging consequences of his choices, largely because he surrounded himself with sycophants who would never dare criticize him.
Rather than offering honest counsel, the minister was a sycophant who praised every royal whim in hopes of securing a lucrative estate.
The director's films declined after she dismissed her frank collaborators and kept only a circle of sycophants who applauded every draft.
Colleagues regarded him as a sycophant: he laughed loudest at the dean's jokes and volunteered for every task that might earn her favor.

def: habitually reserved and uncommunicative

exs.t: While the CEO enthusiastically shares his plans and agenda with all who will listen, the CFO is far more taciturn, rarely revealing his perspective.
The taciturn farmer answered the journalist's lengthy questions with a nod or a single word, leaving her with barely a paragraph of quotations.
Though his letters were expansive and witty, in person the poet was taciturn, sitting through entire dinner parties without offering a remark.
Negotiators found the delegation's leader taciturn and hard to read; unlike his talkative aides, he spoke only when directly addressed.

def: being essentially equal to something

exs.t: In many situations, remaining silent is tantamount to admitting guilt, so speak to prove your innocence.
The judge ruled that the company's refusal to release the records was tantamount to contempt of court, since its effect was the same as open defiance of her order.
In that field, publishing without peer review is tantamount to professional self-sabotage: the work, however sound, will simply be ignored by other scholars.
The ambassador warned that massing troops along the border would be tantamount to a declaration of war, even if no shot were ever fired.

def: the trait of avoiding excesses

exs.t: Welles wasn't known for his temperance--he usually ate enough for two and drank enough for three.
The philosopher praised temperance as the foundation of a good life, arguing that pleasures enjoyed in moderation outlast those pursued to excess.
Despite the lavish banquets that surrounded him, the emperor was known for his temperance, eating simple meals and rarely finishing a cup of wine.
Her financial success owed less to bold speculation than to temperance: she never borrowed beyond her means and resisted every fashionable spending spree.

def: moderated in effect

exs.t: The wide-eyed optimism of her youth was now tempered after she had worked many years in the criminal justice system.
After the accountant warned that costs had been badly underestimated, the committee's once exuberant support gave way to a far more tempered endorsement of the proposal.
Reviewers offered tempered praise for the debut album, admiring its ambition while noting that several tracks felt unfinished.
Years of failed reforms had left the minister with a tempered idealism; she still believed in change but no longer expected it to come quickly.

def: stubbornly unyielding

exs.t: Even the most tenacious advocates for gun ownership must admit some of the dangers that firearms present.
The tenacious reporter filed requests for the documents for six years, refusing to abandon the story even after two editors told her to move on.
Invasive vines are notoriously tenacious, regrowing from tiny root fragments long after gardeners believe they have eradicated them.
Although the defending army was vastly outnumbered, its tenacious resistance held the mountain pass for weeks and upset the invaders' entire campaign.

def: timid by nature or revealing fear and nervousness

exs.t: Since this was her first time debating on stage and before an audience, Di's voice was timorous and quiet for the first 10 minutes.
The timorous deer bolted at the faintest snap of a twig, so the photographer had to wait motionless for hours to capture a single image.
Critics faulted the council's timorous response to the crisis, arguing that fear of offending anyone had kept it from taking decisive action.
Once a timorous student who dreaded speaking in class, she grew into a confident trial lawyer who relished cross-examination.

def: inactivity resulting from lethargy and lack of vigor or energy

exs.t: After work, I was expecting my colleagues to be enthusiastic about the outing, but I found them in a state of complete torpor.
The long summer afternoons induced a pleasant torpor in the villagers, who dozed in the shade instead of tending their fields.
Economists warned that the market had sunk into a torpor, with investment stagnant and few firms willing to expand or hire.
Hibernating bears enter a state of torpor in which their heart rates slow dramatically and they barely move for months.

def: marked by repeated turns and bends; not straightforward

exs.t: Because the logic behind McMahon's side of the debate was so tortuous, his audience came out either completely confused or, worse, feeling they'd been tricked.
The road to the monastery is tortuous, twisting through dozens of hairpin turns as it climbs the side of the gorge.
The bill's tortuous passage through the legislature, with its endless amendments, reversals, and procedural detours, left even its sponsors unsure what it finally contained.
Rather than stating his conclusion plainly, the author led readers through a tortuous chain of qualifications and digressions before revealing his point.

def: readily reacting to suggestions and influences; easily managed (controlled or taught or molded)

exs.t: Compared to middle school students, who have an untamed wildness about them, high school students are somewhat more tractable.
The new foreman found the crew surprisingly tractable, willing to adopt his revised procedures without the complaints he had been warned to expect.
Unlike the stubborn ponies of the northern highlands, this breed is notably tractable, which makes it popular for teaching children to ride.
Once it was broken into smaller components, the problem proved far more tractable than the committee had feared, and a solution emerged within weeks.

def: lasting a very short time

exs.t: The unpredictable and transient nature of deja vu makes it a very difficult phenomenon to study properly.
The drug's side effects are usually transient, fading within a few hours of the first dose and rarely recurring.
Tourists drawn by the festival lend the town a transient prosperity; once they depart in September, the shops close and the streets fall quiet.
The poet dwelt on the transient beauty of cherry blossoms, which fall from the branches only days after they open.

def: an absurd presentation of something; a mockery

exs.t: What I expected to be an intelligent, nuanced historical documentary turned out to be a poorly-produced travesty of the form.
The defendant's lawyers called the trial a travesty of justice, since the judge had excluded their key witnesses and admitted hearsay from the prosecution.
The film adaptation was a travesty of the novel, reducing its subtle meditation on grief to a series of car chases and cheap gags.
Purists regarded the modernized opera production as a travesty, arguing that its garish costumes and rewritten libretto mocked the composer's intentions.

label: adj.1
def: tending to betray

exs.t: Even though Jesse James was an outlaw, his killer, Robert Ford, is remembered more for his treacherous actions than for eliminating a criminal and murder.
The king trusted his chancellor completely, never suspecting that this treacherous adviser was secretly passing state secrets to a foreign court.
Once a loyal partner, he proved treacherous in the end, abandoning the firm and taking its largest clients with him to a rival.
In the epic, the hero's downfall comes not from his enemies but from a treacherous companion who opens the city gates at night to the invading army.

label: adj.2
def: dangerously unstable and unpredictable

exs.t: The bridge built from twine and vine is treacherous to walk across, and so I think I will stay put right here.
After the thaw, the ice on the lake was treacherous: solid in some places, it was thin enough elsewhere to give way beneath a single skater.
Sailors dreaded the treacherous strait, whose shifting sandbars, hidden rocks, and sudden squalls had wrecked countless vessels over the centuries.
The mountain path, though pleasant in summer, grows treacherous after rain, when loose scree can send a careless hiker sliding toward the cliff edge.

def: repeated too often; overfamiliar through overuse

exs.t: Many style guides recommend not using idioms in writing because these trite expressions are uninteresting and show a lack of imagination on the part of the writer.
The judges faulted the essay's trite conclusion, which ended with the stale reminder that every cloud has a silver lining.
Although the melody is pleasant, its chord progression is so trite that listeners feel they have heard the song a hundred times before.
Critics dismissed the novel's romance as trite, a recycling of the same star-crossed formula that countless earlier books had exhausted.

def: reduce the length of something

exs.t: The soccer game was truncated when the monsoon rain began to fall.
Because the broadcast ran over its allotted time, the network truncated the final interview, cutting it off after only two questions.
The editor asked the author to truncate the sprawling third chapter, trimming it to half its length so that the narrative would move faster.
His career as a concert pianist was truncated by an injury to his wrist, which forced him to retire in his early thirties.

def: to weaken (usually paired with an abstract term)

exs.t: The student undermined the teacher's authority by questioning the teacher's judgment on numerous occasions.
Repeated revelations of fabricated data have undermined public confidence in the institute, and even its sound studies are now greeted with suspicion.
The manager's habit of reversing her team's decisions without explanation undermined their morale, and within months several key members had resigned.
Critics argued that the treaty's vague enforcement provisions would undermine its purpose, allowing signatories to ignore their obligations without penalty.

def: give extra weight to (a communication)

exs.t: While the hiking instructor agreed that carrying a first aid kit could be a good idea under certain circumstances, he underscored the importance of carrying enough water.
The minister's surprise visit to the flooded district underscored the government's claim that recovery was its highest priority.
In her closing remarks, the professor underscored the central point of the lecture: correlation, however striking, is not proof of causation.
The rising number of hospital admissions underscores the need for better air quality monitoring, lending weight to warnings that had previously been dismissed.

def: admitting of no doubt or misunderstanding; having only one meaning or interpretation and leading to only one conclusion

exs.t: The President's first statement on the subject was vague and open to competing interpretations, so when he spoke to Congress about the same subject later, he was careful to make his position completely unequivocal.
Unlike the evasive statements of her predecessors, the chancellor's answer was unequivocal: the program would be ended, and no exceptions would be granted.
The trial results were unequivocal; every reviewer, regardless of prior skepticism, reached the same conclusion about the vaccine's effectiveness.
The union demanded an unequivocal commitment to job security, having learned that vaguely worded promises could be reinterpreted whenever management found it convenient.

def: without scruples or principles

exs.t: In the courtroom, the lawyer was unscrupulous, using every manner of deceit and manipulation to secure a victory for himself.
Unscrupulous landlords exploited the housing shortage by charging illegal fees and ignoring repairs, confident that desperate tenants would not complain.
The collector was defrauded by an unscrupulous dealer who sold him forged prints accompanied by fabricated certificates of authenticity.
Though her methods were effective, her unscrupulous willingness to deceive rivals and break promises eventually left her without a single ally.

def: to reproach; to scold

exs.t: Bob took a risk walking into the "Students Barbershop"--in the end he had to upbraid the apparently drunk barber for giving him an uneven bowl cut.
The conductor upbraided the brass section in front of the entire orchestra for arriving late and unprepared for the dress rehearsal.
Rather than praising the junior analyst for spotting the error, the director upbraided her for failing to notice it sooner.
The editorial upbraided city officials for their negligence, listing in stinging detail the years of warnings they had ignored about the aging dam.

def: be undecided about something; waver between conflicting positions or courses of action

exs.t: Some students vacillate between schools when deciding which to attend, while others focus only on one school.
The committee vacillated for months between renovating the old theater and building a new one, and by the time it decided, construction costs had doubled.
Historians attribute the defeat partly to the general's tendency to vacillate: he ordered an advance, rescinded it, and then ordered it again, squandering the element of surprise.
Her opinion of the novel vacillated as she read it, swinging from admiration in one chapter to exasperation in the next.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: marked by extreme intensity of emotions or convictions

exs.t: While the other employees responded to the bad news in a measured way, Andrew responded in a vehement manner, tipping over his desk and shouting at the top of his lungs.
The proposal to close the rural clinic drew vehement opposition from residents, who packed the hearing and shouted down the officials who defended it.
Though he is mild in conversation, the critic is vehement in print, denouncing films he dislikes with a ferocity that startles his readers.
Her vehement denial of the rumor, delivered with a fist pounding the lectern, convinced some listeners and made others suspect she protested too much.

def: the condition of being susceptible to bribes or corruption

exs.t: Even some of the most sacrosanct sporting events are not immune to venality, as many of the officials have received substantial bribes to make biased calls.
If our legal system becomes plagued with venality, then the very notion of justice is imperiled.
Reformers blamed the port's decline on the venality of its customs officials, who routinely waved through smuggled cargo in exchange for cash.
The novel exposes the venality of a city council whose members, one by one, accept payments from a developer in return for favorable zoning votes.
Judges were given generous salaries and lifetime appointments precisely to guard against venality, since poorly paid magistrates had often sold their verdicts.

def: to respect deeply

exs.t: The professor, despite his soporific lectures, was venerated amongst his colleagues, publishing more papers yearly than all of his peers combined.
In many cultures, elders are venerated as keepers of wisdom, and their counsel is sought before any important communal decision.
Though ignored during her lifetime, the painter is now venerated by younger artists, who make pilgrimages to her studio and study her every brushstroke.
The monks venerate the ancient relic, bowing before it each morning and permitting no one to touch it without elaborate rites of purification.

def: truthful

exs.t: While we elect our leaders in the hope that every word they speak will be veracious, history has shown that such a hope is naive.
Historians consider the diarist a veracious witness, since the details she recorded have been confirmed repeatedly by independent archives.
A veracious account of the expedition would have admitted its failures, but the leader's memoir exaggerated every triumph and omitted every blunder.
The court valued the witness precisely because he was veracious to a fault, admitting even details that damaged his own reputation.

def: spread negative information about

exs.t: Todd was noble after the divorce, choosing to say only complimentary things about Barbara, but Barbara did not hesitate to vilify Todd.
The reformer was vilified in the tabloid press, which portrayed her as a reckless schemer bent on destroying the city's institutions.
Rather than engaging with his critics' arguments, the author chose to vilify them, spreading rumors about their motives and their private lives.
Although later historians have rehabilitated his reputation, the engineer was widely vilified in his own time as the man responsible for the bridge's collapse.

def: to clear of accusation, blame, suspicion, or doubt with supporting arguments or proof

exs.t: Even seven Tour de France wins cannot vindicate Lance Armstrong in the eyes of the public--that the athlete used performance enhancing drugs invalidates all those wins.
The scientist's once ridiculed hypothesis was vindicated when new telescopes detected precisely the faint signal she had predicted decades earlier.
The audit vindicated the treasurer, showing that the missing funds had been misplaced through a clerical error rather than stolen.
Accused of plagiarism, the student produced early drafts and notes that vindicated her, proving that the ideas had been her own from the start.

def: conspicuously and offensively loud; given to vehement outcry

exs.t: In giving Marcia a particular vociferous response, Paul caused people at every other table in the restaurant to turn around an look at them angrily.
The plan to pave over the park drew vociferous protests, with hundreds of residents chanting outside city hall late into the night.
A small but vociferous minority of the audience booed and jeered throughout the premiere, drowning out the singers during the final act.
The professor welcomed disagreement but not the vociferous interruptions of one student, who shouted objections before others could finish speaking.

def: the quality of talking or writing easily and continuously

exs.t: The professor's volubility knows no bounds; he could talk through a hurricane and elaborate a point from one St. Patrick's Day to the next.
The host's volubility was an asset on the radio, where she could fill an hour of airtime without a pause, but it exhausted guests who hoped to speak.
Readers of her letters are struck by their volubility: she could write twenty pages about a single afternoon and still apologize for leaving things out.
In contrast to his quiet brother, Paulo was the family's spokesman, and his volubility allowed him to chat with strangers for hours without running out of words.

def: lacking

exs.t: She did not think her vocabulary was wanting, yet there were so many words that inevitably she found a few she didn't know.
The candidate's credentials were impressive, but in the interview her knowledge of the field was found wanting, and the committee chose someone else.
Though the translation is fluent, it is wanting in precision; several technical terms are rendered so loosely that the original meaning is lost.
Critics praised the building's facade but judged its interior wanting, with cramped rooms and too little natural light for its intended use as a gallery.

def: charming in a childlike or naive way

exs.t: She was winsome by nature, and many people were drawn to this free and playful spirit.
The toddler's winsome grin disarmed even the grumpiest passengers, who found themselves waving back at her across the aisle.
The film's heroine is winsome rather than glamorous; audiences who would never envy her find themselves won over by her artless curiosity and her delight in small things.
Though the illustrations are winsome (all round faces and wide, innocent eyes), the story they accompany is surprisingly dark.

def: open and honest

exs.t: The mayor, despite his avuncular face plastered about the city, was hardly aboveboard -- some concluded that it was his ingratiating smile that allowed him to engage in corrupt behavior and get away with it.
To reassure skeptical investors, the charity made its books public, insisting that every transaction had been aboveboard and fully documented.
Rather than negotiating in secret, the two firms kept the merger talks aboveboard, briefing regulators and employees at every stage.
The auditor suspected the deal was not aboveboard, since it had been arranged through an anonymous intermediary and recorded nowhere in the minutes.

def: extremely bad

exs.t: Coach Ramsey took his newest player off the field after watching a few painful minutes of her abysmal performance.
The orchestra's first rehearsal was abysmal: half the players were out of tune, and the brass entered a full bar early.
Despite the restaurant's glowing reputation, the service that evening was abysmal, with diners waiting an hour for food that arrived cold.
Living conditions in the mining camps were abysmal, with workers crowded into unheated shacks and forced to drink contaminated water.

def: the highest point of achievement

exs.t: The new Cessna airplanes will be the acme of comfort, offering reclining seats and ample legroom.
Many critics regard the late string quartets as the acme of the composer's art, the summit toward which all his earlier experiments were leading.
At the acme of her career, the architect was designing museums on three continents; a decade later, she could scarcely find a commission.
For ancient rhetoricians, the funeral oration represented the acme of eloquence, a form that only the most accomplished speakers dared attempt.

label: v.
def: speak, plead, or argue in favor of

exs.t: While the senator privately approved of gay marriage, he was unwilling to advocate for the cause in a public venue.
The report advocates a gradual approach to reform, arguing that sudden changes would disrupt the very communities they are meant to help.
For decades the physician advocated for stricter limits on tobacco advertising, testifying before legislatures and publishing study after study on its harms.
Though she privately doubted the plan, the consultant was hired to advocate it publicly, and she argued its merits with conviction at every meeting.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

label: n.
def: a person who pleads for a cause or propounds an idea

exs.t: Martin Luther King Jr. was a tireless advocate for the rights of African-Americans in the United States.
A passionate advocate of public libraries, the author donated her royalties to rural branches and spoke tirelessly about their importance.
The proposal had few advocates on the committee; most members considered it too costly, and only one spoke in its favor.
Early advocates of the germ theory endured ridicule from established physicians before experiments finally confirmed that microorganisms cause disease.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: likeable; easy to talk to

exs.t: For all his surface affability, Marco was remarkably glum when he wasn't around other people.
The new ambassador was affable and approachable, chatting easily with junior staff and remembering the names of their children.
Although the professor's writing is dense and forbidding, in office hours he is affable, putting nervous students at ease with a joke and a cup of tea.
Guests who expected the famously stern critic to be cold were surprised to find him affable, laughing readily and inviting questions after his talk.

def: wealthy

exs.t: The center of the city had sadly become a pit of penury, while, only five miles away, multi-million dollar homes spoke of affluence.
The suburb grew affluent after the technology firms arrived, and modest bungalows were soon replaced by sprawling houses with private pools.
Charities in affluent neighborhoods often raise more money in a single evening than those in poorer districts collect in a year.
The novelist, born into an affluent family of bankers, never had to worry about money and could spend years on a single manuscript.

def: the quality of unselfish concern for the welfare of others

exs.t: Albert Schweitzer spent most of his life doing missionary work as a doctor in Africa, seeking no reward, apparently motivated only by altruism.
Biologists have long puzzled over altruism in animals, such as the worker bee that dies defending a hive in which only the queen will reproduce.
Some economists doubt that pure altruism exists, arguing that even anonymous donations provide the giver with a hidden reward of self-esteem.
The nurse's altruism was evident to everyone on the ward: she worked unpaid overtime, gave away her lunches, and never asked for recognition.

def: friendly

exs.t: Amy's name was very apt: she was so amiable that she was twice voted class president.
The two rival chefs maintained an amiable relationship, trading recipes and sharing a meal once a month despite competing for the same customers.
Though the negotiations were tense, the delegates' conversations over dinner were amiable, full of laughter and anecdotes about their families.
The guide's amiable manner quickly put the anxious tourists at ease, and by the end of the tour they were treating him like an old friend.

def: more than is adequate

exs.t: The boat was amply supplied for its year at sea--no man would go hungry or thirst.
The theory's predictions have been amply confirmed by experiment, so few physicists now doubt its basic soundness.
The tenants were amply compensated for the disruption, receiving three months of free rent and a generous allowance for moving costs.
The expedition was amply provisioned, carrying enough food and fuel to last twice as long as the planned journey.

def: in a frenzied or uncontrolled state

exs.t: Wherever the bowl haircut teen-idol went, his legions of screaming fans ran through the streets amuck, hoping for a glance at his boyish face.
When the fire alarm sounded, the crowd ran amuck, trampling the exhibits and shoving toward the exits in a disorderly panic.
The satirist imagines a bureaucracy run amuck, generating forms for their own sake until the agency processes nothing but its own paperwork.
Once the escaped goats ran amuck through the market, stalls toppled, vendors shouted, and it took hours to restore any semblance of order.

def: similar in some respects but otherwise different

exs.t: In many ways, the Internet's transformative effect on society has been analogous to that of the printing press.
The researcher argued that the spread of rumors is analogous to the spread of infection, since both pass from person to person and grow rapidly in dense populations.
Although the wings of bats and insects are analogous structures, serving the same function of flight, they evolved independently from entirely different tissues.
The position of a museum curator is in some ways analogous to that of an editor: each selects, arranges, and frames material created by others.

def: intense hostility

exs.t: The governor's animosity toward his rival was only inflamed when the latter spread false lies regarding the governor's first term.
The long-standing animosity between the two families erupted at the wedding, where a trivial slight led to shouting and overturned tables.
Despite months of animosity during the campaign, the two rivals shook hands warmly after the result and pledged to work together.
The historian traces the animosity between the neighboring city-states to a disputed boundary river, over which they fought three wars.

def: precede in time

exs.t: Harry was so unknowledgeable that he was unaware the Egyptian pharaohs antedated the American Revolution.
The newly discovered manuscript antedates all previously known copies of the poem by at least a century, making it invaluable to scholars.
Cave paintings in the region antedate the earliest known writing by tens of thousands of years, suggesting that visual art arose long before the alphabet.
The quarrel between the brothers antedated their father's death; they had fought over the farm for years before the will was ever read.

def: old-fashioned; belonging to an earlier period in time

exs.t: Aunt Betty had antiquated notions about marriage, believing that a man should court a woman for at least a year before receiving a kiss.
The hospital's antiquated computer system, installed decades ago and no longer supported by its manufacturer, frequently crashed during busy shifts.
Critics called the dress code antiquated, noting that its rules about hats and gloves reflected the manners of a bygone era.
Although the statute remained on the books, its antiquated penalties (among them the public stocks) had not been enforced in over a century.

def: the highest point

exs.t: The Ivy League is considered the apex of the secondary education system.
The empire reached its apex under the third dynasty, when its territory stretched from the mountains to the sea, and declined steadily thereafter.
Wolves sit at the apex of the food chain in that ecosystem, preying on elk and deer while having no natural predators of their own.
Winning the international competition marked the apex of the young violinist's career, a height she never again approached.

def: a short instructive saying about a general truth

exs.t: Nietzsche was known for using aphorisms, sometimes encapsulating a complex philosophical thought in a mere sentence.
The essayist condensed her philosophy into a single aphorism, 'A garden reveals the gardener,' which her students still quote decades later.
Rather than building a systematic argument, the moralist wrote in aphorisms, each compressing a lifetime of observation into one memorable line.
The old saying that haste makes waste was an aphorism her grandfather repeated whenever an apprentice rushed a job in his workshop.

def: something that is a concise and instructive of a general truth or principle

exs.t: The philosopher's aphoristic style, in which entire arguments are compressed into a few pointed sentences, makes his books easy to quote but difficult to interpret.
Rather than explaining her decisions at length, the coach offered aphoristic advice such as 'Practice the thing you avoid,' which her players repeated for years.
The novel's dialogue is oddly aphoristic; every character speaks in polished maxims, as if reciting lines from a book of proverbs.
Critics praised the poet's aphoristic closing lines, each of which distills the preceding stanza into a crisp, memorable observation about human nature.

def: large enough to be noticed (usually refers to an amount)

exs.t: There is an appreciable difference between those who say they can get the job done and those who actually get the job done.
The new drug produced no appreciable improvement in patients' symptoms; any differences from the placebo group were too small to measure reliably.
Moving production abroad yielded appreciable savings, enough to lower the product's retail price by nearly a third.
Although the insulation was expensive, it made an appreciable difference to the building's energy use, which fell noticeably within the first winter.

def: fearful expectation

exs.t: Test day can be one of pure apprehension, as many students worry about their test scores.
The villagers watched the rising river with growing apprehension, sandbagging their doorways as forecasters predicted another night of heavy rain.
Despite her apprehension before the surgery, the patient found the procedure far less painful than she had feared.
Investors greeted the new regulations with apprehension, worried that the added costs would erode profits in an already fragile market.

def: so old as to appear to belong to a different period

exs.t: Hoping to sound intelligent, Mary spoke in archaic English that was right out of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice--needless to say, she didn't have many friends.
The legal code is full of archaic terms that even lawyers must look up, relics of statutes drafted centuries ago.
Visitors to the remote island are struck by its archaic customs, such as settling disputes through ritual song contests, practices long vanished from the mainland.
Critics found the translation's diction archaic, since its constant 'thee' and 'thou' made a lively modern play sound like a sermon from a distant age.

def: the state that exists when one person or group has power over another

exs.t: The ascendancy of the Carlsbad water polo team is clear--they have a decade of championships behind them.
By the end of the century the merchant guilds had gained ascendancy over the old aristocracy, controlling both the city council and its treasury.
During the decade of the general's ascendancy, no policy could be adopted without his approval, and rival officers were sidelined or exiled.
The spread of streaming services has ended the long ascendancy of broadcast networks, which once dictated what nearly every household watched each evening.

def: attribute or credit to

exs.t: History ascribes The Odyssey and The Iliad to Homer, but scholars now debate whether he was a historical figure or a fictitious name.
Doctors once ascribed the fever to foul air rising from swamps, not realizing that mosquitoes breeding in the water carried the disease.
The painting was long ascribed to a master of the Florentine school, but recent analysis suggests it came from the workshop of a minor follower.
She ascribed her success not to talent but to discipline, crediting the years she spent practicing scales every morning before dawn.

def: attack in speech or writing

exs.t: In the weekly paper, the editor assailed the governor for wasting hundreds of thousands of dollars in public projects that quickly failed.
Critics assailed the new museum in column after column, denouncing its design as a cold and arrogant intrusion on the historic square.
In his pamphlet, the economist assailed the central bank's policies, accusing its governors of recklessness and demanding their resignation.
The theory, once widely accepted, was assailed in a series of scathing reviews that exposed its reliance on flawed data.

def: make something intense less severe

exs.t: Her fear that the new college would be filled with unknown faces was assuaged when she recognized her childhood friend standing in line.
The airline tried to assuage the anger of stranded passengers by offering free hotel rooms and vouchers for future flights.
Nothing the doctor said could assuage the family's grief, though her patient explanations helped them understand what had happened.
To assuage fears about the new vaccine, health officials published the full trial data and invited independent scientists to review it.

def: enlarge or increase; improve

exs.t: Ideally, the restaurant's augmented menu will expand its clientele and increase its profits.
The museum augmented its modest collection of prints with a bequest of several hundred works, making it one of the largest in the region.
Many teachers augment their salaries by tutoring on weekends, since their regular pay barely covers living costs in the city.
Rather than replacing the aging reservoir, engineers chose to augment its capacity by raising the dam wall several meters.

def: in an autonomous or self-governing manner

exs.t: Many of the factory workers are worried about being replaced by machines and computers that will work completely autonomously.
The rover was designed to operate autonomously, choosing its own path across the terrain, since signals from Earth take too long to allow real-time control.
After the reforms, each province managed its affairs autonomously, setting its own taxes and school curricula without seeking approval from the capital.
Senior researchers in the lab work autonomously, pursuing their own projects with little supervision, while junior members follow a prescribed program.

def: greed (one of the seven deadly sins)

exs.t: The Spanish conquistadors were known for their avarice, plundering Incan land and stealing Incan gold.
The merchant's avarice was legendary: he hoarded gold he would never spend and refused his servants even a crust of bread.
Moralists of the period blamed the financial collapse on avarice, arguing that bankers' insatiable appetite for profit had blinded them to obvious risks.
In the fable, the king's avarice undoes him: forever craving more treasure, he gambles away the kingdom he already had.

label: v.1
def: turn away

exs.t: Afraid to see the aftermath of the car crash, I averted my eyes as we drove by.
Embarrassed by the lavish praise, the young author averted her gaze and stared at the floor until the applause died down.
Squeamish at the sight of the needle, the patient averted his eyes and fixed them on a poster across the room.
Passersby averted their faces from the man pleading for spare change, pretending not to see him as they hurried along the crowded street.

label: v.2
def: ward off or prevent

exs.t: The struggling video game company put all of its finances into one final, desperate project to avert bankruptcy.
Quick action by the air traffic controller averted a collision between the two aircraft, which had been assigned the same altitude by mistake.
Last-minute negotiations averted a strike that would have shut down the city's transit system during the holiday season.
Economists argue that the central bank's timely intervention averted a far deeper recession, although critics say it merely postponed the crisis.

def: marked by active interest and enthusiasm

exs.t: Martin is an avid birdwatcher, often taking long hikes into remote mountains to see some rare eagle.
An avid collector of old maps, the retired judge spent his weekends combing through auctions and dusty bookshops for rare specimens.
The book club's most avid reader finished three novels a week and was always pressing new titles on the other members.
Although she had been an avid gardener for decades, arthritis eventually forced her to give up the hobby she had pursued with such zeal.

def: to pester

exs.t: Badgered by his parents to find a job, the 30-year-old loafer instead joined a gang of itinerant musicians.
The journalist badgered the minister's office with daily phone calls until an aide finally agreed to schedule an interview.
The children in the back seat badgered their parents for hours about stopping for ice cream, repeating the request at every exit.
Rather than badger reluctant donors with a stream of letters, the charity sent a single well-crafted appeal and respected their decision.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: refuse to comply

exs.t: The students were willing to clean up the broken glass, but when the teacher asked them to mop the entire floor, they balked, citing reasons why they needed to leave.
The board initially approved the expansion but balked when it learned that the project would require borrowing nearly twice the original estimate.
Many patients balk at the cost of the new treatment, choosing older therapies that are less effective but far cheaper.
The horse had cleared every earlier fence with ease, so the crowd gasped when it balked at the final jump and its rider had to circle back for another attempt.

def: expel from a community, residence, or location; drive away

exs.t: The most difficult part of the fast was banishing thoughts of food.
After the failed coup, the plotters were banished from the kingdom and forbidden, on pain of death, ever to return.
The new principal banished mobile phones from the classrooms, requiring students to leave them in lockers until the end of the day.
A brisk walk usually banished the composer's gloom, driving away the melancholy that settled on him after long hours at the piano.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: blissfully happy

exs.t: Often we imagine all monks to wear the beatific smile of the Buddha, but, like any of us, a monk can have a bad day and not look very happy.
Marred by the ravages of time, the idols were hardly beautiful, yet each seemed to emanate a beatific aura that not even 500 years could diminish.
The saint in the altarpiece wears a beatific expression, her eyes raised toward heaven as if she were already enjoying paradise.
As she held her first grandchild, the old woman's face took on a beatific glow that none of her family had seen in years.
After finishing the marathon, the runners lay on the grass with beatific smiles, utterly exhausted yet perfectly content.

def: appropriate, and matches nicely

exs.t: Her dress was becoming and made her look even more beautiful.
The actor's modesty after his victory was becoming; rather than boasting, he praised his rivals and thanked the crew.
The historian adopted a sober, measured tone, which was becoming in a report on a national tragedy; sensational language would have seemed disrespectful to the victims' families.
Such petty sniping at a colleague's retirement dinner was hardly becoming in a senior diplomat, and several guests left the room in disgust.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

label: v.1
def: to envy someone for possessing or enjoying something

exs.t: Sitting all alone in his room, Harvey begrudged the happiness of the other children playing outside his window.
Though she had lost the prize to her former student, the sculptor did not begrudge him his success; she was the first to congratulate him.
Neighbors who had struggled through the drought begrudged the rancher his lush pastures, suspecting that he had diverted more than his share of the river.
It is hard not to begrudge a colleague the grants she seems to win without effort, even when one knows that such resentment is unworthy.

label: v.2
def: to give reluctantly

exs.t: We never begrudge money spent on ourselves.
The stingy landlord begrudged every penny spent on repairs, patching leaks with tape rather than paying a plumber.
The overworked surgeon begrudged the hours each week she was required to spend on paperwork, time she would rather have given to her patients.
Though the legislature did fund the museum, it begrudged the money, approving only the bare minimum after months of haggling.

def: to be one's duty or obligation

exs.t: The teacher looked down at the student and said, "It would behoove you to be in class on time and complete your homework, so that you don't repeat freshman English for a third straight year."
It behooves any researcher who handles public funds to publish her results openly, since taxpayers have a right to see what their money produced.
Given the scale of the risk, it would behoove the city council to consult independent engineers before approving the new tower.
It behooves a translator to respect the author's intentions, even when a looser rendering would sound more elegant.

def: lessen the importance, dignity, or reputation of

exs.t: A good teacher will never belittle his students, but will instead empower them.
Rather than acknowledging his assistant's discovery, the professor belittled it as a lucky accident that any undergraduate could have stumbled upon.
Some reviewers belittle genre fiction as mere entertainment, yet many detective novels explore moral questions with remarkable subtlety.
The coach was careful never to belittle a struggling player in front of the team, knowing how public humiliation could destroy an athlete's confidence.

def: warlike; inclined to quarrel

exs.t: Known for their bellicose ways, the Spartans were once the most feared people from Peloponnesus to Persia.
The dictator's bellicose speeches, full of threats against neighboring states, alarmed diplomats who feared that an invasion was imminent.
Normally mild, the scholar turned bellicose whenever his theory was questioned, challenging critics to public debates and denouncing them in print.
Anthropologists once portrayed the tribe as bellicose, but later research showed that its members resolved most disputes through elaborate negotiation rather than raids.

label: adj.1
def: kind

exs.t: I remember my grandfather's face was wrinkled, benign, and calm.
The villagers remembered the old doctor as a benign presence, always ready with a gentle word and never charging those who could not pay.
Far from the tyrant his enemies described, the ruler was benign toward his subjects, lowering taxes after bad harvests and pardoning petty offenders.
The headmistress regarded her pupils with a benign smile, forgiving their small mischiefs as the natural high spirits of youth.

label: adj.2
def: (medicine) not dangerous to health; not recurrent or progressive

exs.t: The tumor located in your ear lobe seems to be benign and should not cause you any trouble.
The biopsy showed that the lump was benign, so the surgeon removed it for the patient's comfort rather than out of any concern that it would spread.
Although most skin moles are benign, dermatologists recommend monitoring any that change in size, shape, or color, since these can signal cancer.
The child's heart murmur turned out to be benign, a quirk of blood flow that required no treatment and posed no threat to her health.

def: harass, as with questions or requests; cause to feel distressed or worried

exs.t: After discovering a priceless artifact in her backyard, Jane was besieged by phone calls, emails, and reporters all trying to buy, hold or see the rare piece of history.
After the lottery win was announced, the family was besieged by distant relatives and strangers, all requesting loans or donations.
Following the controversial ruling, the court's press office was besieged with inquiries from reporters demanding an explanation.
Besieged by doubts about her decision to leave the firm, she spent sleepless nights rehearsing every argument for and against it.

def: damage the good name and reputation of someone

exs.t: The prince's distasteful choice of words besmirched not only his own name, but the reputation of the entire royal family.
The anonymous letters besmirched the reputation of a scientist whose integrity had never before been questioned, and her funding was suspended pending an inquiry.
Rather than debating her proposals, her opponents sought to besmirch her character with insinuations about her finances.
The plagiarism scandal besmirched the proud name of the old publishing house, and authors who had long been loyal began seeking other publishers.

def: having a depressing or gloomy outlook

exs.t: Unremitting overcast skies tend to lead people to create bleak literature and lugubrious music -- compare England's band Radiohead to any band from Southern California.
With no rain forecast for months and the reservoirs nearly empty, the outlook for the region's farmers is bleak.
The novel's bleak vision of the future, in which cities have crumbled and hope has vanished, left many readers shaken.
Although the company's prospects looked bleak after three losing quarters, a surprise licensing deal transformed its fortunes almost overnight.

label: n.
def: a desirable state

exs.t: Modern technology has been a boon to the travel industry.
The new highway proved a boon to local restaurants, which saw their business double as travelers stopped to eat on the way to the coast.
For scholars of medieval history, the digitization of the monastery's archive has been an enormous boon, sparing them long and costly journeys.
Mild winters are a boon for the region's farmers but a hazard for its ski resorts, which depend on reliable snowfall.

label: adj.
def: very close and convivial

exs.t: He was a boon companion to many, and will be sadly missed.
The two poets were boon companions for decades, sharing long dinners, lively conversation, and a lifelong habit of reading each other's drafts.
At the harbor tavern the old sailor found his boon companions from the voyage, and they spent the night toasting one another and swapping stories.
Though they sparred ferociously in print, the two critics were boon companions in private, dining together every week and laughing over each other's reviews.

def: ill-mannered and coarse or contemptible in behavior or appearance

exs.t: Bukowski was known for being a boorish drunk and alienating close friends and family.
The guest's boorish behavior (talking loudly through the toast and helping himself from other diners' plates) embarrassed his hosts.
The diplomat was reprimanded for boorish remarks at the banquet, where he mocked his hosts' cuisine and repeatedly interrupted the foreign minister.
Though the novelist cultivated a boorish persona in public, swearing and sneering at interviewers, his friends insisted he was gracious in private.

def: in a blunt, direct manner

exs.t: Not one for social pleasantries, the Chief of Staff would brusquely ask his subordinates anything he wanted, even coffee.
The clerk brusquely waved the applicants away, telling them to come back tomorrow without bothering to explain which documents they lacked.
Rather than softening the bad news, the consultant delivered it brusquely, announcing the layoffs in two sentences and leaving the room.
Although she answered reporters brusquely, cutting off any question she considered irrelevant, her colleagues knew her as patient and warm.

def: resist

exs.t: The profits at our firm bucked the general downturn that affected the real estate industry.
The young composer bucked the conventions of her conservatory, writing atonal pieces at a time when her teachers prized traditional harmony.
Few legislators were willing to buck the party leadership openly, knowing that dissenters would lose their committee assignments.
Villagers who bucked the chief's authority were rare, since defiance usually meant exclusion from the communal harvest.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: make stronger or defensible

exs.t: China's economy has been buttressed by a global demand for the electronic parts the country manufactures.
The lawyer buttressed her argument with dozens of precedents, leaving opposing counsel little room to challenge it.
New archaeological finds have buttressed the theory that the city was abandoned because of drought rather than invasion.
To buttress its shaky finances, the orchestra launched an endowment campaign and secured long-term pledges from several foundations.

def: emaciated; gaunt

exs.t: Some actors take challenging roles in which they have to lose so much weight that they appear cadaverous.
After months of illness, the poet was cadaverous, his cheekbones jutting sharply beneath skin stretched thin over his skull.
The actor starved himself for the role of the prisoner, and by the final scenes his cadaverous frame and hollow eyes were almost painful to watch.
The painter's portraits of ascetic monks emphasize their cadaverous features: sunken cheeks, bony hands, and eyes set deep in shadowed sockets.

def: frank; honest and direct, holding nothing back

exs.t: Even with a perfect stranger, Charles was always candid and would rarely hold anything back.
In a candid memoir, the former minister admits to mistakes that she had denied throughout her career.
The mentor's candid feedback stung at first, but the young writer came to value it far above the polite flattery she received elsewhere.
Asked whether the project would finish on time, the engineer was candid: without more staff, he said, it would be at least six months late.

def: the quality of being honest and straightforward in attitude and speech

exs.t: Although I was unhappy that the relationship ended, I appreciated her candidness about why she was ready to move on from the relationship.
The committee appreciated the witness's candidness, for unlike previous witnesses, he admitted his own role in the failures without being pressed.
Her candidness in discussing her struggles with anxiety encouraged other students to speak openly about their own mental health.
Some officials valued the envoy's candidness, but others found his blunt assessments of their governments tactless and impolitic.

def: of primary importance; fundamental

exs.t: Most cultures consider gambling a cardinal sin and thus have outlawed its practice.
The cardinal rule of the laboratory is never to eat or drink near the samples; every other guideline is secondary.
Clarity is the cardinal virtue of scientific writing, since an elegant idea is useless if readers cannot understand it.
Historians disagree about many causes of the war, but most regard the collapse of the grain trade as the cardinal factor, without which the others would not have mattered.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: persistently petty and unjustified criticism

exs.t: What seemed like incessant nagging and carping about my behavior from my mother turned out to be wise and useful advice that has served me well.
The director ignored the carping critics who objected to every small liberty his adaptation took, and audiences embraced the film anyway.
Her carping comments about the seating chart, the menu, and the music soured an evening that everyone else found delightful.
Although the review contained some valid points, its carping tone (it fussed over minor typographical errors for three paragraphs) made the reviewer seem petty.

def: something that speeds up an event

exs.t: Rosa Park's refusal to give up her bus seat acted as a catalyst for the Civil Rights Movement, setting into motion historic changes for African-Americans.
The factory's closure proved the catalyst for the town's reinvention, prompting residents to convert the empty buildings into studios and shops.
A chance conversation with a stranger on a train served as the catalyst for the novel, which the author finished within a year.
Enzymes act as catalysts in the body, allowing chemical reactions that would otherwise take years to occur in fractions of a second.

def: given to haughty disregard of others

exs.t: Percy dismissed the issue with a cavalier wave of his hand.
The manager's cavalier attitude toward safety regulations, which he dismissed as bureaucratic nonsense, eventually led to a serious accident.
Critics faulted the archivist's cavalier treatment of the historical record when she discarded boxes of old letters without consulting anyone.
He spoke in a cavalier way about other people's money, promising investors huge returns while brushing aside their questions about risk.

def: to examine and remove objectionable material

exs.t: Every fall, high school English teachers are inundated by requests to censor their curriculum by removing The Catcher in the Rye and Scarlet Letter from their reading lists.
The wartime government censored soldiers' letters, blacking out any mention of troop locations before the mail reached families at home.
Rather than censor the controversial play, the theater added a discussion after each performance so that audiences could debate its themes.
Librarians resisted pressure to censor the collection, insisting that removing books because some patrons found them offensive would betray the library's mission.

def: involving intelligence rather than emotions or instinct

exs.t: A cerebral analysis of most pop music finds it to be simple and childish, but that ignores the point--the music's effect on the listener.
The chess master's style was cerebral rather than aggressive, built on deep calculation instead of daring sacrifices.
Some listeners find the composer's music too cerebral, admiring its intricate structure while wishing that it stirred their feelings.
Unlike his impulsive partner, who acted on gut feeling, the detective took a cerebral approach, reasoning methodically from each clue to the next.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: protect or fight for as a champion
defMasked: protect or fight for as a ____

exs.t: Martin Luther King Jr. championed civil rights fiercely throughout his short life.
The legislator championed the rights of migrant workers for decades, sponsoring bill after bill to guarantee them fair wages and safe housing.
Long before the teaching method was fashionable, a few educators championed it, publishing studies and training colleagues in its use.
The critic championed the neglected novelist, writing essays that restored her to the canon after decades of obscurity.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: a person who believes in the superiority of their group

exs.t: The chauvinist lives on both sides of the political spectrum, outright shunning anybody whose ideas are not consistent with his own.
A committed chauvinist, the historian dismissed every foreign contribution to science and insisted that his own nation had invented nearly everything of value.
The travel writer was accused of being a chauvinist after describing every culture she visited as a pale imitation of her own.
Cultural chauvinists in the academy long ignored non-Western philosophy, assuming that serious thought had flourished only within their own tradition.

label: v.
def: to limit (usually modifying the growth of something)

exs.t: Deserted for six months, the property began to look more like a jungle and less like a residence--weeds grew unchecked in the front yard.
Predators such as wolves check the growth of deer populations, which would otherwise overgraze the forest and strip it of saplings.
The new medication can check the spread of the infection, although it cannot reverse the damage already done.
Constitutional courts were designed to check the ambitions of the executive, preventing any single official from accumulating unlimited power.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

label: n.
def: the condition of being held back or limited

exs.t: When government abuses are not kept in check, that government is likely to become autocratic.
Without natural predators to serve as a check on their numbers, the rabbits introduced to the island multiplied until they had devoured most of its vegetation.
A free press acts as a check on official corruption, since corrupt officials know that their misconduct may be exposed on the front page.
Held in check for years by strict import quotas, domestic demand for foreign cars surged as soon as the restrictions were lifted.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: one that is marked by disreputable happenings

exs.t: One by one, the presidential candidates dropped out of the race, their respective checkered pasts-- from embezzlement to infidelity--sabotaging their campaigns.
Despite a checkered past that included two bankruptcies and a fraud investigation, the entrepreneur persuaded investors to fund his newest venture.
The museum was reluctant to acquire the painting because of its checkered history, which involved theft, forged provenance papers, and several disputed sales.
The nominee's checkered record, marred by leaked scandals and an earlier dismissal for misconduct, made his appointment difficult to defend.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: being attentive to women like an ideal knight

exs.t: Marco's chivalrous ways, like opening doors and pulling out chairs, was much appreciated by his date.
In an age of casual manners, the elderly gentleman remained chivalrous, rising whenever a woman entered the room and insisting on carrying her parcels.
The medieval romance idealizes its chivalrous hero, who risks his life to rescue a lady and treats even his defeated enemies with courtesy.
Some readers find the novel's chivalrous gestures charming, while others see in the hero's protectiveness a condescending assumption that women are helpless.

def: leniency and compassion shown toward offenders by a person or agency charged with administering justice

exs.t: In the final moments of the trial, during his closing speech, Phillips was nearly begging the judge for clemency.
The governor granted clemency to the elderly prisoner, commuting his sentence on the grounds that he had shown genuine remorse and posed no danger.
Despite pleas for clemency from the defendant's family, the judge imposed the maximum sentence, citing the severity of the crime.
The emperor was famed for his clemency, often pardoning rebels who surrendered rather than executing them as his predecessors had done.

def: fuse or cause to grow together

exs.t: Over time, the various tribes coalesced into a single common culture with one universal language.
Over millions of years, dust and gas in the early solar system coalesced into planets, drawn together by their mutual gravity.
Scattered local protests gradually coalesced into a national movement with a single leadership and a shared list of demands.
Only in the final chapter do the novel's separate storylines coalesce, revealing that the three narrators have been describing the same night.

def: clear and persuasive

exs.t: A cogent argument will change the minds of even the most skeptical audience.
The student's essay was so cogent that even the skeptical examiner, who disagreed with its thesis, conceded that the argument was difficult to refute.
Although the proposal was cogent, its lucid reasoning failed to persuade a committee that had already made up its mind.
The defense offered no cogent explanation for the missing funds, only a series of vague and contradictory excuses.

def: well integrated, forming a united whole

exs.t: A well-written, cohesive essay will keep on topic at all times, never losing sight of the main argument.
The new manager turned a group of feuding specialists into a cohesive team that shared information freely and worked toward common goals.
Critics praised the album as unusually cohesive, noting that its songs flowed into one another and developed a single theme.
Although the anthology gathers stories by twenty different writers, it is surprisingly cohesive, since every piece explores the same neighborhood across a single century.

def: agreement on a secret plot

exs.t: Many have argued that Lee Harvey Oswald, JFK's assassin, was in collusion with other criminals; others maintain that Oswald was a lone gunman.
Regulators fined the three airlines for collusion after discovering that their executives had secretly agreed to raise fares on the same day.
The referee was banned for life when investigators uncovered his collusion with gamblers, who had paid him to influence the outcome of matches.
The auction appeared competitive, but the bidders were acting in collusion, having agreed beforehand which of them would win each lot.

def: so great in size or force or extent as to elicit awe

exs.t: Few appreciate the colossal scale of the sun: if hollow, it could contain a million Earths.
The colossal statue towered over the harbor, dwarfing the ships that passed beneath it and awing every visitor who arrived by sea.
The merger proved a colossal mistake, wiping out billions in shareholder value and leading to the dismissal of the entire executive team.
Building the cathedral required a colossal effort, spanning several generations of masons and consuming the resources of an entire region.

def: worthy of high praise

exs.t: The efforts of the firefighters running into the burning building were commendable.
The student's decision to report a grading error in her own favor was commendable, since it cost her several points on the exam.
While the charity's goals are commendable, its management has been so inefficient that little of the money reaches those in need.
The rescue crew showed commendable composure, working calmly through the night despite freezing temperatures and the constant risk of another collapse.

def: contented to a fault with oneself or one's actions

exs.t: After the water polo team won their sixth championship, they became complacent and didn't even make it to the playoffs the next year.
Having led the market for a decade, the company grew complacent, ignoring the smaller rivals whose innovations would eventually overtake it.
Public health officials warned the public not to grow complacent as the outbreak waned, since a single lapse in vigilance could allow it to return.
Although her early novels were daring, critics felt that success had made the author complacent, since each new book simply repeated the formula of the last.

def: enhancing each other's qualities (for two things or more)

exs.t: The head waiter was careful to tell the amateur diners that red wine was complementary with beef, each bringing out subtle taste notes in the other.
The two researchers had complementary skills: she excelled at designing experiments, while he was gifted at interpreting the resulting data.
Painters often place complementary colors side by side, since a patch of red makes a nearby green appear more vivid, and vice versa.
The museum's new wing is complementary to the original building, its sleek glass walls highlighting the ornate stonework of the older facade.

def: make more intense, stronger, or more marked

exs.t: Her headache was compounded by the construction crew outside, which had six jackhammers going at the same time.
The company's initial error was compounded by its attempt to conceal it, which turned a minor recall into a national scandal.
Drought compounded the region's difficulties, adding widespread crop failures to an economic crisis that was already severe.
Rather than easing tensions, the ambassador's clumsy apology compounded the offense, since it seemed to blame the injured party.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: making a situation or outcome more likely to happen
