exs.t: Studying in a quiet room is conducive to learning; studying in a noisy environment makes learning more difficult.
The open-plan office, meant to encourage collaboration, proved hardly conducive to concentration, since constant chatter made focused work impossible.
A warm, humid climate is conducive to the growth of mold, so archivists keep rare manuscripts in cool, dry rooms.
The mediator arranged the chairs in a circle, believing that a setting without a head of the table would be more conducive to open discussion.

def: taking part in immoral and unethical plots

exs.t: The queen was so conniving that, with the help of the prince, she tried to overthrow the king.
The treasurer was accused of conniving with contractors to inflate invoices, splitting the excess payments among the conspirators.
Historians have long suspected that the queen's own ministers were conniving against her, secretly corresponding with a rival claimant to the throne.
Two clerks connived to alter the ledger, hoping that the auditors would never notice the small sums they had siphoned away each month.

def: to make holy or set apart for a high purpose

exs.t: At the church of Notre Dame in France, the new High Altar was consecrated in 1182.
Before the ruined chapel could host services again, the bishop had to consecrate its new altar, formally setting the space apart from ordinary use.
The veterans' committee chose to consecrate the former battlefield as a memorial ground, dedicating it permanently to the memory of those who had fallen there.
She did not merely study music; she consecrated her entire life to it, forgoing marriage, travel and comfort so that nothing could distract from that single devotion.

def: something that limits or restricts

exs.t: He found pop music a constraint on his ability to learn and preferred to listen to classical musical while studying.
The architect's most severe constraint was the narrow lot, which limited the building to a width of barely six meters and forced every room into a vertical arrangement.
Far from stifling the poet, the strict meter of the sonnet proved a productive constraint, compelling her to find precise words she might otherwise never have sought.
Because the grant covered only a single year of fieldwork, the researchers had to design their study around that constraint, abandoning several long-term measurements they had hoped to include.

label: adj.
def: having or revealing supreme mastery or skill

exs.t: Tyler was the consummate musician: he was able to play the guitar, harmonica, and the drum at the same time.
A consummate diplomat, the envoy could soothe furious delegates, extract concessions from rivals and leave both sides believing they had won.
Although the novel's plot is thin, its prose reveals a consummate stylist whose every sentence seems carefully weighed and polished.
The restorer's consummate skill was evident only on close inspection: the repaired sections of the fresco were indistinguishable from the original brushwork.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

label: v.
def: to make perfect and complete in every respect

exs.t: The restoration of the ancient church was only consummated after a twenty years of labor.
The merger was not consummated until regulators approved the final terms, at which point the two firms at last became a single, fully integrated company.
For decades the composer sketched fragments of the symphony, but only in his final year did he consummate the work, supplying the missing finale that made it whole.
The treaty signed in the spring merely outlined a truce; the alliance was consummated months later, when both parliaments ratified every clause and completed the arrangement.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: scornful, looking down at others with a sneering attitude

exs.t: Always on the forefront of fashion, Vanessa looked contemptuously at anyone wearing dated clothing.
The established painters were openly contemptuous of the young impressionists, dismissing their loose brushwork as the careless daubing of amateurs.
Rather than engaging with her critics' arguments, the philosopher adopted a contemptuous tone, implying that their objections were beneath serious consideration.
Although he claimed to respect the local craftsmen, the visiting designer's contemptuous glance at their furniture betrayed how little he thought of their work.

def: to be remorseful

exs.t: Though he stole his little sister's licorice stick with malevolent glee, Chucky soon became contrite when his sister wouldn't stop crying.
Far from defiant, the scientist was contrite after the flawed data came to light, publicly apologizing to her colleagues and retracting the paper herself.
The editor expected a defensive reply, but the columnist's letter was surprisingly contrite, acknowledging each error and expressing genuine regret for the harm done.
Only when he saw how deeply his careless remark had wounded his brother did Paul become contrite, spending the evening trying to make amends.

def: a difficult problem

exs.t: Computers have helped solve some of the mathematical conundrums which have puzzled man for many centuries.
The museum faced a genuine conundrum: displaying the fragile manuscript would expose it to damaging light, yet keeping it hidden would defeat the purpose of acquiring it.
For generations of physicists, reconciling gravity with quantum theory has remained a conundrum that resists even the most ingenious attempts at solution.
Urban planners confront a familiar conundrum when a neighborhood improves, since the very amenities that attract new residents also drive up rents and push longtime tenants out.

def: describing a lively atmosphere

exs.t: The wedding reception was convivial; friends who hadn't seen each other for ages drank and ate together before heading to the dance floor.
Unlike the stiff formal banquets of previous years, this year's reunion was convivial, full of laughter, toasts and old friends lingering late at crowded tables.
The historian argues that coffeehouses thrived not merely because of the coffee but because of their convivial atmosphere, where strangers chatted freely and debates ran late into the night.
Although the conference sessions were dry and technical, the evenings were convivial, with researchers from rival labs sharing meals, stories and music.

def: highly complex or intricate

exs.t: Instead of solving the math problem in three simple steps, Kumar used a convoluted solution requiring fifteen steps.
The tax code has grown so convoluted that even specialists must consult several cross-referenced provisions to answer what seems like a simple question.
Critics praised the film's performances but found its plot convoluted, with so many flashbacks and double crosses that audiences struggled to follow it.
Instead of stating her objection plainly, the committee chair offered a convoluted explanation that looped through three hypotheticals before reaching any point at all.

def: an abundant supply of something good

exs.t: The International Food Expo was a cornucopia of culinary delights: gourmet foods from every continent were under one roof.
For the botanist, the unexplored valley was a cornucopia: nearly every trail revealed orchids, ferns and mosses she had seen only in illustrated guides.
The newly opened archive proved a cornucopia for historians, yielding letters, diaries and ledgers in such abundance that cataloging them will take years.
Rather than the meager offerings they had expected, the travelers found a cornucopia at the village market, its stalls overflowing with fruit, spices and fresh bread.

def: to confirm or lend support to (usually an idea or claim)

exs.t: Her claim that frog populations were falling precipitously in Central America was corroborated by locals, who reported that many species of frogs had seemingly vanished overnight.
The detective refused to rely on the witness's account alone and waited until fingerprints and phone records could corroborate her story.
Although the hypothesis was intriguing, reviewers insisted that independent laboratories must corroborate the results before the journal would publish them.
Newly deciphered tax records corroborate the chronicler's claim that the city was prosperous, supporting what many scholars had dismissed as mere civic boasting.

def: comprising many cultures; global in reach and outlook

exs.t: There are few cities in the world as diverse and cosmopolitan as New York.
The port city had long been cosmopolitan, its streets alive with merchants, sailors and scholars speaking dozens of languages and trading ideas along with goods.
Unlike her provincial contemporaries, who wrote only of their native villages, the novelist had a cosmopolitan outlook shaped by years spent in capitals across three continents.
The restaurant's menu is thoroughly cosmopolitan, drawing on Ethiopian, Korean and Peruvian traditions rather than confining itself to any single national cuisine.

def: belief in something

exs.t: He placed no credence in psychics, claiming that they offered no special powers beyond the ability to make people part with their money.
Because the letter surfaced decades after the events it described and bore no signature, historians gave little credence to its account of the treaty negotiations.
The discovery of similar fossils on two distant continents lent credence to the long ridiculed theory that the landmasses had once been joined.
Investors placed no credence in the startup's projections, which promised profits far beyond anything its modest sales could plausibly support.

def: deserving of praise but not that amazing

exs.t: Critics agreed the movie was creditable, but few gave it more than three out of five stars.
The debut novel is a creditable effort, carefully plotted and cleanly written, though nothing in it suggests the arrival of a major new voice.
Given the limited budget and an inexperienced cast, the community theater staged a creditable production: hardly dazzling, but solid and worthy of respect.
Although the team finished far from first, its creditable showing in the tournament earned polite praise from coaches who had expected it to collapse.

def: tendency to believe readily

exs.t: Virginia's wide-eyed credulity as a five-year old was replaced by suspicion after she learned that Santa Claus didn't really exist.
The swindler relied on the credulity of his investors, who accepted every glowing report without once asking to see the company's accounts.
Medieval bestiaries, with their unicorns and fire-dwelling salamanders, reveal less about zoology than about the credulity of readers who accepted whatever travelers reported.
A good scientist must balance openness with skepticism, since too much credulity toward striking results can lead an entire field astray.

def: difficult to handle or use especially because of size or weight

exs.t: Only ten years ago, being an avid reader and a traveler meant carrying a cumbersome backpack stuffed with books--these days we need only an e-reader.
Early portable computers were so cumbersome that business travelers dreaded hauling them through airports, often wishing they had simply brought paper files.
The expedition left the cumbersome brass telescope behind, since its weight and awkward length made it nearly impossible to carry up the narrow mountain trail.
The old diving suit, with its copper helmet and lead-weighted boots, was so cumbersome on land that divers had to be helped to the ladder before each descent.

def: a lack or shortage

exs.t: I am surprised by the dearth of fast food chains; this is America and I assumed they were on every street.
The region's dearth of rainfall has forced farmers to abandon thirsty crops like rice in favor of hardier grains that tolerate drought.
Despite the abundance of commentary on the poet's life, there is a surprising dearth of careful analysis of the poems themselves.
Historians of the period face a dearth of reliable sources, since most records were destroyed in a fire and only fragments survive.

def: reduce the quality or value of something

exs.t: The third-rate script so debased the film that not even the flawless acting could save it from being a flop.
Critics complained that the studio had debased a subtle literary classic, reducing its moral complexity to a string of chase scenes and explosions.
When the emperor mixed ever more copper into the silver coinage, he debased the currency, and merchants soon demanded more coins for the same goods.
The senator warned that personal insults would only debase public discourse, turning serious disagreements over policy into a contest of cheap ridicule.

def: expose as false ideas and claims, especially while ridiculing

exs.t: Richard Dawkins tries to debunk religious belief, but his ridicule tends to push people away from his points rather than convince them.
In a witty and devastating essay, the physicist set out to debunk the claims of perpetual motion inventors, and by the final page not one of their supposed machines still seemed credible.
Although the myth that we use only a tenth of our brains persists, neuroscientists have repeatedly debunked it by showing activity across virtually every region.
The historian delighted in debunking cherished legends about the town's founding, mocking the tale of a heroic ancestor that turned out to have no documentary basis.

def: destroying or killing a large part of the population

exs.t: The decimation after atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki is incomprehensible.
The decimation of the bison herds in the nineteenth century left the plains nations without the animal on which their food and shelter had depended.
Ecologists fear that the fungal disease could cause the decimation of amphibian populations, since in several regions it has already left ponds that once teemed with frogs almost silent.
Although the town's buildings survived the plague largely intact, the decimation of its inhabitants left entire streets empty and fields untended for a generation.

def: reduce in worth or character, usually verbally

exs.t: Jesse had mockingly pointed out all of Nancy's faults in front of their friends, publicly degrading the poor girl.
The manager had a habit of degrading junior staff in meetings, belittling their suggestions so harshly that most stopped offering ideas at all.
Rather than debate her arguments, the opposing columnist sought to degrade her, describing her work as the scribbling of an unqualified amateur.
Advocates argued that the textbook's crude caricatures degraded the very communities they claimed to depict, presenting them as ignorant and unworthy of respect.

def: give an assignment to (a person)

exs.t: Since the senior manager had to go on many international business trips, she was forced to delegate many of her responsibilities to two lower-level managers.
Overwhelmed by paperwork, the new principal learned to delegate scheduling and budgeting to her assistants so she could focus on the quality of teaching.
A founder who refuses to delegate any responsibility soon becomes a bottleneck, since every decision, however trivial, must wait for her approval.
The director delegated the lighting design to a young technician, trusting him with a task she had always insisted on handling herself.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: think about carefully; weigh the pros and cons of an issue

exs.t: Emergency situations such as this call for immediate action and leave no room to deliberate over options.
Because the testimony of the two key witnesses was flatly contradictory, the jury deliberated for three days before finally reaching a unanimous verdict.
Rather than accept the first offer, Elena deliberated over the two positions for weeks, listing the advantages and drawbacks of each.
The board spent the afternoon deliberating whether to expand overseas, with members weighing the potential profits against the considerable risks.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: to insult; to cause someone to lose dignity or respect

exs.t: At first the soccer players bantered back and forth, but as soon as one of the players became demeaning, calling the other's mother a water buffalo, the ref whipped out a red card.
The coach refused to demean his players after a loss, insisting that public humiliation only erodes the confidence a team needs to improve.
Some critics felt that the actor demeaned himself by appearing in a string of crude commercials, squandering the dignity he had earned on the stage.
Although she disagreed sharply with the intern's analysis, the editor took care not to demean him, criticizing the argument while respecting the person.

def: to be modest and shy

exs.t: The portrait of her in a simple white blouse was sweet and demure.
In the portrait, the young woman appears demure, eyes lowered and hands folded, though her letters reveal a far bolder personality.
Unlike her flamboyant sister, who dominated every gathering, Clara remained demure, speaking softly and rarely drawing attention to herself.
Critics expected the famously outspoken actress to dominate the interview, yet she remained demure throughout, answering briefly with lowered eyes and deflecting every compliment.

def: treat or speak of with contempt

exs.t: The nun derided the students for trying to sneak insects and worms into the classroom.
Early critics derided the novel as sentimental trash, though later generations recognized it as a subtle exploration of class.
Many engineers derided the proposal for a suspension bridge across the wide strait, calling it a fantasy, until the completed span silenced them.
Rather than engage respectfully with rival theories, the professor derided them in lectures, mocking their proponents as naive and uninformed.

def: abusing vocally; expressing contempt or ridicule

exs.t: I was surprised by her derisive tone; usually, she is sweet, soft spoken, and congenial.
When the candidate claimed to have single-handedly balanced the budget, the audience responded with derisive laughter that drowned out the rest of his speech.
The reviewer's derisive dismissal of the exhibition, which he called a collection of expensive doodles, provoked angry letters from the artists.
Although the scientist expected skepticism, she was unprepared for the derisive comments of colleagues who openly mocked her hypothesis at the conference.

def: expressed as worthless or in negative terms

exs.t: Never before have we seen a debate between two political candidates that was so derogative and filthy.
Historians note that the term was originally derogative, coined by critics to belittle the movement, before its members proudly adopted it.
Although the report aimed to be neutral, its derogative descriptions of rural schools as backward and worthless offended many teachers.
The editor removed several derogative adjectives from the review, reasoning that criticism should assess the work rather than simply disparage it.

def: to willfully violate or destroy a sacred place

exs.t: After desecrating the pharaoh's tomb, the archaeologist soon fell victim to a horrible illness.
The felon had desecrated the holy site, and was on the church's Top 10 Anathema list.
Vandals desecrated the ancient burial ground, overturning headstones and scrawling graffiti across a site the community had revered for centuries.
Villagers regarded the proposed mine as an attempt to desecrate their sacred mountain, a place where ceremonies had been held for generations.
Soldiers who looted the cathedral were accused of desecrating it, since they stabled horses in the nave and melted down the holy vessels from the altar.

label: adj.1
def: poor enough to need help from others

exs.t: Jean Valjean, is at first destitute, but through the grace of a priest, he makes something of his life.
The economic collapse left thousands of families destitute, dependent on soup kitchens and charity for their daily meals.
Although the painter now commands high prices, he spent his early years destitute, sleeping in shelters and relying on friends for food.
The charity focuses on elderly widows left destitute by the death of a spouse, providing housing and a small stipend to those with no other means of support.

label: adj.2
def: completely wanting or lacking (usually "destitute of")

exs.t: Now that the mine is closed, the town is destitute of any economic activity.
The committee's report was long and polished yet destitute of original ideas, merely restating recommendations that had been ignored for a decade.
Critics found the sequel destitute of the wit that had made the original so charming, its jokes stale and its dialogue flat.
After years of drought, the valley was destitute of vegetation, its once green hillsides reduced to bare rock and dust.

label: v.1
def: turn away from by persuasion

exs.t: His mother tried to deter him from joining the army, but he was too intoxicated with the idea of war to listen.
Her advisor tried to deter her from switching to philosophy, arguing at length that the academic job market was bleak, but she would not be dissuaded.
Friends attempted to deter Marco from buying the crumbling farmhouse, pointing out the costly repairs, yet their warnings only strengthened his resolve.
No amount of reasoning from her parents could deter Anna from her plan to sail alone across the ocean; she had a ready answer to each of their objections.

label: v.2
def: try to prevent; show opposition to

exs.t: The government's primary job should involve deterring paths to war, not finding ways to start them.
The city installed brighter streetlights in the park, hoping to deter the vandalism that had flourished under cover of darkness.
Steep fines for late filing are meant to deter carelessness, though critics argue they mainly punish those who cannot afford an accountant.
Thorny spines deter grazing animals, allowing the cactus to conserve the precious water stored in its fleshy stems.

def: (sometimes followed by "to") causing harm or injury

exs.t: Many know that smoking is detrimental to your health, but processed sugar in large quantities is equally bad.
Although the pesticide boosted crop yields, it proved detrimental to bee populations, which in turn threatened the pollination the farms relied on.
Researchers found that chronic sleep deprivation is detrimental to memory, impairing the brain's ability to consolidate what was learned during the day.
Far from helping the company, the aggressive cost cutting was detrimental in the long run, since it drove away the experienced engineers who kept its products reliable.

label: v.1
def: pass on or delegate to another

exs.t: The company was full of managers known for devolving tasks to lower management, but never doing much work themselves.
The new constitution devolved authority over schools and hospitals to regional governments, leaving the capital responsible mainly for defense and trade.
When the founder retired, the task of managing daily operations devolved to her deputy, who had quietly prepared for the role for years.
Rather than making every decision herself, the director devolved budgetary control to department heads, trusting them to allocate funds wisely.

label: v.2
def: grow worse (usually "devolve into")

exs.t: The dialogue between the two academics devolved into a downright bitter argument.
What began as a civil exchange about zoning rules soon devolved into a shouting match, with neighbors hurling personal accusations across the hall.
Without a clear leader, the reform movement devolved into rival factions that spent more energy attacking one another than pursuing their shared goals.
Critics lamented that the once thoughtful talk show had devolved into a spectacle of staged quarrels and cheap sensationalism.

def: to be extremely wicked like the devil

exs.t: The conspirators, willing to dispatch anyone who stood in their way, hatched a diabolical plan to take over the city.
In the novel, the villain devises a diabolical scheme to poison the city's wells, relishing in advance the suffering it will cause.
Although the tyrant presented himself as a benevolent father to his people, historians describe his methods of surveillance and punishment as diabolical.
The conspirators' plan was diabolical in its cruelty: they intended to frame an innocent clerk for the fire and watch him be condemned for their crime.

label: v.1
def: be a distinctive feature, attribute, or trait (sometimes in positive sense)

exs.t: Mozart's long melodic lines differentiate his compositions from other works of late 18th century music.
What differentiates the architect's buildings from those of her contemporaries is the use of unfinished timber, which gives even her largest projects a rustic warmth.
A subtle bitterness in the aftertaste differentiates this regional cheese from its more famous cousin, which is otherwise nearly identical in texture.
Economists argue that in a crowded market, reliable customer service may be the only feature that differentiates one airline from another.

label: v.2
def: evolve so as to lead to a new species or develop in a way most suited to the environment

exs.t: Animals on Madagascar differentiated from other similar animal species due to many years of isolation on the island.
Isolated on separate islands for millennia, the finch populations gradually differentiated, each developing a beak suited to the seeds available in its own habitat.
Once a mountain range separated the two groups of salamanders, they began to differentiate, eventually becoming distinct species that can no longer interbreed.
Bacteria living in scalding hot springs and their relatives in the cooler surrounding soil have slowly come to differentiate, each lineage evolving enzymes suited to its own temperature.

def: in terrible condition

exs.t: The main house has been restored but the gazebo is still dilapidated and unusable.
The once grand theater had become dilapidated, its roof leaking, its seats torn and its ornate plaster ceiling crumbling onto the stage.
Investors saw potential in the dilapidated warehouse, reasoning that its sagging floors and broken windows could be repaired more cheaply than a new building could be erected.
Although the landlord advertised the apartments as charming, tenants found them dilapidated, with peeling paint, rotting window frames and plumbing that barely worked.

def: characterized by care and perseverance in carrying out tasks

exs.t: Michael was a diligent gardener, never leaving a leaf on the ground and regularly watering each plant.
A diligent archivist, Maria spent months cross-checking every date in the collection, refusing to publish the catalog until each entry had been verified.
Although she was not the most gifted student in the program, her diligent practice, hours every day without fail, eventually made her its finest pianist.
The auditors were diligent, examining each receipt rather than sampling a few, and so uncovered discrepancies that earlier reviews had missed.

def: lack of agreement or harmony

exs.t: Despite all their talented players, the team was filled with discord--some players refused to talk to others--and lost most of their games.
Discord within the coalition, as partners quarreled over nearly every appointment, eventually brought down the government.
The composer deliberately introduced discord into the final movement, letting clashing chords unsettle listeners before resolving into harmony.
Although the siblings had always been close, disputes over their father's estate sowed a discord that lasted for years.

def: careful to protect one's speech or actions in order to avoid offense or gain an advantage

exs.t: The professor thought that he was discreet, subtly wiping the stain off of his shirt, but as soon as he stepped off the podium a member of the audience pointed out the large ketchup stain.
Wary of embarrassing his colleague, the professor made a discreet remark after class rather than correcting her error in front of the students.
The diplomat was famously discreet, never revealing in public what had been said in private negotiations, which made both sides trust him.
Unlike her predecessor, who announced every rumored acquisition to the press, the new chief executive was discreet, disclosing deals only after contracts were signed.

def: recognize or perceive the difference

exs.t: Sarah couldn't discriminate between a good wine and a bad wine, so she avoided wine tastings.
Young infants can discriminate between many speech sounds that their parents' language does not use, an ability that fades as they grow accustomed to their native tongue.
Because the two species of warbler look nearly identical, birders must discriminate between them by listening closely to differences in their songs.
A skilled radiologist can discriminate a harmless shadow from a dangerous one, detecting slight variations in shape that an untrained eye would overlook.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: deprive of voting rights

exs.t: The U.S. Constitution disenfranchised women until 1920 when they were given the right to vote.
The novel depicts a republic that disenfranchises anyone without property, so that only landowners may cast ballots in its elections.
Reformers argued that the poll tax served chiefly to disenfranchise the poor, who could not afford to pay for the privilege of voting.
When the district's boundaries were redrawn without updating the registry, thousands of residents were effectively disenfranchised, unable to vote anywhere at all.

def: made less hopeful or enthusiastic

exs.t: After the visiting team scored nine times, the home team's fans were disheartened, some leaving the game early.
Disheartened by a string of rejections, the young novelist nearly abandoned writing, until one editor's encouraging note restored her confidence.
The researchers were disheartened when the trial showed no benefit, since they had devoted a decade to developing the drug.
Although volunteers were initially eager, many grew disheartened as the cleanup dragged on and the river seemed as polluted as ever.

def: two things are fundamentally different

exs.t: With the advent of machines capable of looking inside the brain, fields as disparate as religion and biology have been brought together by scientists trying to understand what happens in the brain when people have a religious experience.
The anthology gathers disparate voices, from medieval mystics to contemporary engineers, whose only common thread is an interest in silence.
Unifying such disparate traditions as Baroque counterpoint and West African drumming, the composer created a sound unlike anything her audience had heard.
Although the two witnesses described the same event, their accounts were so disparate that investigators wondered whether they had seen the same accident.

label: n.
def: the property of being prompt and efficient

exs.t: She finished her thesis with dispatch, amazing her advisors who couldn't believe she hadn't written 60 scholarly pages so quickly.
The new clerk handled the backlog of requests with remarkable dispatch, clearing in a single afternoon what had languished for weeks.
Because the patient's condition was worsening rapidly, the surgical team acted with dispatch, wasting no time on unnecessary tests.
Far from the slow bureaucracy she had expected, the permit office processed her application with admirable dispatch, returning the approval within a day.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

label: v.
def: dispose of rapidly and without delay and efficiently

exs.t: As soon as the angry peasants stormed the castle, they caught the king and swiftly dispatched him.
The chess champion dispatched her first three opponents in under twenty moves each, barely pausing to consider their openings.
Eager to reach the more interesting questions, the lecturer dispatched the preliminary definitions in a few brisk minutes.
The seasoned editor could dispatch a stack of routine letters before lunch, answering each one quickly and accurately.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: easily handled or managed; willing to be taught or led or supervised or directed

exs.t: Barnyard animals are considerably more docile than the wild animals.
Unlike their wild ancestors, domesticated sheep are docile, following a shepherd's dog without resistance wherever it steers them.
The regime preferred a docile press, one that printed official statements without question and never challenged those in power.
Although the new recruit was docile during training, obeying every order without complaint, he proved surprisingly independent once he reached the field.

def: to pursue relentlessly; to hound

exs.t: Throughout his life, he was dogged by insecurities that inhibited personal growth.
Rumors of plagiarism dogged the historian for years, resurfacing with every new book despite repeated investigations that cleared him.
Mechanical failures dogged the expedition from the start, delaying its departure and repeatedly stranding the team in remote villages.
Though she had achieved great success, the composer was dogged by a self-doubt that followed her relentlessly from one premiere to the next.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

label: v.
def: to trick or swindle

exs.t: Once again a get-rich-fast Internet scheme had duped Harold into submitting a $5,000 check to a sham operation.
The forger duped several respected museums, selling them paintings so skillfully aged that even experts accepted them as genuine.
Investors were duped by the fund's glossy brochures, which promised steady returns while concealing that early profits came from new deposits.
The con artist duped the elderly couple into signing over their house by posing as a government inspector.

label: n.
def: a person who is easily tricked or swindled

exs.t: The charlatan mistook the crowd for a bunch of dupes, but the crowd was quickly on to him and decried his bald-faced attempt to bilk them.
Believing every advertisement he saw, the gullible collector became an easy dupe for any dealer who claimed to have a rare manuscript for sale.
The spy insisted he had been merely a dupe: his handlers had assured him the sealed envelopes held business contracts, and he never thought to look inside.
Critics argued that the committee had become a dupe of industry lobbyists, since it accepted without question studies whose funding and methods should have aroused suspicion.

def: highly unconventional or usual (usually describes a person)

exs.t: Mozart was well-known for his eccentricities, often speaking words backward to confuse those around him.
The eccentric inventor wore a pith helmet to the laboratory each day and insisted on conducting experiments only at night.
Though her neighbors found her habits eccentric, such as keeping dozens of clocks all set to different times, the retired astronomer insisted the arrangement helped her think.
Scholars once dismissed the poet as merely eccentric, noting his odd habits of writing on wallpaper and refusing to wear shoes, but his experiments now seem visionary.

def: a conceited and self-centered person

exs.t: An egotist, Natasha had few friends because of her inability to talk about anything except her dream of becoming the next American Idol.
An egotist to the core, the conductor claimed full credit for the orchestra's success and never once acknowledged the musicians who performed the music.
Although he presented himself as a humble servant of the public, his memoir reveals an egotist who measured every event by its effect on his own reputation.
Conversations with Victor were exhausting, since the egotist inevitably steered every topic back to his own accomplishments.

def: to live off meager resources, to scrape by

exs.t: Stranded in a cabin over the winter, Terry was able to eke out an existence on canned food.
After the factory closed, many families eked out a living by selling vegetables from their gardens and taking whatever odd jobs they could find.
Through the long drought, the herders eked out their dwindling stores of grain, rationing every handful so that it would last until the rains returned.
Living on a meager stipend as a graduate student, Lena could eke out only the barest subsistence, rarely affording anything beyond rice, beans and used books.

label: adj.
def: marked by complexity and richness of detail

exs.t: Thomas, on returning from Morocco, replaced his dirty gray carpet with an elaborate one he'd brought back with him.
The wedding featured an elaborate ceremony, with three processions, a full choir and costumes embroidered by hand over several months.
Unlike the plain facades of modernist buildings, the cathedral's front is elaborate, crowded with carved saints, gargoyles and intricate tracery.
The heist in the novel relies on an elaborate plan involving forged blueprints, a fake delivery and precise timing, each step depending on the one before.

label: v.
def: explain in more detail

exs.t: Most high school physics teachers find themselves elaborating the same point over and over again, since many concepts confuse students.
When the reviewers asked her to elaborate on her methods, the scientist added a detailed appendix describing each step of the experiment.
The senator declined to elaborate, offering only a brief statement and leaving reporters to speculate about what the vague remark had meant.
In the second chapter, the author elaborates on an idea merely sketched in the introduction, filling it out with historical cases and statistical evidence.

def: escape understanding

exs.t: Even a basic understanding of physics can elude most high schools students.
The meaning of the poem's final stanza eludes even seasoned critics, who continue to propose rival interpretations with little agreement.
Although she could perform the calculation flawlessly, the underlying logic of the proof eluded her until a tutor explained it with a diagram.
Why the ancient builders aligned the monument with that particular star still eludes archaeologists, who have found no inscriptions explaining the choice.

def: difficult to capture or difficult to remember

exs.t: Many first time skydivers say that describing the act of falling from the sky is elusive.
The snow leopard is famously elusive, so wildlife photographers may spend months in the mountains without glimpsing a single one.
The name of the tune remained elusive; Mark could hum its melody perfectly yet could not recall what it was called.
For decades the particle proved elusive, escaping detection in experiment after experiment until more sensitive instruments finally captured its signature.

def: make more attractive by adding ornament, colour, etc

exs.t: ; make more beautiful McCartney would write relatively straightforward lyrics, and Lennon would embellish them with puns and poetic images.
The monks embellished the manuscript's margins with gold leaf and intricate vines, transforming a plain text into a luminous work of art.
Rather than leave the facade bare, the architect embellished it with colored tiles and carved stone flowers that caught the afternoon light.
The singer liked to embellish the simple folk melody with trills and grace notes, decorating it without obscuring the tune.

def: involved in argument or contention

exs.t: These days we are never short of a D.C. politician embroiled in scandal--a welcome phenomenon for those who, having barely finished feasting on the sordid details of one imbroglio, can sink their teeth into a fresh one.
For nearly a decade the two families were embroiled in a bitter dispute over the boundary between their farms, with neither willing to concede an inch.
Hoping to remain neutral, the small nation was nevertheless embroiled in the conflict when both neighboring powers demanded its support.
The professor had hoped to focus on research but instead found herself embroiled in departmental quarrels over hiring and funding.

def: showing understanding and ready comprehension of other peoples' states and emotions

exs.t: Most discrimination and hatred is based on a lack of empathetic awareness of people that have the same aspirations and fears.
An empathetic nurse, Grace could sense a patient's anxiety before a word was spoken and knew exactly how to ease it.
Readers found the memoir's narrator deeply empathetic, since she portrayed even her harshest critics with a keen understanding of the fears that drove them.
Unlike his brusque predecessor, the new counselor was empathetic, listening patiently and responding to each student's worries as though he felt them himself.

def: strive to equal or match, especially by imitating; compete with successfully

exs.t: To really become fluent in a new language, emulate the speech patterns and intonation of people who speak the language.
Young painters of the period sought to emulate the old masters, copying their compositions in museums in hopes of one day equaling their skill.
Many developing economies have tried to emulate the export-led growth of successful neighbors, adopting similar policies in hopes of matching their prosperity.
The apprentice watched the master carpenter closely, striving to emulate his precise joinery until her own work could rival his.

def: native; originating where it is found

exs.t: Irish cuisine makes great use of potatoes, but ironically, the potato is not endemic to Ireland.
Because the tiny frog is endemic to a single mountain forest, conservationists warn that clearing that forest would erase the species from the wild entirely.
The island's long isolation produced many endemic plants, species that grow there naturally and nowhere else on earth.
Although the herb now appears in cuisines worldwide, botanists trace it to a single valley, where it is endemic, and argue that every cultivated variety descends from those wild plants.

def: a state of deep-seated ill-will

exs.t: Charles rude remark toward Sarah yesterday was due to his illness, not due to any real enmity toward Sarah.
The enmity between the two scholars, rooted in a decades-old dispute over credit for a discovery, was so deep that they refused to attend the same conferences.
Despite centuries of enmity, the neighboring kingdoms eventually signed a treaty, surprising observers who had assumed their hostility was permanent.
Rather than a friendly rivalry, the two firms maintained an abiding enmity, each seizing any opportunity to undermine the other.

def: get someone to do something through (often false or exaggerated) promises

exs.t: Harold enticed his wife, Maude, to go on a vacation to Hawaii, with promises of luaus on the beach and all-you-can-eat seafood buffets.
The city tried to entice young professionals to relocate with promises of cheap housing and vibrant nightlife, though the reality proved far less glamorous.
Advertisements for the timeshare enticed buyers with talk of luxurious villas, but the actual units were cramped and far from the beach.
The recruiter enticed the engineer to leave her stable job by describing lavish stock options that, in the end, proved nearly worthless.

label: v.1
def: determine the number or amount of

exs.t: The survey enumerates the number of happy workers and the number of unhappy workers.
Census takers set out to enumerate the region's population, visiting every household to count its residents.
Because the colony is spread across hundreds of cliffs, biologists use aerial photographs to enumerate the nesting birds, tallying individuals from the images.
Before the grant could be renewed, the museum had to enumerate its holdings, arriving at a precise count of every object in storage.

label: v.2
def: specify individually, one by one

exs.t: I sat and listened as she enumerated all of the things she did not like about the past three months.
In her opening statement, the prosecutor enumerated the defendant's alleged offenses, naming each in turn: fraud, forgery and obstruction of justice.
The treaty enumerates the rights guaranteed to each signatory, listing them article by article so that no party can later claim ambiguity.
Rather than summarize the flaws in general terms, the reviewer enumerated them one after another, citing a specific page for each problem.

def: to make an error

exs.t: He erred in thinking that "indigent" and "indignant" were synonyms.
The historian acknowledged that he had erred in dating the manuscript, having mistaken a later scribe's handwriting for the original author's.
When uncertain about a patient's allergies, doctors choose to err on the side of caution, prescribing a safer alternative drug.
Even the most careful translators occasionally err, and the novel's first English edition contains several passages that misrepresent the original.

def: to be wandering; not sticking to a circumscribed path

exs.t: Unlike his peers, who spent their hours studying in the library, Matthew preferred errant walks through the university campus.
Unlike the disciplined monks who kept to the cloister, the errant friar roamed from village to village, preaching wherever he happened to stop.
The shepherd spent the evening searching for an errant lamb that had strayed far from the flock into the rocky hills.
The romances of the period celebrated errant knights, yet real lords distrusted such men, preferring vassals who stayed on their own lands rather than riding off wherever adventure called.

def: unpredictable; strange and unconventional

exs.t: It came as no surprise to pundits that the President's attempt at re-election floundered; even during his term, support for his policies was erratic, with an approval rating jumping anywhere from 30 to 60 percent.
The patient's erratic heartbeat, racing one moment and slowing the next, alarmed the physicians, who could find no pattern in its rhythm.
Investors grew nervous about the company's erratic leadership, as the chief executive reversed major decisions without warning or explanation.
Because the old bus ran on an erratic schedule, sometimes early and sometimes an hour late, commuters never knew when to leave home.

def: a feeling of great (usually exaggerated) elation

exs.t: The euphoria of winning her first gold medal in the 100 meter dash overwhelmed Shelly-Ann Fraser and she wept tears of immense joy.
The euphoria that followed the treaty's signing soon faded, as citizens realized that peace would not immediately restore their ruined economy.
Market analysts cautioned that the euphoria surrounding the new technology was overblown, since few of the companies involved had ever turned a profit.
After years of failed attempts, the team's euphoria at finally detecting the signal was so intense that they celebrated long into the night.

label: adj.1
def: avoiding or escaping from difficulty or danger or commitment

exs.t: His responses were clearly evasive; he obviously did not want to take on any responsibility or any new work.
When the storm shifted course, the captain took evasive action, steering the ship far to the south to avoid the worst of the waves.
The gazelle's evasive zigzagging makes it difficult for a cheetah to close in, since each sudden turn forces the predator to slow down.
Pilots practice evasive maneuvers so that, if another aircraft strays into their path, they can swerve away from danger instantly.

label: adj.2
def: deliberately vague or ambiguous

exs.t: Every time I call the bank, I receive the same evasive answers about our mortgage and never get a clear response.
Asked directly whether the company had known about the defect, the spokesperson gave an evasive answer about ongoing reviews and never said yes or no.
The witness grew evasive under cross-examination, offering vague recollections and conveniently forgetting details she had described clearly the day before.
Frustrated by the minister's evasive replies, reporters pressed him to state plainly whether taxes would rise, but he spoke only of unspecified adjustments.

def: without partiality

exs.t: Teachers often have trouble being evenhanded to all of their varied students.
A good mediator must remain evenhanded, giving each party equal time to speak and refusing to signal sympathy for either side.
Although the biographer clearly admired her subject, her treatment of his failures was evenhanded, neither excusing them nor dwelling on them unduly.
Critics accused the referee of favoring the home team, but a review of the footage showed that his calls had been scrupulously evenhanded.

def: to irritate intensely

exs.t: As a child, I exasperated my mother with strings of never-ending questions.
The composer's constant revisions exasperated the orchestra, which had to relearn the score after every rehearsal only days before the premiere.
Nothing exasperated the professor more than students who asked questions she had answered moments earlier; by the third repetition her patience had worn thin.
The software's frequent crashes so exasperated the staff that several began keeping handwritten records rather than risk losing another day's work.

def: extremely painful

exs.t: After the boulder rolled a couple of feet, pinning my friend's arm, he experienced excruciating pain.
The fractured ankle caused excruciating pain, so severe that the hiker could not put the slightest weight on it and had to be carried down.
Migraine sufferers describe the attacks as excruciating, with throbbing so intense that even dim light and quiet sounds become unbearable.
Although the dentist promised only mild discomfort, the procedure proved excruciating once the anesthetic wore off halfway through.

label: v.1
def: be characteristic of

exs.t: Lincoln exemplified the best of not only America, but also the potential greatness that exists within each person.
The cathedral's soaring arches and stained glass exemplify the Gothic style, displaying nearly every feature that defines the period.
Her patient, meticulous research, conducted over decades without shortcuts, exemplifies the scholarly virtues the prize was created to honor.
With its flat skyline and endless rows of identical houses, the suburb exemplifies the postwar housing boom and its emphasis on affordability over individuality.

label: v.2
def: clarify by giving an example of

exs.t: Please present some case studies that exemplify the results that you claim in your paper.
To exemplify the principle of buoyancy, the teacher dropped a block of wood and a stone into a tank of water and asked students to explain the difference.
The author exemplifies her abstract claim about memory with a vivid anecdote from her own childhood, making the theory concrete for readers.
The lecturer exemplified each grammatical rule with a sentence from a famous novel, so that students could see the rule at work.

def: to strongly urge on; encourage

exs.t: Nelson's parents exhorted him to study medicine, urging him to choose a respectable profession; intransigent, Nelson left home to become a graffiti artist.
The coach exhorted her exhausted players to give one final effort, shouting encouragement from the sideline throughout the last minutes.
In his sermons, the preacher exhorted the congregation to care for the poor, urging them again and again to share what they had.
Public health posters exhorted citizens to wash their hands frequently, pressing the message with bold slogans on every bus and train.

def: making less guilty or more forgivable

exs.t: The jury was hardly moved by the man's plea that his loneliness was an extenuating factor in his crime of dognapping a prized pooch.
The judge reduced the sentence, citing extenuating circumstances: the defendant had stolen the medicine only to treat his gravely ill daughter.
Although late submissions normally receive no credit, the professor accepted Mei's essay, since a family emergency was clearly an extenuating factor.
The committee found nothing extenuating in the official's conduct; his misuse of funds was deliberate and entirely inexcusable.

def: cleverly amusing in tone

exs.t: Facetious behavior will not be tolerated during sex education class; it's time for all of you to treat these matters like mature adults.
The senator's facetious suggestion that the committee simply flip a coin drew laughs, though some colleagues felt the joke trivialized a serious debate.
Although his essays are often facetious, their jokes conceal a serious argument about the decline of public reading that careless readers tend to miss.
Asked why she had become an economist, she gave the facetious reply that she had been too pessimistic for any other profession.

def: try to gain favor by extreme flattery

exs.t: The media fawned over the handsome new CEO, praising his impeccable sense of style instead of asking more pointed questions.
Courtiers fawned over the young king, praising his every remark as brilliant in hopes of winning titles and estates.
The junior associate's habit of fawning on senior partners, laughing at their weakest jokes and lavishing praise on their briefs, earned him little respect.
Instead of offering honest criticism, the reviewers fawned over the celebrated novelist's latest book, heaping flattery on a work that was plainly weak.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: to search for something persistently

exs.t: Ever the resourceful lexicographer, Fenton was able to ferret out the word origin of highly obscure words.
The investigative reporter spent months ferreting out the details of the scheme, combing through records and interviewing dozens of former employees.
A patient archivist, she managed to ferret out the missing letter from a box of unrelated papers that had been mislabeled for decades.
Auditors are trained to ferret out hidden losses, since a company in trouble will often bury its worst figures in footnotes and obscure subsidiary accounts.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: to celebrate a person

exs.t: After World War II, war heroes were feted at first but quickly forgotten.
Upon returning from the expedition, the explorers were feted with banquets and parades, though the public soon forgot their achievement.
The village feted its oldest resident on her hundredth birthday, holding a festival in her honor complete with music and speeches.
Although the scientist was feted abroad, receiving honors and lavish receptions, she remained almost unknown in her own country.

def: liable to sudden unpredictable change, especially in affections or attachments

exs.t: She was so fickle in her politics, it was hard to pinpoint her beliefs; one week she would embrace a side, and the next week she would denounce it.
Fashion designers must cope with a fickle public whose tastes can shift overnight, making last season's bestselling style suddenly unwanted.
The poet's patrons proved fickle, lavishing support on him one year and abandoning him the next for a more fashionable writer.
Voters in the district are notoriously fickle, switching allegiance so often that no candidate can take their support for granted.

def: achieve something by means of trickery or devious methods

exs.t: Steven was able to finagle one of the last seats on the train by convincing the conductor that his torn stub was actually a valid ticket.
By flattering the clerk and hinting at a nonexistent appointment, Leo managed to finagle a meeting with the director that others had waited weeks to get.
The contractor finagled extra payments from the city by submitting invoices for work that had never actually been done.
Unable to get tickets honestly, the students finagled their way into the sold-out concert by posing as members of the stage crew.

def: young and inexperienced; describing any new participant in some activity

exs.t: Murray has years of experience in family practice, but he is just a fledgling in surgery.
The fledgling democracy struggled to establish independent courts, since its leaders had no experience governing outside of a dictatorship.
Although the fledgling company had only a handful of employees, its inexperienced founders boldly bid for contracts against established firms.
As a fledgling reporter, Nadia made mistakes that seasoned journalists would have avoided, such as quoting sources without verifying their claims.

def: to deceive

exs.t: Many people have been fleeced by Internet scams and never received their money back.
The Internet is filled with get-rich-quick schemes that intend only to fleece the Pollyannaish and unsuspecting.
The dishonest mechanic fleeced unsuspecting tourists, charging them for repairs that were never performed on their rental cars.
Investors who trusted the charismatic promoter were fleeced of their savings, discovering the fraud only when the fund suddenly vanished.
Street vendors near the monument were known to fleece visitors, passing off cheap trinkets as rare antiques at extravagant prices.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: behave awkwardly; have difficulties

exs.t: Sylvia has excelled at advanced calculus, but ironically, when she has deal with taxes, she flounders.
Asked an unexpected question about his own data, the graduate student floundered, stammering through half-formed answers until his advisor intervened.
Without clear direction from its new leadership, the once thriving magazine floundered, losing readers and advertisers year after year.
Although Tom excelled at written exams, he floundered in the oral portion, where he struggled to organize his thoughts under pressure.

def: to be in abundance

exs.t: The exam's passage is flush with difficult words, words that you may have learned only yesterday.
Flush with profits from a record harvest, the farmers' cooperative invested in new equipment and a larger storage facility.
The newly endowed library was flush with funds, able at last to purchase rare volumes it had long coveted but never afforded.
The region's rivers are flush with salmon every autumn, providing an abundant food source for bears and eagles alike.

def: a behavioral attribute that is distinctive and peculiar to an individual

exs.t: When their new roommate sat staring at an oak tree for an hour, Marcia thought it indicated a mental problem, but Jeff assured her it was a harmless foible.
The biography treats its subject with affection, noting his foibles, such as his habit of reading the last page of a novel first, without mocking him.
Every great detective in fiction seems to have some foible, whether a fondness for oddly flavored tea or an insistence on arranging objects symmetrically.
Colleagues tolerated the professor's foibles, including his refusal to use email and his penchant for lecturing in rhyme, because his teaching was superb.

def: marked by defiant disregard for danger or consequences

exs.t: The police regularly face dangerous situations, so for a police officer not to wear his bullet-proof vest is foolhardy.
Setting out to climb the peak in winter without a guide or proper gear was foolhardy, and the rescue team was lucky to find the hikers alive.
Although the general admired bold tactics, he considered a frontal assault on the fortified hill foolhardy, likely to waste lives for no gain.
Investing one's entire savings in an untested startup may seem courageous, but most financial advisors would call it foolhardy.

def: characterized by directness in manner or speech; without subtlety or evasion

exs.t: I did not expect the insurance agent to give us any straight answers, but I was pleasant surprised by how forthright he was.
Unlike politicians who hedge every statement, the mayor was forthright about the budget crisis, telling residents plainly that services would be cut.
The reviewer's forthright critique was more useful to the author than polite praise, since it told him in the first paragraph that the novel's second half collapses.
Patients appreciate a forthright doctor who explains the diagnosis directly instead of softening it into vague reassurances.

def: producing no result or effect; unproductive of success

exs.t: I thought I could repair the car myself, but after two days of work with no success, I have to admit that my efforts were futile.
The villagers' attempts to hold back the rising river with sandbags proved futile, as the water poured over the barrier within hours.
Recognizing that further negotiation was futile, since neither side would move from its position, the mediator suspended the talks.
Breeders once tried to tame the wild horses for farm work, but the effort was futile; generation after generation remained as unruly as ever.

def: agreeable, conducive to comfort

exs.t: Betty is a genial young woman: everyone she meets is put at ease by her elegance and grace.
The host's genial manner, warm, relaxed and generous with compliments, quickly put the nervous guests at ease.
Grapes flourish in the valley's genial climate, where mild winters and gentle breezes allow them to ripen slowly.
Although the negotiations had been tense, the genial atmosphere of the closing dinner allowed the delegates to relax and even joke together.

def: marked by refinement in taste and manners

exs.t: A live string quartet would provide a more genteel air to the wedding than would a folk singer.
The novel satirizes a genteel family that prides itself on elegant manners and fine china while quietly sinking into debt.
The tea room retained a genteel air, with lace tablecloths, silver pots and patrons who spoke in hushed, refined voices.
Raised in a genteel household where table manners were strictly observed, Clara was startled by the boisterous customs of the rural boarding school.

def: collect information bit by bit

exs.t: Herb has given us no formal statement about his background, but from various hints, I have gleaned that he grew up in difficult circumstances.
From scattered references in merchants' letters, historians have gleaned a surprisingly detailed picture of daily life in the port.
The reporter gleaned the outlines of the deal bit by bit, piecing together remarks from several officials who refused to speak on the record.
Although the manual was poorly written, the technician gleaned enough from its diagrams and footnotes to repair the machine.

def: (of a person) speaking with ease but without sincerity

exs.t: I have found that the more glib the salesman, the worse the product.
The candidate's glib answers impressed the audience at first, but his polished phrases seemed hollow once reporters asked about specifics.
Rather than a glib apology crafted by the public relations team, the victims wanted a sincere acknowledgment of the harm done.
The salesman was glib, able to talk smoothly about any product, yet customers sensed he believed none of what he said.

def: urge on with unpleasant comments

exs.t: Doug did not want to enter the race, but Jim, through a steady stream of taunts, goaded him into signing up for it.
Opponents goaded the young boxer with insults, hoping to provoke him into a reckless attack that would leave him exposed.
Tired of her brother's teasing that she would never finish a marathon, Rosa was finally goaded into signing up for one.
The columnist deliberately goaded his readers with provocative jabs, knowing that indignant letters would boost the paper's circulation.

def: show submission or fear

exs.t: Every time Susan comes to the office, Frank grovels as if she were about to fire.
After the disastrous launch, the executive groveled before the shareholders, apologizing profusely and begging them not to sell their stock.
Trembling before the throne, the courtier groveled at the emperor's feet, pleading for mercy after his plot was discovered.
Rather than grovel for a raise, Nora calmly presented evidence of her contributions and let her record speak for itself.

def: laugh boisterously

exs.t: Whenever the jester fell to the ground in mock pain, the king guffawed, exposing his yellow, fang-like teeth.
When the comedian mimicked the pompous professor, the audience guffawed so loudly that the next line was drowned out entirely.
Unlike his sister, who merely smiled at the joke, Sam guffawed, slapping the table and roaring until tears filled his eyes.
The solemn ceremony was interrupted when a guest guffawed at the officiant's slip of the tongue, his booming laughter echoing through the hall.

def: prevent the progress or free movement of

exs.t: As the rain water began to collect in pools on the highway, it began to hamper the flow of traffic.
Heavy snowfall hampered rescue efforts for days, blocking mountain roads and preventing helicopters from reaching the stranded villagers.
A lack of reliable data has hampered attempts to measure the policy's effects, leaving economists to rely on rough estimates.
Her progress in learning the cello was hampered by an old wrist injury that made long practice sessions painful.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: made ineffective or powerless

exs.t: The FBI has made so many restriction on the local police that they are absolutely hamstrung, unable to accomplish anything.
Hamstrung by a tiny budget and a shortage of staff, the agency could do little to enforce the environmental rules it was charged with upholding.
The coalition government was hamstrung by internal disagreements, unable to pass even routine legislation for most of its term.
Although the new principal had bold plans, she was hamstrung by district regulations that left her almost no authority to act.

def: the pinnacle or top of a time period or career

exs.t: During the heyday of Prohibition, bootlegging had become such a lucrative business that many who had been opposed to the 18th Amendment began to fear it would be repealed.
In its heyday, the resort town drew visitors from across the continent, but its grand hotels now stand mostly empty.
The critic argues that the novelist's heyday came early; after the triumph of her second book, her work never again reached such heights.
During the heyday of the silk trade, the city's markets overflowed with merchants, and its wealth funded palaces that still dominate the skyline.

def: a confusing mixture or jumble

exs.t: Those in attendance represented a hodgepodge of the city's denizens: chimney sweepers could be seen sitting elbow to elbow with stockbrokers.
The museum's early collection was a hodgepodge of fossils, coins, stuffed birds and folk costumes, assembled without any organizing principle.
Critics dismissed the bill as a hodgepodge of unrelated provisions, lumping farm subsidies, tax breaks and highway funding into a single confusing package.
The town's architecture is a hodgepodge, with medieval cottages jostling against glass office towers and a mock Tudor supermarket.

def: to pursue relentlessly

exs.t: An implacable foe of corruption, Eliot Ness hounded out graft in all forms--he even helped nab Al Capone.
Creditors hounded the failed merchant for years, sending agents to his door and following him from one city to the next.
Because photographers hounded the actress for months after the trial, she finally left the city and moved to a farm where no stranger could approach unseen.
The inspector hounded the suspect with repeated interviews and constant surveillance, refusing to relent until he confessed.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: dull and lacking excitement

exs.t: Having grown up in a humdrum suburb, Jacob relished life in New York City after moving.
After years of daring fieldwork abroad, the anthropologist found her humdrum office routine of meetings and paperwork almost unbearable.
The critics agreed that the first act was humdrum, with little happening beyond polite small talk, though the second act finally sparked to life.
Rather than a humdrum lecture recited from notes, the professor's talk was full of surprising demonstrations that kept students riveted.

def: contrary to or forbidden by law

exs.t: Though Al Capone was engaged in many illicit activities, he was finally arrested for income tax evasion, a relatively minor offense.
Customs officers uncovered an illicit trade in rare orchids, smuggled across the border without the permits required by law.
Although the tavern appeared to sell only coffee, it housed an illicit gambling operation in its cellar, well hidden from the authorities.
The ban did not end consumption of the drug; it merely drove it into illicit markets where quality was uncontrolled and sellers ignored the law.

def: not relevant

exs.t: The judge found the defendant's comments immaterial to the trial, and summarily dismissed him from the witness stand.
Whether the painting was completed on a Tuesday or a Wednesday is immaterial; what matters is that the artist was in Rome when she painted it.
The candidate's height is immaterial to the job, since the position involves analyzing data rather than performing any physical task.
Although the lawyer raised the defendant's past hobbies, the judge ruled the information immaterial, bearing no relation to the fraud at issue.

def: without fault or error

exs.t: He was impeccably dressed in the latest fashion without a single crease or stain.
The pianist's technique was impeccable, yet some critics found her playing emotionally cold, as if she cared more about hitting every note than about the music's meaning.
With his impeccable record of honesty over three decades in office, the treasurer was the last person anyone suspected of embezzlement.
Her manners were impeccable: she remembered every guest's name, wrote thank-you notes promptly and never once interrupted anyone.

def: be a hindrance or obstacle to

exs.t: Since the police sergeant had to train the pair of new hires, progress in his own case was impeded.
Dense undergrowth impeded the explorers' progress, forcing them to hack a path through the jungle a few meters at a time.
Critics warned that excessive regulation might impede innovation, discouraging small firms with limited legal budgets from developing new products.
Scar tissue can impede the flow of blood, which is why surgeons try to minimize damage to the surrounding vessels.

def: close in time; about to occur

exs.t: The impending doom of our world has been a discussed and debated for 2000 years--maybe even longer.
Aware of the impending storm, the fishermen hauled their boats onto the beach and secured their nets before the first winds arrived.
Anxious about her impending retirement, the professor began donating her books and wondering how she would fill her days.
Economists warned of an impending recession, pointing to falling orders and rising unemployment as signs that a downturn was near.

def: does not allow fluids to pass through

exs.t: The sand bags placed on the river formed an impermeable barrier, protecting the town from flooding.
Because clay is nearly impermeable, rainwater pools on its surface rather than soaking into the ground below.
The explorers wrapped their maps in an impermeable oilcloth that kept them dry even as the canoe was swamped.
Engineers lined the landfill with an impermeable membrane so that contaminated liquids could not seep into the groundwater.

label: v.1
def: convey a meaning; imply

exs.t: By saying that some of the guests were uncomfortable, the manager implicated to the hotel staff that it needed to be more diligent.
The pattern of the ruins implicates a gradual abandonment rather than a sudden catastrophe, since the inhabitants appear to have removed their valuables before leaving.
Although the report never states it outright, its careful wording implicates that the delays were foreseeable, a conclusion few readers could miss.
The recurring image of locked doors implicates a theme of isolation that runs through the entire novel, even though the narrator never names it.

label: v.2
def: to indicate in wrongdoing, usually a crime

exs.t: The crime boss was implicated for a long list of crimes, ranging from murder to disturbing the peace.
The accountant's testimony implicated the firm's director in the fraud, revealing that he had personally approved the falsified statements.
Although the burglar confessed, he refused to implicate his accomplices, insisting that he had acted entirely alone.
Forensic evidence found at the scene implicated the gardener, whose fingerprints appeared on the forced window latch.

def: impossible to estimate or figure out

exs.t: According to many lawmakers, the huge variety of factors affecting society make devising an efficient healthcare system an imponderable task.
The planners could estimate construction costs, but the long-term effects of the new highway on the region's culture remained imponderable.
Philosophers have long wrestled with imponderable questions, such as why anything exists at all, that seem to resist any definitive answer.
Because the success of a debut novel depends on imponderable factors like timing and public mood, publishers cannot reliably predict which books will sell.

def: immune to attack; incapable of being tampered with

exs.t: As a child, Amy would build pillow castles and pretend they were impregnable fortresses.
Built on a sheer rock outcrop and ringed by triple walls, the fortress was considered impregnable, and no army ever managed to breach it.
The company's encryption was once thought impregnable, but a team of researchers eventually found a flaw that allowed them to break in.
Her reputation seemed impregnable; decades of scrupulous scholarship had made it proof against the attacks of even her fiercest rivals.

def: happening by chance or unexpectedly or unintentionally

exs.t: Although Prohibition was rooted in noble ideals, the inadvertent and costly consequences of making alcohol illegal in the U.S. led to its repeal.
The spill was inadvertent, caused by a worker who misread a gauge, but it still contaminated miles of the river.
The novelist's inadvertent revelation of the ending during an interview dismayed her publisher, who had carefully kept it secret.
Rather than a calculated snub, his omission of her name from the acknowledgments was inadvertent, the result of a hasty final edit.

def: without or deprived of the use of speech or words

exs.t: Although a brilliant economist, Professor Black was completely inarticulate, a terrible lecturer.
Overcome with grief at the funeral, the normally eloquent senator was inarticulate, able only to nod at mourners who offered condolences.
The toddler's inarticulate cries grew louder as she pointed at the shelf, since she lacked the words to say which toy she wanted.
Although his paintings convey profound emotion, the artist was nearly inarticulate in interviews, groping for words and falling silent in the middle of sentences.

def: make furious

exs.t: When Herb bought football tickets for a game on the day of their wedding anniversary, Jill was incensed.
The proposal to demolish the historic library incensed residents, who packed the council meeting and shouted down the mayor.
The reviewer's dismissive remarks about her life's work so incensed the elderly composer that she wrote a furious rebuttal to the newspaper.
Workers were incensed to learn that executives had awarded themselves bonuses while freezing everyone else's wages.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: uninterrupted in time and indefinitely long continuing

exs.t: I don't mind small children in brief doses, but I think the incessant exposure that their parents have to them would quickly wear me down.
The incessant hammering from the construction site next door, which continued from dawn until dusk every day, made it impossible for the writer to concentrate.
Villagers grew weary of the incessant rain, which had fallen without a break for three weeks and turned every road to mud.
Her incessant chatter, which did not pause once during the entire three-hour journey, left her fellow passengers longing for silence.

label: adj.1
def: (of weather) unpleasant, stormy

exs.t: After a week of inclement weather, we finally are able to go outside and enjoy the sun.
Inclement weather forced the organizers to move the outdoor concert into the gymnasium, as heavy rain and gusting winds battered the park.
Sailors in the region learned to watch the sky for signs of inclement conditions, since sudden squalls could capsize small boats.
Because of the inclement winter, with blizzards arriving week after week, construction of the bridge fell months behind schedule.

label: adj.2
def: used of persons or behavior; showing no mercy

exs.t: Marcus Aurelius, though a fair man, was inclement to Christians during his reign, persecuting them violently.
Debtors who came before the inclement magistrate knew that pleading poverty was useless, since he sentenced even those who owed trifling sums to long terms in prison.
Unlike his forgiving father, the young king proved inclement toward rebels, refusing every plea for pardon and punishing entire villages for the acts of a few.
Students dreaded the inclement headmaster, who punished the slightest infraction severely and never once granted a reprieve.

def: necessary (for someone) as a duty or responsibility

exs.t: Middle managers at times make important decisions, but real responsibility for the financial well-being of the corporation is ultimately incumbent on the CEO.
Because Dr. Reyes was the senior physician on duty, it was incumbent on her to inform the family of the diagnosis, however painful the conversation.
Scholars who publish controversial claims should recognize that it is incumbent upon them to share their data, so that others can verify the results.
Once the city accepted the grant, it became incumbent on officials to report precisely how every dollar had been spent, a duty they could not ignore.

def: to formally charge or accuse of wrong-doing

exs.t: The bank robber was indicted on several major charges, including possession of a firearm.
After a lengthy investigation, the grand jury indicted the former treasurer on charges of embezzlement and filing false reports.
Prosecutors lacked sufficient evidence to indict the executive, so although suspicion lingered, he was never formally charged.
Because the statute of limitations had expired, the state could no longer indict the retired official, even though fresh evidence of his bribery had surfaced.

def: originating in a certain area

exs.t: The plants and animals indigenous to Australia are notably different from those indigenous to the U.S-- one look at a duckbill platypus and you know you're not dealing with an opossum.
The botanist catalogued plants indigenous to the valley, distinguishing them from species introduced by settlers in later centuries.
Rather than importing foreign stone, the architect built the museum from indigenous materials, using timber and slate quarried within a few miles.
Many indigenous languages of the region, spoken there long before colonization, now survive only among a few elderly speakers.

def: feeling anger over a perceived injustice

exs.t: When the cyclist swerved into traffic, it forced the driver to brake and elicited an indignant shout of "Hey, punk, watch where you're going!"
The scientist was indignant when a rival claimed credit for her discovery, and she promptly published her dated notebooks to prove her priority.
Customers grew indignant after learning that the airline had overbooked the flight and bumped them without compensation.
Far from accepting the unfair penalty quietly, the indignant player protested to the referee that he had never touched his opponent.

def: characterized by hard work and perseverance
