exs.t: Pete was an industrious student, completing every assignment thoroughly and on time.
The industrious apprentice rose before dawn each day, finishing her chores and practicing her craft long after the others had gone to bed.
Unlike her easygoing brother, Anna was industrious, turning the neglected family farm into a thriving business through years of relentless work.
Historians credit the town's prosperity to its industrious artisans, who labored tirelessly to produce textiles admired across the region.

def: extremely controversial, incendiary

exs.t: It only takes one person to leave an inflammable comment on an Internet thread for that thread to blow up into pages upon pages of reader indignation.
The editor refused to print the letter, judging its inflammable accusations likely to provoke riots in an already tense city.
Moderators quickly removed the inflammable post, whose insults toward a minority group had already sparked furious arguments in the forum.
Diplomats avoided the inflammable subject of the disputed border, fearing that even mentioning it might derail the fragile negotiations.

def: the power of creative imagination

exs.t: Daedalus was famous for his ingenuity; he was able to fashion his son Icarus with a pair of wings, using wax to hold them together.
With no spare parts available, the stranded crew relied on sheer ingenuity, fashioning a working filter from socks, charcoal and a plastic bottle.
The museum celebrates the ingenuity of medieval engineers, whose inventive use of pulleys and counterweights allowed them to raise enormous stones.
Faced with a tiny budget, the set designer displayed remarkable ingenuity, transforming cardboard and old curtains into a convincing palace.

def: a slight suggestion or vague understanding

exs.t: Lynne speaks four Romance languages, but she doesn't have an inkling about how East Asian languages are structured.
Until the letter arrived, Maria had no inkling that her grandfather had once been a celebrated violinist; he had never mentioned it.
The early experiments gave the researchers only an inkling of the compound's potential, a faint suggestion that would take years to confirm.
Although the plot twist seems obvious in hindsight, most readers have barely an inkling of the truth until the final chapter.

def: dull and uninteresting

exs.t: The movie director was known for hiring beautiful actors in order to deflect attention away from the insipid scripts he would typically use.
The critic found the film's dialogue insipid, a string of bland platitudes that failed to reveal anything about the characters.
The developer's insipid design, a beige box indistinguishable from a thousand others, drew yawns rather than objections from the planning board.
Although the band's early albums were daring and inventive, its later work struck reviewers as insipid, polished but utterly lacking in character.

def: unable to pay one's bills; bankrupt

exs.t: With credit card bills skyrocketing, a shockingly large number of Americans are truly insolvent.
Although the startup's product won several design awards, years of reckless borrowing left the company insolvent, and its creditors seized the warehouse to recover what they could.
Economists warned that if the city kept funding pensions through short-term loans, it would soon be insolvent, and its employees might one day find their paychecks bouncing.
In the novel, the once-wealthy merchant hides from his creditors, too proud to admit that he has become insolvent and can no longer settle even his tailor's bill.

def: stopping and starting at irregular intervals

exs.t: The intermittent thunder continued and the night was punctuated by cracks of lightning--a surreal sleepless night.
The rover's signal was intermittent, arriving in brief bursts separated by long, unpredictable silences that left the engineers anxious for hours at a time.
Because the drug's side effects were intermittent rather than constant, patients often failed to mention them to their doctors during routine appointments.
The composer punctuates the otherwise continuous string melody with intermittent brass chords, so that the listener never quite knows when the next interruption will come.

def: to flood or overwhelm

exs.t: The newsroom was inundated with false reports that only made it more difficult for the newscasters to provide an objective account of the bank robbery.
After the museum announced free admission for a single weekend, it was inundated with visitors, and the guards struggled to manage lines that wrapped around the block.
Rather than being ignored as she had feared, the young scholar found herself inundated with requests for interviews once her dissertation on urban migration was published.
When the levee failed, rising water inundated the low-lying farmland, submerging fields that had produced corn for generations.

def: quickly aroused to anger

exs.t: If Arthur's dog is not fed adequately, he becomes highly irascible, even growling at his own shadow.
The irascible conductor was notorious for hurling his baton at musicians over the slightest missed entrance, so new members of the orchestra approached rehearsals with dread.
Although his letters reveal a tender side, the philosopher was irascible in public, prone to sudden outbursts whenever a student questioned one of his premises.
Chronic pain had made the old sailor irascible; the most innocent question about the weather could provoke a torrent of angry complaint.

def: irritate or vex

exs.t: My little sister has a way of irking and annoying me like no other person.
What irked the reviewers most was not the novel's length but its author's habit of repeating the same point in nearly identical words every few chapters.
The constant interruptions during the budget meeting irked the director, who finally snapped that she would take no further questions until she had finished.
Although the delay was minor, it irks passengers to be told nothing about its cause, and many complained more about the silence than about the wait itself.

def: uncertain how to act or proceed

exs.t: He stood irresolute at the split in the trail, not sure which route would lead back to the camp.
The committee remained irresolute for months, unable to decide whether to renovate the aging library or demolish it, and meanwhile the roof continued to leak.
Unlike her decisive predecessor, the new manager was irresolute, reversing her instructions so often that employees began waiting a day before acting on any of them.
Faced with two equally attractive job offers, Daniel grew irresolute, writing and then deleting acceptance emails to each company throughout the night.

def: a characteristic language of a particular group

exs.t: To those with little training in medicine, the jargon of doctors can be very difficult to understand.
The consultant's report was so thick with financial jargon that the town council, composed mostly of teachers and shopkeepers, could make little sense of its recommendations.
Good science writers translate the jargon of specialists into plain English, so that readers without a laboratory background can follow the argument.
Within weeks of joining the software team, Priya had absorbed its jargon, casually tossing around acronyms and shorthand that had baffled her on her first day.

def: characterized by jokes and good humor

exs.t: My uncle was always in a jocular mood at family gatherings, messing up people's hair and telling knock- knock jokes to anyone who would listen.
Despite the gravity of the negotiations, the ambassador maintained a jocular manner, teasing his counterparts and telling anecdotes that eased the tension in the room.
The eulogy was surprisingly jocular, yet the mourners who laughed through it agreed that nothing could have captured the deceased's irreverent spirit more faithfully.
Readers who know the poet only through his somber elegies may be surprised by his jocular letters, which brim with puns and playful teasing of his friends.

def: a group, usually of military officers, that rules a country after seizing power

exs.t: As dangerous of a threat as North Korea is, some analysts believe that were a junta suddenly to gain power, it could be even more unpredictable and bellicose than the current leadership.
After the army overthrew the elected government, a junta of three generals ruled by decree, suspending the constitution and closing the independent newspapers.
The novel depicts a small island nation where a military junta, having seized power in a single night, struggles to convince the population that its rule is only temporary.
Diplomats hoped that sanctions would pressure the junta to restore civilian rule, but the colonels who had taken over showed no sign of relinquishing control.

def: characterized by effort to the point of exhaustion; especially physical effort

exs.t: The most laborious job I've had was working 20 hours a day as a fisherman in King Salmon, Alaska.
Before the invention of the printing press, copying a manuscript was a laborious process, requiring months of painstaking work by a single scribe.
Restoring the fresco proved far more laborious than the conservators expected: each square inch had to be cleaned by hand with tiny swabs over many exhausting months.
Although the new harvesting machine is expensive, farmers welcome it, since it replaces the laborious task of cutting and bundling the stalks by hand under the summer sun.

def: openly distrustful and unwilling to confide

exs.t: Without checking his references and talking to previous employers, I am leery of hiring the candidate.
Having been misled by glowing projections before, the investors were leery of the founder's promises and insisted on examining the company's books themselves.
Villagers who had watched earlier development schemes fail were understandably leery of the outsiders, answering their questions politely but revealing little.
Although the new treatment showed promise in early trials, many physicians remained leery of prescribing it until independent studies confirmed its safety.

def: lacking energy

exs.t: Nothing can make a person more lethargic than a big turkey dinner.
The heat wave left the entire office lethargic; even the most diligent employees spent the afternoon staring at their screens, too drained to begin new tasks.
Although the zoo's lions appear lethargic during the day, dozing for hours in the shade, they become far more active after sunset.
Economists described the recovery as lethargic: growth was sluggish, hiring was slow, and consumers seemed to lack the energy to spend.

def: (of language) transparently clear; easily understandable

exs.t: Though Walters writes about physics and time travel, his writing is always lucid, so readers with little scientific training can understand difficult concepts.
Although the subject is notoriously difficult, the textbook's lucid explanations allow first-year students to grasp statistical inference without confusion.
The lawyer's closing argument was admirably lucid, reducing a tangle of conflicting testimony to three simple points that every juror could follow.
Her early essays are dense and obscure, but her later work is lucid, as though she had finally learned to trust plain words to carry her meaning.

def: suggesting the horror of death and decay; gruesome

exs.t: Edgar Allen Poe was considered the master of the macabre; his stories vividly describe the moment leading up to--and often those moments after--a grisly death.
The exhibit on Victorian mourning customs held a macabre fascination for visitors, displaying jewelry woven from the hair of the dead alongside elaborate coffin fittings.
The painter's later canvases turned macabre, filled with grinning skulls, rotting fruit, and figures that seemed to be decaying before the viewer's eyes.
Although the story begins as a light comedy of manners, it takes a macabre turn when the guests discover a coffin hidden beneath the dining room floor.

def: a disease or sickness

exs.t: The town was struck by a malady throughout the winter that left most people sick in bed for two weeks.
Physicians of the era had no name for the malady that swept through the port each summer, though they noticed it struck hardest near stagnant water.
The essayist argues that loneliness is not merely a mood but a genuine malady, one that can undermine the body's health as surely as any infection.
Although the patient's symptoms suggested a rare tropical malady, tests eventually revealed a common infection that responded quickly to antibiotics.

def: wishing or appearing to wish evil to others; arising from intense ill will or hatred

exs.t: Villains are known for their malevolent nature, oftentimes inflicting cruelty on others just for enjoyment.
In the folktale, the kindly old woman turns out to be a malevolent witch who lures travelers into her cottage in order to do them harm.
The biographer rejects the view that the minister was malevolent; his disastrous policies, she argues, arose from incompetence rather than any desire to hurt his rivals.
Far from being a mere prank, the computer virus was malevolent by design, engineered to destroy hospital records and cause as much suffering as possible.

label: adj.1
def: capable of being shaped or bent or drawn out

exs.t: The clay became malleable and easy to work with after a little water was added.
Gold is so malleable that a single small nugget can be hammered into a sheet thin enough to let light pass through it without tearing.
Heated in the forge until it glowed, the iron became malleable enough for the blacksmith to bend it into an elaborate scroll for the garden gate.
Engineers chose aluminum for the panels because it is malleable, allowing the sheets to be pressed into curved shapes without cracking.

label: adj.2
def: easily influenced

exs.t: My little brother is so malleable that I can convince him to sneak cookies from the cupboard for me.
Advertisers target young children because their preferences are malleable, readily swayed by a catchy jingle or a cartoon mascot.
The dictator preferred malleable advisers who would echo his opinions, and he quietly dismissed anyone who dared to contradict him.
Research suggests that eyewitness recollections are surprisingly malleable: a single leading question from an investigator can alter what a witness believes she saw.

def: having an unpleasant smell

exs.t: Some thermally active fountains spew sulfur fumes--the air around them is sometimes so malodorous that many have to plug their noses.
The tannery was moved to the edge of town because its vats were so malodorous that residents complained of the stench from half a mile away.
Although the durian is prized for its creamy flesh, the fruit is so malodorous that some hotels forbid guests from bringing it inside.
When the sewage plant malfunctioned, a malodorous haze settled over the neighborhood, forcing residents to keep their windows shut despite the heat.

def: suggesting war or military life

exs.t: Americans tend to remember Abraham Lincoln as kindly and wise, not at all martial, despite the fact that he was involved in the fiercest war America has even fought.
The parade's martial music, with its pounding drums and brassy fanfares, seemed out of place at what was supposed to be a celebration of peace.
The new principal ran the school with an almost martial discipline, insisting that students march in straight lines and stand at attention when a teacher entered.
Although the statue commemorates a general, the sculptor avoided any martial imagery, depicting him without sword or uniform as a weary old man reading a letter.

def: a short saying expressing a general truth

exs.t: Johnson initially suggests that the secret to business can be summarized in a single maxim but then requires a 300-page book to explain exactly what he means.
The old investor lived by a simple maxim, 'never buy what you do not understand,' and he refused to touch any company whose business he could not explain.
Proverbs often contradict one another; for every maxim urging caution, such as 'look before you leap,' there is another that praises boldness.
The essay opens with a confident maxim about ambition and then spends twenty pages qualifying it until almost nothing of the original claim remains.

def: to wander aimlessly

exs.t: A casual observer might have thought that Peter was meandering through the city, but that day he was actually seeking out those places where he and his long lost love had once visited.
With no particular destination in mind, the tourists meandered through the old quarter, pausing wherever a courtyard or bookshop caught their eye.
The lecture meandered from Greek architecture to medieval farming to modern traffic laws, and by the end the students had no idea what its main point had been.
Rather than walking directly to the station, Ana meandered along the riverbank, content to let the afternoon drift by without any plan.

def: a deep, long-lasting sadness

exs.t: Hamlet is a figure of tremendous melancholy: he doesn't have a truly cheerful scene throughout the entire play.
A deep melancholy settled over the composer after his wife's death, and for years he wrote only slow, mournful pieces in minor keys.
Although the novel's characters laugh often, an undercurrent of melancholy runs through every chapter, as each of them mourns a life that might have been.
Travelers often describe a strange melancholy that overtakes them in abandoned towns, a lingering sorrow that persists long after they have left.

def: a wild, confusing fight or struggle

exs.t: After enduring daily taunts about my name, I became enraged and pummeled the schoolyard bully and his sycophantic friends in a brutal melee.
When the referee's disputed call ended the match, fans poured onto the field and a chaotic melee broke out, with dozens of people shoving and swinging at one another.
The painting depicts the battle not as an orderly clash of ranks but as a confused melee, in which soldiers can barely distinguish friend from foe.
What began as a polite argument over a parking space escalated into a melee involving half the street, and the police needed an hour to sort out who had struck whom.

def: to spellbind or enthrall

exs.t: The plot and the characters were so well developed that many viewers were mesmerized, unable to move their eyes from the screen for even a single second.
The pianist's performance mesmerized the audience; for nearly an hour no one coughed, whispered, or even shifted in their seats.
Children at the aquarium stood mesmerized by the jellyfish, watching the glowing creatures pulse through the dark water as if in a trance.
Some critics complain that the documentary's gorgeous aerial footage is meant to mesmerize viewers so thoroughly that they stop questioning its dubious claims.

def: a hater of mankind

exs.t: Hamilton had been deceived so many times in his life that he hid behind the gruff exterior of a misanthrope, lambasting perfect strangers for no apparent reason.
The novel's hero is a bitter misanthrope who retreats to a mountain cabin, convinced that every human being is fundamentally selfish and cruel.
Although the philosopher was often called a misanthrope, his letters reveal a man who despised not humanity itself but the vanity of the society around him.
After decades of watching colleagues betray one another for promotions, the retired diplomat had become a misanthrope, avoiding company and expecting the worst of everyone he met.

def: a person who breaks the law

exs.t: Come back you miscreant! yelled the woman who just had her purse stollen.
The mayor promised to install more streetlights so that the miscreants who had been vandalizing the park at night would have nowhere to hide.
In the colonial settlement, any miscreant caught stealing from the common storehouse was sentenced to months of hard labor on the fortifications.
The detective suspected that the burglaries were the work of a single miscreant, since each break-in followed exactly the same method.

def: a person who doesn't like to spend money (because they are greedy)

exs.t: Monte was no miser, but was simply frugal, wisely spending the little that he earned.
Although he owned three factories, the old miser heated only one room of his house and wore the same threadbare coat for decades, unwilling to part with a single coin.
The play satirizes a miser who hoards gold in a locked chest while his servants go hungry and his daughter is denied a dowry.
Neighbors assumed the reclusive widow was a miser, but after her death they learned she had quietly given a fortune to the local hospital.

def: a person who dislikes women in particular

exs.t: Many have accused Hemingway of being a quiet misogynist, but recently unearthed letters argue against this belief.
The critic argues that the poet was a misogynist, pointing to the contempt with which nearly every female character in his work is portrayed.
The club's rule barring women was defended as tradition, but many saw it as the legacy of a misogynist founder whose diaries ridicule women as unfit for serious conversation.
Although the philosopher was long dismissed as a misogynist, recent scholars note that he championed women's education at a time when few others did.

def: significant and important value

exs.t: Despite the initial hullabaloo, the play was of no great moment in Hampton's writing career, and within a few years the public quickly forgot his foray into theater arts.
Although the treaty was signed with little fanfare, it proved to be of great moment, reshaping trade in the region for the next century.
The committee spent hours on matters of little moment, such as the color of the letterhead, while the urgent question of the budget went undiscussed.
Few at the time recognized the discovery as an event of real moment; only decades later did historians see that it had transformed the practice of medicine.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: open to argument or debate; undecidable in a meaningless or irrelevant way

exs.t: Since the Board just terminated Steve as the CEO, what the finance committee might have thought of his proposed marketing plan for next year is now a moot point.
Whether the bridge should be painted blue or green became a moot question once engineers declared the structure unsafe and scheduled it for demolition.
Since the company had already gone bankrupt, the lawsuit over its advertising practices was moot, and the judge dismissed it without hearing arguments.
Whether the portrait is the artist's own work remains a moot point among scholars, who have argued over the brushwork for decades without reaching agreement.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: ill-tempered and not inclined to talk; gloomy

exs.t: After Stanley found out he was no longer able to go on vacation with his friends, he sat in his room morosely.
After losing the election, the candidate grew morose, retreating to his study and answering his aides' questions with sullen grunts.
Although she had been lively at dinner, Marta became morose on the drive home, staring out the window and ignoring every attempt at conversation.
The novel's narrator is a morose clerk whose sullen silences contrast sharply with the cheerful chatter of his coworkers.

def: to undergo dramatic change in a seamless and barely noticeable fashion

exs.t: The earnestness of the daytime talk shows of the 1970's has morphed into something far more sensational and vulgar: today guests actually standup and threaten to take swings at one another.
Over several decades, the small neighborhood bakery morphed into a regional chain, its transformation so gradual that longtime customers hardly noticed.
In the animated film, the villain's face slowly morphs into that of a wolf, each feature shifting so smoothly that viewers cannot pinpoint when the change occurred.
The protest began as a campaign against a single tax but gradually morphed into a broad challenge to the government's legitimacy, without any single moment marking the shift.

def: softened, subdued

exs.t: Helen preferred muted earth colors, such as green and brown, to the bright pinks and red her sister liked.
Unlike the garish murals downtown, the interior of the chapel was painted in muted grays and soft blues that invited quiet reflection.
The critics' response to the novel was muted: reviewers praised a few passages but showed none of the enthusiasm that had greeted the author's debut.
Through the thick walls of the recording studio, the traffic outside was reduced to a muted hum that the microphones barely picked up.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: stubbornly persistent in changing an opinion or action

exs.t: No number of pleas and bribes would get him to change his obdurate attitude.
Despite months of petitions and protests, the landlord remained obdurate, refusing even to discuss repairs to the crumbling building.
The general's obdurate insistence on a frontal assault, even after his officers presented evidence of its folly, cost the army dearly.
Diplomats hoped that economic pressure would soften the regime's position, but it proved obdurate, rejecting every compromise put forward.

def: showing a cheerful willingness to do favors for others

exs.t: Even after all his success, I found him to be accommodating and obliging, sharing with me his "secret tips" on how to gain wealth and make friends.
The hotel's obliging concierge not only recommended a restaurant but also called ahead to reserve a table and arranged a taxi for us.
Though I had expected the archivist to resent my endless requests, she was remarkably obliging, retrieving dozens of dusty boxes without a word of complaint.
Neighbors described the old man as obliging, and during any vacation on the street it was usually he who watered the plants, collected the mail, and fed the cats.

def: resistant to guidance or discipline; stubbornly persistent

exs.t: The coach suggested improvements Sarah might make on the balance beam, but she remained obstinate, unwilling to modify any of the habits that made her successful in the past.
The farmer coaxed, pulled and bribed with apples, but the obstinate mule refused to take a single step across the shallow stream.
Although the evidence against his theory had become overwhelming, the professor remained obstinate, clinging to his original conclusions and dismissing every critic.
Teachers found the boy obstinate rather than slow: he understood the lessons perfectly well but refused to complete any assignment he considered pointless.

def: marked by elaborate rhetoric and elaborated with decorative details

exs.t: The ornate Victorian and Edwardian homes spread throughout San Francisco are my favorite part of the city.
The architect rejected the ornate style of the previous century, stripping away carved garlands and gilded moldings in favor of clean, unadorned surfaces.
Readers accustomed to plain modern prose often find the novelist's ornate sentences exhausting, weighed down as they are with elaborate metaphors and nested clauses.
The ceremonial sword was far too ornate for battle; its hilt was encrusted with jewels and engraved with intricate hunting scenes.

def: seemingly contradictory but nonetheless possibly true

exs.t: That light could be both a particle and a wave seems paradoxical, but nonetheless, it is true.
It seems paradoxical that adding a new road can worsen traffic, yet planners have found that extra lanes often attract so many new drivers that congestion increases.
The philosopher's paradoxical claim that we are most free when we bind ourselves to rules puzzled his students until he illustrated it with the example of language.
Though it sounds paradoxical, some patients report feeling less anxious after learning a grim diagnosis, because certainty is easier to bear than doubt.

def: relating to the countryside in a pleasant sense

exs.t: Those who imagine America's countryside as a pastoral region are often disappointed to learn that much of rural U.S. is filled with cornfields extending as far as the eye can see.
The painting offers a pastoral vision of shepherds resting beneath oak trees, a far cry from the grimy industrial cities where most of its buyers lived.
Weary of the noise of the capital, the poet retreated to a pastoral village of meadows and grazing sheep, where he wrote his most tranquil verses.
The symphony's slow movement is pastoral in mood, evoking birdsong, flowing streams and gentle green hills rather than the storms of the preceding section.

def: treat condescendingly

exs.t: She says she genuinely wanted to help me, but instead she patronized me, constantly pointing out how I was inferior to her.
The tour guide patronized the visitors, explaining the simplest facts in a slow, exaggerated voice as though they were small children.
Although the senior partner meant to be encouraging, his habit of praising junior colleagues for 'trying so hard' made them feel patronized.
Critics accused the documentary of patronizing its rural subjects, portraying them as quaint and simple rather than as people capable of understanding their own lives.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: a lack of something

exs.t: There is a paucity of jobs hiring today that require menial skills, since most jobs have either been automated or outsourced.
The paucity of reliable records from the period means that historians must reconstruct daily life largely from a handful of letters and tax receipts.
Despite the paucity of rainfall, the desert farmers coaxed impressive harvests from the land by using ancient irrigation techniques.
Reviewers praised the film's visuals but lamented the paucity of genuine ideas in its script, which relied almost entirely on stock situations and cliches.

def: easily irritated or annoyed

exs.t: Our office manager is peevish, so the rest of us tip-toe around him, hoping not to set off another one of his fits.
Deprived of his afternoon nap, the toddler grew peevish, whining at every small frustration and pushing away the toys he usually loved.
The editor's peevish marginal notes, complaining about everything from comma placement to the font, made the author dread receiving her manuscripts back.
Long delays at the airport had made the passengers peevish, and the gate agent endured a steady stream of petty complaints about trivial inconveniences.

def: lasting an indefinitely long time; eternal; everlasting

exs.t: Even at the old-timers games, Stan Musial would get the loudest cheer: he was a perennial favorite of the fans there.
Flooding is a perennial problem in the delta; every generation builds new levees, and every generation watches the river overwhelm them.
Questions about the nature of justice are perennial, debated by ancient philosophers and modern jurists alike without ever being settled.
Although fashions in children's literature come and go, fairy tales remain perennial favorites, read aloud to children century after century.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: cause to continue

exs.t: If you do not let him do things for himself, you are merely perpetuating bad habits that will be even harder to break in the future.
Critics argue that the textbook perpetuates outdated stereotypes, repeating myths about immigrant groups that historians discredited decades ago.
By rewarding only short-term profits, the bonus system perpetuated the very risk-taking that had nearly ruined the firm.
The festival was founded to perpetuate the region's folk music, ensuring that songs once passed down orally would survive for future generations.

def: a right reserved exclusively by a particular person or group (especially a hereditary or official right)

exs.t: Even as the dishwasher at the French restaurant, Josh quickly learned that he had the perquisite of being able to eat terrific food for half the price diners would pay.
A chauffeured car was among the perquisites of the ambassador's office, along with an official residence and a generous entertainment allowance.
In feudal society, the right to hunt in the royal forests was a perquisite of the nobility; a commoner caught with a deer faced severe punishment.
When the company cut costs, executives lost many of the perquisites they had come to expect, including first-class travel and memberships at exclusive clubs.

def: having precise or logical relevance to the matter at hand

exs.t: While the salaries of the players might draw attention in the media, such monetary figures are not pertinent to the question of who plays the best on the field.
The judge ruled that the defendant's childhood was not pertinent to the charges and ordered the lawyer to limit his questions to the night of the crime.
Before the interview, the reporter gathered every pertinent document, discarding hundreds of pages that had no bearing on the story.
The student's essay was eloquent but rarely pertinent, drifting into anecdotes that had little to do with the question she had been asked.

def: disturb in mind or cause to be worried or alarmed

exs.t: Now that Henry is recovering from a major illnesses, he no longer lets the little trivialities, such as late mail, perturb him.
The captain's calm voice over the intercom did little to reassure the passengers, who were perturbed by the sudden drop in altitude.
Nothing seemed to perturb the veteran surgeon; even when alarms sounded in the operating room, she continued working with steady hands.
Reports of irregularities in the vaccine trial perturbed regulators, who immediately ordered an independent review of the data.

def: to read very carefully

exs.t: Instead of perusing important documents, people all too often rush to the bottom of the page and plaster their signatures at the bottom.
Before signing the lease, Hana perused every clause, underlining ambiguous phrases and noting questions to raise with the landlord.
Rather than skimming the report as his colleagues had, the auditor perused it line by line, and so he alone noticed the discrepancy in the third appendix.
Scholars who have perused the diaries closely argue that the poet's supposed breakdown was exaggerated by her early biographers.

def: to yearn for

exs.t: Standing forlornly by the window, she pined for her lost love.
Exiled to a remote island, the deposed king pined for the capital, writing letter after letter begging to be allowed to return.
Though she had longed to leave her small hometown, after a year in the crowded city Clara found herself pining for its quiet streets and familiar faces.
Months at sea, the sailors pined for fresh fruit and the company of their families, and they talked of little else during the long evenings.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: the highest point

exs.t: At its pinnacle, the Roman Empire extended across most of the landmass of Eurasia, a feat not paralleled to the rise of the British Empire in the 18th and 19th century.
Winning the national prize marked the pinnacle of her career; she never again produced work that earned such acclaim.
Many critics regard the cathedral as the pinnacle of Gothic architecture, since later builders, unable to surpass its soaring vaults, turned instead to heavier and less daring designs.
Although he had risen to the pinnacle of the legal profession, the judge often said he had been happier as a struggling young lawyer.

def: having an agreeably pungent taste

exs.t: The chef, with a mere flick of the salt shaker, turned the bland tomato soup into a piquant meal.
A squeeze of lime and a pinch of chili made the otherwise bland stew piquant, and the guests asked for second helpings.
The chef balances the richness of the pork with a piquant sauce of mustard, vinegar and pickled peppers that sharpens every bite.
Though some diners found the aged cheese too strong, others relished its piquant flavor, which lingered pleasantly on the tongue.

def: concise and full of meaning

exs.t: I enjoy reading the Daodejing for its pithy and insightful prose; it always gives me something to think about.
Rather than delivering a long speech, the departing senator offered a pithy farewell of two sentences that the audience quoted for years afterward.
The editor trimmed the rambling paragraph into a single pithy line that conveyed the argument more forcefully than the original page had.
Aphorisms endure because they are pithy: a handful of words can capture an insight that would take a philosopher chapters to explain.

def: a small amount (of money)

exs.t: Vinny's uncle beamed smugly about how he'd offered his nephew fifty dollars for his Harvard tuition; even twice the amount would have been a mere pittance.
The seamstresses worked twelve-hour days for a pittance, earning barely enough to buy bread and coal for their families.
The company offered the inventor a pittance for his patent, a sum that looked absurd once his device began earning millions.
Although the grant was a pittance compared with the budgets of large laboratories, it allowed the young researcher to buy the one instrument she needed.

def: not easily irritated

exs.t: Doug is normally placid, so we were all shocked to see him yelling at the television when the Mets lost the game.
The placid librarian listened to the patron's furious complaint without raising her voice, then calmly explained the late-fee policy once more.
Unlike his volatile brother, Tomas was placid by nature; delays, insults and broken appliances all failed to ruffle him.
Breeders prize the horse for its placid temperament, since it remains unbothered even amid the noise and crowds of a busy city street.

def: (of movement) slow and laborious

exs.t: Charlie may seem to run at a plodding pace, but he is an ultramarathoner, meaning he runs distances of up to 100 miles, and can run for ten hours at a stretch.
The old ox moved at a plodding pace, dragging the heavy cart up the muddy slope one slow, heavy step at a time.
Weighed down by their packs, the hikers fell into a plodding rhythm, their boots sinking deep into the snow with each weary stride.
The tortoise's plodding progress across the garden seemed hopeless, yet by evening it had reached the far wall.

def: a clever plan to turn a situation to one's advantage

exs.t: Dennis arranged an elaborate ploy, involving 14 different people lying for him in different situations, so that it could appear that he was meeting Mary completely by chance at the wedding reception.
The offer of a free trial was merely a ploy to collect customers' credit card numbers, which were then charged automatically once the month ended.
The general's retreat was a clever ploy: once the enemy pursued his troops into the narrow valley, his reserves closed in from both sides.
Some critics dismissed the author's announcement that this would be her final novel as a marketing ploy designed to boost sales.

def: an informal meeting or discussion

exs.t: Before the team takes the field, the coach always calls for a powwow so that he can make sure all the players are mentally in the right place.
Before presenting the proposal to the board, the designers held a quick powwow in the hallway to agree on who would answer which questions.
What was scheduled as a formal negotiation turned into a relaxed powwow over coffee, with both sides sketching ideas on napkins.
Every Friday afternoon the editors gather for an unstructured powwow, trading gossip and story ideas without an agenda or minutes.

def: fraught with danger

exs.t: People smoke to relax and forget their cares, but ironically, in terms of health risks, smoking is far more precarious than either mountain-climbing or skydiving.
The climbers' camp was perched on a precarious ledge, where a single misstep or a gust of wind could send them over the edge.
With no savings and a temporary job that could vanish without notice, the family's finances were precarious, one unexpected bill away from disaster.
The coalition government was precarious from the start, depending on the support of a small party that threatened to withdraw at every disagreement.

def: an example that is used to justify similar occurrences at a later time

exs.t: The principal explained that even though one student had done modelling work outside of school, the outfits that student wore in those photographs in no way established a precedent for what could be worn at school dances.
The judge's ruling set a precedent that later courts cited repeatedly when deciding similar disputes over digital privacy.
Administrators refused the student's request for an extension, fearing that it would create a precedent that every other student could then invoke.
Lacking any precedent for such a case, the tribunal had to reason from general principles rather than from earlier decisions.

def: take the place of or have precedence over

exs.t: A governmental warning about an imminent terrorist attack would preempt ordinary network programming on television.
Under the new treaty, national law preempts any conflicting provincial regulation, so local rules on pesticide use no longer apply.
The chief executive's surprise announcement preempted the rest of the agenda; the board set aside its planned discussion and spent the afternoon on the merger.
Urgent repairs to the roof preempted the museum's plans for a new wing, consuming the funds originally set aside for expansion.

def: done before someone else can do it

exs.t: Just as Martha was about to take the only cookie left on the table, Noah preemptively swiped it.
Anticipating criticism of the delay, the mayor issued a preemptive statement blaming the contractor before any reporter could raise the issue.
Suspecting that a rival firm was about to lure away her best engineer, the director made a preemptive offer of a promotion and a raise.
The chess player's preemptive advance on the queen's side prevented her opponent from launching the attack he had been preparing for several moves.

label: n.1
def: an assumption that is taken for granted

exs.t: When Mr. Baker found out the family car was gone, he acted under the presumption that his rebellious son had taken the car, calling his son's phone and yelling at him; only later did Mr. Baker realize that Mrs. Baker had simply gone out to get her nails d.
The study challenges the presumption that older workers are less adaptable, showing that they learn new software as quickly as their younger colleagues.
The legal system operates on the presumption of innocence: a defendant need not prove anything, since the burden falls entirely on the prosecution.
Early astronomers worked under the presumption that the heavens were perfect and unchanging, so the appearance of a new star in the sky astonished them.

label: n.2
def: audacious (even arrogant) behavior that you have no right to

exs.t: The new neighbor quickly gained a reputation for her presumption; she had invited herself to several of the neighbors homes, often stopping over at inopportune times and asking for a drink.
The courtier's presumption in addressing the queen by her first name shocked the assembled nobles, who waited to see how she would punish his insolence.
She was astonished at his presumption: having met her only once, he had already announced their engagement to his friends.
The junior clerk had the presumption to rewrite his supervisor's report without asking, and he was promptly reprimanded for overstepping his role.

def: excessively forward

exs.t: Many felt that Barney was presumptuous in moving into the large office before the management even made any official announcement of his promotion.
The campaign manager warned her overconfident staff that it would be presumptuous to plan a victory celebration before a single vote had been counted.
The graduate student's presumptuous critique of the eminent professor, delivered uninvited at their very first meeting, left the room in stunned silence.
Though he meant only to help, the guest struck his hosts as presumptuous when he rearranged their kitchen cabinets on his first evening in the house.

label: v.1
def: be widespread in a particular area at a particular time; be current

exs.t: During the labor negotiations, an air of hostility prevailed in the office.
In the years after the war, a mood of cautious optimism prevailed, and families spent freely on new homes and appliances.
The custom of arranged marriage still prevails in some rural districts, although it has largely disappeared from the cities.
The belief that illness was caused by bad air prevailed among physicians for centuries, until microscopes revealed the role of microorganisms.

label: v.2
def: prove superior

exs.t: Before the cricket match, Australia was heavily favored, but India prevailed.
Although the underdog team was outmatched in size and experience, it prevailed in overtime, stunning the favored champions.
In the long legal battle between the inventor and the corporation, the inventor eventually prevailed, winning both the patent and substantial damages.
The debate grew heated, but in the end the cautious faction prevailed over the ambitious one, and the committee voted to postpone the expansion.

label: adj.1
def: unspoiled, untouched (usually of nature)

exs.t: The glacial lake was pristine and we filled our canteens to drink deeply.
The expedition found the valley pristine, and the surveyors, who had grown used to clear-cut slopes and polluted streams elsewhere, could scarcely believe no one had ever settled there.
Conservationists fought to keep the remote coral reef pristine, banning fishing boats and tourists from its most fragile sections.
Once pristine, the coastline is now lined with hotels and parking lots, and its wetlands have been drained for development.

label: adj.2
def: immaculately clean and unused

exs.t: Drill sergeants are known for demanding pristine cabinets, uniforms, and beds, and often make new recruits clean and clean and clean until they meet the expected high standards.
Although the novel was printed a century ago, the collector's copy is pristine, its pages crisp and its binding uncracked as though no one had ever opened it.
The rental agency demanded that the apartment be returned in pristine condition, and it deducted fees for even the faintest scuff on the walls.
The chef insisted that every knife and cutting board be pristine before service began, and he sent back any utensil bearing the faintest smudge.

def: plentiful; pouring out in abundance

exs.t: During mile 20 of the Hawaii Marathon, Dwayne was sweating so profusely that he stopped to take off his shirt, and ran the remaining six miles wearing nothing more than skimpy shorts.
The actor's profuse apologies for arriving late seemed excessive; he spent more time apologizing than the delay had actually cost.
After the spring rains, the blossoms on the hillsides were so profuse that the grass beneath them was barely visible from the road.
The patient's profuse sweating alarmed the nurse, who noticed that his sheets were soaked through within a few minutes.

def: the property of being extremely abundant

exs.t: When Maria reported that she had been visited by Jesus Christ and had proof, a profusion of reporters. and journalists descended on the town.
The market offered a dazzling profusion of spices, from saffron and cardamom to dozens of chili varieties the visitors had never seen.
The Baroque chapel is decorated with a profusion of gilded angels, carved flowers and painted clouds, leaving hardly an inch of wall unadorned.
Rather than a scarcity of data, modern researchers face a profusion of it, and the challenge lies in separating meaningful signals from noise.

def: a person who pleads for a cause or propounds an idea

exs.t: Ironically, the leading proponent of Flat-Earth Theory flies all over the world in an effort to win more adherents.
A leading proponent of renewable energy, the engineer spent decades urging legislators to fund wind and solar research.
Although she was once a vocal proponent of the plan, the council member turned against it after learning of its true cost.
Proponents of the four-day workweek argue that it improves productivity, while critics warn that it may strain small businesses.

def: under terms not final or fully worked out or agreed upon

exs.t: Until the corporate office hands down a definitive decision on use of the extra offices, we will share their use in a provisional arrangement.
The rebels formed a provisional government to run the country until elections could be held and a permanent constitution drafted.
The committee reached a provisional agreement on the budget, but members stressed that several details remained to be negotiated.
Scientists regard every theory as provisional, subject to revision or even abandonment should new evidence contradict its predictions.

def: eager to fight or argue; verbally combative

exs.t: The comedian told one flat joke after another, and when the audience started booing, he pugnaciously spat back at them, "Hey, you think this is easy -- why don't you buffoons give it a shot?"
The pugnacious senator seemed to relish every confrontation, interrupting opponents and challenging them to debate at every opportunity.
Although he was mild-mannered at home, the critic was pugnacious in print, attacking rival scholars with a ferocity that shocked his readers.
The little terrier was absurdly pugnacious, snarling at dogs five times its size and lunging at anyone who approached the gate.

def: uneasiness about the fitness of an action

exs.t: While he could articulate no clear reason why Harkner's plan would fail, he nevertheless felt qualms about committing any resources to it.
The accountant had no qualms about reporting her employer's fraud, even though she knew that speaking up might cost her the job.
Despite his qualms about the ethics of the experiment, the young researcher agreed to take part, silencing his conscience with the promise of a publication.
Voters who had once supported the project began to express qualms after reports suggested that its environmental impact had been underestimated.

def: state of uncertainty or perplexity especially as requiring a choice between equally unfavorable options

exs.t: Steve certainly is in a quandary: if he doesn't call Elaine, she will blame him for everything, but if he does call her, the evidence of where he currently is could cost him his job.
The doctor faced a quandary: the only drug that might save the patient could also trigger a fatal allergic reaction.
Offered a promotion that required moving far from her aging parents, Leila found herself in a quandary, unable to accept or refuse without regret.
Rising sea levels have placed the island nation in a painful quandary, forced to choose between seawalls it cannot afford and abandoning its coastal towns.

def: a witty saying or remark

exs.t: In one of the most famous quips about classical music, Mark Twain said: "Wagner's music is better than it sounds."
Asked whether he was nervous before the debate, the candidate replied with a quip about having survived far tougher audiences at family dinners, and the reporters laughed.
Her lectures were dry and technical, but an occasional quip about the absurdities of academic life kept the students awake.
The novelist was famous for his quips at dinner parties, though friends noted that many of his supposedly spontaneous witticisms had been rehearsed in advance.

def: marked by a carefree unconventionality or disreputableness

exs.t: The men found him raffish, but the women adored his smart clothes and casual attitude.
The poet cultivated a raffish image, wearing rumpled velvet jackets, keeping disreputable company and paying his debts only when pressed.
The neighborhood had a raffish charm, with its dimly lit jazz clubs, secondhand bookshops and bohemian residents who ignored the conventions of polite society.
His conservative parents disapproved of his raffish friends, a band of gamblers and struggling actors who stayed out until dawn.

def: a large number of something

exs.t: Despite a raft of city ordinances passed by an overzealous council, noise pollution continued unabated in the megalopolis.
The new administration introduced a raft of reforms, from changes in tax policy to an overhaul of the school curriculum.
The drug's approval was delayed after regulators raised a raft of concerns about side effects, dosage, and the design of the clinical trials.
A raft of recent studies has challenged the notion that bilingual children are slower to speak, finding instead that they reach milestones at the same pace.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: marked by a carefree unconventionality or disreputableness

exs.t: As soon as he arrived in the city, the rakish young man bought some drugs and headed straight for the seedy parts of town.
With his hat tilted at a rakish angle and his reputation for gambling and dueling, the young officer was the despair of respectable mothers.
The novel's rakish hero drinks, duels, and runs up debts across Europe, yet readers cannot help being charmed by his careless wit.
Although she was raised in a strict household, Julia was drawn to rakish companions whose disregard for convention and propriety thrilled her.

def: gnaw into; make resentful or angry

exs.t: His constant whistling would rankle her, sometimes causing her to leave in a huff.
Years after the contest, it still rankled the runner-up that the judges had awarded first prize to a close friend of the organizer.
The committee's decision to ignore her research rankled, and she spent months composing a detailed and indignant rebuttal.
Small slights, left unaddressed, can rankle for decades; the historian traces the bitter feud between the two families to a single unreturned greeting.

def: marked by defiant disregard for danger or consequences; imprudently incurring risk

exs.t: Although Bruce was able to make the delivery in time with a nighttime motorcycle ride in the rain, Susan criticized his actions as rash.
Investing his entire savings in a company he had read about only that morning was a rash decision, and he regretted it within the week.
The general urged patience, warning that a rash attack across the open field would expose his troops to devastating fire.
Although critics called the explorer rash for crossing the ice without a guide, she had in fact studied the route for years.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: an act of making something right

exs.t: Barry forgot his wife's birthday two years in a row, and was only able to redress his oversight by surprising his wife with a trip to Tahiti.
The workers who had been injured by the faulty machinery sought redress in court, demanding compensation for their medical bills and lost wages.
When the airline lost her luggage, Emma spent weeks seeking redress, but the company offered only a voucher that barely covered a new toothbrush.
The commission was established to provide redress for families whose land had been seized without payment decades earlier.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: assign to a lower position

exs.t: When Dexter was unable to fulfill his basic duties, instead of firing him, the boss relegated him to kitchen cleanup.
Once the star of the rotation, the aging pitcher was relegated to the bullpen, appearing only in games whose outcome had already been decided.
Early historians relegated women's contributions to footnotes, treating them as marginal to the main story of the era.
After the new model arrived, the old computer was relegated to a corner of the storeroom, where it gathered dust.

def: to be negligent in one's duty

exs.t: Remiss in his duty to keep the school functioning efficiently, the principle was relieved of his position after only three months.
The inspector was remiss in his duties, signing off on the building's wiring without ever actually examining it.
At the ceremony, the director said she would be remiss not to thank the volunteers, whose unpaid labor had made the entire festival possible.
Although the hospital's staff worked tirelessly, its administrators had been remiss, neglecting to replace outdated equipment despite repeated warnings.

def: fail to fulfill a promise or obligation

exs.t: We will no longer work with that vendor since it has reneged on nearly every agreement.
After promising to fund the new library, the council reneged, diverting the money to road repairs and leaving the architects unpaid.
Voters grew cynical when the governor reneged on his pledge not to raise taxes, introducing a new levy on fuel within six months of taking office.
Having signed the contract, the publisher could not easily renege, though executives privately regretted the enormous advance they had agreed to pay.

def: completely stocked or furnished with something

exs.t: Only weeks after the hurricane made landfall, the local supermarket shelves were replete with goods, so quick was the disaster relief response.
The anthology is replete with forgotten masterpieces, poems that had languished unread in obscure journals for more than a century.
The ship's hold was replete with provisions for the long voyage: barrels of salted meat, casks of water, and sacks of flour stacked to the ceiling.
Far from being a dry legal document, the treaty is replete with poetic flourishes and elaborate expressions of goodwill.

def: a person who is disapproved of

exs.t: Those old reprobates drinking all day down by the river--they are not going to amount to much.
The town regarded the old gambler as an incorrigible reprobate, and mothers warned their sons never to visit his card games.
In the novel, the heroine's family disowns her brother as a reprobate after he squanders the inheritance and is jailed for fraud.
Although the press painted the defendant as a reprobate with no redeeming qualities, several witnesses described his generosity toward the poor.

def: an unstated doubt that prevents you from accepting something wholeheartedly

exs.t: I was initially excited by the idea of a trip to Washington, D.C. but now that I have read about the high crime statistics there, I have some reservations.
Although the committee approved the design, several members expressed reservations about its cost, and the vote was far from unanimous.
She accepted the job offer without reservation, confident that the position was exactly what she had been seeking for years.
Critics admired the film's visual ambition but had reservations about its ending, which seemed to undercut everything that came before.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: the acceptance of something unpleasant that can't be avoided

exs.t: Since Jack could not think of a convincing reason why he had to miss the seminar, he attended it with a sense of resignation.
When the doctor explained that nothing more could be done, the old farmer received the news with quiet resignation, thanking her and turning to gaze at his fields.
Rather than protesting the new rules, the employees greeted them with weary resignation, having learned long ago that complaints changed nothing.
The poems of her final years show not despair but resignation: she writes of failing eyesight and absent friends calmly, as facts to be lived with rather than fought.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: reach a conclusion after a discussion or deliberation

exs.t: After much thought, Ted resolved not to travel abroad this summer because he didn't have much money in his bank account.
After weeks of debate, the council resolved to postpone construction until an independent study of its environmental impact was complete.
Having nearly missed her flight twice, Nadia resolved never again to leave her packing until the last minute.
The delegates argued late into the night before they finally resolved that the organization would admit new members only by unanimous vote.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: a pause from doing something (as work)

exs.t: Every afternoon, the small company has a respite in which workers play foosball or board games.
The brief cease-fire gave the exhausted villagers a respite from the shelling, allowing them to repair their roofs and gather supplies.
For the overworked nurses, the quiet hour before dawn offered a welcome respite, a chance to sit down with coffee before the next wave of patients arrived.
The heat wave continued for weeks without respite, and residents began sleeping on rooftops in search of any cooler air.

def: to be shy, and to be inclined to retract from company

exs.t: Nelson was always the first to leave soirees--rather than mill about with "fashionable" folk, he was retiring, and preferred the solitude of his garret.
Although her novels are bold and outspoken, the author herself had a retiring disposition, rarely granting interviews and slipping away from parties early.
By temperament retiring, the young scholar let his colleagues present their joint findings, content to sit unnoticed at the back of the lecture hall.
Guests were surprised that the host, so retiring in everyday life, gave such a confident speech; normally he avoided even small talk with his neighbors.

def: pull inward or towards a center; formally reject or disavow a formerly held belief, usually under pressure

exs.t: Email is wonderfully efficient, but once something awkward or damaging has been sent, there is no way to retract it.
Faced with evidence that the data had been fabricated, the journal retracted the article and issued an apology to its readers.
Under intense pressure from the authorities, the astronomer publicly retracted his claim, though many suspected he privately held the same view.
When threatened, the snail retracts its soft body into its shell and remains there, motionless, until the danger has passed.

def: cause annoyance in; disturb, especially by minor irritations

exs.t: Dan is usually calm and balanced, but it takes only one intense glare from Sabrina to rile him.
The umpire's questionable calls riled the home crowd, and by the ninth inning spectators were hurling insults at the field.
Few things rile the patient old professor more than students who check their phones while he is explaining a difficult proof.
Although the proposed fee was small, it riled local merchants, who saw it as one more petty annoyance imposed by a distant bureaucracy.

def: sturdy and strong in form, constitution, or construction

exs.t: Chris preferred bland and mild beers, but Bhavin preferred a beer with more robust flavor.
Designed to survive rough seas, the research vessel was robust enough to withstand waves that would have capsized a lighter ship.
Despite his age, the farmer remained robust, lifting heavy sacks of grain and working from dawn until dusk without apparent fatigue.
Unlike the fragile economy of its neighbor, the country's economy proved robust, weathering the global downturn with only a mild slowdown.

def: making a show of being pious; holier-than-thou

exs.t: Even during the quiet sanctity of evening prayer, she held her chin high, a sanctimonious sneer forming on her face as she eyed those who were attending church for the first time.
The minister's sanctimonious lectures on thrift rang hollow once reporters discovered his own lavish spending on private jets.
Readers find the narrator insufferably sanctimonious, forever congratulating himself on his virtue while condemning the moral failings of his neighbors.
Although she genuinely cared about the environment, Leah tried not to sound sanctimonious when discussing it, knowing that preaching tends to alienate listeners.

def: cheerful; optimistic

exs.t: With the prospect of having to learn 3,000 words during the course of the summer, Paul was anything but sanguine.
Despite the poor early returns, the campaign manager remained sanguine, insisting that the late-reporting districts would swing the election in their favor.
Economists are less sanguine than the government about the recovery, warning that rising debt could halt growth within a year.
Having survived several previous crises, the veteran captain was sanguine about the storm, cheerfully assuring the passengers that they would reach port by morning.

label: n.
def: a perceptive understanding

exs.t: Although a great CEO, he did not have the political savvy to win the election.
The young director lacked experience but not savvy, and she quickly learned which producers could be trusted and which would undercut her.
It took real financial savvy to recognize that the struggling company's patents were worth far more than its share price suggested.
Although the candidate had impressive credentials, critics doubted that she possessed the media savvy needed to handle hostile interviewers.

label: v.
def: get the meaning of something

exs.t: The student savvies the meaning of astrophysics with little effort.
The foreman rattled off the procedure in rapid slang and then asked, 'Savvy?', and the new hire nodded, though in truth he had understood almost nothing.
The trapper spoke little English, but he savvied enough of the traders' gestures and broken phrases to grasp that they wanted furs in exchange for rifles.
The jokes at the market turned on dialect puns, and the visiting reporter, who didn't savvy half of them, laughed a beat late to hide his confusion.

label: adj.
def: well-informed or perceptive

exs.t: With his savvy business partner, the company was able to turn a profit within a year.
Savvy travelers book their flights well in advance and avoid peak seasons, often paying half of what less informed passengers spend.
The museum's savvy curator anticipated which young artists would become famous and acquired their work while it was still inexpensive.
Though she had no formal training in politics, the mayor proved remarkably savvy, reading the mood of the council and timing her proposals perfectly.

def: describes someone who is brilliant and lively

exs.t: Richard Feynman was renowned for his scintillating lectures--the arcana of quantum physics was made lucid as he wrote animatedly on the chalkboard.
The host was a scintillating conversationalist, darting from art to astronomy to gossip with a wit that kept her guests enthralled until midnight.
Although his books are dry, the historian is scintillating in person, and students crowd his seminars for the sheer brilliance of his improvised arguments.
The dinner was expected to be dull, but a scintillating young physicist enlivened the evening with quick-witted, dazzling stories about her research.

def: an abusive rant (often tedious)

exs.t: Joey had difficulty hanging out with his former best friend Perry, who, during his entire cup of coffee, enumerated all of the government's deficiencies--only to break ranks and launch into some screed against big business.
Instead of a reasoned review, the critic published a screed, three thousand words of invective against the novel, its publisher, and anyone who had enjoyed it.
The neighbor's letter to the editor was a rambling, angry screed about parking regulations that the newspaper printed only to fill space.
Far from offering a balanced history, the book is a screed, relentlessly attacking the author's rivals while ignoring any evidence that complicates her thesis.

def: effusively or insincerely emotional, especially in art, music, and literature

exs.t: I don't like romanticism for the same reason I don't like melodramatic acting and soap operas--overly sentimental.
The film's ending is shamelessly sentimental: swelling violins, a tearful reunion, and a dog racing across a meadow to greet its long-lost owner.
Unlike the sentimental verse popular in her day, which wallowed in tears and deathbed scenes, her poems treat grief with restraint and irony.
Critics dismissed the painter's portraits of wide-eyed orphans as sentimental, arguing that they manipulated viewers' emotions rather than revealing anything true.

def: the instance in which an accidental, fortunate discovery is made

exs.t: The invention of the 3M Post It Note was serendipitous, because the scientist who had come up with the idea was looking for a strong adhesive; the weak adhesive he came up with was perfect for holding a piece of paper in place but made it very easy for someone to pull the paper free.
Many scientific breakthroughs owe as much to serendipity as to planning; a contaminated culture or a misread instrument can reveal something no one was looking for.
By sheer serendipity, the archivist searching for a tax record stumbled upon a lost letter from the city's founder tucked between its pages.
Some urban planners argue that cities should be designed for serendipity, with crowded sidewalks and mixed uses that invite unplanned but fruitful discoveries.

def: calm and peaceful

exs.t: I'd never seen him so serene; usually, he was a knot of stress and anxiety from hours of trading on the stock exchange.
Despite the chaos in the terminal around her, the elderly woman remained serene, knitting calmly as flight after flight was canceled.
The monastery's garden is serene, its raked gravel and still pond offering visitors a refuge from the clamor of the city.
In the portrait, the queen's expression is serene, betraying none of the anxiety that historians know she felt during that turbulent year.

def: carelessly and hastily put together

exs.t: The office building had been constructed in a slapdash manner, so it did not surprise officials when, during a small earthquake, a large crack emerged on the façade of the building.
The report was so slapdash that it misspelled the client's name, repeated entire paragraphs, and cited figures from the wrong year.
Unlike the careful restoration of the east wing, the repairs to the west wing were slapdash, completed in a single weekend with mismatched bricks and sloppy mortar.
The editor rejected the article not for its argument but for its slapdash research, which relied on unverified sources and hastily copied quotations.

def: a slight or superficial understanding of a subject; a small amount of something

exs.t: I know only a smattering of German, but Helen is able to read German newspapers and converse with natives.
He had only a smattering of Latin, enough to recognize a few legal phrases but nowhere near enough to read the classical authors.
The lecture hall, which usually overflows, held only a smattering of students on the Friday before the holiday.
Though the novel's setting is exotic, the author displays little more than a smattering of knowledge about the region, relying on cliches rather than genuine research.

def: marked by excessive complacency or self-satisfaction

exs.t: When Phil was dating the model, he had a smug attitude that annoyed his buddies.
Having predicted the market crash, the analyst wore a smug expression throughout the meeting, reminding colleagues at every turn that he had warned them.
The team's smug confidence after its early lead proved costly, as its players relaxed and allowed the underdogs to score three late goals.
Critics found the essay smug, its author so pleased with his own cleverness that he never seriously considered opposing views.

def: expressive of contempt; derogatory or mocking in an indirect way

exs.t: The chairman interpreted Taylor's question about promotions as a snide remark, but in all innocence Taylor was trying to figure out the company's process.
Rather than criticizing the proposal openly, the manager made snide remarks about 'ambitious newcomers,' leaving everyone to guess whom he meant.
The reviewer's snide aside, praising the actor for 'remembering most of his lines,' hurt more than an outright attack would have.
Although the columnist claimed to admire her rival, her snide insinuations about the rival's sources suggested a very different attitude.

def: refuse to acknowledge; reject outright and bluntly

exs.t: Wheeler was completely qualified for the committee, but the board snubbed him, choosing an obviously lesser qualified candidate instead.
The celebrated novelist snubbed the literary festival, declining its invitation without explanation and appearing at a rival event the same weekend.
At the reception, the ambassador pointedly snubbed his counterpart, turning his back when she offered her hand in greeting.
Although the academy snubbed the film, awarding it no prizes at all, audiences embraced it and it became the year's most popular release.

def: involving ignoble actions and motives; arousing moral distaste and contempt; foul and run-down and repulsive

exs.t: The nightly news simply announced that the senator had had an affair, but the tabloid published all the sordid details of the interaction.
The biography exposes the sordid dealings behind the tycoon's fortune: bribes, blackmail and the betrayal of his closest partners.
The detective's search led him to a sordid rooming house, its hallways reeking of mildew and its walls stained with years of grime.
Readers expecting a romantic tale of adventure were dismayed by the novel's sordid portrait of greed, in which every character acts from the basest motives.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: one who spends money extravagantly

exs.t: Taking weekly trips to Vegas, Megan was a spendthrift whose excesses eventually caught up to her.
Having inherited a vast fortune, the young spendthrift squandered it within a decade on racehorses, yachts, and lavish parties.
Critics called the council a spendthrift with public money, noting that it had bought marble fountains while the schools lacked textbooks.
Unlike her frugal sister, who saved every spare coin, Rosa was a spendthrift, buying whatever caught her eye and worrying about the bills later.

def: reject with contempt

exs.t: She spurned all his flattery and proposals, and so he walked off embarrassed and sad.
The proud artist spurned the wealthy patron's offer, declaring that he would rather starve than paint portraits to flatter the rich.
Spurned by the established journals, whose editors dismissed her as an untrained amateur, the young mathematician published her proof in an obscure newsletter, where it went unnoticed for years.
The union spurned management's final offer as insulting, and its members voted overwhelmingly to continue the strike indefinitely.

def: spend thoughtlessly; waste time, money, or an opportunity

exs.t: Fearing his money would be squandered by his family, he gave all of it to charity when he died.
The team squandered a ten-point lead in the final minutes, missing easy shots and turning the ball over repeatedly.
By squandering the windfall from oil exports on grand monuments, the government left nothing for schools or roads when prices collapsed.
Teachers lamented that the gifted student was squandering his talent, spending his evenings idly rather than practicing the violin he had once loved.

def: characterized by dignity and propriety

exs.t: Frank came from a staid environment, so he was shocked that his college roommate sold narcotics.
The staid old bank, with its marble columns and soft-spoken clerks, seemed an unlikely place for the daring investment strategy the new director proposed.
Readers accustomed to the staid tone of the previous editor were startled when the magazine's next issue appeared full of irreverent essays and bold graphics.
Although the professor was staid in the lecture hall, never raising his voice or departing from his notes, his friends knew him as a lively storyteller at dinner.

def: to suddenly move in a particular direction

exs.t: All alone in the mansion, Henrietta started when she heard a sound.
The deer started at the snap of a twig and bounded into the forest before the photographer could raise her camera.
Dozing over his books, the student started violently when the librarian tapped his shoulder, knocking his coffee across the table.
When the door slammed behind her, Mei started and dropped her keys, her heart pounding from the sudden noise.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: marked by firm determination or resolution; not shakable

exs.t: A good captain needs to be steadfast, continuing to hold the wheel and stay the course even during the most violent storm.
Through years of ridicule from his colleagues, the physician remained steadfast in his belief that handwashing could prevent infections.
The small nation's steadfast neutrality, maintained even when powerful neighbors pressured it to take sides, earned it respect as a mediator.
Her friends drifted away when her business failed, but her brother was steadfast, lending her money and visiting every week until she recovered.

def: to hold back or limit the flow or growth of something

exs.t: To stem the tide of applications, the prestigious Ivy requires that each applicant score at least 330 on the Revised GRE.
To stem the spread of the invasive beetle, officials banned the transport of untreated firewood across county lines.
The central bank raised interest rates sharply in an effort to stem inflation, which had been eroding workers' savings for months.
Nothing seemed able to stem the flood of complaints once customers learned that their personal data had been exposed.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: a regular allowance (of money)

exs.t: He was hoping for a monthly allowance loan from the government, but after no such stipend was forthcoming he realized he would have to seek other means of paying for his college tuition.
Graduate students receive a modest stipend each month, enough to cover rent and groceries but little else besides.
The foundation awarded the young poet a yearly stipend so that she could devote herself to writing without taking a second job.
Although the volunteer position offered no salary, participants received a small weekly stipend to cover travel and meals.

def: having or revealing little emotion or sensibility; not easily aroused or excited

exs.t: Elephants may appear stolid to casual observers, but they actually have passionate emotional lives.
The stolid guard stared straight ahead, his face betraying no reaction even as tourists shouted jokes and waved cameras inches from his nose.
The detective's stolid manner, unmoved by tears or threats alike, unnerved suspects who expected either sympathy or anger.
Although the townspeople seemed stolid to visitors, rarely laughing or showing surprise, they celebrated their harvest festival with remarkable exuberance.

def: hinder or prevent the progress or accomplishment of

exs.t: The engineers found their plans stymied at every turn and were ultimately able to make almost no progress on the project.
The investigation was stymied by missing records, and the auditors could not trace where the funds had gone.
A shortage of skilled workers has stymied the city's plan to rebuild its bridges, leaving several projects years behind schedule.
Every attempt to reform the tax code was stymied by lobbyists, who found ways to block the proposals before they reached a vote.

label: n.1
def: the peak or highest point

exs.t: After hiking for two days, the climbers finally reached the summit of Mount Kilimanjaro.
From the summit, the climbers could see three countries spread out below them, their borders invisible from such a height.
The trail grows steeper and rockier near the summit, and many hikers turn back within sight of the top.
Snow lingered on the mountain's summit well into July, long after the valleys below had turned green and the lower slopes were covered in wildflowers.

label: n.2
