def: a meeting of high-level leaders

exs.t: Since climate change policy has been mired in congressional fighting, this summit should help set the goals for president's next term.
Leaders of the neighboring nations met at a three-day summit to negotiate a treaty on sharing the river's water.
The summit ended without a joint statement, as the presidents could not agree on how to respond to the refugee crisis.
Ahead of the economic summit, finance ministers from each country met privately to draft proposals for their heads of state to sign.

def: inclined to anger or bad feelings with overtones of menace

exs.t: Every morning, Bhavin was a surly unhappy person, but once he ate breakfast, he became loving, laughing, and a joy to be around.
The surly ferryman answered every question with a scowl and a growl, as if the passengers had personally insulted him.
After a sleepless night, the usually genial chef was surly, snapping at his assistants and slamming pots onto the stove.
The waiter's surly manner, all glares and muttered threats about the kitchen's closing time, drove customers to the restaurant across the street.

def: consideration in dealing with others and avoiding giving offense

exs.t: In a tremendous display of tact, Shelly was able to maintain a strong friendship with Marcia, even though Marcia's husband, Frank, confessed to finding Shelley more attractive than Marcia.
Delivering bad news to patients requires great tact, since a single careless word can deepen a frightened family's anxiety and grief.
The diplomat's tact was legendary: she could refuse a request so gracefully that the other party left feeling flattered.
Lacking tact, the new manager told the team bluntly that their previous work had been worthless, and several employees resigned within the month.

def: make dirty or spotty, as by exposure to air; also used metaphorically

exs.t: Pete Rose was one of the best baseball players of his generation, but his involvement with gambling on baseball games has tarnished his image in the eyes of many.
Exposure to damp air had tarnished the silver candlesticks, and the housekeeper spent an afternoon polishing them back to a shine.
A single plagiarism scandal tarnished the historian's reputation, and even his earlier, scrupulously honest work came under suspicion.
The company's image, once synonymous with reliability, was tarnished by a series of embarrassing product recalls and lawsuits.

def: tastelessly showy; cheap and shoddy

exs.t: Carol expected to find New York City magical, the way so many movies had portrayed it, but she was. surprised how often tawdry displays took the place of genuine elegance.
The once elegant hotel had become tawdry, its lobby filled with plastic flowers, flickering neon, and cheap souvenir stands.
Critics dismissed the musical as a tawdry spectacle, all glitter and sequins with no genuine artistry beneath the surface.
Rather than the refined jewelry she had expected, the shop offered only tawdry trinkets that lost their shine within days.

def: use to the limit; exhaust

exs.t: The hike to the summit of Mt. Whitney was so taxing that I could barely speak or stand up.
Caring for a newborn while finishing her dissertation proved so taxing that Mariam slept barely four hours a night for months.
The final exam was less taxing than the students had feared; most finished within an hour and left the room relaxed.
Although the route is short, the climb is taxing, with steep switchbacks that leave even experienced hikers gasping for breath.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: significant and revealing of another factor

exs.t: Her unbecoming dress was very telling when it came to her sense of fashion.
The most telling detail in the letter is not what the general wrote but what he omitted: any mention of the soldiers he had lost.
It was telling that the company's founder sold all his shares a week before the scandal broke, and investigators took note.
Her hesitation before answering the question about her previous employer was telling, and the interviewers began to suspect she had been dismissed.

def: revealing

exs.t: The many telltale signs of chronic smoking include yellow teeth, and a persistent, hacking cough.
The telltale smell of smoke in the hallway alerted the tenants to the fire long before any alarm sounded.
Tree rings bear telltale marks of past droughts, allowing scientists to reconstruct centuries of climate history from a single trunk.
Although the forger was skillful, a telltale anachronism, a pigment not invented until decades after the painter's death, exposed the canvas as a fake.

def: offer up something formally

exs.t: The government was loath to tender more money in the fear that it might set off inflation.
Following the scandal, the minister tendered her resignation, though the premier persuaded her to stay until a successor was found.
The company tendered an offer to buy all outstanding shares at a premium, hoping to win control before rivals could organize.
At the close of the negotiations, the envoy tendered his government's apology, reading it aloud before the assembled delegates and then presenting a signed copy to their chair.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: very thorough; complete

exs.t: As a thoroughgoing bibliophile, one who had turned his house into a veritable library, he shocked his friends when he bought a Kindle.
The new director ordered a thoroughgoing reform of the agency, replacing its leadership, rewriting its rules and closing half its regional offices.
Far from a superficial revision, the second edition is a thoroughgoing reworking of the text, with nearly every chapter rewritten from scratch.
A thoroughgoing skeptic, the philosopher doubted not only religious claims but also the reliability of his own senses and memory.

def: spending money wisely

exs.t: He was economical, spending his money thriftily and on items considered essential.
Thrifty shoppers wait for end-of-season sales, buying winter coats in spring at a fraction of their original price.
Raised by thrifty parents who repaired everything rather than replacing it, Elena was appalled by her roommates' habit of throwing away barely worn clothes.
Although the town's budget was small, its thrifty council managed to build a new library by reusing materials from the old courthouse.

def: hinder or prevent (the efforts, plans, or desires) of

exs.t: I wanted to spend a week in New York this autumn, but the high costs of travel and lodging thwarted my plans.
The engineers had designed the levee to withstand a century of storms, but an unforeseen shift in the riverbed thwarted their efforts within a decade.
Although the reformers enjoyed broad public support, a handful of entrenched committee chairs managed to thwart the bill by refusing even to schedule a hearing.
The detective's patient surveillance finally thwarted the forger's scheme: every counterfeit canvas was seized before it could reach the auction house.

def: an angry speech

exs.t: In terms of political change, a tirade oftentimes does little more than make the person speaking red in the face.
Rather than offering the measured critique the editors expected, the reviewer delivered a tirade, denouncing the novelist's prose as lazy, dishonest, and unworthy of print.
The coach's furious halftime tirade, in which he berated each player by name for a full ten minutes, left the team more rattled than motivated.
Though the professor usually answered objections with calm patience, a student's accusation of plagiarism provoked a furious tirade that silenced the seminar.

def: advertise in strongly positive terms; show off

exs.t: At the conference, the CEO touted the extraordinary success of his company's Research & Development division.
The pharmaceutical firm touted its new drug as a breakthrough, yet the published trials showed only a marginal improvement over existing treatments.
Real estate brochures routinely tout a property's 'charming character,' praising as a virtue what often turns out to be cramped rooms and aging plumbing.
Eager to attract investors, the startup's founders touted every modest milestone in glowing press releases, as if each were a triumph of engineering.

def: lasting a very short time

exs.t: If we lived forever and life was not transitory, do you think we would appreciate life less or more?
The economist cautioned that the spike in consumer spending was transitory, driven by a one-time tax rebate rather than by any lasting rise in wages.
Unlike the cathedral's stone, which has endured for centuries, the sand mandala is deliberately transitory: the monks sweep it away soon after completing it.
Critics dismissed the fashion for minimalist interiors as transitory, predicting that ornament would return as soon as the novelty wore off.

def: use of physical or mental energy; hard work; agony or anguish

exs.t: While they experienced nothing but travails in refinishing the kitchen, they completed the master bedroom in less than a weekend.
The biography chronicles the composer's travails in exile: poverty, illness, and years of rejection by publishers who had once courted him.
After months of travail in the archives, deciphering faded ledgers line by line, the historian finally reconstructed the merchant's trading network.
Far from the effortless genius of legend, the painter's letters reveal constant travail, with each canvas reworked dozens of times before she was satisfied.

def: something, especially an event, that causes difficulty and suffering

exs.t: As of 2013, nearly 1.5 million Syrians have fled their country hoping to escape the tribulations of a civil war tearing their country to pieces.
The memoir recounts the tribulations of a family of immigrant farmers: failed harvests, crushing debt, and a flood that swept away their only barn.
Despite the many tribulations of the expedition, including frostbite and a lost supply cache, the team completed its survey of the glacier.
Every generation of settlers on the frontier faced some fresh tribulation, so the town's founders came to regard hardship as the ordinary condition of life.

def: a state of chaos, noise and confusion

exs.t: Riots broke out just in front of our apartment building, and the tumult continued late into the night.
When the verdict was announced, the courtroom erupted into tumult, with reporters shouting questions and spectators pushing toward the doors.
The composer deliberately follows the movement's opening tumult, all clashing brass and pounding drums, with a passage of almost unbearable stillness.
Amid the tumult of the trading floor, where hundreds of brokers were shouting orders at once, the young clerk could barely hear his own thoughts.

def: suggesting the operation of supernatural influences; surpassing the ordinary or normal

exs.t: Reggie has an uncanny ability to connect with animals: feral cats will readily approach him, and sometimes even wild birds will land on his finger.
The forger possessed an uncanny talent for mimicry; even the museum's experts could not distinguish his copies from the originals.
Visitors to the abandoned lighthouse often report an uncanny sense of being watched, though no one has lived there for decades.
The novelist has an uncanny ability to anticipate social trends: themes she explored years ago now seem to describe the present with eerie precision.

def: not making concessions

exs.t: The relationship between Bart and Hilda ultimately failed because they were both so uncompromising, never wanting to change their opinions.
An uncompromising architect, she refused every request from the developers to cheapen the materials, even when it meant losing the commission.
Rather than softening his findings to placate the funding agency, the scientist published an uncompromising report that confirmed every alarming result.
Negotiations collapsed because both delegations remained uncompromising: neither would yield an inch on the disputed water rights.

def: unreasonable; unscrupulous; excessive

exs.t: The lawyer's demands were so unconscionable that rather than pay an exorbitant sum or submit himself to any other inconveniences, the defendant decided to find a new lawyer.
Consumer advocates argued that the lender's interest rates were unconscionable, since borrowers could end up repaying several times what they had borrowed.
The judge voided the contract as unconscionable, noting that it stripped the tenant of nearly every right while imposing no obligations on the landlord.
Delaying the vaccine shipment merely to raise its price struck even the company's own board as unconscionable, and the executive responsible was dismissed.

def: to support financially

exs.t: The latest symphony broadcast was made possible with underwriting from the Carnegie Endowment.
A consortium of local banks agreed to underwrite the restoration of the old opera house, covering costs that the city could no longer afford.
Because a wealthy patron underwrote the expedition, the archaeologists could spend an entire season excavating without worrying about their budget.
The foundation declined to underwrite the documentary, so the filmmakers had to finance it themselves through years of freelance work.

def: to make nervous or upset

exs.t: At one time unnerved by math problems, she began avidly "Magoosh-ing", and soon became adept at even combinations and permutations questions.
The candidate had rehearsed every answer, yet the interviewer's long, unblinking silences unnerved her so much that she began to stammer.
Seasoned climbers are rarely unnerved by heights, but the sudden crack of the ice shelf beneath them left even the guide visibly shaken.
Nothing seemed to unnerve the veteran diplomat: while his aides panicked over the leaked memo, he calmly drafted a reply.

def: having never been done or known before; novel

exs.t: When America first created its national parks, the idea of setting aside the most beautiful land in a country was unprecedented in the history of mankind.
The drought was unprecedented in the region's recorded history; not even the oldest farmers could remember the river running completely dry.
When the museum allowed visitors to handle the original manuscripts, curators elsewhere called the decision unprecedented and, in some cases, reckless.
The treaty granted the small nation an unprecedented degree of autonomy, a privilege that no colonial territory had ever before received.

def: (of persons) noisy and lacking in restraint or discipline; unwilling to submit to authority

exs.t: Walk in to any preschool and I am sure that you will find an unruly and chaotic scene--unless it's nap time.
The substitute teacher, faced with an unruly class that ignored every instruction, finally abandoned the lesson plan and sent for the principal.
Although the crowd began peacefully, it grew unruly as the evening wore on, and stewards had to remove spectators who were throwing bottles onto the field.
Early parliaments were often unruly assemblies in which members shouted down speakers and openly defied the chair's calls for order.

def: not in keeping with accepted standards of what is right or proper in polite society

exs.t: He acted in an unseemly manner, insulting the hostess and then speaking ill of her deceased husband.
Mourners found it unseemly that the heirs began arguing over the estate before the funeral service had even ended.
The official's eagerness to accept lavish gifts from contractors struck many observers as unseemly, even though no law had technically been broken.
In the rigidly formal court, it was considered unseemly for a courtier to laugh aloud or to turn his back on the king.

def: showing a high degree of refinement and the assurance that comes from wide social experience

exs.t: Because of his service as an intelligence officer and his refined tastes, W. Somerset Maugham became the inspiration for the urbane and sophisticate spy James Bond.
Unlike his provincial cousins, who were awkward at formal dinners, the diplomat was urbane, gliding effortlessly between conversations in four languages.
The essayist's urbane wit, polished through years in the salons of several capitals, made even his harshest criticisms sound gracious.
Though raised on a remote farm, she had become thoroughly urbane after decades abroad, as comfortable discussing opera as negotiating a contract.

def: devoid of intelligence, matter, or significance

exs.t: To the journalist's pointed question, the senator gave a vacuous response, mixing a few of his overall. campaign slogans with platitudes and completely avoiding the controversial subject of the question.
The advertisement's vacuous slogans promised 'excellence' and 'innovation' without saying a single concrete thing about the product.
Critics praised the lead actor's performance but found the script vacuous, a series of glossy scenes with no discernible ideas beneath them.
The student's vacuous answers, which merely repeated each question in slightly different words, convinced the examiners that he had not read the assigned texts.

def: come out better in a competition, race, or conflict

exs.t: For years, Argentina would dominate in World Cup qualifying matches, only to be vanquished by one of the European countries during the late stages of the tournament.
The underdog chess player vanquished the reigning champion in only twenty moves, stunning commentators who had predicted an easy defeat for her.
Although the rebel army was vastly outnumbered, it vanquished the imperial forces by luring them into a narrow mountain pass.
Having vanquished every rival bidder, the company now controlled the only railway line through the valley.

def: the quality of varying

exs.t: The cynic quipped, "There is not much variance in politicians; they all seem to prevaricate".
Researchers were surprised by the variance in patients' responses to the drug: some recovered within days, while others showed no improvement at all.
Because the vineyard's soil changes so markedly from one row of vines to the next, there is considerable variance in the flavor of grapes picked only yards apart.
Critics of standardized curricula warn that eliminating variance among schools would also eliminate the experimentation that produces better teaching methods.

def: covering consisting of a thin superficial layer that hides the underlying substance

exs.t: Mark Twain referred to the Victorian Period in America as the "Gilded Age", implying the ample moral corruption that lay beneath a mere veneer of respectability.
Beneath the firm's veneer of prosperity, with its marble lobby and lavish parties, lay a mountain of unpaid debt.
The diplomat's courtesy was only a veneer; in private negotiations he proved ruthless and contemptuous of his counterparts.
The novel exposes the thin veneer of civility in a small town, where polite greetings conceal decades of feuds and resentments.

def: felt or undergone as if one were taking part in the experience or feelings of another

exs.t: The advent of twitter is a celebrity stalker's dream, as he or she can--through hundreds of intimate "tweets"--vicariously live the life of a famous person.
Unable to travel because of her illness, she took vicarious pleasure in her grandson's letters from abroad, savoring every description of the places he visited.
Some psychologists argue that sports fans derive a vicarious sense of achievement from their team's victories, as if they themselves had been on the field.
Parents who push their children into careers they themselves abandoned may be seeking vicarious fulfillment rather than serving the child's interests.

def: compete for something

exs.t: While the other teams in the division actively vie for the championship, this team seems content simply to go through the motions of playing.
Three architectural firms vied for the commission to design the new library, each submitting elaborate models to the city council.
In the crowded market for electric cars, dozens of startups now vie with established manufacturers for the attention of cautious buyers.
As the aging king's health declined, his nephews began to vie for the loyalty of the nobles, each hoping to secure the throne.

def: to have a very strong desire for revenge

exs.t: Though the other girl had only lightly poked fun of Vanessa's choice in attire, Vanessa was so vindictive that she waited for an entire semester to get the perfect revenge.
Rather than forgiving the critic who had panned her debut, the novelist grew vindictive, mocking him by name in every book she published afterward.
The deposed minister's vindictive campaign against his former colleagues, whom he blamed for his downfall, eventually alienated even his supporters.
Historians note that the victors' terms were vindictive rather than prudent: designed to punish the defeated nation, they instead bred lasting resentment.

def: an ill-tempered or violent woman

exs.t: Poor Billy was the victim of the virago's invective--she railed at him for a good 30-minutes about how he is the scum of the earth for speaking loudly on his cellphone in public.
In the play, the landlady is portrayed as a virago who berates her tenants at the slightest provocation and once hurls a teapot at a lodger.
Contemporary pamphlets caricatured the outspoken duchess as a virago, exaggerating her occasional sharp words into a reputation for constant rage.
The villagers avoided the miller's wife, a notorious virago whose furious outbursts could be heard across the square.

def: very hungry; approaching an activity with gusto

exs.t: Steven was a voracious reader, sometimes finishing two novels in the same day.
A voracious collector, the banker filled three warehouses with paintings, manuscripts, and antique instruments, yet was always hunting for more.
After the long winter, the bears emerged voracious, stripping berry bushes and raiding campsites in their search for food.
Her appetite for languages was voracious: by the time she finished graduate school, she had learned Greek, Arabic, Persian, and Russian.

def: without check or limitation; showing no moral restraints to one's anger, desire, or appetites

exs.t: Due to wanton behavior and crude language, the drunk man was thrown out of the bar and asked to never return.
The invading soldiers engaged in wanton destruction, burning libraries and smashing statues that had no military value whatsoever.
The court condemned the factory owners' wanton disregard for safety, noting that they had ignored repeated warnings about the crumbling walls.
Moralists of the period denounced the courtier's wanton extravagance, since he indulged every appetite while the peasants on his estates went hungry.

def: to gradually increase in size or intensity

exs.t: Her enthusiasm for the diva's new album only waxed with each song; by the end of the album, it was her favorite CD yet.
As the campaign against the tax wore on, public anger only waxed, and by autumn the protests had spread to every major city.
The composer's reputation waned after his death but waxed again a century later, when conductors rediscovered his forgotten symphonies.
Interest in the obscure philosopher has been waxing steadily among graduate students, whose dissertations now cite him more often than ever.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: determined by impulse or whim rather than by necessity or reason

exs.t: Adults look to kids and envy their whimsical nature at times, wishing that they could act without reason and play without limitation.
The dictator's whimsical decrees, issued without consultation and often reversed within days, left his ministers unable to plan anything.
Rather than follow a systematic research agenda, the eccentric chemist pursued whimsical lines of inquiry, abandoning each one the moment a new idea struck him.
The garden's layout appears whimsical, with paths that wander aimlessly, but the designer insists that every curve was carefully calculated.

def: the highest point; culmination

exs.t: At the zenith of his artistic career, Elvis was outselling any other artist on the charts.
At the zenith of its power, the trading city controlled nearly every port along the coast; within a century, however, it had faded into obscurity.
Critics regard the late quartets as the zenith of the composer's achievement, the culmination of decades of experimentation.
The company reached its zenith in the year it bought out its largest rival; after that, a series of poor decisions sent it into steady decline.

def: formally reject or give up (as a belief)

exs.t: While the church believed that Galileo abjured the heliocentric theory under threat of torture, he later wrote a book clearly supporting the theory.
Upon entering the monastery, the young nobleman abjured his inheritance and every worldly pleasure, vowing before the abbot to live in poverty.
Under pressure from the inquisitors, the philosopher publicly abjured his heretical doctrines, though his private letters suggest he never ceased to hold them.
The former militant has abjured violence entirely, and he now travels to schools to warn students against the ideology he once embraced.

def: revoke formally

exs.t: As part of the agreement between the labor union and the company, the workers abrogated their right to strike for four years in exchange for better health insurance.
The new government abrogated the treaty its predecessor had signed, declaring that the agreement had been negotiated under duress.
When the legislature abrogated the old licensing law, small vendors who had been barred from the market for years were suddenly free to trade.
Critics argued that the emergency decree effectively abrogated citizens' right to assemble, since it banned all public gatherings indefinitely.

def: to serve as a judge in a competition; to arrive at a judgment or conclusion

exs.t: Only those with the most refined palates were able to adjudicate during the barbeque competition.
A panel of three retired judges was appointed to adjudicate the dispute between the neighboring towns over water rights.
Having been asked to adjudicate the regional piano competition, the conservatory professor listened to forty performances before announcing the winners.
International courts often lack the power to adjudicate border conflicts effectively, since sovereign states may simply refuse to accept their rulings.

def: provide with an opportunity

exs.t: The summit of Mt. Kilimanjaro affords a panoramic view that encompasses both Tanzania and Kenya.
The residency affords young composers a rare chance to hear their works performed by a professional orchestra before they are published.
Because the archive was only recently opened, it affords historians an unusual glimpse into the private deliberations of the council.
The balcony of the old observatory affords a sweeping prospect of the harbor, which is why painters have long set up their easels there.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: an eager willingness to do something

exs.t: The first three weeks at his new job, Mark worked with such alacrity that upper management knew it would be giving him a promotion.
The interns accepted the challenging assignment with alacrity, volunteering to stay late even before the supervisor had finished explaining it.
Expecting resistance to the new policy, the manager was surprised by the alacrity with which the staff embraced it.
She answered the invitation to lecture abroad with such alacrity that her colleagues suspected she had been hoping for it for years.

def: something that is inappropriate for the given time period (usually something old)

exs.t: Dressed in 15th century clothing each day, Edward was a walking anachronism.
The historical film was riddled with anachronisms: Roman soldiers wore wristwatches, and a medieval peasant casually referred to germs.
In a firm that had long since digitized its records, the elderly clerk's handwritten ledger seemed a charming anachronism.
Critics argue that the hereditary title is an anachronism, a relic of feudal privilege with no place in a modern democracy.

def: a detested person; the source of somebody's hate

exs.t: Hundreds of years ago, Galileo was anathema to the church; today the church is anathema to some on the left side of the political spectrum.
To the purist chefs of the old school, frozen ingredients were anathema; they would sooner close the restaurant than serve a thawed fish.
The very idea of borrowing money was anathema to my grandfather, who had watched his own father ruined by debt.
Once celebrated as a reformer, the minister became anathema to his party after he voted with the opposition, and former allies refused even to speak his name.

def: lacking energy and vigor

exs.t: After three straight shows, the lead actress gave an anemic performance the fourth night, barely speaking loudly enough for those in the back rows to hear.
Despite heavy investment in advertising, the company's sales remained anemic, barely rising above the previous year's disappointing figures.
Critics found the orchestra's anemic rendition of the symphony puzzling, since the same players had performed it with fire only a month before.
Economists blamed the country's anemic recovery on weak consumer confidence, which kept households from spending even as interest rates fell.

label: n.
def: something that soothes or relieves pain

exs.t: Muzak, which is played in department stores, is intended to be an anodyne, but is often so cheesy and over-the-top that customers become irritated.
For the grieving widow, gardening became an anodyne, a quiet routine that dulled the ache of loss when nothing else could.
Before modern pharmaceuticals, physicians relied on herbal preparations as their chief anodyne, prescribing them for everything from toothaches to broken bones.
The philosopher regarded music as an anodyne for the anxieties of modern life, recommending an hour of Bach to any student tormented by worry.

label: adj.
def: inoffensive

exs.t: Wilbur enjoyed a spicy Mexican breakfast, but Jill preferred a far more anodyne meal in the mornings.
Hoping to offend no one, the committee approved an anodyne mission statement so vague that it could have described almost any organization.
Although the comedian was once known for provocative material, his recent routines have become anodyne, carefully avoiding any subject that might stir controversy.
The press secretary's anodyne remarks about 'continuing dialogue' revealed nothing and ruffled no one, which was precisely their purpose.

def: ludicrously odd

exs.t: The clown's antic act was too extreme for the youngest children, who left the room in tears.
The play's antic humor, with actors tumbling over furniture and speaking in absurd rhymes, delighted children but baffled some older critics.
Though the scholar was solemn in his lectures, his letters reveal an antic streak: he signed them with invented titles and doodled ridiculous animals in the margins.
The film's antic energy, all pratfalls and absurd chases, gives way in the final act to an unexpectedly somber meditation on grief.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: great coolness and composure under strain

exs.t: Nancy acted with aplomb during dangerous situations--she once calmly climbed up an oak tree to save a cat.
When the power failed midway through her keynote address, the speaker continued with aplomb, finishing her talk by lamplight as if nothing had happened.
The young pilot handled the engine failure with remarkable aplomb, calmly guiding the aircraft to a safe landing while passengers panicked.
Though the negotiators across the table grew openly hostile, the ambassador responded with aplomb, never raising her voice or losing her train of thought.

def: the highest point

exs.t: The apogee of the Viennese style of music, Mozart's music continues to mesmerize audiences well into the 21st century.
The empire reached its apogee under its third ruler; thereafter, costly wars and internal feuds brought about a long decline.
Many critics consider the novel the apogee of the author's career, the point at which her experiments with form finally achieved full mastery.
At the apogee of the speculative frenzy, investors paid absurd sums for shares in companies that had never earned a profit; within months, the market collapsed.

def: a person who has abandoned a religious faith or cause

exs.t: An apostate of the Republican Party, Sheldon has yet to become affiliated with any party and dubs himself an independent.
Once the movement's most zealous preacher, he became an apostate after witnessing its leaders' corruption, and he spent his later years writing against them.
The community treated the apostate harshly, refusing to trade with a woman who had publicly renounced the faith of her ancestors.
To the party loyalists, the economist was an apostate: having abandoned the free-market doctrines he once championed, he now advocated sweeping regulation.

def: a short, pithy instructive saying

exs.t: Winston Churchill is famous for many apothegms, but this might be his most famous: "It has been said that democracy is the worst form of government except all the others that have been tried."
The old sea captain was fond of apothegms, and his favorite, 'a calm sea never made a skilled sailor,' was repeated to every new recruit.
The philosopher's notebooks contain few sustained arguments; instead, they are filled with terse, memorable maxims, each apothegm distilling a lesson on friendship, death, or virtue.
Rather than deliver a lengthy lecture on thrift, my grandmother offered a single apothegm that has guided me ever since: 'Mend today, spare tomorrow.'

def: exaltation to divine status; the highest point of development

exs.t: As difficult as it is to imagine, the apotheosis of Mark Zuckerberg's career, many believe, is yet to come.
The ceiling fresco depicts the apotheosis of the slain hero, who rises through the clouds to take his place among the gods.
Many critics regard the cathedral as the apotheosis of Gothic architecture, the culmination of centuries of refinement in vaulting and stained glass.
Within a generation of his death, the general had undergone a kind of apotheosis: statues of him filled every town square, and schoolchildren recited his sayings as if they were scripture.

def: expressing praise or approval

exs.t: Although it might not be her best work, Hunter's new novel has received generally approbatory reviews.
The committee's approbatory letter commended the young scientist for work that, in its words, had transformed the field.
Although the director had braced himself for scathing reviews, the notices were almost uniformly approbatory, and within a week the theater had extended the play's run.
Her usually stern mentor offered only an approbatory nod, but from him even that small gesture felt like lavish praise.

label: v.1
def: to give or take something by force

exs.t: The government appropriated land that was occupied by squatters, sending them scurrying for another place to live.
The occupying army appropriated the farmers' grain and livestock without compensation, leaving the villages to face the winter with nothing.
Critics accused the regime of having appropriated church lands under the pretext of reform, seizing property that had been held for centuries.
The lawsuit arose when the larger firm appropriated the startup's patented design without permission and began selling it as its own.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

label: v.2
def: to allocate

exs.t: The committee appropriated the funds to its various members.
Each year the legislature appropriates a portion of the state budget for the maintenance of rural roads and bridges.
Because the council had appropriated too little for snow removal, the city ran out of road salt in the middle of January.
The university appropriated a separate fund for graduate fellowships, ensuring that research assistants would be paid even if grant money dried up.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: belonging to something as an accessory or supporting part

exs.t: In hiking Mt. Everest, sherpas are appurtenant, helping climbers both carry gear and navigate treacherous paths.
The deed conveyed not only the farmhouse but also the barns and water rights appurtenant to it, which the buyers regarded as essential to working the land.
The main hospital performs the surgeries, while the appurtenant clinics supply the follow-up care and rehabilitation that support each patient's recovery.
In the orchestra's plan, the smaller chamber ensembles were appurtenant to the main ensemble, supplementing its season with educational concerts in local schools.

def: to be deliberately teasing

exs.t: The baroness was arch, making playful asides to the townspeople; yet because they couldn't pick up on her dry humor, they thought her supercilious.
He shrugged off her insults because he knew she was only being arch.
Her arch reply to the pompous critic, delivered with a raised eyebrow and a faint smile, made it clear she was mocking him without ever saying so.
Readers who take the narrator at face value miss the joke, for his tone is arch throughout, and his solemn promises about the ending are made only to be slyly broken.
Though the professor seemed stern, his arch asides during lectures, playful jabs at famous theorists, revealed a mischievous sense of humor.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: complete and wholly (usually modifying a noun with negative connotation)

exs.t: An arrant fool, Lawrence surprised nobody when he lost all his money in a pyramid scheme that was every bit as transparent as it was corrupt.
The reviewer dismissed the supposed memoir as arrant nonsense, pointing out that half of its episodes could not possibly have occurred.
Only an arrant coward would abandon his wounded comrades to save himself, the sergeant declared before the court-martial.
Calling the hastily drafted plan a strategy was arrant flattery; in truth, it was little more than a list of wishes.

def: a person who has recently reached a position of power; a social climber

exs.t: The city center was aflutter with arrivistes who each tried to outdo one another with their ostentatious sports cars and chic evening dress.
The old aristocratic families sneered at the arriviste, whose fortune from railway shares had bought him a mansion but not their acceptance.
Eager to prove she belonged among the city's elite, the arriviste threw extravagant parties and dropped famous names constantly, which only confirmed the established families' disdain.
The novel satirizes an arriviste who, having recently clawed his way into the cabinet, flaunts his new power with petty displays of authority.

def: seize and control without authority

exs.t: Arriving at the small town, the outlaw arrogated the privileges of a lord, asking the frightened citizens to provide food, drink, and entertainment.
Without consulting the board, the new director arrogated to herself the power to hire and fire staff, a privilege the bylaws reserved for the trustees.
Historians note that the general gradually arrogated civilian authority, first controlling the press and then dissolving the elected assembly.
The committee chair was accused of arrogating decisions that belonged to the full membership, announcing policies that no one else had approved.

def: cunning tricks used to deceive others

exs.t: The mayoral candidates both spent much of the campaign accusing each other of artifices designed to mislead the voting public.
The swindler's artifice was elaborate: forged letters, a rented office, and a staff of actors who posed as satisfied investors.
Wary of diplomatic artifice, the negotiator insisted that every promise be written into the treaty rather than trusting the envoy's charming assurances.
Far from being spontaneous, the executive's tearful apology was pure artifice, rehearsed for days with a team of public relations consultants.

def: without cunning or deceit

exs.t: Despite the president's seemingly artless speeches, he was a skilled and ruthless negotiator.
The child's artless questions exposed contradictions that the adults had tactfully ignored for years, precisely because she had no idea that such things were not supposed to be asked.
Unlike the polished testimony of the other witnesses, the farmer's account was artless and plainly sincere, which is why the jury believed him.
Some readers mistake the poet's artless voice for naivete, but her utter lack of pretense is precisely what gives the poems their honesty.

def: the quality of innocence

exs.t: I, personally, found the artlessness of her speech charming.
The novelist captures the artlessness of her young heroine, who says exactly what she thinks and cannot imagine that anyone would lie to her.
Voters found the candidate's artlessness refreshing; unlike his rehearsed rivals, he admitted mistakes openly and never seemed to calculate his answers.
What the court mistook for cunning was in fact artlessness: the defendant had simply signed whatever papers his trusted accountant placed before him.

def: harshness of manner

exs.t: The editor was known for his asperity, often sending severe letters of rejection to amateur writers.
The judge rebuked the lawyer with such asperity that the courtroom fell silent and the attorney's face turned crimson.
Although her letters to friends were warm, the critic wrote about untalented playwrights with an asperity that made her reviews feared throughout the theater world.
The mediator's gentle manner stood in sharp contrast to the asperity of the two parties, who addressed each other only in curt, cutting phrases.

def: with care and persistence

exs.t: The top college football program recruits new talent assiduously, only choosing those who were the top in their county.
The graduate student assiduously checked every citation in her dissertation, spending weeks in the library to ensure that no source was misquoted.
Having assiduously cultivated relationships with local farmers over many years, the chef could obtain produce that no competitor could match.
Though the restorers worked assiduously, removing centuries of grime one square inch at a time, the project took more than a decade to complete.

def: a reappearance of an earlier characteristic; throwback

exs.t: Much of the modern art movement was an atavism to a style of art found only in small villages through Africa and South America.
The sociologist described the revival of blood feuds in the remote province as an atavism, a return to customs the region had seemed to abandon generations ago.
Occasionally a foal is born with small extra toes, an atavism that recalls the horse's distant ancestors, which walked on several digits.
Critics dismissed the heavy stone library as an atavism: in an age of glass and steel, its architect had given it turrets and arrow slits as though the city still feared siege.

def: to weaken (in terms of intensity); to taper off/become thinner

exs.t: Her animosity towards Bob attenuated over the years, and she even went so far as to invite him to her party.
The stick is attenuated at one end to allow the villagers to forage for ants.
As the river spreads across the delta, its current gradually attenuates, until it becomes little more than a sluggish seep through the reeds.
A second layer of insulation attenuated the roar of the highway so effectively that residents could finally sleep through the night.
The drug's side effects usually attenuate after the first few weeks, so doctors urge patients not to abandon treatment during the initial discomfort.

label: adj.1
def: characteristic of an absolute ruler or absolute rule; having absolute sovereignty

exs.t: The last true autocratic country is certainly North Korea; nowhere does a leader exercise the absolute control over all aspects of a people the way that Kim Jong-un does.
Under the autocratic system of the old empire, the emperor alone could make law, and no council or court could overrule his decrees.
The constitution was designed to prevent a return to autocratic rule, dividing power among three branches that could check one another.
Although it held elections, the state remained essentially autocratic, since the president could dissolve parliament and govern by decree whenever he wished.

label: adj.2
def: offensively self-assured or given to exercising usually unwarranted power

exs.t: The manager was finally fired for his autocratic leadership, which often bordered on rude and offensive.
The orchestra's autocratic conductor made every decision himself, dismissing musicians who dared to suggest a different tempo.
Employees chafed under the autocratic new department head, who overruled her team's plans without explanation and demanded obedience rather than input.
Though he held no official rank in the family business, the eldest son behaved in an autocratic manner, issuing orders to cousins who were technically his superiors.

def: threatening or foreshadowing evil or tragic developments

exs.t: Movies often use storms or rain clouds as a baleful omen of evil events that will soon befall the main character.
The villagers took the circling vultures as a baleful sign, and many refused to begin the harvest until the birds had gone.
In the painting, a baleful red moon hangs over the sleeping army, foreshadowing the defeat that the next panel depicts.
Economists issued baleful warnings about the housing bubble, predicting widespread foreclosures that, unfortunately, soon came to pass.

def: the lowest, class were without any moral principles

exs.t: She was not so base as to begrudge the beggar the unwanted crumbs from her dinner plate.
The prosecutor argued that only base greed could explain the embezzlement, since the defendant had stolen from a fund for orphaned children.
Although the courtier professed noble ideals, his conduct revealed base motives: he betrayed his patron the moment a richer lord offered him a bribe.
The novelist refuses to portray her villain as merely base; even his cruelest acts spring from a wounded and recognizably human pride.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: an act that debases or corrupts

exs.t: The movie World War Z is a complete bastardization of the book with little more in common than zombies and a title.
Purists condemned the pop arrangement as a bastardization of the folk song, since it stripped away the haunting modal melody and replaced it with a generic beat.
The translator complained that the publisher's heavy edits amounted to a bastardization of the original, cutting whole chapters and softening its political critique.
Scholars view the watered-down curriculum as a bastardization of the philosopher's teachings, reducing a rigorous ethical system to a list of slogans.

def: (in 'beg the question') to assume the very point that is in dispute
defMasked: (in '____ the question') to assume the very point that is in dispute

exs.t: By assuming that Charlie was headed to college--which he was not--Maggie begged the question when she asked him to which school he was headed in the Fall.
The pamphlet merely begs the question, since it argues that the ancient chronicle must be reliable on the grounds that the chronicle itself claims to be accurate.
Critics noted that the study begged the question by measuring intelligence with a test designed on the assumption that the favored group was already more intelligent.
The witness begged the question by asserting that the document was genuine because it bore a genuine signature, which was exactly what the court had asked him to establish.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: express discontent or a strong regret

exs.t: While the CFO carefully explained all the reasons for the cuts in benefits, after the meeting employees bemoaned the cuts as further evidence that management was against them.
Veteran journalists often bemoan the decline of long-form reporting, lamenting that editors now prefer quick stories that attract clicks.
Rather than spend months bemoaning the loss of their grant, as some colleagues did, the researchers redesigned the study around their existing equipment.
In his final essays, the aging critic bemoaned the passing of an era when poetry was read aloud in every household, a loss he considered tragic.

def: fallen into a state of ignorance

exs.t: Far from being a period of utter benightedness, The Medieval Ages produced some great works of theological speculation.
The reformers regarded the villagers as benighted, yet the villagers' traditional farming methods proved better suited to the arid soil than the experts' modern techniques.
The pamphlet argued that censorship had left the population benighted, cut off from the scientific discoveries that were transforming neighboring countries.
Enlightenment writers often portrayed the preceding centuries as a benighted age of superstition, a caricature that later historians have challenged.

label: adj.1
def: deprived of a loved one through death; grieving

exs.t: After 64 years of marriage, William was bereft after the death of his wife.
Bereft after her father's sudden death, the young historian set aside her dissertation for a year and spent long afternoons sorting through the letters he had left behind.
The opera's second act finds the heroine bereft, mourning at the tomb of the brother who fell defending the city and refusing every attempt to console her.
The villagers rallied around the bereft parents after the fever claimed their only son, bringing meals to the house and sitting with them through the long nights of mourning.

label: adj.2
def: sorrowful through loss or deprivation

exs.t: You are not bereft if you haven't played on your Xbox in the past week, his mother said.
When the flood destroyed the library that had been his life's work, the old scholar was bereft, wandering among the ruined shelves in silence.
Bereft after the closing of the factory that had employed three generations of their families, the townspeople struggled to imagine any future for their community.
The orchestra seemed bereft after its concert hall burned down, and several musicians said that playing in a borrowed gymnasium only reminded them of everything they had lost.

label: adj.1
def: strongly affectionate towards

exs.t: Even though her father did not approve, Juliet became besotted with the young Romeo.
The critic was so besotted with the young novelist's debut that his review read less like an assessment than a love letter.
Besotted with his new bride, the prince neglected affairs of state, spending whole days composing poems in her honor.
Though her parents warned that the suitor was a fortune hunter, the heiress was too besotted to heed them, and she married him within a month.

label: adj.2
def: very drunk

exs.t: Never before have I seen my mom so besotted, and honestly, I hope it's the last time she drinks so much.
By midnight the sailors were thoroughly besotted, staggering along the docks and singing after emptying the tavern's last barrel of rum.
The coachman arrived besotted, reeking of gin and barely able to hold the reins, so the travelers refused to board.
The novel's feckless squire is rarely sober; he spends each evening besotted after a bottle of cheap brandy and each morning nursing the consequences.

def: irritable; always angry

exs.t: Rex was bilious all morning, and his face would only take on a look of contentedness when he'd had his morning cup of coffee.
The critic's bilious reviews, which found fault with nearly every production he saw, made him feared by actors and ignored by audiences.
Plagued by chronic pain, the old admiral grew increasingly bilious, snapping at his servants and quarreling with every visitor.
Although the columnist was genial in person, her prose was bilious, and readers learned to expect that politicians, neighbors, and even her own subscribers would feel the sting of her pen.

def: to have a limited outlook or understanding

exs.t: In gambling, the addict is easily blinkered by past successes and/or past failures, forgetting that the outcome of any one game is independent of the games that preceded it.
The committee's blinkered focus on short-term profits led it to ignore warnings that the mine would poison the town's water supply.
Critics called the historian's account blinkered, since it examined only the diplomats' correspondence and ignored the soldiers and civilians who bore the war's costs.
Raised in a sheltered community that forbade outside books, she had a blinkered view of the world until she left for university.

def: edit by omitting or modifying parts considered indelicate

exs.t: To receive an R rating, the entire movie was bowdlerized because it contained so much violence and grotesque subject matter.
The publisher bowdlerized the old ballads for a children's anthology, removing the coarse verses and softening the violence.
Scholars were dismayed to discover that the only surviving edition of the diary had been bowdlerized by the author's prudish nephew, who excised every indelicate passage.
Rather than bowdlerize the playwright's profane dialogue for the school production, the director chose a different play entirely.

label: v.1
def: the act of restraining power or action or limiting excess

exs.t: New curfew laws have bridled people's tendency to go out at night.
The new regulations were intended to bridle the banks' appetite for risk, capping the amount they could lend against speculative assets.
The diplomat learned to bridle her impatience during long negotiations, knowing that any show of irritation would only strengthen the other side.
Constitutional term limits were designed to bridle presidential ambition, preventing any one leader from entrenching himself in office.

label: v.2
def: anger or take offense

exs.t: The hostess bridled at the tactless dinner guests who insisted on eating before everybody had gotten their food.
The veteran surgeon bridled at the suggestion that a young resident should review her technique, and she left the meeting in a huff.
Proud of their town's history, the council members bridled when the visiting consultant described it as a place with no identity.
Accustomed to deference, the professor bridled at his student's blunt correction, his face flushing as he insisted the error was merely a slip.

def: react in an offended or angry manner

exs.t: As we discussed the painting, I noticed the artist's wife bristling at our criticisms, ready to defend her husband's work.
The novelist bristled when an interviewer suggested that her books were merely autobiography, and she curtly ended the conversation.
Local farmers bristled at the new regulations, which they regarded as an insult from officials who had never worked the land.
Although he tried to appear calm, the mayor visibly bristled at the reporter's implication that he had accepted bribes from developers.

def: a strong verbal attack

exs.t: Political broadsides are usually strongest in the weeks leading up to a national election.
In a scathing broadside published in the morning paper, the retired general accused the ministry of squandering soldiers' lives through incompetence.
The biologist's broadside against the journal's editors, delivered in a public letter, charged them with suppressing research that contradicted their own theories.
Although the review began politely, it soon became a broadside, and by the final paragraph the critic was questioning not only the book but also the author's integrity.

def: a trite or obvious remark

exs.t: Instead of sharing his umbrella, the cheeky stranger offered Martha the following bromide: "Looks like it's raining."
The commencement speaker offered little beyond bromides such as 'follow your dreams' and 'never give up,' which the graduates had heard countless times.
Rather than address the committee's specific concerns, the executive retreated into a familiar bromide about teamwork being the key to success.
The novelist's characters rarely speak in bromides; even in casual conversation, they say things that are surprising and precise.

def: put up with something or somebody unpleasant

exs.t: While she was at the chalkboard, the teacher did not brook any form of talking--even a tiny peep resulted in afternoon detention.
The editor would brook no errors in the magazine's fact-checking, and a single misspelled name was enough to cost a researcher her job.
The general, who brooked no dissent, dismissed any officer who questioned his strategy, even those whose objections later proved correct.
Accustomed to unquestioned authority, the founder refused to brook interference from the new board of directors, and he resigned rather than share control.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: be bossy towards; discourage or frighten with threats or a domineering manner

exs.t: During the interrogation, the suspect was browbeaten into signing a false confession.
The prosecutor tried to browbeat the elderly witness, shouting questions and sneering at her answers, until the judge ordered him to show some respect.
Rather than persuading the committee with evidence, the chairman browbeat its members into approving the plan by threatening to cut their budgets.
Employees who had been browbeaten for years by a tyrannical manager were at first suspicious of their new supervisor's genuine requests for their opinions.

def: intricate and complex

exs.t: Getting a driver's license is not simply a matter of taking a test; the regulations and procedures are so byzantine that many have found themselves at the mercy of the Department of Motor Vehicles.
The tax code has grown so byzantine, with exemptions layered upon exemptions, that even professional accountants struggle to interpret it.
The novel's plot is byzantine: dozens of characters, several interlocking conspiracies, and a narrator who reveals crucial information only in footnotes.
Newcomers to the ministry quickly learned that its byzantine chain of approvals meant that even ordering paper required signatures from four departments.

def: young and inexperienced

exs.t: Both Los Angeles and New York are known for callow out-of-towners hoping to make it big.
The callow lieutenant, fresh from the academy and eager to prove himself, ignored the veteran sergeant's advice and led his men into an ambush.
Reading her first published poems years later, the poet winced at their callow sentimentality, so different from the hard-won restraint of her mature work.
Investors were reluctant to entrust millions to such a callow founder, who had never managed a company or even held a full-time job.

def: a deliberately misleading fabrication

exs.t: The public will always be fooled by the media's canards.
Opponents spread the canard that the reformer had embezzled campaign funds, a fabrication that an independent audit later thoroughly disproved.
The rival firm planted a canard in the trade press, falsely claiming that the new product had failed safety tests, in hopes of delaying its release.
Historians have long since debunked the canard, invented by wartime propagandists, that enemy soldiers had poisoned the wells of occupied villages.

def: to surrender (usually under agreed conditions)

exs.t: Paul, losing 19-0 in a ping-pong match against his nimble friend, basically capitulated when he played the last two points with his eyes closed.
After a siege of several months, the starving garrison capitulated, and the victors allowed its soldiers safe passage home in return for the keys to the fortress.
The union had vowed never to accept the pay cuts, but facing mounting debts and dwindling strike funds, its leaders finally capitulated.
Rather than capitulate to the censors' demands, the editor shut down the newspaper, declaring that she would not print a sanitized version of the truth.

def: an event resulting in great loss and misfortune

exs.t: The introduction of smallpox was a cataclysm for Native Americans, killing off more than half of their population.
For the island's farmers, the volcanic eruption was a cataclysm: ash buried their fields, and the harvest that year was entirely lost.
Many economists feared that the collapse of the largest bank would trigger a cataclysm, wiping out savings and throwing millions out of work.
The paleontologist argued that the extinction was not a single sudden cataclysm but a slow decline spread over hundreds of thousands of years.

def: of broad scope; universal

exs.t: Jonah's friends said that Jonah's taste in music was eclectic; Jonah was quick to point out that not only was his taste eclectic but it was also catholic: he enjoyed music from countries as far-flung as Mali and Mongolia.
Her tastes in literature were remarkably catholic, ranging from ancient epic poetry to contemporary graphic novels and obscure scientific treatises.
The museum's catholic acquisitions policy, which welcomed everything from folk quilts to abstract sculpture, set it apart from institutions devoted to a single period.
The scholar's catholic curiosity led her to write books on medieval music, deep-sea biology, and the history of mapmaking.

def: relinquish possession or control over

exs.t: Eventually, all parents must cede control of their growing children's educations and allow their offspring some autonomy.
Under the terms of the peace treaty, the defeated kingdom was forced to cede its coastal provinces to its victorious neighbor.
The founder was reluctant to cede control of the company to professional managers, even after it had grown far beyond his ability to run it.
In return for federal funding, the state agreed to cede authority over the river's management to a regional commission.

def: speed, rapidity

exs.t: We aim to respond to customers' questions with celerity and accuracy, with no longer than a 24 hour wait time.
The firefighters responded with such celerity that the blaze was contained before it could spread beyond the kitchen.
Critics praised the translator's accuracy but not her celerity; the long-awaited edition appeared a full decade after she began the project.
Messages that once took weeks to cross the ocean by ship traveled with astonishing celerity once the telegraph cable was laid.

label: n.
def: strong feelings of embarrassment

exs.t: Much to the timid writer's chagrin, the audience chanted his name until he came back on the stage.
To the chagrin of the proud host, the souffle collapsed just as he carried it triumphantly into the dining room.
The scientist discovered, much to her chagrin, that the result she had announced at the conference was caused by a contaminated sample.
The visiting official's chagrin was obvious when he mispronounced the name of the town he was addressing, and he apologized repeatedly to the crowd.

label: v.
def: cause to feel shame; hurt the pride of

exs.t: She never cared what others said about her appearance but was chagrined by the smallest comment from her mother.
The veteran chess master was chagrined to lose to a twelve-year-old in only fifteen moves, and he declined all interviews afterward.
The minister was deeply chagrined when reporters revealed that his celebrated speech had been lifted almost word for word from an old textbook.
It chagrined the proud engineer that his bridge, praised at its opening, had to be closed within a year because it swayed alarmingly in the wind.

def: a flamboyant deceiver; one who attracts customers with tricks or jokes

exs.t: You may call him a "motivational speaker," but I call him a charlatan--he doesn't have any idea what he's really talking about.
The traveling doctor was a charlatan who dazzled crowds with jokes and conjuring tricks before selling them bottles of colored water as a cure for every ailment.
Though he presented himself as a renowned psychic, investigators soon exposed him as a charlatan who relied on hidden accomplices to feed him information.
Serious economists dismissed the television guru as a charlatan, since his flamboyant predictions were designed to sell books rather than to withstand scrutiny.

def: cautious

exs.t: Jack was wary of GRE words that looked similar, because they usually had different definitions; not so with chary, a word that he began to use interchangeably with wary.
Having been cheated by a fraudulent partner once before, the investor was chary of any deal that promised quick returns.
The famously reclusive novelist is chary of interviews, granting perhaps one a decade and even then refusing to discuss her private life.
Doctors are often chary of prescribing new drugs until long-term studies have confirmed their safety.

def: fanatical patriotism; belief that one's group/cause is superior to all other groups/causes

exs.t: Vegetarians argue that man is chauvinistic in his belief that animals do not consciously feel the pain we humans do.
The historian argued that the war was fueled by chauvinism, as each nation's press insisted on its own people's superiority and mocked the other side.
The critic's dismissal of all foreign films as inferior revealed a cultural chauvinism that his broader writings otherwise concealed.
Physicists and biologists rarely collaborated at the institute, largely because a disciplinary chauvinism led each group to dismiss the other's methods as crude.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: something desired or wished for but is only an illusion and impossible to achieve

exs.t: Many believe that a world free of war is a chimera--a dream that ignores humanity's violent tendancies.
For centuries, inventors pursued the chimera of a perpetual motion machine, though physics had long shown such a device to be impossible.
The dream of a single universal language that would end all misunderstanding proved a chimera; each attempt splintered into rival dialects within a generation.
Some philosophers regard perfect objectivity as a chimera, arguing that every observer inevitably brings assumptions that shape what she sees.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: prone to outbursts of temper; easily angered

exs.t: While a brilliant lecturer, Mr. Dawson came across as choleric and unapproachable--very rarely did students come to his office hours.
The choleric headmaster was known to fly into a rage over a single untucked shirt, and students tiptoed past his office.
Although the composer's music is serene, his contemporaries described him as choleric, prone to smashing chairs when rehearsals went badly.
Diplomats found the envoy's choleric temperament a liability, since his sudden outbursts repeatedly derailed delicate negotiations.

def: lacking manners or refinement

exs.t: The manager was unnecessarily churlish to his subordinates, rarely deigning to say hello, but always quick with a sartorial jab if someone happened to be wearing anything even slightly mismatching.
It seemed churlish to refuse the villagers' hospitality, so the weary travelers accepted the meal despite having already eaten.
The guest's churlish behavior at the banquet, ignoring his hosts and grumbling loudly about the food, embarrassed everyone at the table.
Although the champion had been gracious in victory, her opponent was churlish in defeat, refusing to shake hands and storming off the court.

def: showing a cheerful willingness to do favors for others

exs.t: On her first day at the job, Annie was complaisant, fulfilling every request of her new employee and. anticipating future requests.
The complaisant innkeeper cheerfully rearranged rooms, cooked late meals, and fetched a doctor for his guests, never once grumbling about the extra work.
Unlike her demanding predecessor, the new assistant was complaisant, happily agreeing to run errands that fell well outside her official duties.
The minister's complaisant attitude toward foreign envoys, whose every request he was eager to grant, alarmed advisers who feared he was being exploited.

def: associated with or participating in an activity, especially one of a questionable nature

exs.t: While the grand jury cleared the senator of all criminal charges, in the public mind he was still complicit in the corruption.
Although the accountant had not personally stolen any money, the court found her complicit in the fraud, since she had knowingly falsified the ledgers to conceal it.
Historians debate whether the townspeople were complicit in the deportations or simply too frightened to protest.
By remaining silent about the safety violations he had witnessed, the inspector became complicit in the disaster that followed.

def: to make peace with

exs.t: His opponents believed his gesture to be conciliatory, yet as soon as they put down their weapons, he unsheathed a hidden sword.
Hoping to conciliate the angry farmers, the governor promised emergency relief and personally visited the flooded districts.
The new manager tried to conciliate the rival factions within the department by giving each a voice in planning the budget.
Rather than conciliate his critics, the author published a furious rebuttal that only deepened the feud.

def: describing an event or situation that happens at the same time as or in connection with another

exs.t: Concomitant with his desire for nature was a desire for the culture and energy of a big city.
The rapid growth of the city brought concomitant problems: traffic congestion, rising rents, and overcrowded schools all arrived along with the new residents.
Doctors warned that the medication's benefits came with concomitant risks, including dizziness and insomnia, that patients should weigh carefully.
The spread of literacy in the period, and the concomitant rise of cheap printed pamphlets, transformed how ordinary people encountered political ideas.

def: a very intense and uncontrolled fire

exs.t: In the summer months, conflagrations are not uncommon in the southwest, do to the heat and lack of rain.
A carelessly discarded match sparked a conflagration that swept through the dry forest, consuming thousands of acres before the rains arrived.
The old wooden theater was destroyed in a conflagration so intense that firefighters could only keep it from spreading to neighboring buildings.
City planners rebuilt the district in brick and stone, determined that no future conflagration would ever again reduce whole streets to ashes.

def: mix together different elements or concepts

exs.t: In her recent book, the author conflates several genres--the detective story, the teen thriller, and the vampire romance--to create a memorable read.
Critics complained that the documentary conflated two distinct historical figures who shared a name, attributing one man's achievements to the other.
Many people conflate weather and climate, yet a single cold winter reveals little about long-term trends in global temperature.
The architect conflates classical columns, industrial steel, and traditional Japanese joinery, producing buildings that belong to no single tradition.

def: likely to argue

exs.t: Since old grandpa Harry became very contentious during the summer when only reruns were on T.V., the grandkids learned to hide from him at every opportunity.
She became increasingly contentious, misconstruing even an innocuous statement as a hostile one.
As soon as the discussion turns to politics, Uncle Hank becomes highly contentious, vehemently disagreeing with those who endorse the same positions.
The contentious board member objected to nearly every proposal, often prolonging meetings for hours over matters that others considered trivial.
Known as the most contentious scholar in the department, he seemed to relish disputes and would challenge a colleague's claim merely to provoke a debate.
Although the twins were close as adults, they had been contentious children, quarreling constantly over toys, chores, and even who got the last word.

def: a practical consequence that follows naturally

exs.t: A corollary of Hurricane Sandy, which ravaged the east coast of the U.S., is a push to build higher sea walls to protect against future hurricanes.
Higher tuition has had an unfortunate corollary: students graduate with heavier debts and are therefore less willing to take low-paying public service jobs.
Cheaper air travel produced a natural corollary in the coastal towns, where hotels multiplied to accommodate the new crowds of visitors.
If the theory is correct, then a corollary follows: the same plants should flower earlier wherever winters are warmer.

def: treat with excessive indulgence

exs.t: The king and queen cosseted the young prince, giving him a prized miniature pony for his fifth birthday.
The heir had been cosseted since infancy, attended by servants who anticipated his every wish, so he was ill prepared for life on his own.
Critics argue that protective tariffs cosset domestic manufacturers, sparing them the competition that would otherwise force them to innovate.
Rather than cosseting her students with easy praise, the piano teacher insisted on relentless drills and blunt criticism.

def: being of equal extent or scope or duration

exs.t: The border of the state is coterminous with geographic limits on travel; the east and north are surrounded by a nearly uncrossable river and the south by a desert.
The parish's boundaries were coterminous with those of the old manor, so the same families had worshipped and worked within the same lines for centuries.
The chairman's influence proved coterminous with his term of office; once he stepped down, his proposals were quickly abandoned.
In this region, the watershed and the county are coterminous: every stream within the county's borders drains into the same lake, and no stream beyond them does.

def: a contrary command cancelling or reversing a previous command

exs.t: By the time the colonel countermanded his soldiers not to land in enemy territory, a few helicopters had already touched down amid heavy gunfire.
The general countermanded the order to retreat, instructing his troops to hold their positions until reinforcements could arrive.
Shortly after the manager announced the office closure, the chief executive countermanded the decision, and the staff were told to report to work as usual.
The captain countermanded the first officer's order to change course, insisting that the original heading was safer despite the approaching storm.

def: to intimidate

exs.t: Do not be cowed by a 3,000-word vocabulary list: turn that list into a deck of flashcards!
The dictator's secret police cowed the population so effectively that even private conversations among friends avoided any mention of politics.
Refusing to be cowed by the powerful landowner's threats, the young lawyer filed suit on behalf of the evicted tenants.
The committee members, cowed by the chairman's reputation for vindictiveness, approved his proposal without raising a single question.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: brought low in spirit

exs.t: I asked Maria on a date and she refused without a moment's thought; I was crestfallen.
The young scientist was crestfallen when the journal rejected her paper, having spent three years on the research it described.
The crowd, so jubilant at halftime, filed out of the stadium crestfallen after the home team surrendered its lead in the final minutes.
Expecting praise for his first novel, the author was crestfallen to find that his mentor had written only a single, lukewarm line in the margin.

def: cause to take on a definite and clear shape

exs.t: Only after fifteen minutes of brainstorming did Samantha's ideas for the essay crystallize.
Only after reading the survey data did the team's vague concerns about the product crystallize into a clear list of design flaws.
The philosopher's scattered early notes gradually crystallized into a coherent theory of justice, which she published a decade later.
Years of diffuse discontent crystallized into a movement when the government raised bread prices, giving protesters a single, concrete grievance.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: greed for money

exs.t: Some believe people that amassing as much wealth as possible is the meaning to life--yet they often realize that cupidity brings anything but happiness.
The merchant's cupidity was legendary; he charged interest even on loans to his own brother and hoarded coins while his employees went unpaid.
The novel traces how cupidity corrupts a once honorable family, as each generation sacrifices loyalty and love for a larger share of the inheritance.
Regulators blamed the financial crisis less on ignorance than on cupidity, noting that bankers had knowingly sold worthless securities to enrich themselves.

def: a grouchy, surly person

exs.t: Since Uncle Mike was the family curmudgeon, each Thanksgiving he was plied with copious amounts of wine, in the hope that she would become less grouchy.
The neighborhood curmudgeon complained about everything, from children playing in the street to the color of the new mailboxes.
Though the old critic cultivated a reputation as a curmudgeon, grumbling at every premiere, his private letters reveal a surprisingly tender heart.
Even the office curmudgeon, who rarely had a kind word for anyone, grudgingly admitted that the new intern's report was excellent.

def: having a sophisticated charm

exs.t: James Bond is known for his good looks, high tech gadgets, and debonair manner.
The debonair diplomat, impeccably tailored and effortlessly witty, charmed even the hostile delegates at the tense summit.
Though he had grown up in a cramped farmhouse, the actor projected a debonair elegance on screen that made audiences assume he was born to wealth.
Guests at the gala were captivated by their debonair host, who greeted each of them by name and moved through the crowded ballroom with easy grace.

def: express strong disapproval of

exs.t: The entire audience erupted in shouts and curses, decrying the penalty card issued by the referee.
Environmental groups decried the decision to open the protected wetlands to drilling, calling it a betrayal of future generations.
Although many critics decried the novel as immoral when it was first published, it is now taught in schools as a classic.
The medical association decried the proliferation of unproven remedies, warning that patients were abandoning effective treatments in favor of them.

def: to help pay the cost of, either in part of full

exs.t: In order for Sean to attend the prestigious college, his generous uncle helped defray the excessive tuition with a monthly donation.
A grant from the historical society helped defray the cost of restoring the chapel's fragile frescoes, though the parish still had to raise the remainder.
To defray the expenses of her research trip, the graduate student taught evening classes and sold several of her photographs.
Conference organizers offered small stipends to defray travel costs for scholars from underfunded universities, though the sums rarely covered the full fare.

def: do something that one considers to be below one's dignity

exs.t: The master of the house never deigned to answer questions from the servants.
The celebrated conductor did not deign to acknowledge the student musicians who had waited hours to meet him, sweeping past them to his car.
The aristocrat rarely deigned to speak with shopkeepers, instead sending servants to conduct any business she considered beneath her.
