When the famous author finally deigned to answer the young critic's letter, his reply consisted of a single dismissive sentence.

def: given to or marked by the open expression of emotion

exs.t: When Sally told James that she wanted to break up with him, she expected he would react demonstratively, but he quietly nodded his head and left without saying a word.
Unlike her reserved husband, who rarely showed any emotion, she was demonstrative, embracing guests at the door and weeping openly at weddings.
Her cousins were far more demonstrative than the stoic family she had married into, greeting her with kisses, tears, and loud declarations of affection.
Though the coach was not demonstrative by nature, he leapt from the bench and hugged each player when the team clinched the championship.

def: the final resolution of the many strands of a literary or dramatic work; the outcome of a complex sequence of events

exs.t: At the denouement of the movie, all questions were answered, and the true identity of the robber was revealed.
In the novel's denouement, the long-lost heir is revealed, the feuding families are reconciled, and every mystery introduced in the first chapter is finally explained.
The protracted legal battle reached its denouement when the appeals court ruled in the tenants' favor, ending a dispute that had dragged on for fifteen years.
Critics admired the play's first two acts but found its denouement rushed, as if the playwright had grown tired of untangling the plot threads he had so carefully woven.

label: adj.
def: (of a person) not doing one's duties

exs.t: The teacher was derelict in her duties because she hadn't graded a single student paper in three weeks.
The inspector was found derelict in his duties, having approved the bridge as safe without ever visiting the site.
Parents accused the school board of being derelict, since it had ignored complaints about bullying for years without taking any action.
A night watchman who sleeps through his shift is plainly derelict, however loyal he may otherwise be to his employer.

label: n.
def: (of a building) abandoned

exs.t: At one time the waterfront factories were busy and productive, but now they stand derelict and will be torn down.
After the canneries closed, a row of derelict warehouses lined the harbor, their windows smashed and their doors left open to the wind and the gulls.
Urban explorers are drawn to the derelict asylum, whose empty wards and collapsing roof have stood untouched since the last patients left decades ago.
Rather than let it crumble further, the council voted to convert the derelict railway station, boarded up and unused for thirty years, into a public library.

def: uninteresting, lacking vitality

exs.t: Few novelists over 80 are able to produce anything more than desiccated works--boring shadows of former books.
The composer's late works struck critics as desiccated, technically flawless but devoid of the passion that had animated his youthful symphonies.
Students found the textbook's desiccated prose so lifeless that they turned instead to the lively lectures of a popular historian.
Once a spirited forum for debate, the society had become a desiccated institution by the century's end, its meetings reduced to reading the minutes aloud.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: something desired as a necessity

exs.t: The desideratum of the environmental group is that motorists should rely on carpooling.
For the new laboratory, a stable supply of electricity was the chief desideratum, since even a brief outage could ruin months of experiments.
Affordable housing near the city center remains a desideratum for young families, yet few developers have found a way to provide it profitably.
In choosing a site for the observatory, the astronomers listed dark skies as their foremost desideratum, followed closely by dry weather and high altitude.

def: a cruel and oppressive dictator

exs.t: The Emperor Claudius was regarded as a fair-minded leader; his successor, Nero, was an absolute despot.
The despot silenced every critic, imprisoning journalists and confiscating the property of anyone suspected of disloyalty.
Though he came to power promising democratic reforms, the general soon revealed himself as a despot, dissolving the legislature and ruling through terror.
Historians debate whether the emperor was an enlightened reformer or merely a despot whose harsh decrees occasionally happened to benefit his subjects.

def: a strong verbal attack against a person or institution

exs.t: Steve's mom launched into a diatribe during the PTA meeting, contending that the school was little more than a daycare in which students stare at the wall and teachers stare at the chalkboard.
The retired professor's letter to the editor was a diatribe against the university administration, accusing it of betraying every principle of scholarship.
Instead of a reasoned critique, the pamphlet offered a lengthy diatribe against modern architecture, condemning glass towers as monuments to greed.
Audience members expected a gracious acceptance speech, but the novelist launched into a diatribe against the publishers who had rejected her early work.

label: n.
def: to indicate smallness

exs.t: He prefers to be called a diminutive of his name: "Bill" instead of "John William."
In many languages, adding a suffix to a noun creates a diminutive: a word for a little house or a small dog is formed from the ordinary word.
Linguists note that speakers often use a diminutive, such as 'booklet' or 'piglet,' to express affection as well as small size.
Although he was named Juan after his grandfather, the family always called him by the diminutive 'Juanito' to distinguish the boy from the old man.

label: adj.
def: very small

exs.t: When he put on his father's suit and shoes, his appearance was that of a diminutive youth.
The diminutive gymnast, barely reaching her coach's shoulder, generated astonishing power on the vault.
Despite its diminutive size, the hummingbird defends its territory fiercely, chasing off birds many times larger than itself.
The architect's diminutive cottage, with rooms scarcely large enough to turn around in, was a deliberate rebuke to the sprawling mansions nearby.

def: to persuade somebody that his/her belief is not valid

exs.t: As a child, I was quickly disabused of the notion that Santa Claus was a rotund benefactor of infinite largess--one night I saw my mother diligently wrapping presents and storing them under our Christmas tree.
A single semester of organic chemistry disabused him of the notion that medical school would be easy.
The tour guide tried to disabuse visitors of the popular belief that the castle was haunted, explaining that the eerie noises came from wind in the chimneys.
Early investors were quickly disabused of their faith in the company when an audit revealed that its reported profits had been invented.

def: (of speech or writing) tending to depart from the main point

exs.t: Many readers find it tough to read Moby Dick since the author is discursive, often cutting the action short to spend 20 pages on the history of a whale.
The lecturer's discursive style, which wandered from medieval poetry to modern economics to his own childhood, left students unsure what the lecture was actually about.
Although the memoir is discursive, frequently straying into anecdotes about minor acquaintances, its detours are so charming that few readers mind.
The editor urged the author to trim the discursive middle chapters, which abandoned the main argument for long excursions into family history.

def: not straightforward; giving a false appearance of frankness

exs.t: Many adults think that they can lie to children, but kids are smart and know when people are disingenuous.
It was disingenuous of the company to claim it had no knowledge of the defect, since internal memos showed engineers had warned executives years earlier.
The official's disingenuous show of surprise at the scandal fooled no one, as reporters soon revealed that he had helped to orchestrate it.
Critics called the author's modest disclaimer disingenuous: while claiming to offer 'mere impressions,' she in fact presented a carefully argued indictment.

def: an exemption from a rule or obligation

exs.t: Since her father is a billionaire, she is given dispensation from many of the school's policies.
The athlete received a special dispensation from the league, allowing her to compete despite missing the qualifying deadline because of injury.
Because of the drought, farmers were granted a dispensation from the usual restrictions on drawing water from the river.
The monastery's rule forbade speaking at meals, but the abbot granted a dispensation to the novice who had to translate for visiting guests.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: conceal one's true motives, usually through deceit

exs.t: To get close to the senator, the assassin dissembled his intentions, convincing many people that he was a reporter for a well-known newspaper.
The spy dissembled so skillfully that her colleagues never suspected she was passing their secrets to a foreign government.
When questioned about the missing funds, the treasurer dissembled, feigning confusion and insisting that the records must have been misfiled.
Rather than dissemble about his reasons for resigning, the minister openly admitted that he could no longer support the government's policy.

label: v.1
def: squander or spend money frivolously

exs.t: The recent graduates dissipated their earnings on trips to Las Vegas and cruises in Mexico.
Within five years the heir had dissipated the family fortune on racehorses, gambling, and lavish parties, and the ancestral estate had to be sold.
Rather than dissipate their lottery winnings as so many others had, the couple invested the money and continued to live modestly.
Auditors charged that the ministry had dissipated its entire reconstruction budget on consultants and ceremonies, leaving the damaged bridges unrepaired.

label: v.2
def: to disperse or scatter

exs.t: Kathleen's perfume was overwhelming in the cramped apartment, but once we stepped outside the smell dissipated and we could breathe once again.
Although the morning fog lay thick over the harbor, it dissipated within an hour of sunrise, leaving the fishing fleet a clear view of the channel.
The crowd that had gathered outside the courthouse slowly dissipated once the verdict was announced, its members drifting back to offices and cafes across the city.
Engineers designed the heat sink with dozens of thin fins so that warmth from the processor would dissipate into the surrounding air rather than accumulate inside the case.

def: a living full of debauchery and indulgence in sensual pleasure

exs.t: Many Roman emperors were known for their dissolution, indulging in unspeakable desires of the flesh.
The novel traces the young heir's slide into dissolution: nights of gambling, drinking and carousing gradually consumed both his inheritance and his once promising reputation.

Contemporary moralists blamed the city's decline on the dissolution that prevailed among its ruling class, whose lavish banquets and open vices contrasted starkly with the austerity of earlier generations.
Far from living in dissolution, as rumors in the capital suggested, the exiled poet spent his final years in sober routine, rising early and drinking nothing stronger than tea.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: filled with or evoking sadness

exs.t: No event is more doleful than the passing of my mother; she was a shining star in my life, and it brings me great sadness to think that she is now gone.
The doleful tolling of the village bell announced to every household that the fishing boat lost in the storm would not be coming home.
Although the children's book ends happily, its middle chapters are so doleful that several parents reported their children weeping at bedtime.
The shelter dog's doleful expression, with drooping ears and downcast eyes, persuaded the visiting family to take him home rather than the livelier puppy beside him.

def: showing sorrow

exs.t: Chopin's ballades are filled with sharp changes in moods--a dolorous melody can give way to a lighthearted tempo.
The soprano's dolorous final aria, sung as her character mourns a lost child, left much of the audience quietly wiping their eyes.
Rather than celebrating the treaty, the veteran's memoir adopts a dolorous tone, lingering over the friends he buried and the villages he saw reduced to ashes.
Medieval painters often gave the Virgin a dolorous countenance at the foot of the cross, her eyes lowered and her hands clasped in grief.

def: brave; bold; courageous

exs.t: I enjoy films in which a doughty group comes together to battle a force of evil.
The doughty explorer pressed on across the ice sheet even after two of her companions turned back, undaunted by the storms that battered their camp nightly.
Though small and outnumbered, the doughty garrison refused to surrender the fortress, repelling three assaults before reinforcements finally arrived.
Critics dismissed the reformer as naive, yet she proved a doughty opponent of entrenched interests, facing down threats and lawsuits without once retreating from her position.

def: fit together tightly, as if by means of a interlocking joint

exs.t: Although Darwin's evolution and Mendel's genetics were developed in isolation from one another, they dovetail each other very well.
The historian's findings dovetail neatly with the archaeological record: the documents describe a fire in the granary, and excavators found charred grain precisely where the texts indicated.
Because her research interests dovetailed with the laboratory's ongoing project, Priya was able to contribute meaningful work within her first week.
Planners hoped the new bus routes would dovetail with the train schedule, so that commuters arriving at the station would never wait more than a few minutes for a connection.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: deceitfulness, pretending to want one thing but interested in something else

exs.t: A life of espionage is one of duplicity: an agent must pretend to be a totally different person than who she or he actually is.
The diplomat's duplicity became clear only later: while publicly championing the alliance, he had been secretly negotiating a separate treaty with its rivals.
Voters forgave the candidate's occasional blunders, but they would not forgive duplicity, and the revelation that he had promised opposite things to rival donors ended his campaign.
In the play, the servant's duplicity drives the plot, as he professes loyalty to each of the feuding brothers while quietly working to ruin them both.

def: joyously unrestrained

exs.t: Can you blame him for his ebullient mood? He just graduated from medical school.
Normally reserved, the professor grew almost ebullient when her student's thesis won the prize, laughing, embracing colleagues and toasting everyone in the room.
The composer's ebullient finale, with its rushing strings and triumphant brass, stands in deliberate contrast to the somber movement that precedes it.
Investors were ebullient after the successful launch, though the chief financial officer cautioned that such exuberance might prove premature.

def: marked by high spirits or excitement

exs.t: After the sales result, the manager was in an effervescent mood, letting several employees leave work early that day.
The host's effervescent personality kept the long evening lively; she moved from table to table, sparking conversation and laughter wherever she paused.
Critics praised the young actor's effervescent performance as the heroine's sister, whose bubbling enthusiasm offers relief from the play's darker scenes.
Although the book's subject is grave, its author remained effervescent throughout the promotional tour, greeting each audience with obvious delight and boundless energy.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: audacious (even arrogant) behavior that you have no right to

exs.t: The skateboarders acted with effrontery, skating through the church grounds and spray-painting signs warning trespassers.
After arriving an hour late to the interview, the applicant had the effrontery to ask whether the company could rearrange its schedule to suit his preferences.
The committee was astonished by the effrontery of the contractor, who, having delivered a flawed bridge design, submitted an invoice demanding a bonus for early completion.
Few junior scholars would presume to correct the eminent historian in public, yet Dana showed the effrontery to interrupt his keynote and dispute his central claim.

def: expressing sorrow

exs.t: Few can listen to the elegiac opening bars of the Moonlight sonata without feeling the urge to cry.
The documentary's closing scenes are frankly elegiac, lingering over empty factories and shuttered storefronts as the narrator mourns a way of life that has vanished.
Written after the death of her brother, the poet's final collection is elegiac in tone, each poem circling back to memories of their shared childhood.
Instead of a triumphant march, the composer ended the symphony with an elegiac adagio, a quiet lament for the soldiers who never returned.

def: in an early stage of development

exs.t: The Board of Directors is hoping to launch a new product soon, but planning for the Z7 is in an embryonic stages.
Research on the new battery chemistry is still embryonic; the team has produced promising results in the laboratory but has yet to build a working prototype.
Though the city's arts district is only in its embryonic phase, a handful of galleries and studios have already begun to draw visitors to the old warehouses.
Historians trace the embryonic forms of modern banking to medieval merchants, whose crude letters of credit would eventually develop into sophisticated financial instruments.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: any method that derives knowledge from experience, used in experimental science as a way to gain insight and knowledge

exs.t: Empiricism does not always lead to knowledge; an experience or experiment may raise more questions than it answers.
The philosopher rejected pure speculation in favor of empiricism, insisting that any claim about the natural world must ultimately be tested against observation.
Early physicians often relied on tradition rather than empiricism, so remedies persisted for centuries even when careful observation would have shown them to be useless.
The economist's empiricism set her apart from colleagues who built elegant theoretical models; she trusted only conclusions drawn from carefully gathered data on actual households.

def: fill with love or strong attraction (usually 'enamored of')
defMasked: fill with love or strong attraction (usually '____ of')

exs.t: She is completely enamored with Justin Bieber, and goes to all his concerts on the East coast.
The young architect was so enamored of glass towers that she proposed one for every site, even where local planners had requested low brick buildings.
Visitors who arrive expecting to dislike the city often leave enamored of its narrow streets and lively markets, vowing to return the following year.
Though critics had long scorned the genre, the director was openly enamored of old musicals, and his new film lovingly recreates their lavish dance numbers.

def: hold back

exs.t: The costume encumbered all my movements and caused me to sweat profusely.
The startup's growth was encumbered by debt from its early years, which forced the founders to spend revenue on interest payments rather than new hires.
Hikers are advised not to encumber themselves with heavy gear on the steep ascent, since every extra pound slows progress up the narrow trail.
Reformers argued that layers of outdated regulations encumbered small farmers, who spent more time filling out forms than tending their fields.

def: give instructions to or direct somebody to do something with authority

exs.t: The government agency enjoined the chemical company to clean up the hazardous dump it had created over the years.
The physician enjoined her patient to rest for a full week, warning that returning to work too soon could turn a minor strain into a lasting injury.
The monastic rule enjoins novices to keep silence during meals, and the abbot enforces this command without exception.
In his will, the merchant enjoined his heirs to keep the family library intact, directing that no volume ever be sold or divided among them.

def: an act of extreme wickedness

exs.t: The enormity of Pol Pot's regime is hard to capture in words--within months hundreds of thousands of Cambodians lost their lives.
Only when the archives were opened did historians grasp the enormity of the regime's crimes, which included the systematic persecution of entire villages.
The novel refuses to soften the enormity of the tyrant's deeds; it records his cruelties toward prisoners in plain, unflinching prose.
Although the official claimed he had merely followed orders, the tribunal insisted that no directive could excuse an enormity as monstrous as the burning of a defenseless town.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: hold spellbound

exs.t: She was so enthralled by the movie that she never heard people screaming, "Fire! Fire!" in the neighboring theater.
The storyteller enthralled the children so completely that not one of them stirred until the tale ended and the lanterns were lit.
Although the lecture concerned the seemingly dry subject of medieval tax records, the historian's vivid anecdotes enthralled an audience that had expected to doze.
Birdwatchers are often enthralled by the courtship dance of the crane, standing motionless in the cold for hours to watch it unfold.

def: a witty saying

exs.t: My favorite epigram from Mark Twain is "A man who carries a cat by the tail learns something he can learn no other way."
Rather than building a sustained argument, the essayist relied on the epigram, compressing each insight into a pithy, witty line that readers could easily quote.
At the retirement dinner, the dean offered a single epigram instead of a long speech, and the guests laughed at how neatly his clever phrase summed up a forty-year career.
The play's dialogue sparkles with epigrams, clever quips that the characters toss off so casually that the audience scarcely has time to laugh before the next one arrives.

def: a sudden revelation or moment of insight

exs.t: Gary one day had an epiphany that he was a people person; he promptly quit his factory job and began working as a salesman.
While staring at the tangled data late one night, the chemist had an epiphany: the anomaly was not an error but evidence of an unknown compound.
The novel's turning point is a quiet epiphany on a train, when the heroine suddenly understands that the life she has been building belongs to her parents rather than to herself.
For years the composer struggled with the finale, until a sudden epiphany during a walk in the rain revealed how the opening theme could return transformed.

def: the name derived from a person (real or imaginary); the person for whom something is named

exs.t: Alexandria, Egypt is an eponym because it is named after Alexander the Great.
The clinic's founder became the eponym of the syndrome she first described, and medical students now learn her name alongside its symptoms.
Few residents realize that their town has an eponym: it was named for an eighteenth-century surveyor whose portrait still hangs in the courthouse.
The word 'boycott' preserves the surname of its eponym, a land agent whose tenants refused to deal with him, so that his name became a general term for organized refusal.

def: fair to all parties as dictated by reason and conscience

exs.t: The equitable distribution of ice cream to a group of 5 year olds will ensure little to no fighting--at least until the ice cream is gone.
The mediator sought an equitable settlement, one that neither the landlord nor the tenants could reasonably claim favored the other side.
Critics argued that the flat tax was not equitable, since it asked a struggling family to sacrifice a far larger share of its necessities than a wealthy one.
To ensure an equitable division of the workload, the manager rotated the least desirable assignments so that no single employee bore them every month.

def: to speak vaguely, usually with the intention to mislead or deceive

exs.t: After Sharon brought the car home an hour after her curfew, she equivocated when her parents pointedly asked her where she had been.
Pressed by reporters about whether the factory would close, the spokesperson equivocated, offering vague references to 'ongoing reviews' rather than a straight answer.
A witness who equivocates under oath, phrasing each reply so that it can later be read two ways, may damage a case more than one who simply lies.
Unlike her predecessor, who would equivocate whenever a question became uncomfortable, the new director answered directly, even when the truth was unwelcome.

def: not real or genuine; phony

exs.t: The car dealer's ersatz laughter was immediately followed by a price quote, one that Shelley found highly inflated.
During the wartime shortages, households brewed an ersatz coffee from roasted chicory and acorns, a poor substitute that fooled no one.
The theme park's ersatz Venetian canals, complete with painted skies and chlorinated water, struck the critic as a charmless imitation of the real city.
The memoir's ersatz humility, apparent in passages where the author praises himself while pretending to be modest, irritated reviewers more than open boasting would have.

def: deserving of esteem and respect

exs.t: After serving thirty years, in which he selflessly served the community, Judge Harper was one of the more estimable people in town.
Although she never achieved fame, the librarian led an estimable life, quietly teaching generations of children to read and earning the gratitude of the entire town.
The committee chose the most estimable candidate for the ethics post, a judge whose integrity even her political opponents admired.
The novel has estimable qualities, including careful research and graceful prose, though its sluggish plot may test some readers' patience.

def: characterized by lightness and insubstantiality

exs.t: Because she dances with an ethereal style, ballet critics have called her Madame Butterfly.
The choir's ethereal harmonies seemed to float above the congregation, so light and delicate that they hardly seemed produced by human voices.
The designer favored ethereal fabrics such as chiffon and silk gauze, which drifted around the models like mist as they walked.
Unlike the heavy, earthbound figures of his early sculpture, the artist's late work is almost ethereal, with slender forms that appear weightless.

def: tending to vanish like vapor

exs.t: The storm flashed into existence above us and lasted only a short time--an evanescent turbulence of wind and cloud.
The painter tried to capture the evanescent colors of dusk, which shifted and faded so quickly that she had only minutes to work each evening.
Much online fame is evanescent: a video that captivates millions on Monday is often forgotten entirely by the end of the week.
Chemists struggled to study the evanescent intermediate compound, since by the time their instruments could register it, it had already broken down into more stable products.

def: to criticize very harshly

exs.t: Entrusted with the prototype to his company's latest smartphone, Larry, during a late night karaoke bout, let the prototype slip into the hands of a rival company--the next day Larry was excoriated, and then fired.
The review excoriated the new opera, condemning its libretto as incoherent and its score as a clumsy imitation of better composers.
Although the governor had expected mild criticism, the editorial board excoriated her proposal, calling it reckless, cynical and an insult to taxpayers.
The auditor's report excoriates the charity's management in unsparing terms, faulting its leaders for years of careless bookkeeping and misleading statements to donors.

def: to curse and hiss at

exs.t: Though the new sitcom did decently in the ratings, Nelson railed against the show, saying that it was nothing more than an execrable pastiche of tired clichés and canned laughter.
Villagers execrated the landlord whose evictions had scattered their families, and his name became a byword for cruelty in local songs.
Though celebrated in his lifetime, the general is now widely execrated, as historians have documented the brutal reprisals he ordered against civilians.
The reformers did more than disagree with child labor; they execrated it from every pulpit and podium, denouncing it as a moral stain on the nation.

def: critical explanation or analysis, especially of a text

exs.t: The Bible is fertile ground for exegesis--over the past five centuries there have been as many interpretations as there are pages in the Old Testament.
Her exegesis of the poem's final stanza, which traced each image back to classical sources, persuaded many scholars to reconsider its meaning.
Rather than offering a close exegesis of the constitution's text, the judge relied on broad appeals to fairness, a method her colleagues found insufficiently rigorous.
Students in the seminar spend entire sessions on the exegesis of a single paragraph, weighing every word and debating how medieval readers would have understood it.

def: something to be imitated

exs.t: Lena's homework is on the wall because it is an exemplar of clean, neat, and thoughtful work.
The restored town hall is regarded as an exemplar of civic architecture, and designers from neighboring cities study it when planning their own public buildings.
Young scientists were encouraged to model their conduct on the retired chemist, an exemplar of rigor who rechecked every result before publishing.
Teachers often hold up the essay as an exemplar for their students to imitate, pointing to its clear thesis and economical prose.

def: the quality of being meager

exs.t: After two months at sea, the exiguity of the ship's supplies forced them to search for fresh water and food.
The exiguity of the museum's budget meant that the curators had to borrow display cases and rely on volunteers to guard the galleries.
Historians must work around the exiguity of surviving records from the period; a handful of letters and a single tax roll are nearly all that remain.
Despite the exiguity of their rations, a thin soup and a crust of bread each day, the prisoners organized lectures and concerts to sustain their morale.

def: greatly exceeding bounds of reason or moderation

exs.t: Shelley made one exorbitant purchase after another, buying new clothes and taking vacations even though she earned a limited salary.
Tenants protested the exorbitant rent increase, which would have doubled their monthly payments despite no improvements to the building.
The critic found the film's running time exorbitant: at nearly four hours, it far exceeded what its slender plot could justify.
Hospitals were accused of charging exorbitant prices for routine supplies, billing patients many times what the items cost wholesale.

def: communicative, and prone to talking in a sociable manner

exs.t: After a few sips of cognac, the octogenarian shed his irascible demeanor and became expansive, speaking fondly of the "good old days".
Usually taciturn at meetings, the engineer grew expansive at the reunion dinner, chatting freely with old colleagues and telling stories late into the night.
The interviewer's warm manner made the reclusive novelist unexpectedly expansive, and she spoke at length about her childhood, her influences and her doubts.
In his letters the statesman is far more expansive than in his guarded public speeches, sharing opinions and confidences with friends in long, garrulous paragraphs.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: to eliminate completely

exs.t: When I turned 18, all of the shoplifting and jaywalking charges were expunged from my criminal record.
The editor expunged every trace of the retracted study from the journal's archive, so that later researchers would not cite its fabricated data.
Although the council voted to expunge the offensive remarks from the official minutes, many residents had already recorded them and shared them widely.
The new regime tried to expunge the deposed king from national memory, removing his portraits, renaming streets and rewriting textbooks.

def: to remove objectionable material

exs.t: The censor expurgated every reference to sex and drugs, converting the rapper's raunchy flow into a series of bleeps.
The publisher agreed to print the novel only if the author would expurgate the passages that censors had deemed obscene.
Students were surprised to learn that the version of the play they had studied was expurgated, with its bawdy jokes and coarse insults removed for classroom use.
Rather than expurgating the diaries to spare the relatives' feelings, the family published them in full, including every harsh remark the author had made about them.

def: draw from specific cases for more general cases

exs.t: By extrapolating from the data on the past three months, we can predict a 5% increase in traffic to our website.
From a few fossilized teeth, paleontologists extrapolated the size and diet of the entire animal, an inference some colleagues considered too bold.
It is risky to extrapolate from a single successful classroom to an entire school district, since conditions that worked for one teacher may not hold elsewhere.
By observing how the glacier retreated over the past decade, the team extrapolated a date by which the valley would be free of ice altogether.

def: arrived at without due care or effort; lacking depth

exs.t: Many news shows provide facile explanations to complex politics, so I prefer to read the in-depth reporting of The New York Times.
The report offered a facile explanation for the company's decline, blaming a single bad quarter while ignoring years of mismanagement.
Although the debut novel is fluently written, its facile ending, in which every conflict melts away in a final reconciliation, betrays the complexity of the themes it raises.
Serious historians resist facile comparisons between ancient and modern empires, insisting that the differences matter as much as any superficial resemblance.

def: produced by, or characterized by internal dissension

exs.t: The controversial bill proved factious, as dissension even within parties resulted.
The factious committee could not agree even on an agenda, as rival blocs spent each meeting accusing one another of bad faith.
The founders warned that a factious spirit, in which citizens place loyalty to their party above the common good, could tear the young republic apart.
What had been a unified reform movement grew factious after its leader's death, splintering into competing groups that each claimed to be her true heirs.

def: artificial; not natural

exs.t: The defendant's story was largely factitious and did not accord with eyewitness testimonies.
The town's prosperity proved factitious, propped up entirely by a single government contract that vanished as soon as the war ended.
Collectors learned that the dealer's antiques were factitious: the patina on the furniture had been produced with chemicals rather than centuries of use.
The advertising campaign created a factitious demand for the gadget, persuading consumers that they needed a product that solved no real problem.

def: lazy and irresponsible

exs.t: Two years after graduation, Charlie still lived with his parents and had no job, becoming more feckless with each passing day.
The feckless nephew squandered every opportunity his aunt arranged, skipping interviews, missing deadlines and blaming others for each failure.
Critics described the regulatory agency as feckless, noting that it had issued warnings for years but never once enforced a penalty.
Though her brother was charming, he was also feckless, so the family entrusted the estate to the sister, whose diligence was beyond question.

def: intellectually productive

exs.t: The artist had entered a fecund period, producing three masterpieces in the span of two months.
The decade the physicist spent at the institute was her most fecund; she published a dozen influential papers and trained a generation of students.
The novelist possessed a fecund imagination, producing plots, characters and whole invented languages faster than his editors could review them.
Rather than exhausting the subject, the conference proved remarkably fecund, generating new collaborations and research questions that occupied the participants for years.

def: terribly evil

exs.t: For fans of the Harry Potter series, the fell Lord Voldemort, who terrorized poor Harry for seven lengthy installments, has finally been vanquished by the forces of good--unless, that is, JK Rowling decides to come out of retirement.
In the old ballads, the fell sorcerer poisons the kingdom's wells and curses its children, and only a humble shepherd dares to oppose him.
The plague was a fell visitor to the medieval town, sweeping through its crowded streets and sparing neither rich nor poor.
Although the tyrant styled himself a benevolent father to his people, his fell deeds, including the imprisonment of dissenters and the seizure of their lands, told a different story.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: someone who deliberately creates trouble

exs.t: Freddie is a firebrand: every time he walks into the office, he winds up at the center of heated argument.
The young firebrand stirred up the dockworkers with speeches urging them to strike immediately, alarming even the union leaders who shared his goals.
Once a firebrand who delighted in provoking her colleagues, the professor mellowed with age and became a patient mediator in departmental disputes.
The pamphleteer was a born firebrand, writing tracts designed to inflame the public and provoke confrontation with the authorities.

def: droop, sink, or settle from or as if from pressure or loss of tautness; become less intense

exs.t: After the three crushing defeats in the last three games, the team's enthusiasm began to flag.
By the fourth hour of the negotiation, the delegates' energy had begun to flag, and even the chair struggled to keep her eyes open.
Public interest in the reform flagged once the initial scandal faded from the headlines, and the bill quietly died in committee.
The marathoner's pace never flagged; if anything, she ran the final miles faster than the first ones.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: showing inappropriate levity

exs.t: Although Sam was trying to honor Mark's sense of humor, many found it quite flippant that he wore a comic nose and glasses mask to Mark's funeral.
The minister's flippant reply to questions about the flood, in which he joked that residents needed swimming lessons, provoked outrage across the region.
Although the teacher welcomed humor in class discussion, she objected to flippant remarks during the solemn lesson on wartime refugees.
His tone in the apology was so flippant that the clients concluded he did not take the data breach seriously at all.

def: be a mystery or bewildering to

exs.t: Mary's behavior completely flummoxes me: I never have any idea what her motivations might be.
The puzzle flummoxed even the seasoned mathematicians at the conference, none of whom could explain why the obvious approach failed.
Tourists are often flummoxed by the city's transit map, whose overlapping colored lines seem designed to bewilder rather than guide.
The sudden failure of the experiment flummoxed the researchers, since they had followed the protocol exactly and could find no plausible cause.

def: irritable and is likely to cause disruption

exs.t: We rarely invite my fractious Uncle over for dinner; he always complains about the food, and usually launches into a tirade on some touchy subject.
The fractious toddler resisted every attempt to calm him, kicking his feet and wailing through the entire flight.
Managing the fractious board was the chairman's hardest task, as its members quarreled constantly and stormed out of meetings in protest.
The horse was so fractious that only the most experienced riders dared mount it, and it threw even them on occasion.

def: a socially awkward or tactless act

exs.t: In a famous gaffe, Vice President Quayle attempted to correct the spelling of a grade school student, only to find that the child was correct.
At the state dinner, the ambassador committed an embarrassing gaffe, toasting the host country by the name of its historic rival.
The new manager's gaffe of praising the department's former head, who, as everyone else knew, had been dismissed for misconduct, produced an awkward silence.
Etiquette guides for travelers warn of common gaffes, such as refusing food offered by a host or pointing with a single finger, that can offend local customs.

def: a maneuver or risk in a game or conversation, designed to secure an advantage

exs.t: Randy played a gambit, telling his boss that he would leave at the end of the week if he didn't get a raise.
Her opening gambit in the negotiation, a generous concession on price, was calculated to make the supplier more flexible on delivery terms.
The lawyer's gambit of calling the defendant's own mother as a witness was risky, but it ultimately won the jury's sympathy.
Sensing that his rival was nervous, the chess player sacrificed a pawn in an audacious gambit, betting that the resulting attack would outweigh the lost material.

def: to manipulate voting districts in order to favor a particular political party

exs.t: Years ago, savvy politicians had gerrymandered the city center to ensure their re-election.
By drawing the district as a narrow, winding strip that captured only friendly neighborhoods, the legislature gerrymandered the map to protect incumbents.
Reformers proposed an independent commission to redraw boundaries, arguing that lawmakers could not be trusted not to gerrymander seats in their own party's favor.
The court struck down the plan because it was clearly gerrymandered: districts snaked across the state to dilute the votes of one party's supporters.

def: corruption, usually through bribery

exs.t: In countries with rampant graft, getting a driver's license can require no more than paying an official.
The new mayor promised to root out graft in the building department, where inspectors had long accepted cash to overlook safety violations.
Because contracts were awarded to whoever paid the largest kickback, graft rather than merit determined which firms built the city's roads.
The historian argues that graft was so pervasive in the colonial administration that officials viewed bribes as an ordinary supplement to their salaries.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: puffed up with vanity

exs.t: The dictator was known for his grandiloquent speeches, puffing his chest out and using big, important- sounding words.
The mayor's grandiloquent speech, full of references to destiny and glory, seemed absurdly inflated for the opening of a municipal parking garage.
Readers found the memoir grandiloquent, as the author described his modest business career in the lofty rhetoric usually reserved for great conquerors.
Unlike her grandiloquent predecessor, who delivered every announcement as though addressing posterity, the new principal spoke plainly and briefly.

def: resourcefulness and determination

exs.t: Wallace Stegner lamented the lack of gumption in the U.S. during the sixties, claiming that no young person knew the value of work.
It took real gumption for the young baker to open a shop across the street from the town's most beloved bakery, but her ingenuity and persistence paid off.
Stranded when their bus broke down, the students showed gumption, arranging rides with local farmers and reaching the conference only an hour late.
The founder lacked capital and connections, but she had gumption: she taught herself accounting, pitched to dozens of investors and refused to quit after each rejection.

def: excessively flattering toward someone's life or work

exs.t: Most accounts of Tiger Woods life were hagiographic, until, that is, his affairs made headlines.
The authorized biography is frankly hagiographic, omitting every scandal and presenting the industrialist as a flawless benefactor.
Scholars have grown wary of hagiographic accounts of the explorer, which celebrate his courage while ignoring his brutal treatment of the people he encountered.
The documentary avoids a hagiographic tone; although it admires the conductor's genius, it also records his tyrannical treatment of musicians.

def: enthusiastically acclaim or celebrate something

exs.t: Many college superstar athletes are hailed as the next big thing, but then flop at the professional level.
Critics hailed the young architect's library as a masterpiece, praising its luminous reading rooms and its graceful integration with the surrounding park.
Although the treaty was hailed as a triumph when it was signed, within a decade most historians regarded it as a costly failure.
Researchers hail the new vaccine as a breakthrough, citing trial results far better than any previous candidate had achieved.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: idyllically calm and peaceful; suggesting happy tranquillity; marked by peace and prosperity

exs.t: The first decade after WWI was a halcyon period in America with new-found wealth and rapidly improving technology.
Retirees in the village often reminisce about the halcyon summers of their youth, when the lake was clear and days passed in unhurried calm.
The decade after the civil war proved a halcyon interval for the republic, marked by steady trade, peaceful elections and growing prosperity.
The novel opens in a halcyon setting, a sunlit estate where nothing disturbs the family's tranquility, only to shatter that peace in the second chapter.

def: overbearing pride evidenced by a superior manner toward inferiors

exs.t: As soon as she won the lottery, Alice begin displaying a hauteur to her friends, calling them dirty-clothed peasants behind their backs.
The duchess received the petitioners with icy hauteur, barely glancing at them and addressing her replies to her secretary instead.
Although the new partner was talented, his hauteur toward junior associates, whom he treated as beneath his notice, soon made him unpopular.
The waiter's hauteur, evident in his disdainful glance at diners who mispronounced the wine list, spoiled an otherwise excellent meal.

def: to bully or intimidate

exs.t: The boss's hectoring manner put off many employees, some of whom quit as soon as they found new jobs.
The coach hectored his players from the sidelines, shouting insults and threats until several of them refused to return for the next season.
Rather than persuade the committee, the lobbyist tried to hector its members, warning that he would ruin the career of anyone who voted against his client.
Witnesses complained that the prosecutor had hectored them during questioning, raising his voice and badgering them until they contradicted themselves.

def: to limit or qualify a statement; to avoid making a direct statement

exs.t: When asked why he had decided to buy millions of shares at the very moment the tech companies stock soared, the CEO hedged, mentioning something vague about gut instinct.
Asked whether the drug was safe for children, the researcher hedged, noting that the data were limited and that further trials might change the picture.
Good scientific writing avoids overstatement, but some authors hedge so heavily, with 'perhaps' and 'possibly' in every clause, that readers cannot tell what they actually believe.
Instead of giving a clear forecast, the economist hedged her prediction, saying growth could rise or fall depending on factors no one could yet measure.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: to be overly theatrical

exs.t: Though she received a B- on the test, she had such a histrionic outburst that one would have thought that she'd been handed a death sentence.
The lawyer's histrionic closing argument, complete with tears and a dramatic collapse into his chair, struck the judge as more theater than reasoning.
Although the novel's heroine faces real hardship, her histrionic reactions, fainting at bad news and declaiming her woes to strangers, undercut the reader's sympathy.
Unlike her histrionic co-star, who wept and shouted in every scene, the veteran actress conveyed grief through restrained, almost imperceptible gestures.

def: ancient

exs.t: Most workout gurus are young, fit people, whereas most yoga gurus are hoary men with long white beards.
The professor dismissed the argument as a hoary cliche, one that had been repeated in textbooks for so many generations that no one questioned it anymore.
At the center of the village stands a hoary oak, so old that local legend claims it sheltered travelers long before the church was built.
The comedian's routine relied on hoary jokes about mothers-in-law and bad cooking that had been old even in his grandfather's day.

def: to hold back the progress of something

exs.t: Bad weather has hobbled rescue efforts, making it difficult for crews to find bodies in the wreckage.
Chronic underfunding has hobbled the city's transit system, leaving it unable to replace aging trains or extend service to growing suburbs.
The reform was hobbled from the start by a clause requiring unanimous approval, so that a single objection could block any change.
Investors worried that the lawsuit would hobble the startup's expansion, tying up its funds and distracting its leaders for years.

def: to deceive or trick someone

exs.t: Someone tried to hoodwink Marty with an email telling him that his uncle had just passed away, and to collect the inheritance he should send his credit card information.
The swindler hoodwinked dozens of retirees into investing in a nonexistent gold mine, supplying them with forged reports of rich deposits.
Although the forger's painting hoodwinked several experts, a chemical analysis revealed pigments that had not existed in the artist's lifetime.
Voters resent being hoodwinked, and the candidate's lead vanished once it emerged that his celebrated tax plan contained hidden fees.

def: overbearing pride or presumption

exs.t: Bill Clinton was criticized for his hubris, since he believed he could get away with anything once in the White House.
The engineer's hubris proved disastrous: convinced that his design could not fail, he dismissed the warnings of colleagues who had spotted a flaw in the supports.
In Greek tragedy, a hero's hubris typically invites ruin, as when a mortal presumes to rival the gods and is punished for his arrogance.
The company's hubris after a decade of success led it to ignore smaller competitors, whose cheaper products eventually captured most of its market.

def: widely known and esteemed; having or conferring glory

exs.t: Einstein was possibly the most illustrious scientist in recent history.
The conservatory boasts an illustrious roster of alumni, including celebrated conductors, soloists and composers whose names are familiar worldwide.
Although she came from an illustrious family of statesmen, the young lawyer preferred to earn her own reputation rather than trade on her ancestors' renown.
The scientist's illustrious career, crowned by numerous prizes and honorary degrees, began modestly in a cramped basement laboratory.

def: to drink or absorb as if drinking

exs.t: Plato imbibed Socrates' teachings to such an extent that he was able to write volumes of work that he directly attributed, sometimes word for word, to Socrates.
Children imbibe the prejudices of their surroundings long before they can articulate them, absorbing attitudes from overheard conversations and casual remarks.
Travelers crossing the desert were warned to imbibe water regularly, even when they did not feel thirsty, since dehydration can set in without warning.
The plant's roots imbibe moisture from the soil so efficiently that it can survive for months without rain.

def: a confusing and potentially embarrassing situation

exs.t: The chef cook-off featured one gourmand who had the unfortunate distinction of mixing the wrong broths, creating an imbroglio that diners would not soon forget.
What began as a minor dispute over a parking space escalated into a neighborhood imbroglio, involving lawyers, the city council and an embarrassing story in the local paper.
The ambassador spent weeks trying to extricate his government from the diplomatic imbroglio caused by a misdirected letter that insulted an allied leader.
The museum's board found itself in an awkward imbroglio when it emerged that a donated painting had been stolen and that two trustees had known of its origin.

def: to enclose, usually in walls

exs.t: The modern supermarket experience makes many feel claustrophobic, as they are immured in walls upon walls of products.
In the gothic novel, a jealous baron immures his wife in a tower, sealing the only door with stone so that she can never leave.
Preferring solitude, the scholar immured herself in the library for months, emerging only for meals and rarely speaking to anyone.
Some medieval hermits chose to be immured in small cells built against the church wall, receiving food through a narrow window for the rest of their lives.

def: lacking money; poor

exs.t: In extremely trying times, even the moderately wealthy, after a few turns of ill-fortune, can become impecunious.
The impecunious graduate student lived on rice and borrowed textbooks, unable to afford even the modest fee to attend the conference.
Although he died impecunious, leaving his widow nothing but debts, the painter's canvases now sell for fortunes at auction.
Many of the city's greatest benefactors had once been impecunious immigrants who arrived with empty pockets and worked their way to wealth.

def: having or showing arrogant superiority to and disdain of those one views as unworthy

exs.t: Children are imperious with each other before they learn that earning someone's respect is better than demanding.
The imperious director demanded that the entire cast wait in silence until she arrived, and she never once thanked anyone for their work.
With an imperious wave of his hand, the landlord dismissed the tenants' complaints as unworthy of his attention and ordered them out of his office.
Although the professor was brilliant, his imperious manner toward students, whom he treated as servants summoned to hear his pronouncements, alienated many of them.

def: not admitting of passage or capable of being affected

exs.t: I am not impervious to your insults; they cause me great pain.
The new coating renders the fabric impervious to water, so that rain beads on its surface and rolls away without soaking through.
The senator seemed impervious to criticism; no matter how fiercely editorials condemned him, he never altered a single position.
Because the clay layer is impervious, groundwater collects above it rather than seeping down into the deeper rock.

def: characterized by undue haste and lack of thought or deliberation

exs.t: Herbert is rarely impetuous, but on the spur of the moment, he spent thousands of dollars on a motorcycle today.
The impetuous investor sold all her shares the moment the market dipped, without consulting her advisers or waiting to learn the cause of the decline.
Unlike his impetuous younger brother, who proposed marriage after a week, Daniel deliberated for years before making any important decision.
The general's impetuous charge, launched before scouts had returned with information about the terrain, led his cavalry straight into a marsh.

def: beg persistently and urgently

exs.t: After weeks of importuning the star to meet for a five-minute interview, the journalist finally got what she wanted.
The street vendors importuned every tourist who passed, following them for blocks and pleading with them to buy just one more trinket.
For months the charity importuned the foundation for a grant, submitting letter after letter until the directors finally agreed to meet.
Tired of being importuned by relatives seeking loans, the lottery winner changed her phone number and moved to another city.

def: not given careful consideration

exs.t: Marty was improvident, never putting money aside for the future but spending it on decorating the interior of his home.
The improvident decision to build the stadium on a floodplain, made without any environmental study, cost the city millions when the river rose.
Economists blamed the crisis on improvident lending, as banks had extended credit to borrowers without examining whether they could ever repay.
Having spent his entire inheritance in a single year, the improvident heir had nothing left when the harvest failed and his creditors called in their debts.

def: attack as false or wrong

exs.t: Though many initially tried to impugn Darwin's theory, in scientific circles today, the is idea taken as truth.
The defense attorney tried to impugn the witness's credibility by pointing out inconsistencies between her testimony and her earlier statements to police.
Critics impugned the study's conclusions, arguing that its small sample and flawed controls made its findings unreliable.
Rather than engaging with her argument, her opponents chose to impugn her motives, claiming she was secretly funded by the industry she criticized.

def: attribute (responsibility or fault) to something

exs.t: He imputed his subpar performance on the test to a combination of stress and poor sleep.
The inquiry imputed the collapse to faulty welding rather than to the design itself, clearing the architects of blame.
It is unfair to impute malice to a colleague whose mistake was plainly the result of inexperience rather than ill will.
Historians once imputed the empire's fall entirely to moral decay, but newer research emphasizes drought, disease and economic strain.

def: total lack of meaning or ideas

exs.t: Bill's poem was nothing more than a list of impressive sounding words, so there was no point in trying to take meaning from the inanity.
The talk show's inanity was relentless: for an hour, the hosts traded empty chatter about nothing in particular while serious news went unmentioned.
After reading dozens of applications filled with vague slogans, the committee was relieved to find one essay that rose above the inanity with a genuine argument.
The satirist mocked the inanity of corporate jargon, quoting memos so full of meaningless buzzwords that they conveyed no information whatsoever.

def: only partly in existence; imperfectly formed

exs.t: Inchoate ideas about the relation of humans to other animals had been discussed since the Middle Ages but the modern theory really began with Darwin.
The student's thesis was still inchoate; she had a promising intuition but had not yet shaped it into a coherent argument.
The protest movement remained inchoate for months, a loose collection of grievances without leaders, demands or a clear strategy.
In the composer's sketchbooks one can see the symphony's inchoate themes, rough fragments that would later be developed into its soaring melodies.

def: necessarily or demonstrably true; impossible to deny or disprove

exs.t: Unless you can provide incontrovertible evidence, I will remain skeptical.
The DNA results provided incontrovertible proof that the man had been wrongly convicted, and he was released within the week.
Although some still dispute the details, the core finding is incontrovertible: every independent laboratory that repeated the experiment obtained the same result.
The auditor presented incontrovertible evidence of the fraud, including signed invoices and bank records that no explanation could reconcile with the company's claims.

label: adj.
def: poor; having very little

exs.t: In the so-called Third World, many are indigent and only a privileged few have the resources to enjoy material luxuries.
The clinic provides free care to indigent patients, many of whom cannot afford even the bus fare to reach a hospital.
Born to indigent parents who often lacked money for food, the novelist later wrote vividly about childhood hunger.
The law guarantees that indigent defendants, who cannot pay for their own lawyers, will be represented by counsel at public expense.

label: n.
def: a poor or needy person

exs.t: The indigents, huddled under the overpass, tried to start a small bonfire in the hope of staying warm.
The charity's founders devoted their fortune to feeding indigents, opening soup kitchens in every district where poverty was most severe.
Under the old poor laws, an indigent could be sent to the workhouse, where food and shelter were provided in exchange for grueling labor.
The hospital's charter required it to treat any indigent who arrived at its doors, regardless of whether the patient could pay.

def: too sacred to be uttered; defying expression or description

exs.t: While art critics can occasionally pinpoint a work's greatness, much of why a piece captures our imaginations is completely ineffable.
Mystics across many traditions describe an ineffable experience of union with the divine, and their writings are full of apologies for the inadequacy of the words they must use.
The mountaineer tried to convey the view from the summit, but finally admitted that its beauty was ineffable and that photographs did it no justice.
Some names were considered too holy to speak aloud, so worshippers substituted a title for the ineffable word whenever they prayed.

def: impossible to avoid or evade:

exs.t: For those who smoke cigarettes for years, a major health crisis brought on by smoking is ineluctable.
The tragedy's power lies in its sense of ineluctable fate: from the first scene, the audience knows the hero cannot escape his doom.
Many economists regard some degree of automation as ineluctable, arguing that no policy can halt it and that societies should plan for its consequences.
Though the climbers tried every route, the storm made retreat ineluctable, and they descended without reaching the summit.

def: injustice by virtue of not conforming with rules or standards

exs.t: After decades of racial inequity, the "separate but equal" doctrine was successfully overturned.
The report documented a glaring inequity in school funding: districts in wealthy suburbs spent twice as much per student as those in poorer towns.
Workers protested the inequity of a pay system in which newcomers doing identical jobs earned far less than their longer-serving colleagues.
Reformers argued that the tax code's many loopholes created inequities, allowing some to pay almost nothing while others with similar incomes paid in full.

def: inappropriate

exs.t: During the executive meeting, the marketing director continued to make infelicitous comments about the CEO's gambling habit.
The speaker's infelicitous choice of a joke about illness at a hospital fundraiser drew uncomfortable silence rather than laughter.
The translation is accurate but often infelicitous, rendering the poet's graceful lines in awkward phrasing that jars the ear.
'Exciting opportunity' was an infelicitous way to describe the layoffs, and the chief executive later apologized for the insensitivity of the phrase.

def: defying imitation; matchless

exs.t: Mozart's music follows a clear pattern that, anyone could imitate, but his music gives an overall sense of effortlessness that is inimitable.
No other cook could reproduce the grandmother's inimitable stew, though many relatives tried to copy it from her handwritten recipe.
The comedian's inimitable timing, a split-second pause before each punchline, has baffled generations of performers who have attempted to reproduce it.
Critics agree that the novelist's style is inimitable; the many writers who have tried to copy her sentences produce only pale parodies.

def: lack of concern

exs.t: Surprisingly, Hank had become a high-powered CEO; his high school friends remembered him as "Hanky Panky", who shrugged off each failed class with insouciance.
The pianist approached the fiendishly difficult concerto with remarkable insouciance, chatting with the conductor minutes before walking onstage as if nothing were at stake.
Investors were alarmed by the chief executive's insouciance about mounting debts, since he seemed not the least bit worried about the looming payments.
Far from displaying the anxiety one might expect, the defendant sat through the trial with insouciance, idly sketching in a notebook while witnesses testified.

def: intolerable, difficult to endure

exs.t: Chester always tried to find some area in which he excelled above others; unsurprisingly, his co-workers found him insufferable and chose to exclude him from daily luncheons out.
The critic's insufferable arrogance, evident in his habit of correcting everyone's pronunciation at dinner, eventually cost him most of his friends.
The heat in the unventilated factory became insufferable by midafternoon, and several workers fainted before management opened the doors.
Though his early novels were charming, his later narrators became insufferable, lecturing readers for pages on subjects no one had raised.

def: (of conflict) within a group or organization

exs.t: The guerilla group, which had become so powerful as to own the state police, was finally destroyed by an internecine conflict.
The party spent the campaign in internecine squabbling, as rival wings attacked one another instead of addressing the voters.
The empire's collapse owed less to foreign invaders than to internecine struggles among the emperor's sons, each of whom sought the throne for himself.
Internecine feuds within the research institute, in which departments sabotaged one another's grant applications, left it unable to compete with outside laboratories.

def: an indirect suggestion

exs.t: At first the hostess tried intimation, praising the benefits of cutlery; when Cecil continued eating with his hands, the hostess told him to use a fork at dinner.
The first intimation that the company was in trouble came when the executives quietly canceled the annual holiday party.
Rather than state her objections outright, the editor offered only an intimation of her displeasure, a raised eyebrow and a pointed question about the deadline.
The late poems contain faint intimations of the poet's illness, hints that most readers noticed only after her death.

def: to make accustomed to something unpleasant

exs.t: Three years of Manhattan living has inured her to the sound of wailing sirens; she could probably sleep through the apocalypse.
Years of working in the emergency ward had inured the nurse to scenes that would have unsettled most visitors, and she remained calm amid the chaos.
Residents of the flood-prone delta have become inured to hardship, rebuilding their homes after each storm without complaint.
The acoustician warned that constant exposure to background noise would inure listeners to it, so that they would no longer notice or object to the din.

def: abusive or denunciatory language

exs.t: The Internet has unleashed the invectives in many of us; many people post stinging criticism on the comments section underneath newspaper articles or YouTube videos.
The debate degenerated into invective, with each candidate hurling insults at the other rather than discussing policy.
Although the critic was known for scathing reviews, his invective against the new museum, which he called a monument to vulgarity, shocked even his admirers.
The pamphlet abandoned reasoned argument for pure invective, denouncing its opponents as traitors, liars and fools.

def: likely to cause resentment

exs.t: At a time when many others in the office were about to be laid off, many considered Cheryl's fine clothes that day an invidious display.
The manager avoided invidious comparisons between team members, knowing that praising one employee at another's expense would breed resentment.
Awarding the corner offices only to senior partners' relatives proved invidious, and junior staff grumbled about favoritism for months.
Scholarship committees must make invidious choices among equally deserving applicants, inevitably disappointing and embittering those who are passed over.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: never to be broken, infringed, or dishonored

exs.t: Too many the grass at Wimbledon is inviolable and only greater tennis players are able to enjoy a game there.
For the monks, the vow of silence was inviolable; not even a fire in the kitchen could persuade them to speak.
The constitution treats freedom of conscience as an inviolable right, one that no legislature may abridge under any circumstances.
Among the old merchants, a handshake agreement was inviolable, and breaking one meant permanent exclusion from the guild.

def: must be kept sacred

exs.t: While the literary critic subjected most of the classics to the harshest reviews, he regarded Cervantes as inviolate, and had nothing but praise for him.
Although the invading army looted the city, the ancient shrine remained inviolate, as even the conquerors feared to desecrate it.
The founder insisted that the trust's central principle remain inviolate: the land was never to be sold or developed, no matter the offer.
Throughout decades of upheaval, the family kept its grandmother's letters inviolate, sealed in a chest that no one was permitted to open.

def: impossible to deny or disprove

exs.t: The existence of life on earth is irrefutable; the existence of intelligent life on earth is still hotly debated.
The fingerprints on the vault provided irrefutable evidence that the guard had been involved, and he confessed shortly afterward.
Her logic was irrefutable; although her opponents searched for a flaw in the proof, none could find a step that failed.
Satellite images offered irrefutable confirmation that the forest was shrinking, silencing officials who had long denied any deforestation.

def: to be biased against due to envy or prejudice

exs.t: Shelly was jaundiced towards Olivia; though the two had once been best friends, Olivia had become class president, prom queen, and, to make matters worse, the girlfriend of the one boy Shelly liked.
After years of broken campaign promises, voters regarded every new pledge with a jaundiced eye, assuming it would be abandoned after the election.
The critic's jaundiced view of the young novelist, whose success he openly resented, colored every review he wrote of her work.
Having been passed over for promotion, Martin grew jaundiced toward his rival, dismissing even her genuine achievements as luck or flattery.

label: adj.1
def: dull; lacking flavor

exs.t: Although many top chefs have secured culinary foam's popularity in haute cuisine, Waters criticizes it for being jejune and unfilling.
Students struggle to stay awake through a single chapter of the textbook, whose jejune prose reduces even the most dramatic events of the century to a list of dates.
Diners expecting the bold spices promised on the menu were disappointed by the jejune curry, which tasted of little more than boiled vegetables.
Compared with the vivid, witty letters of her youth, the aging writer's final essays seem jejune, as though the years had drained all the flavor from her prose.

label: adj.2
def: immature; childish

exs.t: Her boss further cemented his reputation for being jejune after throwing a fit when the water cooler wasn't refilled.
The senior diplomats dismissed the intern's proposal as jejune, the kind of naive scheme that ignores every practical obstacle an experienced negotiator would foresee.
Although the poet later disowned her jejune early verses, with their adolescent posturing and borrowed melodrama, they reveal the roots of her mature style.
The professor found the debate club's arguments jejune, relying on schoolyard taunts and simplistic slogans rather than the reasoning expected of adults.

def: a person who thinks that their country should be at war

exs.t: In the days leading up to war, a nation typically breaks up into the two opposing camps: doves, who do their best to avoid war, and jingoists, who are only too eager to wave national flags from their vehicles and vehemently denounce those who do not do the same.
The jingoist newspaper editor called for an immediate invasion after the border incident, mocking anyone who urged diplomacy as a coward.
Historians have noted how quickly moderate voices were drowned out by jingoists eager for battle once the naval dispute became public.
Though he had once been a jingoist, demanding war with every neighboring state, the veteran returned from the front a committed advocate for peace.

def: a force that cannot be stopped

exs.t: Napoleon was considered a juggernaut until he decided to invade Russia in winter; after which, his once indomitable army was decimated by cold and famine.
The upstart retailer grew into a juggernaut, crushing small competitors and expanding into every market it entered despite regulators' efforts to slow it.
The campaign seemed an unstoppable juggernaut until a single scandal, revealed days before the vote, finally halted its momentum.
Once the reform movement gained broad public support, it became a juggernaut that no coalition of entrenched interests could resist.

def: to bow or act in a subservient manner

exs.t: Paul kowtowed to his boss so often the boss herself became nauseated by his sycophancy.
Rather than kowtow to the wealthy donor's demands, the museum director refused to alter the exhibition and risked losing the gift.
Courtiers kowtowed to the emperor, bowing low and agreeing with every pronouncement, however absurd.
The editorial accused the regulators of kowtowing to the industry they were supposed to police, approving every request without objection.

def: deeply hurt the feelings of; distress

exs.t: The teacher was fired for lacerating a student who wrote a poor essay.
The review lacerated the young playwright, who had poured years into the script and was devastated to see it described as worthless.
Her sister's cruel remarks at the wedding lacerated Julia's feelings, and the two did not speak for nearly a year.
Though intended as constructive, the supervisor's criticism lacerated the sensitive intern, who left the meeting in tears.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: showing sorrow

exs.t: Lachrymose and depressed, Alexei Alexandrovich walked two miles home in the rain after learning that his wife was having an affair.
The lachrymose widower wept openly throughout the memorial service, unable to finish the eulogy he had prepared.
Critics complained that the film was lachrymose to excess, with nearly every scene engineered to make the audience cry.
Although the children's author usually wrote cheerful adventures, her final book was lachrymose, dwelling on loss and ending with a tearful farewell.

def: ridicule with satire

exs.t: Mark Twain understood that lampooning a bad idea with humor was the most effective criticism.
The satirical magazine lampooned the city's pompous officials, depicting them as bumbling peacocks strutting about the town hall.
The playwright lampoons the pretensions of the art world, portraying collectors who pay fortunes for blank canvases they cannot tell apart.
Rather than argue earnestly against the bureaucracy, the columnist chose to lampoon it, inventing absurd regulations so plausible that readers mistook them for real ones.

def: become feeble

exs.t: Stranded in the wilderness for four days, the hiker languished, eating protein bars and nuts.
Deprived of sunlight in the dim apartment, the potted ferns languished, their fronds yellowing and drooping week by week.
Without regular visits from family, the elderly patient began to languish, eating little and growing weaker each day.
The once thriving port languished after the railway bypassed it, its warehouses emptying and its population steadily declining.

def: lecherous; sexually perverted

exs.t: Lolita is a challenging novel for many, not necessarily because of the elevated prose style but because of the depravity of the main character, Humbert Humbert, who, as an old, lascivious man, falls in love with a girl.
The censor objected to the novel's lascivious passages, which dwelt so openly on lust that he feared they would corrupt young readers.
In the morality play, the lascivious courtier, forever leering at the ladies of the household, serves as a warning against unchecked desire.
The curator defended the painting against charges that it was lascivious, arguing that its nude figures were depicted with classical restraint rather than lecherous intent.

def: clarity in terms of expression

exs.t: Her limpid prose made even the most recondite subjects accessible to all.
Her limpid explanation of quantum mechanics, free of jargon and needless complication, allowed even novices to follow the argument.
The philosopher's early essays are dense and tangled, but his later prose became limpid, each sentence as transparent as a pane of glass.
Students prize the textbook for its limpid style: even the most difficult proofs are laid out so clearly that the logic seems obvious.

def: any long and tedious account of something

exs.t: Mr. Rogers spoke to a Senate committee and did not give a litany of reasons to keep funding the program, but instead, appealed to the basic human decency of all present.
The customer recited a litany of complaints, from the late delivery to the scratched table to the rude driver, that lasted nearly half an hour.
The report is less an analysis than a litany of failures, listing one missed deadline after another without explaining why any occurred.
Voters, weary of the candidate's litany of grievances against his opponents, began to wonder whether he had any proposals of his own.

def: unwillingness to do something contrary to your custom (usually followed by 'to')

exs.t: I was loath to leave the concert before my favorite band finished playing.
The committee was loath to abandon a tradition that had lasted a century, even though few members could remember why it had begun.
Scientists are often loath to speculate in public, preferring to wait until the data are conclusive before making any claims.
Though she needed the money, Elena was loath to borrow from friends, since she had always prided herself on paying her own way.

def: excessively mournful

exs.t: At the funeral, lugubrious songs filled the small church.
The actor's lugubrious expression, with drooping eyes and a mournful sigh, made even his comic lines sound like announcements of a death.
The chair delivered the minor budget news in such a lugubrious tone that several members assumed the organization was about to close.
Visitors found the memorial garden's music lugubrious, a slow, funereal dirge played on repeat that seemed designed to deepen rather than console their grief.

def: engage in plotting or enter into a conspiracy, swear together

exs.t: The rebels met at night in an abandoned barn to machinate.
