While publicly pledging loyalty to the king, the ambitious duke machinated with foreign envoys to seize the throne.
The board members who had machinated to oust the founder met secretly for months, drafting their plan before a single employee suspected it.
The novel's villain spends every chapter machinating against the heroine, forging letters and bribing servants to ruin her reputation.

def: offensively self-assured or given to exercising unwarranted power

exs.t: Though she was only a third grade teacher, Ms. Martinet was magisterial in dealing with her class, lording over them like a queen.
The new supervisor's magisterial manner, issuing decrees without consultation and brooking no dissent, quickly alienated a staff accustomed to collaboration.
In a magisterial tone that invited no disagreement, the senior partner informed the associates that his interpretation of the contract was final.
Readers bristled at the critic's magisterial pronouncements, which dismissed entire genres as unworthy without offering any reasons.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: the confusion of a word with another word that sounds similar

exs.t: Whenever I looked glum, my mother would offer to share "an amusing antidote" with me--an endearing malapropism of "anecdote" that never failed to cheer me up.
Students laughed at the malapropism when their classmate announced that the explorer had died of 'ammonia' rather than pneumonia.
The sitcom's landlord speaks almost entirely in malapropisms, confidently assuring tenants that the lease is 'legally biting' and that he will never 'take them for granite.'
The best man's toast is remembered chiefly for one malapropism: he wished the newlyweds a lifetime of 'marital blitz,' and the guests laughed so hard that he never finished his speech.

def: misconduct or wrongdoing (especially by a public official)

exs.t: Not even the mayor's trademark pearly-toothed grin could save him from charges of malfeasance: while in power, he'd been running an illegal gambling rink in the room behind his office.
The auditors uncovered evidence of malfeasance in the treasurer's office, where public funds had been diverted to accounts controlled by the treasurer's relatives.
Although the commissioner insisted that his errors were honest mistakes, investigators concluded that his conduct amounted to deliberate malfeasance in office.
Voters who had tolerated the council's inefficiency lost patience once they learned of outright malfeasance, including bribes accepted in exchange for zoning approvals.

def: someone shirking their duty by pretending to be sick or incapacitated

exs.t: At one time, our country was full of hardworking respectful people, but now it seems that everyone is a malingerer with little inclination to work.
The foreman suspected that the worker was a malingerer, since his mysterious back pain always seemed to flare up on the days heavy crates arrived.
Army doctors were trained to distinguish genuinely wounded soldiers from the occasional malingerer who feigned illness to avoid returning to the front.
Far from being a malingerer, as her skeptical manager had assumed, the employee turned out to have a serious illness that she had tried to work through.

def: a strict disciplinarian

exs.t: The job seemed perfect to Rebecca, until she found out that her boss was a total martinet; after each project the boss would come by to scrutinize--and inevitably criticize--every little detail of the work Rebecca had done.
The conductor was a notorious martinet, dismissing musicians for arriving a minute late and demanding that every note be played exactly as marked.
Cadets who expected a lenient commander were dismayed to find that the new colonel was a martinet who inspected their boots and beds every morning.
Although her students called her a martinet for her rigid rules about deadlines and formatting, many later credited her discipline with their success.

def: overly emotional and sad

exs.t: Just as those who were alive during the 70's are mortified that they once cavorted about in bellbottoms, many who lived during the 80's are now aghast at the maudlin pop songs they used to enjoy--really, just what exactly is a total eclipse of the heart?
By the end of the reunion, the guests had grown maudlin, tearfully toasting departed friends and lamenting lost youth in speeches that went on far too long.
The screenplay avoids the maudlin sentimentality typical of the genre; even the grandmother's death is handled with restraint rather than swelling violins and weeping relatives.
Critics found the singer's ballad maudlin, its syrupy lyrics about lost love wallowing in self-pity rather than expressing genuine grief.

label: v.1
def: wander aimlessly

exs.t: Max liked to maunder down by the seaside and pick up whatever sea shells he would stumble upon.
With no destination in mind, the retired professor would maunder through the old quarter each afternoon, drifting from bookshop to bookshop without any plan.
The stray cattle maundered across the open range, ambling wherever the grass looked greenest rather than following any path.
Lacking a map, the tourists maundered along the riverbank for hours, idly turning down one lane and then another until the sun had set.

label: v.2
def: speak in a rambling, aimless way about unimportant matters

exs.t: After drinking two espressos each, the animated couple would maunder loudly, annoying the other patrons in the coffee shop.
The guest speaker maundered on about his vacation photographs for forty minutes, never reaching the topic the audience had come to hear.
Rather than answer the question directly, the witness maundered about the weather, his neighbors and his health until the judge interrupted him.
Her uncle would maunder endlessly over dinner about trivial grievances, chattering so incessantly that no one else could get a word in.

def: smooth and sweet-sounding

exs.t: Chelsea's grandmother thought Franz Schubert's music to be the most mellifluous ever written; Chelsea demurred, and to her grandmother's chagrin, would blast Rihanna on the home stereo speakers.
Listeners who found the audiobook's chapters dull kept listening anyway, because the narrator's voice was so mellifluous that even lists of dates sounded pleasant.
Unlike the harsh, clattering consonants of the northern dialect, the southern accent sounded mellifluous to visitors, its vowels flowing gently together.
The violinist's tone was praised as mellifluous, though some critics felt that such unfailing sweetness suited Mozart better than the jagged modern works on her program.

def: a pauper who lives by begging

exs.t: Tolstoy was an aristocrat, but he strove to understand the Christianity of the Russian peasants by wandering among them as a mendicant.
Having given away his possessions, the friar lived as a mendicant, relying on the charity of villagers for every meal he ate.
Pilgrims approaching the medieval shrine passed long lines of mendicants holding out bowls and pleading for coins.
The novel's hero falls from wealthy merchant to mendicant, and in the final chapter he stands with an outstretched hand outside the very warehouses he once owned.

def: like a meteor in speed or brilliance or transience
defMasked: like a ____ in speed or brilliance or transience

exs.t: The early spectacular successes propelled the pitcher to meteoric stardom, but a terribly injury tragically cut short his career.
The startup's meteoric rise, from a garage workshop to a billion-dollar valuation in three years, astonished even its founders.
Her fame was meteoric in every sense: dazzling for a single season, it faded almost as abruptly as it had appeared.
Few scientists enjoy so meteoric a career; within five years of his doctorate, he directed an institute and had won nearly every major award.

def: filled with courage or valor

exs.t: For its raid on the Bin Laden's compound in Abbottabad, Seal Team Six has become, for many Americans, the embodiment of mettle.
The mettlesome reporter continued to investigate the cartel despite repeated threats, refusing to abandon the story.
Though hers was the smallest boat in the regatta, it had a mettlesome crew that sailed straight into the storm while larger vessels turned back.
The seventeen-year-old proved a mettlesome advocate for her village, confronting the mining company's executives at a public hearing where adults had stayed silent.

def: to erroneously attribute; to falsely ascribe; used especially of authorship

exs.t: I made a mistake; I misattributed "Crime and Punishment" to Leo Tolstoy when it was actually written by Fyodor Dostoyevsky.
Quotations are frequently misattributed to famous figures, since a clever line gains authority when it seems to come from a celebrated author.
The museum had long misattributed the portrait to the master himself, until an analysis of the brushwork revealed that one of his apprentices had painted it.
Historians warn against misattributing the anonymous pamphlet to the revolutionary leader simply because its style resembles his; several contemporaries wrote in the same manner.

def: a small or moderate or token amount

exs.t: If my sister had even a modicum of sense, she wouldn't be engaged to that barbarian.
The reforms granted the colonies only a modicum of self-government; the governor still appointed every official and could veto any law.
Although the documentary is mostly bleak, it offers a modicum of hope in its final scenes, showing a few families returning to rebuild.
The negotiators agreed that at least a modicum of trust, however slight, would be necessary before any larger agreement could be reached.

def: biting and caustic in thought, manner, or style

exs.t: While Phil frequently made mordant remarks about company policy overall, he always was considerably gentler in discussing any person in particular.
The columnist's mordant wit spared no one; her caustic remarks about the city council were quoted, and resented, for weeks.
Though his novels deal with grim subjects, they are leavened by a mordant humor that skewers the pretensions of his characters.
Rather than offering gentle suggestions, the editor scrawled mordant comments in the margins, mocking clumsy sentences with biting sarcasm.

def: being on the point of death; declining rapidly losing all momentum in progress

exs.t: Whether you like it or not, jazz as a genre is moribund at best, possibly already dead.
The once bustling mill town is now moribund, its factories shuttered and its young people departing for cities elsewhere.
Critics declared the epic poem a moribund form, but a few contemporary writers have revived it with surprising vigor.
The physician recognized that the patient was moribund and gently advised the family to gather at her bedside while there was still time.

def: to defraud or swindle

exs.t: The so-called magical diet cure simply ended up mulcting Maria out of hundreds of dollars, but did nothing for her weight.
The fraudulent contractor mulcted elderly homeowners of their savings, charging for roof repairs that were never performed.
Investigators found that the fund's managers had mulcted investors by inflating fees and concealing losses for nearly a decade.
Posing as a tax official, the con artist mulcted dozens of shopkeepers, collecting fictitious penalties that went straight into his own pocket.

def: the lowest point

exs.t: For many pop music fans, the rap and alternative-rock dominated 90s were the nadir of musical expression.
Mike had walked in cold to the new GRE and was not surprised afterwards that he'd hit a standardized test nadir.
The team reached its nadir in the final month of the season, losing ten straight games and finishing in last place.
Historians regard the famine years as the nadir of the kingdom's fortunes, after which a slow recovery began.
At the nadir of his career, with no publisher willing to read his manuscripts, the novelist took a job washing dishes to pay the rent.

def: causing irritation or annoyance

exs.t: Maria found her coworkers cell phone nettlesome, because every few minutes it would buzz to life with another text message.
The software's nettlesome habit of freezing whenever a file was saved drove the office staff to distraction.
Negotiators set aside the most nettlesome issue, the division of water rights, to avoid derailing agreement on the rest of the treaty.
The constant hum of the neighbor's generator was more nettlesome than genuinely harmful, but it frayed everyone's nerves by the end of the week.

def: having an extremely bad smell

exs.t: Each August, when the winds moved in a south easterly direction, the garbage dump would spread noisome vapors through the small town.
The noisome odor of rotting fish drifted from the abandoned cannery, forcing pedestrians to cover their noses as they passed.
Before the sewer system was built, the city's canals were noisome channels whose stench sickened residents every summer.
The chemist opened the flask and immediately regretted it, as noisome fumes reminiscent of rotten eggs filled the entire laboratory.

def: coming across as coolly uninterested

exs.t: The twenty-somethings at the coffee shop always irked Sheldon, especially the way in which they acted nonchalantly towards everything, not even caring when Sheldon once spilled his mocha on them.
Despite having just won the championship, the player gave a nonchalant shrug when reporters asked how she felt, as though the victory meant little to her.
The pilot's nonchalant announcement that one engine had failed, delivered in the tone of a weather update, somehow reassured the anxious passengers.
Though his hands trembled beneath the table, the candidate tried to appear nonchalant during the interview, leaning back and answering questions with studied indifference.

def: express strong disapproval of

exs.t: The manager spent an hour objurgating the employee in the hopes that he would not make these mistakes again.
Rather than offering the gentle correction the young clerk expected, the magistrate chose to objurgate him before the entire courtroom, denouncing his carelessness in the harshest terms.
Critics who had once praised the architect's daring now objurgated her latest tower, condemning its blank facade as an insult to the historic square it overshadowed.
Although the committee chair was known for her mild manners, she objurgated the auditors sharply for concealing the deficit, making clear that such conduct would not be tolerated.

def: not straightforward; indirect

exs.t: Herbert never explicitly revealed anything negative about Tom's past, but at times he would obliquely suggest that Tom was not as innocent as he seemed.
Instead of stating her objection outright, the diplomat made only an oblique reference to 'certain unresolved concerns,' leaving her counterparts to guess what she actually opposed.
The novel's criticism of the regime is oblique rather than explicit: the author never names the dictator, conveying her judgment through allegory and carefully chosen silences.
Because direct questions about his finances made the tycoon defensive, the biographer took an oblique approach, asking about his childhood and letting the subject of money arise on its own.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: noisily and stubbornly defiant; willfully difficult to control

exs.t: When the teacher asked the obstreperous student simply to bus his tray, the student threw the entire tray on the floor, shouted an epithet, and walked out.
The seminar ran smoothly until an obstreperous attendee began shouting objections over every speaker and refused to yield the microphone even when the moderator pleaded with him.
Far from the docile animals described in the brochure, the goats proved obstreperous, bleating loudly, butting the gate, and resisting every attempt to lead them into the pen.
The conductor could manage temperamental soloists, but the obstreperous brass section, which played loudly out of turn and ignored his cues, finally exhausted his patience.

def: be valid, applicable, or true

exs.t: The custom of waiting your turn in line does not obtain in some countries, in which many people try to rush to front of the line at the same time.
Customs that obtain in a small village, where everyone knows everyone else, often fail to hold in a large city, where anonymity changes how people behave.
The economist cautioned that the link between interest rates and inflation, though reliable in the past, may no longer obtain under the new global conditions.
Newton's laws obtain for everyday objects such as falling apples and rolling carts; at the scale of atoms, however, they cease to apply and quantum mechanics must take over.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: slow to learn or understand; lacking intellectual acuity; lacking in insight or discernment

exs.t: Jackson was the most obtuse member of the team: the manager's subtle ironies were always lost on him.
The clues in the detective story were so heavy-handed that only the most obtuse reader could fail to identify the murderer by the second chapter.
Though brilliant with numbers, the analyst was strangely obtuse about people, never noticing that his colleagues' polite smiles concealed growing irritation.
The editor's letter was gently worded, but the author was so obtuse that he mistook her rejection for a request to submit more chapters.

def: intrusive in a meddling or offensive manner

exs.t: The professor had trouble concentrating on her new theorem, because her officious secretary would barge in frequently reminding her of some trivial detail involving departmental paperwork.
The officious hall monitor insisted on inspecting every visitor's bag and lecturing each one on the building's history, though no one had asked for either service.
Maria appreciated help with the move, but her officious neighbor rearranged the kitchen cabinets without asking and then criticized where she had placed the dishes.
Tourists found the museum guard officious: he hovered beside each group, correcting their pronunciation of artists' names and telling them how long to look at each painting.

def: make rigid and set into a conventional pattern

exs.t: Even as a young man, Bob had some bias against poor people, but during his years in social services, his bad opinions ossified into unshiftable views.
Once a lively forum for dissent, the academy gradually ossified, its members repeating the same doctrines year after year and rejecting any painter who departed from them.
The reformer warned that without periodic review, even well-intentioned regulations tend to ossify into rigid procedures whose original purpose no one remembers.
Linguists note that phrases once used creatively can ossify into cliches, fixed expressions that speakers repeat without any awareness of their original imagery.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: arrogant; presumptuous

exs.t: Mark was so convinced of his basketball skills that in his overweening pride he could not fathom that his name was not on the varsity list; he walked up to the basketball coach and told her she had forgotten to add his name.
The general's overweening confidence led him to dismiss his scouts' warnings, and he marched his army straight into the ambush they had predicted.
Her colleagues admired her talent but resented her overweening manner: she routinely claimed credit for group projects and interrupted senior partners to correct them.
Critics faulted the new director's overweening ambition, noting that he had presumed to redesign the historic galleries without consulting a single curator.

def: acceptable to the taste or mind

exs.t: Mikey didn't partake much in his friends' conversations, but found their presence palatable.
The proposal to raise taxes was unpopular, but the mayor made it more palatable by pairing it with a promise to repair every school roof in the district.
Though the medicine was bitter, the pharmacist mixed it with honey so that it would be palatable to the children who had to take it.
Many voters found neither candidate appealing, yet the moderate's platform was at least palatable, containing nothing they considered outright objectionable.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: speak (about unimportant matters) rapidly and incessantly

exs.t: During the rain delay, many who had come to see the game palavered, probably hoping that idle chatter would make the time go by faster.
While the kitchen prepared the next course, the waiters palavered by the door about the weather and their weekend plans, ignoring the diners who needed attention.
The committee members palavered for an hour about parking spaces and coffee brands, so the substantive budget question was never even raised.
Rather than get to the point, the salesman would palaver endlessly about his vacation and his nephew's soccer games until the customer finally walked out.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: something that has been changed numerous times but on which traces of former iterations can still be seen

exs.t: The downtown was a palimpsest of the city's checkered past: a new Starbucks had opened up next to an abandoned, shuttered building, and a freshly asphalted road was inches away from a pothole large enough to swallow a small dog.
The old manor house is a palimpsest: Victorian wallpaper peels away to reveal Georgian paneling, and beneath the modern floor lie traces of a medieval hearth.
Scholars read the heavily amended constitution as a palimpsest, since each revision layered new principles over older clauses that were never fully erased.
The artist's canvas became a palimpsest of her changing intentions; x-rays revealed at least three earlier compositions beneath the final painted surface.

def: hypothetical remedy for all ills or diseases; a universal solution

exs.t: While the company credit card has made most large purchases easier, it is no panacea: some smaller basic transactions still must be conducted in cash.
Enthusiasts touted the new software as a panacea for every inefficiency in the office, but staff soon found that it solved some problems while creating several others.
Economists cautioned that free trade is not a panacea; although it can raise overall wealth, it cannot by itself cure unemployment, inequality, or poor infrastructure.
Nineteenth-century peddlers hawked tonics said to cure everything from baldness to heartbreak, yet each supposed panacea usually contained little but alcohol and sugar.

def: a formal expression of praise

exs.t: Dave asked Andrew to do just a simple toast, but Andrew launched into a full panegyric, enumerating a complete list of Dave's achievements and admirable qualities.
The retirement dinner featured a lengthy panegyric in which the dean praised the professor's scholarship, generosity, and wit in the most elevated language.
Reviewers expected a balanced biography, yet the book reads as a panegyric, lavishing admiration on its subject while ignoring his well-documented failures.
Far from delivering the sharp critique the audience anticipated, the rival poet offered a panegyric, extolling the laureate's verse as the finest of the century.

label: n.1
def: model of excellence or perfection of a kind; one having no equal

exs.t: Even with the rise of Kobe Bryant, many still believe that Michael Jordan is the paragon for basketball players.
Among the violinists of her generation, she was considered a paragon, the standard against which every young performer's technique and tone were measured.
The old textbook held up the cathedral as a paragon for students of architecture to emulate, arguing that no later building had matched its harmony of proportion.
Colleagues regarded the surgeon as a paragon without rival in the hospital; when difficult cases arrived, other doctors sought her judgment before making any decision.

label: n.2
def: an ideal instance; a perfect embodiment of a concept

exs.t: Some say that Athens was the paragon of democracy, but these people often forget that slaves and women were still not allowed to vote.
With its punctual trains, spotless stations, and clear signage, the city's transit system is often cited as a paragon of efficiency.
The novelist's heroine is a paragon of patience: through years of betrayal and hardship, she never once loses her temper or her compassion.
Though the founder was celebrated as a paragon of thrift, his private letters reveal lavish spending that contradicted the frugal image he cultivated.

def: an outcast

exs.t: The once eminent scientist, upon being found guilty of faking his data, has become a pariah in the research community.
After testifying against his former partners, the accountant became a pariah in the financial district; old friends crossed the street to avoid him.
After the novelist mocked the town's founding family in a thinly veiled satire, she became a pariah there, greeted with silence at the market and barred from the reading club she had started.
Once welcomed at every gala, the collector found himself a pariah after the forgeries were exposed, shunned by the very circles that had courted him.

def: a person who has suddenly become wealthy, but not socially accepted as part of a higher class

exs.t: The theater was full of parvenus who each thought that they were surrounded by true aristocrats.
Although the parvenu had purchased the grandest house on the avenue, the old families never invited him to dinner, regarding his fortune as too recent to be respectable.
In the novel, the heroine's father is a parvenu who made millions in railways, yet his ostentatious carriages only confirm the aristocrats' view that money cannot buy breeding.
The dowager dismissed the young industrialist as a parvenu, observing that he had acquired a fortune in a single decade but none of the manners that old wealth supposedly confers.

def: glaringly obvious

exs.t: Since the book had been through no fewer than six proof runs, the staff was shocked to see such a patent spelling mistake remaining, right in the middle of the front cover!
The witness's story was a patent fabrication; she claimed to have seen the suspect clearly from a window that, as the photographs showed, faced a brick wall.
Despite the manager's efforts to appear calm, his anxiety was patent to everyone in the room: he stammered, fumbled with his notes, and kept glancing toward the door.
The flaw in the argument was so patent that even first-year students spotted it at once, which made the author's failure to address it all the more puzzling.

def: relating to or involving money

exs.t: The defendant was found guilty and had to serve a period of community service as well as pay pecuniary damages to the client.
The volunteers insisted their motives were entirely charitable, and indeed none of them received any pecuniary reward for the hundreds of hours they contributed.
Although the scholarship carried great prestige, its pecuniary value was modest, covering little more than the cost of textbooks for a single semester.
The ethics board required each member to disclose any pecuniary interest in the project, such as stock holdings or consulting fees, before voting on it.

def: transparently clear; easily understandable

exs.t: The professor had a remarkable ability make even the most difficult concepts seem pellucid.
Unlike the dense treatises of his predecessors, the philosopher's essays were pellucid, explaining even abstract questions of logic in prose that any educated reader could follow.
The instruction manual, written by engineers for engineers, was anything but pellucid; lay readers found its jargon and diagrams utterly baffling.
Her lecture on tax law was so pellucid that students who had dreaded the topic left the hall confident they understood every provision she had discussed.

label: adj.1
def: lacking money; poor

exs.t: Truly penurious, Mary had nothing more than a jar full of pennies.
The composer spent his final years penurious, living in a single unheated room and selling his manuscripts for whatever meager sums the local publishers would pay.
Many of the immigrant families were penurious when they arrived, possessing only the clothes they wore and a few borrowed coins.
Though the family had once owned vast estates, a series of disastrous investments left them penurious, unable even to afford the rent on a modest cottage.

label: adj.2
def: miserly

exs.t: Warren Buffett, famous multi-billionaire, still drives a cheap sedan, not because he is penurious, but because luxury cars are gaudy and impractical.
Sarah chose to be penurious and drive a beat-up VW, though with her wealth she could have easily afforded an Italian sports car.
Despite his considerable fortune, the landlord was so penurious that he refused to repair the building's broken heating, preferring to let tenants shiver rather than spend a dime.
The wealthy patron proved surprisingly penurious; after promising to fund the entire exhibition, she haggled over the cost of every frame and label.
Although the company earned record profits, its penurious owners cut employees' holiday bonuses and rationed office supplies as though bankruptcy were imminent.

def: highly perceptive

exs.t: Even the most percipient editor will make an occasional error when proofreading.
A percipient critic, she noticed that the novel's seemingly random chapter titles actually formed an acrostic that the author had never publicly acknowledged.
Most visitors saw only a charming village, but the percipient anthropologist recognized in its festival calendar the remnants of an ancient agricultural cycle.
The therapist was unusually percipient, detecting from a client's hesitations and slight changes in tone the anxieties he had not yet admitted even to himself.

def: bossy and domineering

exs.t: My sister used to peremptorily tell me to do the dishes, a chore I would either do perfunctorily or avoid doing altogether.
The new supervisor's peremptory manner, issuing orders without explanation and tolerating no questions, quickly alienated a staff accustomed to collaborative decisions.
Rather than politely requesting the documents, the official sent a peremptory note demanding them by noon and threatening penalties for any delay.
Guests were taken aback by the host's peremptory tone as he directed them where to sit, when to eat, and which topics they were permitted to discuss.

def: done routinely and with little interest or care

exs.t: The short film examines modern perfunctory cleaning rituals such as washing dishes, doing laundry and tooth-brushing.
The inspector gave the factory only a perfunctory glance before signing the safety certificate, missing the frayed wiring that later caused a fire.
After years of performing the same role, the actor delivered his lines in a perfunctory manner, reciting them accurately but without any trace of feeling.
His apology was perfunctory, a mumbled 'sorry' offered without eye contact, and it did little to repair the trust his careless remarks had damaged.

def: traveling by foot

exs.t: Jim always preferred a peripatetic approach to discovering a city: he felt that he could see so many more details while walking.
The medieval friars led a peripatetic existence, walking from village to village to preach and seldom sleeping under the same roof two nights in succession.
Rather than lecturing from a podium, the philosopher preferred a peripatetic style of teaching, strolling along the garden paths while his students walked beside him.
A peripatetic naturalist, she covered hundreds of miles of trail on foot each year, recording birdsong along routes that no vehicle could reach.

def: acutely insightful and wise

exs.t: Many modern observers regard Eisenhower as perspicacious, particularly in his accurate prediction of the growth of the military.
While other investors were dazzled by the company's growth, one perspicacious analyst noticed that its revenue depended almost entirely on a single contract due to expire.
The judge was perspicacious enough to see that the two witnesses, though apparently strangers, had rehearsed their testimony together.
Historians praise the minister as perspicacious, for she foresaw the consequences of the treaty's vague borders decades before disputes over them erupted.

def: illusive; unreal

exs.t: Those suffering from malaria fall into a feverish sleep, their world a whirligig of phantasmagoria; if they recover, they are unsure of what actually took place and what was simply a product of their febrile imaginations.
The painter's late canvases are phantasmagorical: melting towers, floating staircases, and figures that dissolve into smoke, as though each scene came from a fevered dream.
Critics found the film's plot phantasmagorical rather than realistic, a shifting parade of illusions in which viewers could never tell what was actually happening.
Recovering from a high fever, the patient described phantasmagorical visions of dancing shadows and talking statues that he knew, in retrospect, had never existed.

def: smug and ignorant towards artistic and cultural values

exs.t: Jane considered Al completely philistine, because he talked almost exclusive about video games; she was entirely unaware of how well read he really was.
The council's philistine decision to demolish the historic theater for a parking lot outraged residents who valued the building's ornate architecture.
He scoffed at the symphony as mere noise and called poetry a waste of paper, a philistine attitude that dismayed his literature-loving wife.
Critics accused the publisher of philistine priorities, since he refused to print any novel without a car chase and dismissed literary fiction as pretentious and unprofitable.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: showing little emotion

exs.t: Arnold is truly noble, remaining reserved until an issue of significance arises, but Walter is simply phlegmatic: he doesn't have the energy or inclination to care about anything.
Even when the stock market collapsed and colleagues panicked, the phlegmatic trader merely shrugged, sipped his coffee, and continued reviewing his spreadsheets.
The fans screamed and wept as the final goal went in, but the phlegmatic coach barely changed expression, simply noting the time on his watch.
Her phlegmatic temperament made her an ideal emergency dispatcher, since frantic callers rarely managed to disturb her steady, unemotional voice.

def: trifling or petty (a person)

exs.t: English teachers are notorious for being picayune; however, the English language is so nuanced and sophisticated that often such teachers are not being contrary but are only adhering to the rules.
The editor's comments were so picayune, quibbling over commas and fonts, that the author wondered whether she had engaged with the manuscript's actual arguments at all.
Rather than address the substance of the proposal, the council members raised picayune objections about the color of the binder and the width of the margins.
Colleagues found him picayune, a manager who would reprimand staff for arriving two minutes late while ignoring serious problems in the department's budget.

def: ridicule or expose to public scorn

exs.t: After the candidate confessed, the press of the opposing party took the opportunity to pillory him, printing editorials with the most blatantly exaggerated accusations.
The tabloids pilloried the actor after his ill-judged remarks, running mocking cartoons and headlines that held him up to nationwide ridicule.
Although her findings were later vindicated, the young scientist was pilloried at the conference, where senior researchers openly mocked her data before a laughing audience.
Satirists of the eighteenth century loved to pillory pompous aristocrats, and pamphlets mocking their vanity and hypocrisy were read aloud to jeering crowds in coffeehouses.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: the most essential part of something

exs.t: When Cynthia hears a speaker presenting a complex argument, she is always able to discard the irrelevant details and extract the pith of what the speaker is trying to convey.
The senator's speech rambled for an hour, but its pith could be summed up in a single sentence: the bridge would be built, and taxpayers would fund it.
Good editors cut away ornamental digressions and tangents so that the pith of an argument stands out clearly, no longer buried beneath material the reader could safely skip.
After three days of testimony, the jurors struggled to identify the pith of the case amid all the technical detail and conflicting expert opinions.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: marked by courage and determination

exs.t: Some scouts initially doubted Pedroia because of his short stature, but he is a plucky player, surprising everyone with his boundless energy and fierce determination.
Though the plucky little firm had no capital and only three employees, it challenged the industry giant in court and ultimately won.
Despite a broken wrist, the plucky climber insisted on finishing the ascent, determined not to abandon her team a few hundred meters from the summit.
Critics dismissed the underfunded expedition as doomed, yet its plucky members pressed on through blizzards and food shortages until they reached the pole.

def: extremely optimistic

exs.t: Even in the midst of a lousy sales quarter, Debbie remained Pollyannaish, never losing her shrill voice and wide smile, even when prospective customers hung up on her.
Even as floodwaters rose around the town, the mayor issued Pollyannaish statements assuring residents that the levees would certainly hold and nothing would be damaged.
The analyst warned that the company's Pollyannaish forecasts ignored rising costs and shrinking demand, projecting growth where the evidence pointed toward decline.
Critics called the novel's ending Pollyannaish, since every character, however badly wronged, is reconciled and rewarded in a single cheerful chapter.

def: weighed-down; moving slowly

exs.t: Laden with 20 kilograms of college text books, the freshman moved ponderously across the campus.
Unlike the nimble gazelles that scattered at the first sound, the elephants made their ponderous way across the plain, each heavy step raising a cloud of dust.
Burdened with heavy armor, the knights advanced at a ponderous pace, allowing the lightly equipped archers to outmaneuver them with ease.
The freighter, loaded far beyond its usual capacity, made ponderous progress through the harbor while smaller vessels darted nimbly past it.

def: talk in a dogmatic and pompous manner

exs.t: The vice-president would often pontificate about economic theory, as if no one else in the room were qualified to speak on the topic.
At every family dinner, Uncle Richard would pontificate about foreign policy as though he were the only person present who had ever read a newspaper.
Instead of listening to the farmers' concerns, the consultant pontificated on the principles of agronomy, lecturing them with a certainty his limited experience hardly justified.
The critic tended to pontificate rather than argue, handing down grand pronouncements on which films were masterpieces without ever explaining his reasons.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: ominously prophetic

exs.t: When the captain and more than half the officers were sick on the very first night of the voyage, many of the passengers felt this was portentous, but the rest of the voyage continued without any problems.
The sudden silence of the birds seemed portentous to the villagers, who had learned that such stillness often preceded a violent storm.
Economists found the sharp drop in shipping orders portentous, interpreting it as an early sign of the recession that arrived six months later.
In the play, a portentous dream in which the king sees his crown crack foreshadows the rebellion that will eventually cost him his throne.

label: adj.
def: hasty or rash

exs.t: Instead of conducting a thorough investigation after the city hall break-in, the governor acted precipitately, accusing his staff of aiding and abetting the criminals.
The board regretted its precipitate decision to close the factory, made in a single afternoon without consulting engineers who could have fixed the problem cheaply.
Cautious by temperament, the scientist warned against precipitate conclusions drawn from a single experiment, insisting that the results be replicated first.
The general's precipitate retreat, ordered before scouts had even confirmed the enemy's strength, abandoned a position that could easily have been held.

label: v.
def: to cause to happen

exs.t: The government's mishandling the hurricane's aftermath precipitated a widespread outbreak of looting and other criminal activity.
The minister's careless remark precipitated a diplomatic crisis, prompting both countries to recall their ambassadors within days.
A single failed harvest can precipitate famine in regions where grain reserves are already dangerously low.
Historians debate whether the assassination actually precipitated the war or merely provided a pretext for a conflict that existing tensions had made inevitable.

def: a feeling of evil to come

exs.t: On the night that Lincoln would be fatally shot, his wife had a presentiment about going to Ford's Theater, but Lincoln persuaded her that everything would be fine.
Before boarding the ship, the traveler had a vague presentiment of disaster, and though he could not explain it, he canceled his passage at the last moment.
Throughout the novel, the heroine is haunted by a presentiment that her brother will not return from the war, a dread the final chapter sadly confirms.
Although the morning was bright and calm, Elena woke with a presentiment of misfortune that she could not shake as she prepared for the interview.

def: the state of being first in importance

exs.t: The primacy of Apple Computers is not guaranteed, as seen in the recent lawsuits and weak growth.
The historian argued that the city's primacy among Mediterranean ports rested less on its geography than on the stability of its banking institutions.
Throughout his career, the philosopher insisted on the primacy of experience over theory, maintaining that no abstract system should override what observation reveals.
Once unchallenged, the company's primacy in the market began to erode as smaller rivals introduced cheaper and more innovative products.

def: integrity, strong moral principles

exs.t: The ideal politician would have the probity to lead, but reality gravely falls short of the ideal of morally upright leaders.
The treasurer's probity was never questioned; in forty years of handling the charity's funds, not a single penny was misplaced or misused.
Voters had grown weary of scandal, so the candidate's reputation for probity, rather than any specific policy, became her greatest electoral asset.
The auditors expected to find fraud, but instead the records revealed the manager's probity: every expense was documented and every conflict of interest disclosed.

def: a statement made about the future

exs.t: When the Senator was asked about where the negotiations would lead, he said that any guess he could make would be an unreliable prognostication.
The economist's prognostication of a housing collapse was ridiculed at the time, but within two years prices had fallen exactly as she had predicted.
Weather forecasting has progressed from folklore to science, yet any prognostication beyond ten days remains notoriously unreliable.
The astrologer's vague prognostication that great changes lay ahead was carefully worded so that almost any future event could be claimed as its fulfillment.

def: boring verbosity

exs.t: I loved my grandfather dearly, but his prolixity would put me to sleep, regardless of the topic.
The lawyer's prolixity tested the jury's patience; a point that required a single sentence would stretch, in his telling, over twenty tedious minutes.
Editors trimmed the manuscript by half, since the author's prolixity had buried a genuinely original argument beneath pages of repetitive digression.
In contrast to the prolixity of his earlier novels, the writer's final book is spare and concise, with no chapter longer than a few pages.

def: state or announce

exs.t: The President wanted to promulgate the success of the treaty negotiations, but he had to wait until Congress formally approved the agreement.
After months of deliberation, the council promulgated new building codes, publishing them in the official gazette so that every contractor would know the requirements.
The monarch promulgated the edict throughout the kingdom, ordering heralds to read it aloud in every town square.
Early advocates of the germ theory worked tirelessly to promulgate their findings, lecturing to physicians and publishing pamphlets to make the discovery widely known.

def: to placate or appease

exs.t: The two sons, plying their angry father with cheesy neckties for Christmas, were hardly able to propitiate him -- the father already had a drawer full of ones he had never worn before or ever planned to.
The ancient farmers offered the first fruits of each harvest in an effort to propitiate the gods they believed controlled the rain.
Hoping to propitiate the furious client, the architect apologized for the delay and offered to redesign the lobby at no extra cost.
The new manager tried to propitiate the disgruntled employees with a round of raises, but their anger over the layoffs was not so easily soothed.

def: dull and lacking imagination

exs.t: Unlike the talented artists in his workshop, Paul had no such bent for the visual medium, so when it was time for him to make a stained glass painting, he ended up with a prosaic mosaic.
Visitors expecting a romantic castle were disappointed by the prosaic reality: a squat concrete building housing the regional tax office.
Though the poet's early work was bold and inventive, her later verse struck critics as prosaic, full of flat statements and predictable imagery.
The detective in the novel solves crimes not through brilliant leaps of imagination but through prosaic methods such as checking receipts and interviewing neighbors.

def: command against

exs.t: My doctor proscribes that I not eat donuts with chocolate sauce and hamburger patties for breakfast.
The new regulations proscribe smoking in all public buildings, including the lobbies and stairwells where it had long been tolerated.
Many ancient legal codes proscribed marriage between close relatives, imposing severe penalties on those who violated the prohibition.
Although the club's charter did not explicitly proscribe political debate at dinner, members observed an unwritten rule against it that newcomers quickly learned.

def: convert to another religion, philosophy, or perspective

exs.t: Lisa loves her Mac but says little about it; by contrast, Jake will proselytize, interrogating anyone with an Android about why she didn't purchase an iPhone.
Having discovered the benefits of a plant-based diet, Tom began to proselytize at every dinner party, urging each guest to give up meat as he had.
The ruler allowed the foreign monks to practice their faith privately but forbade them to proselytize, fearing that they would win his subjects over to their religion.
Rather than proselytize for her economic theory, the professor presented it alongside its rivals and let students decide which account they found persuasive.

def: readily taking on different roles; versatile

exs.t: Peter Sellers was truly a protean actor--in Doctor Strangelove he played three very different roles: a jingoist general, a sedate President and a deranged scientist.
A protean performer, she could play a tragic queen one night and a slapstick maid the next, fully convincing in both roles.
The virus proved protean, mutating so rapidly that each season's vaccine was nearly obsolete by the time it reached pharmacies.
The protean intellectual moved easily among the roles of novelist, diplomat, and composer, excelling in each while never settling into one.

def: careful in regard to your own interests; providing carefully for the future
defMasked: careful in regard to your own interests; ____ carefully for the future

exs.t: In a move that hardly could be described as provident, Bert spend his entire savings on a luxurious cruise, knowing that other bills would come due a couple months later.
Provident farmers stored grain during the good years, so that when drought struck the region, their families did not go hungry.
Unlike his spendthrift brother, Marcus was provident, setting aside part of every paycheck for retirement and keeping an emergency fund for unexpected repairs.
The city's provident decision to build reservoirs decades earlier spared it the water rationing that afflicted its neighbors during the long dry spell.

def: of or characteristic of a child; displaying or suggesting a lack of maturity

exs.t: Helen enjoyed blowing soap bubbles, but Jim regarded this as puerile, totally unworthy of a woman with a Ph.D.
The debate degenerated into puerile name-calling, with the candidates mocking each other's hairstyles rather than discussing policy.
Although the comedy was marketed to adults, critics found its humor puerile, relying on jokes that would amuse only a young schoolboy.
Rather than responding maturely to criticism, the executive sulked and slammed doors, behavior his staff considered puerile in a man of fifty.

def: powerful

exs.t: Over the years of service, and quite to his surprise, he became a puissant advisor to the community.
The duke was a puissant lord whose vast armies and wealth allowed him to defy even the king.
Once a puissant force in regional politics, the party had dwindled to a handful of elderly members with no real influence.
Myths describe the storm god as puissant enough to split mountains with a single thunderbolt, and even the other deities feared his wrath.

def: marked by precise accordance with details

exs.t: The colonel was so punctilious about enforcing regulations that men fell compelled to polish even the soles of their shoes.
The punctilious accountant checked every figure three times, refusing to sign off on the report until even a discrepancy of a few cents had been explained.
Guests at the embassy dinner were expected to observe punctilious etiquette, from the precise order of toasts to the correct form of address for each diplomat.
Although some authors found her tiresome, the editor's punctilious attention to citations meant that no error in her journal ever went uncorrected.

def: describing a victory that comes at such a great cost that the victory is not worthwhile

exs.t: George W. Bush's win in the 2000 election was in many ways a pyrrhic victory: the circumstances of his win alienated half of the U.S. population.
The company won its lawsuit, but the victory was pyrrhic: legal fees exceeded the damages awarded, and the bad publicity drove away its biggest clients.
Although the army held the ridge, it lost so many soldiers doing so that the triumph proved pyrrhic, leaving it too weak to continue the campaign.
The strike secured the union a small raise, yet many regarded the outcome as pyrrhic, since the plant closed within a year and every worker lost a job.

def: draw back, as with fear or pain

exs.t: Craig always claimed to be a fearless outdoorsman, but when the thunderstorm engulfed the valley, he quailed at the thought of leaving the safety of his cabin.
The young lawyer, confident in rehearsal, quailed when the stern judge fixed her with a withering stare.
Seasoned sailors did not quail before the approaching storm, but the passengers huddled below deck in terror.
Many people would quail at the prospect of speaking before thousands, yet the shy student delivered her commencement address without a tremor.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: a traitor

exs.t: History looks unfavorably upon quislings; indeed they are accorded about the same fondness as Nero--he who watched his city burn down while playing the violin.
When the occupying forces installed a puppet government, the resistance denounced its leader as a quisling who had sold out his own people.
The official was branded a quisling after it emerged that he had passed his country's secrets to the enemy in exchange for money.
Although he claimed to be protecting his fellow citizens, the mayor who collaborated with the invaders was remembered as a quisling who had betrayed his town.

def: wildly idealistic; impractical

exs.t: For every thousand startups with quixotic plans to be the next big name in e-commerce, only a handful ever become profitable.
Her quixotic plan to end world hunger by planting a single orchard in every town ignored the practical problems of transport, funding, and climate.
Colleagues admired his idealism but considered the campaign quixotic: a lone candidate with no funds hoping to unseat an incumbent who had never lost.
Rather than pursue the quixotic dream of a perfectly just society, the pragmatic reformer focused on small, achievable improvements to local courts.

def: a person skilled in telling anecdotes

exs.t: Jude is entertaining, but he is no raconteur: beyond the handful of amusing stories he has memorized, he has absolutely no spontaneous story-telling ability.
A gifted raconteur, the retired ambassador kept dinner guests enthralled for hours with tales of misadventures in distant capitals.
Although his lectures were dry, the professor was a superb raconteur at faculty gatherings, where his amusing anecdotes about eccentric scientists drew crowds.
The host fancied himself a raconteur, but his stories rambled without punch lines, and guests drifted away before he reached the end of each one.

def: light teasing

exs.t: The new recruit was not bothered by the raillery, finding most of it light-hearted and good-natured.
Her colleagues' raillery about her fondness for bow ties was affectionate, and she laughed along with the good-natured jokes.
The friendly raillery between the two old rivals, full of gentle jibes about each other's golf swing, masked a deep mutual respect.
What began as playful raillery at the dinner table turned hurtful when her brother's teasing touched on her recent divorce.

def: the reestablishing of cordial relations

exs.t: Although Ann hoped that her mother and her aunt would have a rapprochement, each one's bitter accusations against the other made any reconciliation unlikely.
After decades of hostility, the two nations achieved a rapprochement, reopening embassies and signing trade agreements that would have been unthinkable a generation earlier.
The estranged brothers' rapprochement began slowly, with a few tentative letters, and culminated in a warm reunion at their mother's birthday.
Despite the mediator's efforts, no rapprochement between the feuding departments proved possible, since each blamed the other for the project's failure.

def: esoteric and refined; remote from the lives of ordinary people

exs.t: Jack's vulgar jokes were not so successful in the rarefied environment of college professors.
Accustomed to the rarefied world of manuscript auctions and private collectors, the curator was bewildered by the noisy bargaining at the county fair's antique stalls.
The seminar's debates about medieval Latin grammar were so rarefied that even well-read visitors from other departments could not follow a single exchange.
Critics complained that the opera house, with its steep prices and strict dress code, had become a rarefied enclave for connoisseurs rather than a place where ordinary citizens might hear music.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: a summary (think of recap)

exs.t: Every point of the professors lesson was so clear that the students felt his concluding recapitulation was not necessary.
At the end of each chapter, the textbook provides a brief recapitulation of its main points, helping students review before the exam.
Rather than introduce new evidence, the prosecutor's closing statement was a recapitulation of the testimony the jury had already heard.
The chair opened the meeting with a brief recapitulation of last week's decisions, running through each in a sentence or two for members who had been absent.

def: mutual accusations

exs.t: The two brothers sat and cried, pointing fingers and making elaborate recriminations of the other's guilt.
After the project failed, the meeting dissolved into bitter recrimination, with engineers blaming managers and managers blaming engineers in turn.
The divorce proceedings were marked by recriminations on both sides, each spouse accusing the other of having wrecked the marriage.
Rather than trade recriminations over the lost election, the party's leaders agreed to analyze what had gone wrong and plan together for the next campaign.

def: to break out or happen again

exs.t: After years of gamblers anonymous, Tony thought he'd broken his compulsive slot machine playing, but it took only one trip to the Atlantic City for a full recrudescence--he lost $5k on the one armed bandit.
Doctors warned that the infection might recrudesce if the patient stopped taking the antibiotics before completing the full course.
Just when the border dispute seemed settled, old hostilities recrudesced, and skirmishes broke out once more along the contested river.
The historian notes that anti-intellectual sentiment tends to recrudesce in times of economic hardship, reappearing after long periods of dormancy.

def: inspiring fear or awe

exs.t: On television basketball players don't look that tall, but when you stand in front of a seven-foot tall NBA player, he is truly redoubtable.
The chess champion was a redoubtable opponent, and many challengers conceded defeat after only a few moves against her.
Protected by thick walls and a deep moat, the castle was redoubtable, and invading armies usually chose to bypass it rather than risk a siege.
Even seasoned lawyers were intimidated by the redoubtable judge, whose sharp questions and formidable memory left unprepared counsel speechless.

def: to make objections while pleading

exs.t: The mothers of the kidnapped victims remonstrated to the rogue government to release their children, claiming that the detention violated human rights.
The residents remonstrated with the council against the highway plan, pleading that it would split their neighborhood in two and destroy its historic park.
When the headmaster announced that the library would close, students remonstrated, begging him to reconsider and pointing out how many of them relied on it for study.
The scientist remonstrated with her funders, protesting the decision and urging them not to cancel the project when it was so close to yielding results.

def: a retaliatory action against an enemy in wartime

exs.t: The Old Testament doctrine of an eye for an eye is not the kind of retaliation practiced in war; rather, an. arm, a leg, and both ears are the reprisal for the smallest scratch.
After the rebels ambushed a supply convoy, the occupying army launched a harsh reprisal, shelling the villages it suspected of sheltering them.
The treaty explicitly forbade reprisals against prisoners of war, so commanders could not punish captured soldiers for attacks carried out by their comrades.
Fearing reprisal from the enemy fleet, the admiral hesitated to strike its harbor, knowing that his own coastal cities lay undefended.

def: humorously vulgar

exs.t: The speaker was famous for his ribald humor, but the high school principal asked him to keep the talk G- rated when he spoke to the student body.
The tavern songs were ribald, full of bawdy jokes that delighted the sailors but made the visiting clergyman blush.
The medieval collection mixes pious sermons with ribald tales of foolish husbands and scheming wives, a blend of the sacred and the crudely comic.
The comedian toned down his usually ribald routine for the charity luncheon, replacing his vulgar punch lines with gentler observations about family life.

def: an angry dispute

exs.t: The Prime Minister looked very foolish after his row with the foreign dignitary was caught on video and posted on youtube.
The neighbors had a furious row over the fence line, shouting at each other across the hedge until the police were called.
A public row between the conductor and the lead soprano, carried on through angry letters to the newspaper, overshadowed the opera's premiere.
What began as a polite disagreement over the budget escalated into a bitter row, with ministers accusing each other of incompetence in front of reporters.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: having good judgement and acute insight

exs.t: Steve Jobs is surely one of the most sagacious CEOs, making Apple the most recognizable and valuable companies in the world.
The sagacious elder advised the villagers to plant drought-resistant crops, a recommendation that saved them when the rains failed the following year.
Although young, the judge was remarkably sagacious, weighing each argument carefully and delivering rulings that even veteran lawyers admired for their wisdom.
Investors who followed the sagacious fund manager avoided the crash, since she had recognized the bubble long before others and quietly sold her holdings.

def: calmness or poise in difficult situations

exs.t: The hostage negotiator exhibited a sangfroid that oftentimes was more menacing than the sword at his throat, or the gun at his head.
The pilot's sangfroid during the engine failure reassured the passengers; she announced the emergency landing as calmly as if she were describing the weather.
Even as the audience jeered and the lights failed, the pianist continued playing with remarkable sangfroid, never missing a note.
Negotiators prized her sangfroid, since no threat or insult across the table could provoke her into losing her composure.

def: disdainfully or ironically humorous; scornful and mocking

exs.t: A stand-up comedian walks a fine line when making jokes about members of the audience; such fun and joking can quickly become sardonic and cutting.
When the proposal was rejected yet again, the engineer gave a sardonic laugh and remarked that the committee's vision was truly breathtaking in its smallness.
The columnist's sardonic wit spared no one; she mocked politicians' pieties with a scornful irony that delighted readers and infuriated her targets.
Rather than offering sympathy, the older brother responded with a sardonic smile, as if the younger boy's misfortune merely confirmed his low opinion of him.

def: related to fashion or clothes

exs.t: Monte was astute at navigating the world of finance; sartorially, however, he was found wanting--he typically would attempt to complement his beige tie with a gray suit and white pants.
The professor's sartorial choices, a rumpled tweed jacket and mismatched socks, suggested a man more concerned with ideas than with appearance.
The film's costume designer took great care with sartorial detail, ensuring that every cufflink and hat matched the fashions of the period.
Although he knew little about politics, the commentator had strong sartorial opinions and devoted most of his column to the candidates' suits and ties.

def: morose or gloomy

exs.t: Deprived of sunlight, humans become saturnine; that's why in very northerly territories people are encouraged to sit under an extremely powerful lamp, lest they become morose.
The saturnine old librarian rarely smiled, and his gloomy silences made the reading room feel even more somber than it already was.
In contrast to his cheerful sister, Paul had a saturnine temperament, brooding for days over minor setbacks and expecting the worst from every venture.
The composer's late works reflect a saturnine mood, their slow, dark harmonies conveying a melancholy that his earlier, sunnier pieces never approached.

def: joy from watching the suffering of others

exs.t: From his warm apartment window, Stanley reveled in schadenfreude as he laughed at the figures below, huddled together in the arctic chill.
Rivals watched the celebrated chef's restaurant fail with barely concealed schadenfreude, delighted that his arrogance had finally been punished.
Psychologists suggest that schadenfreude is strongest when the sufferer is envied, since another's misfortune can make us feel better about our own position.
Though she publicly expressed sympathy, the novelist admitted to a twinge of schadenfreude when the critic who had savaged her book was himself harshly reviewed.

def: done diligently and carefully

exs.t: An avid numismatist, Harold sedulously amassed a collection of coins from over 100 countries--an endeavor that took over fifteen years and trips to five continents.
The sedulous researcher spent years combing through archives, checking every letter and ledger until she had reconstructed the merchant's entire trading network.
Thanks to the gardener's sedulous care, weeding daily and watering by hand, the neglected estate was transformed into a flourishing showpiece.
Unlike his careless predecessor, the new archivist was sedulous, cataloging each document meticulously and double-checking every entry.

def: reluctant to draw attention to yourself

exs.t: The most admirable teachers and respected leaders are those who are self-effacing, directing attention and praise to their students and workers.
Despite winning the prize, the self-effacing scientist credited her laboratory assistants and declined to give interviews about her own contributions.
The captain's self-effacing manner surprised reporters, who had expected boasting but heard him attribute the victory entirely to his teammates.
Rather than dominating the conversation, the self-effacing host kept the spotlight on his guests, asking about their work and saying little about his own accomplishments.

def: an outward or token appearance or form that is deliberately misleading

exs.t: While the banker maintained a semblance of respectability in public, those who knew him well were familiar with his many crimes.
The regime held elections to create a semblance of democracy, though the results were determined long before any ballots were cast.
Beneath a semblance of cooperation, the two firms were secretly working to undermine each other's bids.
The con artist maintained a semblance of wealth, renting a luxury car and an elegant office, while in fact he owed money to nearly everyone he knew.

def: to be moralizing, usually in a pompous sense

exs.t: The old man, casting his nose up in the air at the group of adolescents, intoned sententiously, "Youth is wasted on the young."
The novel's narrator is insufferably sententious, pausing every few pages to deliver pompous moral lessons about the virtues of hard work and thrift.
Rather than offering practical advice, the retiring executive gave a sententious speech full of lofty maxims about integrity that he had rarely practiced himself.
Critics found the film sententious, complaining that its characters spoke in sanctimonious aphorisms rather than natural dialogue.

label: n.1
def: a representation of a person (especially in the form of sculpture)

exs.t: The Shanghai Urban Planning Exhibition Center showcases a simulacrum of all the present and approved buildings in the city of Shanghai.
In the town square stands a bronze simulacrum of the founder, depicting him on horseback with one hand raised toward the harbor.
The wax museum's simulacrum of the old queen was so lifelike that visitors often paused before it, half expecting the figure to speak.
Ancient mourners placed a small clay simulacrum of the deceased in the tomb, believing that the likeness would house the spirit in the afterlife.

label: n.2
def: a bad imitation

exs.t: The early days of computer graphics made real people into a simulacrum that now seems comical.
The chain's so-called Italian restaurants offer only a simulacrum of Italian cooking, with bland sauces and frozen pasta that no cook in Rome would recognize.
Critics dismissed the reconstructed village as a hollow simulacrum, a theme-park version of history with plastic beams and costumed staff reciting scripts.
The dictator's parliament was a mere simulacrum of a legislature: it met rarely, debated nothing, and approved every decree unanimously.

def: an office that involves minimal duties

exs.t: The position of Research Director is a sinecure: the job entails almost no responsibilities, nor does the person in that position have to answer to anyone.
The title of honorary consul proved a sinecure: it paid a generous stipend but required nothing more than attending an annual reception.
Critics charged that the governor had created the post as a sinecure for his brother-in-law, who collected a salary without ever visiting the office.
Far from being the sinecure he had imagined, the chairmanship demanded long hours, constant travel, and difficult negotiations with unions.

def: a socially awkward or tactless act

exs.t: Mother Anna was always on guard against any solecism from her children and scolded them immediately if any of them talked out of place in public.
At the formal banquet, the young diplomat committed a solecism by addressing the ambassador by her first name, and an awkward hush fell over the table.
Arriving at a funeral in bright beach attire would be regarded as a grave solecism in almost any culture.
The etiquette manual catalogs every conceivable solecism, from using the wrong fork to interrupting one's host, so that anxious readers might avoid social embarrassment.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: showing hovering attentiveness

exs.t: Our neighbors are constantly knocking on our door to make sure we are ok, and I don't know how to ask them to stop being so solicitous about our health.
The nurse was solicitous of her elderly patient, checking his pillows every hour and asking repeatedly whether he needed anything.
The hotel staff were almost too solicitous; within an hour of arrival, three different employees had called to ask whether the room was satisfactory.
Although his colleagues were solicitous about his recovery after surgery, offering meals and rides, he found their constant attention exhausting.

note: Has other meanings too; this is the one the GRE tests.

def: a feeling of excessive concern

exs.t: I walked to his house in the rain to make sure he had enough to eat while he was sick, but he seemed not to appreciate my solicitude.
Her mother's solicitude could be suffocating: she telephoned three times a day to ask whether her adult daughter was eating properly and dressing warmly.
The mayor's sudden solicitude for the neglected neighborhood, expressed only weeks before the election, struck residents as insincere.
Despite the doctors' assurances that the injury was minor, the coach's solicitude never wavered, and he insisted on examining the player's ankle before every practice.

def: unsparing and uncompromising in discipline or judgment; practicing great self- denial

exs.t: After losing everything in a fire, Tim decided to live in spartan conditions, sleeping on the floor and owning as little furniture as a possible.
The monks lived a spartan life, sleeping on wooden boards, eating a single plain meal each day, and owning nothing beyond a robe and a bowl.
The training camp was notoriously spartan: athletes woke before dawn, ran in freezing weather, and were denied any comforts that might soften their resolve.
Though the founder was a billionaire, his office was spartan, containing only a metal desk, a single chair, and no decoration whatever.

def: very irritable

exs.t: Ever since the car accident, Frank has been unable to walk without a cane, and so he has become splenetic and unpleasant to be around.
The critic's columns grew increasingly splenetic in his old age, bristling at actors, sets, and even audiences as though every evening at the theater were a personal affront.
Chronic pain made the old sailor splenetic, and he would snap at anyone who asked him even the simplest question.
Unlike his patient predecessor, the new editor was splenetic, flying into a temper over minor typos and berating staff for trivial delays.

def: suppress or crush completely

exs.t: After the dictator consolidated his power, he took steps to squelch all criticism, often arresting any journalist who said anything that could be interpreted as negative about his regime.
The authorities moved quickly to squelch the rumor of a bank failure, releasing audited statements before panic could spread among depositors.
A dismissive teacher can squelch a child's curiosity entirely, so that questions once eagerly asked are never voiced again.
The studio squelched the director's ambitious ending, replacing it with a conventional conclusion that test audiences found more comfortable.

def: dependable; inured to fatigue or hardships

exs.t: Despite all the criticism directed at the President during this scandal, Lisa has remained his stalwart supporter.
Through decades of funding cuts, the librarian remained a stalwart defender of public access, never missing a council meeting where the budget was discussed.
The stalwart pioneers endured blizzards, failed harvests, and disease, yet they refused to abandon the homesteads they had built.
Although many donors withdrew after the scandal, a few stalwart supporters continued to fund the charity, confident that its mission remained worthy.

def: cause one, through routine, to lose energy and enthusiasm

exs.t: As an undergraduate Mark felt stultified by classes outside his area of study; only in grad school, in which he could focus solely on literary analysis, did he regain his scholarly edge.
Years of filling out identical forms in the records office stultified the once-ambitious clerk, until he could no longer summon any interest in his work.
Critics argue that endless rote memorization can stultify young students, draining the curiosity and enthusiasm they bring to school.
The novelist found that the monotonous routine of her day job was stultifying her imagination, so she resigned in order to recover the energy she needed to write.

def: something intended to misrepresent the true nature of an activity

exs.t: Finally deciding to abandon all subterfuge, Arthur revealed to Cindy everything about his secret affair over the past two years.
Unable to get permission to enter the archive, the journalist resorted to subterfuge, posing as a visiting scholar to gain access to the files.
The company used an elaborate subterfuge to hide its losses, transferring debts to shell firms so that its balance sheet appeared healthy.
The general's victory depended on subterfuge: dummy tanks and false radio traffic convinced the enemy that the attack would come from the north.

def: haughty and disdainful; looking down on others

exs.t: Nelly felt the Quiz Bowl director acted superciliously towards the underclassmen; really, she fumed, must he act so preternaturally omniscient each time he intones some obscure fact, as though everybody knows that Mt. Aconcagua is the highest peak in South America?
The supercilious waiter raised an eyebrow at the couple's choice of wine, as though their taste were beneath his notice.
Though brilliant, the professor alienated students with his supercilious manner, answering their questions with sighs and condescending remarks.
The aristocratic family treated the new neighbors with supercilious disdain, refusing to acknowledge them simply because their fortune came from trade.

def: an excessive amount of something

exs.t: There was no such thing as a surfeit of shopping for Nancy--she could stay at the outlet stores from opening to closing time.
The housing market suffered from a surfeit of apartments, and with far more units than buyers, prices fell sharply.
After a surfeit of rich holiday feasts, the family longed for simple meals of soup and bread.
Modern researchers face not a scarcity of information but a surfeit, so that the real challenge lies in filtering out what is irrelevant.

def: stealthy, taking pains not to be caught or detected

exs.t: Since his mom was a light sleeper, Timmy had to tiptoe surreptitiously through the entire house, careful to not make the floors creak, until he at last was able to enjoy his plunder: a box of chocolate chip cookies.
During the long lecture, several students cast surreptitious glances at their phones, hiding them beneath their desks whenever the professor looked their way.
The spy made surreptitious copies of the documents late at night, careful to return each file to its exact position before dawn.
Though the museum banned photography, one visitor took a surreptitious snapshot of the painting, concealing the camera inside his coat.

def: a person who indulges in luxury

exs.t: Despite the fact that he'd maxed out fifteen credit cards, Max was still a sybarite at heart: when the police found him, he was at a $1,000 an hour spa in Manhattan, getting a facial treatment.
A confirmed sybarite, the heir spent his days in silk robes, dining on delicacies and bathing in perfumed water while ignoring the family business.
The resort catered to the sybarite, offering champagne breakfasts, private masseuses, and suites with marble baths.
Friends were astonished that the former sybarite, who had once refused to travel without his wine cellar and silk sheets, had taken vows of poverty and moved to a remote monastery.

def: fearless daring

exs.t: No child has the temerity to go in the rundown house at the end of the street and see if it is haunted.
The junior clerk had the temerity to contradict the chairman in front of the entire board, a boldness that astonished everyone present.
Few scholars had the temerity to challenge the eminent historian's thesis, but one young researcher published a rebuttal that dismantled it point by point.
It took considerable temerity for the explorers to cross the uncharted ice sheet with only a compass and a few weeks' provisions.

def: as if driven by turbulent or conflicting emotions; highly energetic and wildly changing or fluctuating

exs.t: Chuck and Kathy had always been stable and agreeable people on their own, but when they got involved, it was a tempestuous relationship.
The composer's tempestuous temperament, swinging from rapture to fury within minutes, made him difficult to work with but gave his music its passion.
Their tempestuous friendship was marked by fierce loyalty and furious quarrels, followed by tearful reconciliations that never lasted long.
Historians describe the revolution's early years as tempestuous, with governments rising and falling in rapid succession amid violent swings of public feeling.

def: likely to lean towards a controversial view

exs.t: Because political mudslinging has become a staple of the 24-hour media cycle, most of us, despite protestations to the contrary, are tendentious on many of today's pressing issues.
The documentary was criticized as tendentious, since it presented only the evidence that supported its thesis and omitted every dissenting expert.
Rather than an impartial history, the textbook offered a tendentious account that consistently portrayed one faction as heroes and the other as villains.
The reviewer warned readers that the author's tendentious summary of the research distorted the studies to favor his controversial theory of diet.

def: change or alter in form, appearance, or nature
