exs.t: One of the goals of alchemy was to find the substance or process that would transmute lead into gold.
The poet had a gift for transmuting ordinary experiences, such as washing dishes or waiting for a bus, into moments of luminous significance.
Over the centuries, the folk tale was transmuted from a grim cautionary story into a gentle fable for children.
In a nuclear reactor, certain elements can be transmuted into others as their atoms absorb neutrons and change their fundamental nature.

def: characterized by or full of force and vigor; having keenness and forcefulness and penetration in thought, expression, or intellect

exs.t: Jill presented a rather superficial treatment of sales in Asia, but her trenchant analysis of sales in Europe inspired a number of insights into how to proceed in that market.
The critic's trenchant review cut through the film's lavish spectacle to expose the emptiness of its plot.
Although most commentators offered vague praise, one economist delivered a trenchant analysis that pinpointed exactly why the policy would fail.
Her trenchant wit made her a formidable debater; opponents found that a single incisive remark from her could demolish their entire argument.

def: defiant aggressiveness

exs.t: When the boss confronted Aaron about his earlier remarks, Aaron responded with utter truculence, simply throwing a glass of water in the boss' face and walking away.
The prisoner's truculence, glaring at the guards and shoving anyone who approached, earned him extra days in solitary confinement.
Diplomats were alarmed by the envoy's truculence; instead of negotiating, he pounded the table and threatened war over the smallest concession.
The coach hoped the player's truculence would fade with maturity, but he continued to challenge referees and pick fights with his teammates.

def: having a fierce, savage nature

exs.t: Standing in line for six hours, she became progressively truculent, yelling at DMV employees and elbowing other people waiting in line.
The truculent warlord ruled through terror, ordering brutal raids on any village that resisted his demands.
Visitors were warned to stay clear of the truculent guard dogs, which snarled and lunged at anyone who approached the gate.
Despite his genial public image, the tycoon was truculent in negotiations, attacking rivals with a ferocity that left them shaken.

def: (of language) pompous and tedious

exs.t: The amount of GRE vocabulary he used increased with his years--by the time he was 60, his novels were so turgid that even his diehard fans refused to read them.
The committee's report was so turgid that few members read beyond the first page, where a single inflated sentence took forty words to announce that the budget was late.
Students dreaded the textbook's turgid prose, which buried simple ideas beneath inflated phrases and interminable sentences.
Although his early essays were lively and direct, the philosopher's later writing grew turgid, swollen with grandiose terminology and tiresome repetition.

def: depravity; a depraved act

exs.t: During his reign, Caligula indulged in unspeakable sexual practices, so it not surprising that he will forever be remembered for his turpitude.
The lawyer was disbarred for moral turpitude after it emerged that he had defrauded elderly clients of their life savings.
The historian catalogs the tyrant's turpitude, from bribery and extortion to the betrayal of allies who had trusted him.
Novels of the period often contrast the virtue of rural life with the turpitude of the city, depicting urban society as a sink of corruption.

def: someone new to a field or activity

exs.t: All great writers, athletes, and artists were tyros at one time--unknown, clumsy, and unskilled with much to learn.
Though a tyro in the kitchen, the new cook learned quickly, and within a few months he was preparing dishes that impressed even veteran chefs.
The seasoned investor warned tyros not to trade on margin until they had gained enough experience to understand the risks.
As a tyro in politics, the candidate made mistakes that a more experienced campaigner would have avoided, such as answering hypothetical questions with reckless candor.

def: a feeling of anger caused by being offended

exs.t: Since he was so in love with her, he took umbrage at her comments, even though she had only meant to gently tease him.
The senior partner took umbrage at being left off the invitation list, interpreting the oversight as a deliberate insult.
Though the reviewer intended her comments as constructive, the author took umbrage, firing back an angry letter to the editor.
The delegates took umbrage when the host remarked that their country's cuisine was bland, and they left the banquet early in protest.

def: immune to attack; without flaws

exs.t: Professor Williams is so self-assured as to seem arrogant, presenting each and every opinion as an unassailable fact.
With a twenty-point lead and only two games left, the team's position at the top of the league was unassailable.
The prosecution's case seemed unassailable, resting on DNA evidence, security footage, and three independent eyewitnesses.
Perched on a sheer cliff with a single narrow approach, the fortress was considered unassailable, and no army had ever captured it.

def: not easily perturbed or excited or upset; marked by extreme calm and composure

exs.t: The house shook and the ground quaked, but my dad was unflappable and comforted the family.
The unflappable air traffic controller calmly guided the damaged plane to the runway while alarms blared around her.
Reporters tried to provoke the spokesperson with hostile questions, but she remained unflappable, answering each one in the same even tone.
Even when the power failed during the operation, the surgeon was unflappable, instructing staff to switch to backup lights as if nothing unusual had occurred.

def: uncooperative, not willing to give up information

exs.t: The teacher demanded to know who broke the window while he was out of the room, but the students understandably were unforthcoming.
When pressed about the missing funds, the treasurer was unforthcoming, offering only vague answers and refusing to show investigators the ledgers.
The witness proved unforthcoming, declining to name the other people present and claiming not to remember anything useful.
Although the company publicized its successes eagerly, it was unforthcoming about the safety tests that its new product had failed.

def: free of guilt; not subject to blame; beyond doubt or reproach

exs.t: After his long and unimpeachable service to the company, Sharat felt that a gold watch was a slap in the face rather than an honor.
The source of the report was unimpeachable, a respected scientist whose data had never once been called into question.
Because the judge's integrity was unimpeachable, even the losing party accepted her ruling as fair.
The historian's credentials were unimpeachable, yet her controversial thesis still met resistance from colleagues who disliked its conclusions.

def: creating an unfavorable or neutral first impression

exs.t: World leaders coming to meet Gandhi would expect a towering sage, and often would be surprised by the unprepossessing little man dressed only in a loincloth and shawl.
The restaurant's unprepossessing exterior, a peeling sign above a cramped doorway, gave no hint of the exceptional food served inside.
Though the candidate seemed unprepossessing at first, with his rumpled suit and halting speech, his sharp answers soon won over the committee.
Collectors overlooked the unprepossessing little painting, dark with grime and hung in a corner, until restoration revealed it as a lost masterpiece.

def: (of a circumstance) with little chance of success

exs.t: With only a bottle of water and a sandwich, the hikers faced an unpropitious task: ascending a huge mountain that took most two days to climb.
The timing was unpropitious for launching a luxury brand, since the economy had just entered a recession and consumers were cutting back.
Despite unpropitious beginnings, including a leaking roof, no funding, and only two students, the school eventually became one of the finest in the region.
The weather looked unpropitious for the outdoor concert, with dark clouds gathering and forecasters predicting heavy rain by evening.

def: very generous

exs.t: Helen is unstinting with her time, often spending hours at the house of a sick friend.
The volunteers' unstinting efforts, working through nights and weekends without pay, allowed the shelter to open ahead of schedule.
In her memoir, the scientist expresses gratitude for her mentor's unstinting support, which included countless hours of advice and even personal loans.
Critics are rarely unanimous, but their praise for the young pianist was unstinting, with every reviewer lavishing superlatives on her performance.

def: (of theories etc) incapable of being defended or justified

exs.t: With the combination of Kepler's brilliant theories and Galileo's telescopic observations, the old geocentric theory became untenable to most of the educated people in Europe.
Once new fossils showed that the two species had coexisted rather than one evolving from the other, the old theory became untenable.
The minister's position grew untenable after documents contradicted his denials, and he resigned within the week.
Critics argued that the author's claim, which rested on a single ambiguous letter, was untenable in the face of so much contrary evidence.

def: unfavorable; inconvenient

exs.t: Some professors find teaching untoward as having to prepare for lectures and conduct office hours prevents them from focusing on their research.
The expedition met with untoward circumstances almost at once: unseasonable storms closed the mountain passes, and supplies ran short within weeks.
Unless something untoward occurs, such as a strike or a supply shortage, the bridge should be completed on schedule next spring.
The negotiators feared that any untoward publicity before the agreement was signed might cause one side to withdraw.

def: not confined or limited

exs.t: The whole notion of living untrammeled inspired the American Revolution and was enshrined in the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.
Freed from the constraints of her former employer, the designer enjoyed untrammeled creativity, pursuing whatever projects interested her.
The frontier offered settlers an untrammeled existence, far from the laws and customs that had governed their lives in the crowded cities of the east.
Critics warned that untrammeled development along the coast, with no zoning or environmental review, would destroy the wetlands.

def: not able to work, survive, or succeed (also spelled inviable)

exs.t: The plan was obviously unviable considering that it lead to complete environmental destruction in the river valley.
Without a reliable water supply, the proposed settlement was unviable, and planners abandoned it after the preliminary survey.
Rising fuel costs made the airline's discount routes unviable, forcing it to cancel flights that could no longer cover their expenses.
The seeds proved unviable, failing to sprout despite the botanists' careful attention to soil, light, and moisture.

def: highly or widely praised or boasted about

exs.t: For years, they had heard of New York City's vaunted skyline, and when they finally saw it, the spectacular cityscape did not disappoint them in the least.
The team's vaunted defense collapsed in the final, conceding four goals in the first half and leaving columnists to wonder how they had ever called it the league's best.
The much vaunted reforms, which the government had trumpeted for months, turned out to change very little in practice.
Diners expecting the vaunted cuisine of the famous restaurant were disappointed to find the dishes bland and overpriced.

def: easily excused or forgiven; pardonable

exs.t: His traffic violations ran the gamut from the venial to the egregious--on one occasion he simply did not come to a complete stop; another time he tried to escape across state lines at speeds in excess of 140 mph.
The teacher treated forgetting homework as a venial offense, deserving a gentle reminder, but regarded plagiarism as a serious breach requiring formal discipline.
Compared with the embezzlement uncovered later, the manager's habit of taking home extra office supplies seemed a venial lapse.
Readers forgive the narrator's venial faults, such as vanity and occasional laziness, because his deeper loyalty and kindness are never in doubt.

def: the appearance of truth

exs.t: All bad novels are bad for numerous reasons; all good novels are good for their verisimilitude of reality, placing the readers in a world that resembles the one they know.
To lend the historical novel verisimilitude, the author studied period diaries and letters so that every detail of daily life would ring true.
The forger's work possessed such verisimilitude that experts examined the painting for months before detecting the modern pigments.
Although the film is pure fantasy, its careful attention to the physics of flight gives the dragon scenes a surprising verisimilitude.

def: truthfully, without a doubt

exs.t: Frank is a veritable life-saver -- last year, on two different occasions, he revived people using CPR.
The attic proved a veritable treasure trove, containing rare first editions, antique maps, and letters from long-forgotten statesmen.
When the dam burst, the quiet stream became a veritable torrent, sweeping away bridges and flooding the valley within minutes.
Her office, stacked floor to ceiling with papers and books, was a veritable labyrinth that visitors could scarcely navigate.

def: change in one's circumstances, usually for the worse

exs.t: Even great rulers have their vicissitudes--massive kingdoms have diminished overnight, and once beloved kings have faced the scorn of angry masses.
The biography follows the family through the vicissitudes of three generations, from prosperity to bankruptcy and exile.
Farmers learn to accept the vicissitudes of weather, knowing that a single hailstorm can destroy a season's work.
Despite the vicissitudes of her career, including two bankruptcies and a bitter lawsuit, the entrepreneur never lost her optimism.

def: abusive or venomous language used to express blame or bitter deep-seated ill will

exs.t: His vitriol spewed forth from a deep-seated racism that consumed his whole life.
The online forum was filled with vitriol, as anonymous users hurled insults and threats at anyone who disagreed with them.
The candidate's speech, full of vitriol toward his opponents, alarmed moderates who had hoped for a more civil campaign.
Years of rivalry had left the two scholars with nothing but vitriol for each other, and their reviews of each other's books were venomous attacks.

def: harsh or corrosive in tone

exs.t: While the teacher was more moderate in her criticism of the other student's papers, she was vitriolic toward Peter's paper, casting every flaw in the harshest light.
The critic's vitriolic review, which called the novel a monument to incompetence, devastated the young author.
Although the debate began courteously, it soon became vitriolic, with each speaker harshly attacking the other's character.
Unlike his measured public statements, the senator's private letters were vitriolic, full of caustic remarks about colleagues he despised.

def: to criticize harshly; to berate

exs.t: Jason had dealt with disciplinarians before, but nothing prepared him for the first week of boot camp, as drill sergeants vituperated him for petty oversights such as forgetting to double knot the laces on his boots.
The coach would vituperate his players after every loss, berating them in the locker room for mistakes both large and small.
Rather than offering constructive criticism, the reviewer vituperated the playwright, and even readers who disliked the play found the abuse out of proportion to its faults.
For months the pamphleteers vituperated the governor, denouncing him in the harshest language as corrupt and incompetent.

def: spirit of the times

exs.t: Each decade has its own zeitgeist--the 1990's was a prosperous time in which the promise of the American Dream never seemed more palpable.

The zeitgeist of the 2000's was a curious admixture of fear and frivolity; when we were not anxious over the state of the economy and the world, we escaped into reality T.V. shows, either those on popular networks or the ones we would create ourselves on YouTube.
The novel captured the zeitgeist of the postwar years, its restless characters embodying a generation's disillusionment and hunger for change.
Fashion designers try to anticipate the zeitgeist, sensing the moods and values that will define a season before consumers can articulate them.
Historians argue that the architecture of the era reflects its zeitgeist, since the soaring glass towers expressed an optimistic faith in technology and progress.
